en: The Clarification of the Intent of the Nyāyavārttika.
O Mother Sarasvatī, having bowed again and again with palms joined in reverence, I make this petition; please understand it. Be thus attentive toward both my speech and my mind.
Just as these do not falter in the words of Vācaspati.
In the expression "worshipped by all" (*viśvārādhya*), the word "all" (*viśva*) is intended to refer to the class of sentient beings within saṃsāra, because they alone are its worshippers.
In the expression "Lord of all" (*viśveśāna*), it refers to the multitude of desired fruits.
Because that [world] is dependent solely upon the Blessed One;
and in the phrase "the creator of the universe," it refers to the collection of material causes, since it is precisely that which is pervaded by his creative activity.
In the phrase "the agent of the universal destruction," it refers to the entire multitude of impermanent things,
because they alone are subject to destruction by him;
in the phrase "the power of the universe," it refers to the totality of all effects.
Because that very [reality] is the object of its power;
for in the phrase "known by the All-Knowing One," the entire expansion of all that is knowable is precisely the object of His knowledge.
It is all-pervasive here because, among all the aggregates of material substances, it specifically pervades them;
whereas for others, it does so by means of those [substances].

In the context of the term "Viśvamūrti" (the Universal Form), because the entire collection of causal factors is directly presided over by His effort, it is identical to the bodies of those such as ourselves;
for this very reason, there is no dependence on any other body therein.
For that [efficacy] would belong to things that are not directly presided over by effort, like a staff and so forth;
but it does not belong to things that are directly presided over by effort, like a body.

However, by the invocation of the name "Pinākī," which is based on the attribute of wielding a specific weapon, it indicates that the intended goal is precisely the dispelling of obstacles that have already begun.
The application [of the text] by way of the relationship between cause and effect through the presentation of an objection and its resolution is superior;
for if it were applied according to the literal state of affairs, the consequence of tautology regarding the meaning would arise, and thus "praise" itself must be determined as the resolution.
"I bow," and so forth.
Dharma is that which turns one back [from worldly existence].
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the direct realization of the self as distinct from the body and other such things.
Dispassion is the absence of attachment;
sovereignty is mastery over the elements and the senses. In that regard:
For this very reason, [it is] for the sake of the treasure of the purification of speech;
for non-discrimination has unrighteousness as its cause,
and lack of dispassion has non-discrimination as its cause.
Lack of sovereignty has its root in the absence of dispassion;
and the impurities of speech have that as their root.
Indeed, these [impurities] are threefold.
In that regard, the first is the state of being without denotation;
the second is the state of having a contrary denotation;
the third is the state of having a purposeless denotation.
How, then, will these [defects] belong to a great sage who has conquered the elements and the senses?
For one who has not conquered the elements, when he wishes to speak, speech becomes devoid of meaning because such effort is not produced;
and for one who has not conquered the senses, a composition of words results in a contrary meaning, caused by error and the desire to deceive.
And for one whose mind is unconquered and who is intoxicated by negligence, [speech] is purposeless.

Furthermore, the author of the Sūtras himself will elaborate upon these impurities of speech within the context of quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
Thus, he is not like them; he is a treasury of pure speech.
For this very reason, he is a protector (tāyin), one who initiates a tradition capable of preserving the determination of reality.

Having thus bowed to the successive lineages of gurus, he demonstrates the specific excellence of his own composed work in order to steady the intellect of the disciples—beginning with the words "The book," etc.
Now, one might object: by saying "Tātparyaṭīkā" (Commentary on the Intent), you have shown the brevity of the work for the sake of facilitating its commencement;
yet, for disciples who are devoid of an awakening to their fundamental inquiry (*kathantā*), is it not intended that they grasp merely the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) in brief?
If that were the case, let there be only the Upaniṣads;
or let there be the instructions of the teacher according to the maxim of the "corpse's fist" (i.e., useless and hidden).
To the question "What is the use of this?", he says: "With all defects dispelled."

[Objection: "In that case, one must explain the intended meaning of the text and refute the objections; thus, there will again be the burden of a voluminous work. To this, he says: "Precisely under the guise of explaining the text..."
[Objection: "But since there are many such treatises in this long interval that have been accepted by great authorities, what is the purpose of this one? To this he says: "I desire [it].
[Objection: "But if those treatises are [valid] due to the continuity of the author's tradition, how can they be considered bad treatises?"

Now, if the tradition is broken, how is it that this *Tātparyaṭīkā* of yours is also a well-composed work despite its tradition being broken? To this he says: "Of those who are very old. For the tradition of Uddyotakara is indeed their youth.
And that [teaching] has, as it were, dissolved away through the power of the ripening of time.
Is it not therefore appropriate that this elixir of instruction, obtained from the presence of the Guru Trilocana, be given for the sake of their rejuvenation?

Nor is it fitting to give it to those mired in the mud of bad compositions; rather, the proper course is its extraction from there and its placement within the context of one's own composition—this is the meaning.
In this regard, the preeminence of the Blessed Akṣapāda among sages is already well-established through the Vedas and other sources; what, then, is the purpose of this specific mention?
Nor is such an excellence currently required [for our purpose].
Furthermore, his status as the author of the treatise that is the cause for the pacification of the world is already made manifest by the very act of its composition.
What is the point of making that explicit as well?
Since even the fact that one's own composition has that as its subject matter is obtained simply from the commentary on it,
what is the use of stating that too?
Furthermore, it is not appropriate to merely present the superficial appearance of this great ocean of reasoning;
therefore, one must apply oneself with intent to its true meaning.
Thus he says: "Now" (atha).
Regarding the phrase "that is to be removed":

by referring to "that" as the darkness of fallacious reasons (*kuhetu*) which obscures the treatise (*śāstra*) and is produced by bias toward [specific] directions and so forth—intending it as something to be removed—it is shown that this composition belongs to the treatise itself.

Furthermore, since the commentary (*bhāṣya*), which takes the form of an exposition of that [treatise], constitutes the very body of the treatise, it is not considered to be anything additional to the treatise.
[It is] as [the Mīmāṃsā is derived] from the Veda.
For this very reason, there is no contradiction between this commentary (*ṭīkā*) and the end of the *Vārttika*.

By this, the interpretation that "the composition of the treatise, namely the *Bhāṣya* text, will be made as a means for removing the ignorance of bad logicians" should be disregarded due to its contradiction with the *ṭīkā*.

[Objection: But for what purpose is there this restatement of the purpose already stated in the Sūtra? For here, nothing remains to be enjoined or prohibited after having restated this. To this he says: "By the Sūtra...
[And] to the question, "What is accomplished by demonstrating that one's own composition possesses a purpose? he says: "For those who are discerning..."
Now, it might be argued: "Those who desire to learn proceed with the aim of learning;
therefore, since their engagement in the process of instruction has learning itself as its purpose, what need is there for another purpose? To this, he replies: "Of mere instruction...
For indeed, a purpose is of two kinds: primary and secondary.
In this regard, the primary [purpose] is indeed the human goal itself;
the other, however, is its subordinate part.
Since those who seek the primary purpose engage in that [subordinate part] while requesting its accomplishment, that too is indeed a purpose.
Therefore, when the primary purpose exists, there is a secondary purpose;
but if that [primary purpose] does not exist, even that [secondary purpose] would not exist, and thus it remains entirely purposeless.

Furthermore, since this [secondary purpose] does not have its own primary purpose independently, the intention is that once it is shown that "this belongs as a subsidiary to something else, and that [something else] has the primary purpose," the discerning person is thereby induced to act.

The meaning is "by the author of the Vārttika. For this reason as well— namely, from this fragment of the *Ṭīkā*— it should be understood that, according to the maxim that "that which lacks a fruit [is subsidiary] when in proximity to that which possesses a fruit," this is indeed a limb of the *Śāstra* itself and not a limb of the *Bhāṣya*.
For the Bhāṣya has no primary purpose in its own right, by virtue of which the Vārttika would become a subordinate part of it;
therefore, it is beautiful exactly as it is heard in the text.

Now, one might object: "Is it not well known in the Upaniṣads—such as 'He who is tranquil and self-controlled'—that restraint of the organs of action is 'śama,' and yet this is not a human goal (puruṣārtha)?
Therefore, it cannot be the primary purpose. To this, he says: "And here... [etc.].
Now, it may be objected that "for the sake of the world's peace" is difficult to accomplish,
because it is both improbable and impossible.
For no one ever sets out to act for the benefit of the world, such that we could even conceive of a sage doing so.
And they recite: "Even for a sage dwelling in the forest," and so forth.
But this is not possible, because it is impossible to induce those who desire worldly enjoyment [to follow such a path].
Nor does the world as a whole desire liberation;
therefore, it is only the practitioner—the disciple who has already attained the status of a *brāhmaṇa* and so forth through other scriptures—who is to be instructed.

And his characteristics are: the perfection of tranquility (*śama*), self-restraint (*dama*), and the like; the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal; detachment from worldly and heavenly enjoyments; and the desire for liberation (*mumukṣutā*).
However, he who engages in the section on Brahman while being entirely ineligible—just as one might in the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*)—does not partake in the fruit.
In this regard, it might be argued:
"This consideration of eligibility does not concern the object that is to be attained (*upeya*)."
Because that [liberation] is not an object of human effort, and because mere desirability cannot be negated; rather,
what indeed is the object of the means?
Because that alone is the subject matter of the treatise and because it is the object of human endeavor;
and here, just as liberation is the goal, the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) is likewise to be sought as a means to that end.

Because it is unestablished [as a means]. However, the means is valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and unlike the study of the Veda, the employment of inference and direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not prohibited for Śūdras and others.
By which [reason] there would be no qualification for this [person] even in that case;
if that were so, one who understands fire from smoke or through perception would be a transgressor, just like one who studies the Veda [without authorization].

Furthermore, perception and inference regarding the self are not specifically prohibited for Śūdras and others; moreover, since no penance is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa or others upon seeing a Caṇḍāla—unlike the case of a bathed person seeing one—it is concluded, on the contrary, that they do indeed possess the qualification [for knowledge], as per such Smṛti texts as: "Women, Vaiśyas, likewise Śūdras, and others who are of low birth... and so forth.

Therefore, just as that very same distinguished heaven is accomplished by means other than Vedic sacrifices and so forth— even by one not authorized for them— such as through service to the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) and the like, so too, if the realization of the Self is achieved by a *śūdra* through another means such as inference, what kind of fault could there be?
True; however, even inference, when pursued in a manner that does not contradict scripture, is determinative of the meaning, but not if it contradicts it.
As it has been said: "That which contradicts perception and scripture is a fallacy of reasoning (nyāyābhāsa)."
And that determination of non-contradiction, which arises from the lack of contradiction with scripture, is dependent upon the determination of its meaning.
In this regard, a Śūdra is indeed not authorized [to determine it].
One who disregards that [scripture] and relies solely on inference would encounter nothing but calamity, just as in the case of [the argument for] the purity of human heads and so forth.

Therefore, since this treatise proceeds in syntactic unity with the sacred tradition (āgama), its intended audience is precisely that [qualified by the tradition]; thus, Śūdras and others are as if unqualified.
Consequently, some maintain that this word "jagat" (the world) refers only to those who possess such qualification.
To this, he replies: "For [the author] is supremely compassionate," and so forth.
For there certainly are some whose minds are softened by compassion, for whom the entire world is a friend;
otherwise, the injunction "having granted fearlessness to beings" would result in futility. Compassion is simply the desire to eliminate the suffering of others without any ulterior motive.
And just as that [compassion] arises in one who sees a single suffering being, why should it not arise in one who sees the entire world as suffering?
If it does arise, what inconsistency could there be in engaging in the means to eliminate it? Indeed, [there is none].
Even one whose heart is moistened by compassion should instruct only those who are capable of understanding, and not those who are the opposite;
for a singer does not sing for the deaf. Therefore, he says: "In that case, if there were no one [capable].

The meaning is that it is not as if a sick person, due to misfortune, would fail to engage with the instructions of Caraka and others, such that the purpose of those instructions would thereby be nullified.
Now, if he perceives nothing but a transgression in teaching those who are not qualified, how could his words be worthy of attention?
Or, even if he perceives such a transgression, why would he not refrain from acting?
If it is argued that he acts despite perceiving it out of compassion, [then...]
He might become negligent; and since he would thus have no fear of the next world, who would have faith in his words? Therefore, he says: "And not...
Although, because he has abandoned delusion, there is simply no arising of either sin or merit for him, [he speaks thus].
For he will say later that "there is no rebirth for one whose afflictions have been destroyed.

Nevertheless, because the abandonment of afflictions is difficult to achieve, the power of asceticism has been described as a means to prevent the arising of transgression, even while accepting its occurrence [in other cases].
[Objection: "Even so, it is better not to touch mud from afar than to wash it off.
To this, he says: "And thus...
For cows submerged in mud do not, out of compassion and being overcome by it, fail to lift themselves up for fear of being smeared by the mud.
Rather, the meaning is that they wash [the mud] after having removed the mire.
Now, one might object: "If he is not qualified [for the ritual], how can he be a partaker of the fruit?
And if that is so, why is he said to be unqualified? Anticipating this, the author explains in detail: "For it is indeed the power of austerity... and so forth.

For just as such evils are dissolved by the power of their austerity (tapas) alone, so too, by the power of austerity alone, they become partakers of the fruit through the possession of true resolve (satya-saṃkalpa), even though they lack formal qualification; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
Nor is it the case that they lack qualification with respect to the fruit itself.
What then? It depends on the ritual action (*karman*).
Furthermore, it is not the case that an action performed by one who is unqualified, being deficient, is incapable of yielding a fruit;
for its perfection arises precisely from the excellence of the distinguished officiating priest (*yajaka*).
The officiating priest (yājaka), while officiating for one who is unworthy to sacrifice (ayājya), would incur sin, just as a learned man incurs sin by accepting gifts from a king;
and the meaning is that he is dissolved by means of intense austerity (tapas) alone.
"In that case, according to the maxim 'the path is that which the great multitude has taken,' we too shall instruct those who are unqualified"; to this he says, "And not... [The opponent objects]:
"But what benefit would be rendered to the scripture by one who merely dispels the ignorance of fallacious logicians (kutārkika)? To this he replies, "By the fallacious logicians... [and so forth].
Ignorance is incorrect knowledge.
In this world, when beginning an undertaking, wise persons proceed by first paying homage to their chosen deity, desiring the completion of what has been commenced without obstacles; yet,
it is observed in many instances that there is deviation from this rule, in that for one who has performed the salutation the desired goal may not be achieved,
while for one who has not, the desired goal may nonetheless be achieved.
For even in the case of one who acts erroneously, the desired result is not achieved;
nor is there any scriptural injunction here such as, "One desiring rain should perform the Kārīrī sacrifice," or "One desiring the completion of what has been begun should pay homage to the deity."

Since we would otherwise have to postulate a deficiency in the action, the agent, or the means even when there is no deviation [from the result], [the opponent] intends to argue that this is merely a manifestation of unauthentic popular tradition—just like the saying, "One who desires wealth should worship the Yakṣa dwelling here at the banyan tree"—and asks: why did the author of the Vārttika not perform a salutation to his chosen deity?
To this, he replies: "Uncontested" (*avigīta*).

Even the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭācāra), when it is uncontradicted, is indeed a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) just like direct perception, provided that a Vedic text exists; for conduct of the learned cannot possibly be without a foundation,
nor can it be established as authoritative if its root is non-authoritative, since that would be inconsistent with the absence of contradiction among those who accept valid knowledge.
And this being so, the existence [of an effect] depends upon the deficiency of the action, the agent, and the instruments;
whereas its non-existence depends upon the perfection of merit acquired in another birth.

The meaning is that the observation of the absence of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) sets aside the causal relationship, which is the domain of means of knowledge other than scripture (āgama).
If this is so, one might ask: "What has not been done by him? To this he says: "Supremely" (parama).
If it has been done, then why has it passed away like a stroke of lightning (indralupta), such that it is no longer seen? To this he says: "It was not established" (na niveśita).
Regarding this very point, the example is "na khalu" (indeed not).
The meaning is that, unlike the salutation to one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), even its inclusion [in a treatise] is of no use anywhere.
[Objection: But in such a manner, the disciples should also be made to adopt the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*).
And since they could not be made to grasp [the meaning] apart from that insertion, he says: "like another auspicious word."
Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): it refers to the treatise (*śāstra*) that is to be explained.
Now, one might object that there is no restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *daṇḍaka-sūtra*; therefore, it is said [here] "in brief" (*saṃkṣepataḥ*).
"Now, its status as the initial sūtra is indeed well-known, since it is a sentence expressing a connection;
so what is the point of stating this? To this he replies: "By the inclusion of the word 'initial' (ādi)."

[Objection: But surely, since the relationship between the treatise (*śāstra*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) is described by this [verse], it is appropriate that this is a statement of the relationship; why, then, is there a mention of "intended" (*abhimata*)? To this he says: "intended" (*abhimata*).

For there is indeed a relationship between the treatise and the supreme good characterized by the status of the signifier and the signified; however, that [relationship] is not intended here, because it is not a factor for the engagement of a discerning person.
For the manifestation of the signified does not arise from the signifier such that one seeking liberation would engage with the signifier;
rather, it is for the sake of the goal (upeya) that one engages with the means (upāya).
The meaning is that by this [statement], the relationship of cause and effect alone is intended.

Now, one might object: "In this context, neither the treatise (*śāstra*) nor its status as the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) is heard"; to this he says: "Valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and so forth."
To the question, "What is the intended meaning (*tātparya*) regarding the transgression of established usage? he says: "For not...

Although the causality is understood here as well through the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) that "a treatise" (*śāstra*) is so called because by it one is taught (*anuśiṣyate*) or instructed in the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, nevertheless, [it is understood] by virtue of its possessing an activity connected with the instructor (*śāsaka*).
But it is not by virtue of possessing an activity connected with a disciple;
rather, that [activity] is what is intended here.
Otherwise, one would not be liberated even after knowing the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth in their true nature.

"As long as he has not yet instructed [him]"—this is what was meant by saying [the treatise functions] "as the instrument for the comprehension of the reality of categories" and not "by its own nature.

Now, one might object that the states of being a cause (*hetutva*) and being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) cannot exist without a difference in their respective objects; to this, he says: "By that [instrument]."
The treatise (śāstra) is the cause and the instrument for both;

however, the meaning is that it functions as a means of cognition regarding the true nature of categories (padārthatattva), whereas regarding the supreme good (niḥśreyasa), it functions as an instrument by virtue of possessing its [the treatise's] specific operation.
This very point has been stated: "And thus..."

This being the case, when it is shown by the force of the definition that the knowledge of the true nature of categories (*padārtha-tattvajñāna*) functions as the operation (*vyāpāra*) for the treatise (*śāstra*) in its task of achieving the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), there exists a cause-and-effect relationship between the operation and the agent of the operation.

Likewise, there exists a relationship of the "expounded" and the "expounder" (*pratipādya-pratipādaka-bhāva*) between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth—the objects of the operation—and the treatise which possesses that operation.

Similarly, there exists a relationship of "object" and "subject" (*viṣaya-viṣayi-bhāva*) between the knowledge of the true nature—the operation—and the means of valid cognition and so forth, which are the objects of that operation.
Likewise, through that operation, the causal relationship between the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) as the operation and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) as the result is indicated;

similarly, the relationship of cause and effect between the object of the operation and its fruit is indicated because of their inseparability (*nāntarīyakatva*). For indeed, an operation cannot be said to belong to something unless it has that thing as its cause.

Nor is that which is not its action the object of its activity, nor is its activity non-conducive to its result, nor is it the case that the object of its activity is [something else]. Among these five points to be stated, he mentions two as an illustration: "because of the authority of the treatise."

Intending this very function obtained through etymological derivation, the author of the Bhāṣya has shown the genitive case in "tattvasya jñānam" (the knowledge of reality) as being used in the sense of the object; thus, the derivation based on the instrument is not contradictory.
Now, one might object: "Have not the relationships between disciple, teacher, scripture, and its commentary also been demonstrated by certain followers of the same tantra?
Why are those not presented here? To this, he says: "This [work] has as its subject matter... For it is not sufficient to merely state that something exists; it must be demonstrated.

What is it called? Whatever is necessary so that the engagement of a discerning person (*prekṣāvat*) would not occur if it were not set forth—that much is demonstrated. Furthermore, relationships such as those between disciple and teacher are not a requisite for the engagement of a discerning person.
Because they have activity as their fruit;
for it is only after activity has occurred that there can be a disciple who is to be instructed and a teacher who instructs.
It is established that the treatise is to be explained and that he is the commentator, and so forth;
furthermore, even the presentation of the essential nature of the treatise, the teacher, and so on, is not [merely] for its own sake.
Because [the subject matter] is established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Therefore, the purpose (*prayojana*) must be stated; their relationship (*saṃbandha*) is the subject matter (*abhidheya*), and through that, the relationship between the treatise and its purpose is established. It is reasonable that the first sūtra has this as its meaning.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that for one whose false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) extends the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), it is precisely the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) that is the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*)?"
The self is likewise [the subject], but as for the other categories denoted by the treatise, they do not serve as causes for the supreme good (niḥśreyasa).
And thus, there would be no connection with the supreme good; therefore, he says: "That which consists of the categories... and so forth.

Now, if the knowledge of the true nature of categories such as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), then since this is already established by the means of valid cognition prior to the commencement of the treatise, the statement of the purpose in the treatise would be useless; for there is no need for instruction regarding what is already established by other means of knowledge.
On the other hand, if that certainty is derived from this very [treatise] itself, it is difficult to avoid the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
For one who has already engaged in an action would determine the purpose, and having determined the purpose, one would engage;
yet one does not determine it prior to engagement, based on the words of the Sage.
Because engagement [with the treatise] would be impossible at the very first sūtra if the purpose were not determined;
and if, for the sake of engaging with that [first sūtra], another purpose were stated, there would be an infinite regress.
If it is argued that the initial engagement occurs even when that [purpose] is not determined, [then the same applies to all subsequent ones].
Some maintain that even if there is a successive progression [of topics], the same undesirable consequence would follow;
therefore, the statement of the purpose and so forth is useless. That is untenable.
For the mental modifications of persons are threefold: experience, desire, and effort.
Among these, experience does not conform to desire.
For even that which is undesirable is perceived;
however, desire arises spontaneously toward the human goal,
and toward its means, it is produced by the inference of their being so.
Effort, however, pertains exclusively to the means [of accomplishment]. In that regard, desire and effort directed toward the sphere of the means are called the initial engagement (*pravṛtti*).
But experience is not [the cause],
nor is desire directed toward the result the motive, such that even those two would require a determination of the purpose. No.
It is not experienced that what is to be disregarded is purposeless;
nor is it accepted that pleasure is devoid of any other purpose;
nor is it the case that, because heaven is not desired by one seeking liberation, sacrifice and the like are not experienced as its means.
However, activity directed toward the accomplishment of human goals is characterized by desire or effort, and is not established by its own inherent nature.
For no one, when hungry, desires to eat food or exerts effort toward it without intending to eliminate the suffering of hunger or to attain the pleasure of satiety and fullness.
Therefore, wherever someone is to be prompted to act, that person must first be shown the goal to be accomplished by that action.
And since he who is to be turned away from [unwholesome conduct] must first be shown the disadvantage that is to be accomplished by that [turning away],
the purpose and so forth have been stated;
but how will the listener then have faith in it?
It remains to be explained how one who lacks faith would proceed [to study]. To this, he says: "Having ascertained" (*viniścitya*).

Even if the specific purpose is not stated when determining the reliability (*āptatva*) of the Sage, there certainly arises a general determination of the purpose, namely: "This treatise possesses a purpose because it was spoken by a reliable person."
Nevertheless, that [purpose] is not a factor for engagement.
For one does not engage merely because something has a purpose;
rather, one does so by thinking, "This possesses a purpose desired by me."
And since that specific purpose is determined from the statement itself, this expression is meaningful.
This is what was said: "having ascertained the purpose and so forth";
the word "specifically" (*viśeṣataḥ*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sense].

Furthermore, the ascertainment (*viniścaya*) is merely the form "this is the means to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) according to the treatise," and not necessarily the form of a [guaranteed] result,
because obstacles are possible here as well, just as drought and so forth occur in agriculture.
Thus, this capacity of the purpose to impel action exists by way of being the objective.
But it is not [known] as an object of engagement;
therefore, there is no contradiction with the injunction regarding the status of being a means to a desired end.
Now, one might ask: "If there is no certainty regarding the sage's status as a reliable authority (āpta), is there then absolutely no engagement with his word?
If that were so, how could there even be a certainty regarding his being a reliable authority?
To this, he says: "But when there is no certainty of reliability, [engagement occurs] because of doubt regarding the matter."
The phrase "by means of being accomplished through the treatises" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
Now, one might ask: how can a discerning person who is in doubt proceed to act? To this he says: "Indeed, not...
Although there is no doubt that the attainment of grain is accomplished through agriculture and so forth, [the case here is different].
Nevertheless, it exists indeed by way of its future state;
nevertheless,
discerning persons proceed toward it with that very [future state] as their objective.

And just as in that case there is a hundredth part consisting of the absence of a result while the peak of results is predominant, so it is here as well. For this doubt does not arise from the mere impact of the senses; what then? It is drawn forth by the suspicion of non-validity caused by the lack of certainty regarding the speaker's reliability (*āptatva*).
In reality, however, the meaning is that from the Sūtra itself, consciousness arises precisely in the form of a determination regarding the purpose and so forth.

Now, one might object: "Doubt is easily produced even in the absence of statements concerning the purpose and so on; moreover, the recollection of specific details will occur due to a particular desire for knowledge. To this, he says: "And not... (na ca).
For when someone acts on the basis of a particular statement, they depend on that very statement for the recollection of specific details, rather than acting independently.
Indeed, one afflicted by disease does not act impulsively on their own, speculating here and there whether "this might or might not be the means for curing my illness."

What is its name? It is simply the word of a physician, even if his reliability has not been definitively established. Otherwise, failing to perceive the stated purpose, one might suspect it is useless, wondering:
"Is this work devoid of purpose, like a treatise on examining the teeth of a crow?"
Furthermore, it may be useless because its accomplishment is impossible, like explaining the *saṃjīvanī* herb found on the northern peaks of the Snowy Mountain that removes death;
or it may have an undesirable purpose, like a Southerner’s instruction to an inhabitant of Āryāvarta regarding the process of marrying his maternal uncle’s daughter;

or even if the purpose is desired and achievable, this method may be too cumbersome when a simpler one exists, like instructing a thirsty man to dig a well near the bank of the celestial river instead of drinking from it.
And one does not engage in these possibilities of harmful consequences;
nor is there any room for them even when a purpose is stated, because that would entail the undesirable consequence of destroying worldly convention.
The meaning is that no one desists from eating meat merely because of a physician’s word, as they would do based on their own conjecture;
therefore, it is "useless," meaning it serves no purpose.
The claim that the means [of knowledge] is impossible to carry out is unproven; therefore, he says: "For instance" (*tathā hi*).

Here, the word *pramāṇa* has two meanings: it is a *pramāṇa* in the sense that "by this, something is correctly cognized" (*pramīyate 'nena*), and it is a *pramāṇa* in the sense that "the correct cognition itself is the *pramāṇa*" (*pramitiḥ pramāṇam*). And so on.

With reference to that first [category], it has been stated: "The knowledge of the reality of the objects of cognition (prameya) and so forth is dependent upon the knowledge of the reality of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)."
One might object: "Even while observing that the sense organs and so forth produce the determination of their own objects while remaining themselves unknown, how can you say this? To this, he says:
"For not... A means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) determines its own object while being known as a means of knowledge; it does not, however, ascertain [it] [as such].
The meaning is that this is what is intended here. Why does he not determine [the cause]?
For it is not the case that a sense faculty, while itself unknown, produces a cognition whose form is indeterminate; therefore, he says: "of that much alone" (tāvanmātrasya).

The meaning is this: although cognition indeed produces a determinate form, nevertheless, because one repeatedly obtains the absence of the object of knowledge in that very manner, and because no specific difference [in the object] is perceived, doubt invades that [cognition].
Is it then the case that there is no determination whatsoever anywhere? If that were so, then how could such worldly cognitions as "this is water indeed" exist?
Furthermore, [the author] says "But rather" (*api tu*) because the opponent's conceit— that there is no certainty whatsoever anywhere— would otherwise be contradicted.

If the determination of the reality of the object of knowledge (*prameya-tattva-avadhāraṇa*) were to exist in some sense as an ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it would be possible only through the determination of the reality of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-tattva-avadhāraṇa*).
The meaning is that if it exists by means of another valid cognition (*pramā*), it is not ultimately real (*pāramārthika*).

"Cognitiveness" (*bodhakatva*) is the state of producing cognition; that is to say, existence delimited by the production of cognition. "Non-erroneousness" (*avyabhicāritva*) is the state of producing non-erroneous experience; that is to say, existence delimited by the production of non-erroneous experience.

And thus, the inherence (*samavāya*) of existence—which, though delimited by two distinct conditions, appears as if divided due to the difference between those conditions—in a single object is not contradictory, just like [the coexistence] of producedness (*kṛtakatva*) and impermanence (*anityatva*). The phrase "by that which is known through its non-deviation" is the ellipsis to be supplied. To the question, "In what way, then, is the determination of validity (*prāmāṇya*) useful?", he says: "For that very... and so forth.

For a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*) of valid cognition (*pramā*). Furthermore, there are no such specific universals as "instrument-ness" (*karaṇatva*) and so forth,
because that would entail the undesirable consequence of a confusion of universals (*sāmānyasaṃkara*).

What is this [instrumentality]? It is simply the state of being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*). Its specific qualification, however, is the very nature of the particular action; and in this context, that [action] is characterized as valid cognition (*pramā*).
Valid cognition (*pramā*) is non-erroneous apprehension.

Therefore, the meaning is that validity consists precisely in non-deviation (*avyabhicāritva*), which is characterized by being the producer of a non-erroneous experience. If this is so, one might ask: "In that case, let the determination of the object of cognition (*prameya*) and so forth occur only after the determination of that [validity]. To this, he says: "And that... (*tac ca*).

The meaning is that the status of being an instrument of valid cognition (*pramākaraṇatva*) cannot indeed be determined as long as the valid cognition (*pramā*) itself has not been determined. [Objection: "In that case, let the validity (*pramātva*) itself be determined;
for that too is not adventitious (*aupādhika*), such that it could not be determined unless the adventitious condition (*upādhi*) were determined. To this, he says: "For instance" (*tathā hi*).

The validity (*prāmāṇya*) of a cognition— that is, its being a valid means of knowledge (*pramātva*)— is "intrinsic" (*svataḥ*); the meaning of this phrase is that it is either by itself (*svātmanā*) or by that which apprehends it (*svagrāhakeṇa*).
Therein, he first refutes [the opponent's position] with the words "Certainly not" (*na khalu*).

In the view that the property (*dharma*) and the substrate (*dharmin*) are non-different, the very point of refutation is that there would be no self-cognition (*anātma-saṃvedana*). And it will be demonstrated that such a lack of self-cognition follows; this is the intended meaning (*hṛdaya*).
Regarding the position that they are distinct, [the author says] "precisely as before":
for it might indeed be possible that one who perceives a thing would also perceive its property;
however, one who does not even apprehend the substratum itself—
Where is even the mention of grasping its properties?
And although sound, smell, and so forth are perceived even when space, earth, and so on are not perceived, nevertheless, the meaning is that they are not [perceived] as properties of those [latter].
He refutes [the view] with the words "nor by its own grasper," beginning with "not even.
For would that [grasping] be mental or inferential?

In either case, since it would arise from a mark (*liṅga*) characterized by the "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*) of the mind—which is indistinguishable [from the object itself]—how could it possibly grasp [the object] as qualified by that appearance?

If, however, [invalidity] were apprehended in that way simply due to the particularity of the object, it would follow that invalidity (*apramāṇya*) would also be apprehended intrinsically (*svataḥ*), because the specific qualification of the object is present there as well. Furthermore, because valid cognition (*pramā*) is more frequent, its latent impression (*vāsanā*) is more intense; consequently, even invalid cognition is apprehended as being "valid" precisely because of that intensity.

If it is argued that invalidity is thus dependent solely on a subverting cognition— just as the nature of being mother-of-pearl is [recognized] in a piece of mother-of-pearl where silver was superimposed— even so, if the status of being a superimposer is itself understood [in that case], why does the consequence not follow that invalidity is apprehended intrinsically (*svataḥ*)?
Furthermore, if validity is superimposed even in that case, how can there not be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*)?
Furthermore, a perception that does not disregard a fabricated form is not called a "perception," because it is overwhelmed by doubt,
like the immediate cognition of a wandering mendicant regarding one who possesses the marks of a magician.
Therefore, it is not the case that knowledge is necessarily grasped;
however, if by chance it is grasped,
then it is simply "knowledge."
The meaning is not that it is either a valid means of knowledge or an invalid one.
Now, if it is not tenable that [validity] arises from itself, and if,
according to the reasoning to be stated, it does not arise from another either,
then how is this practice of distinguishing between valid and invalid means of knowledge possible without hesitation?
Therefore, let there be the very system of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*); for by that alone this [process] can be sustained.
Indeed, we do not perceive therein any fault such as infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and so forth; thus he says: "By this... (*eteneti*).
For the doctrine of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is not established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
It might perhaps be accepted on the grounds of the excellence of its practical application to valid cognition, provided that it could function through that [application],
but this is not the case.
For just as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), in apprehending itself, also apprehends its own validity, so too it should apprehend its own appearance as being an appearance;
and in that case, the consequence of non-activity resulting from all false cognitions remains exactly as it was.
Nor can there be activity even in that case through the superimposition of validity [upon the appearance].
If it is argued that because invalidity is identical with its own nature, there can be no superimposition upon it when it is apprehended through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*),
or that if it were not apprehended, self-awareness would be untenable; and furthermore,

since there is a distinction between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*), even if the essential nature is apprehended, the property consisting of invalidity is not apprehended— then [the following must be considered]:
In that case, there would also be no apprehension of validity (*prāmāṇya*).
Therefore, even according to the doctrine of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), there would be only the awareness of its own nature;
it would not be the awareness of validity and so forth—this is the meaning.

He refutes the alternative view with the words "nor even from another," meaning "not even from that which has that as its object"— that is, from that which has as its object the object of that [original cognition], by means of eliding the middle term.
This implies that in the case of a perceptual cognition of fire, there must be another perceptual cognition of fire.
And that [recognition] is of two kinds:
produced by the same sense organ and produced by a different sense organ.
Likewise, in the case of inference as well, there is another inferential cognition produced by its mark (liṅga).
And [there is] that arising from another mark (*liṅga*).

Thus, in the case of verbal cognition as well, after a verbal cognition, there is [cognition] arising from the word of that trustworthy person (*āpta*) and [cognition] arising from the word of another trustworthy person; in this way, corroboration by means of a cognition of the same class has been shown.

By the phrase "purposeful action" (*arthakriyā*) and so forth, the three types of inference based on dissimilar corroboration have been shown: that which has an effect as its mark (*kāryaliṅgaka*), that which has a non-cause-and-effect relation as its mark (*akāryakāraṇaliṅgaka*), and so forth.
This is merely an illustration;
for even knowledge arising from the instruction of a reliable person (āpta) is indeed a concordant cognition.

Although this concordance is extrinsic (vyadhikaraṇa) when it comes to ascertaining the validity [of the first cognition], nevertheless, by determining the actual state of the object, it determines the efficacy of that which prompts action; it is by this much alone—
It has been described in exactly that way.
He refutes it with the words "And all that...

Having thus established that the nature of validity (prāmāṇya) is difficult to apprehend, he applies the status of being a means of valid cognition (pramāṇatva) to the instruments of knowledge (pramāṇas) which depend upon that [validity], with the words "And when..."

Now, if activity occurs only through the ascertainment of validity, then that very [ascertainment] will render nugatory all the worldly alternatives such as "intrinsic" and so forth. On the other hand, if activity proceeds without impediment even in the absence of such ascertainment, then let validity not be ascertained at all.
To the question, "What is cut off for us?", he says: "Thus, therefore.
The intention is that this treatise has proceeded with reference to Vedic practice, not worldly practice.
He applies this to the subject at hand with the words "therefore" (tasmāt).
Now, one might object that the use of the suffix *matup* in the sense of a permanent connection (*nityayoga*) is difficult to justify,
since both the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and its object (*artha*) are indeed impermanent.
And because there is no mutual inherence [between them], he says: "and eternality.

Now, one might object that even non-deviation (avyabhicāra), characterized as the relation between the pervaded and the pervader, does not exist between the means of knowledge and its object; to this he says: "and this very [thing].
This non-contradiction—that is, the absence of contradiction—is the definition of non-deviation.
However, the nature of non-deviation is that which constitutes the definiendum (lakṣya), namely, the capacity to determine a real object;
for the locus of both the definition (lakṣaṇa) and the definiendum is identical.
Indeed, the nature of non-deviation is the definiendum, which consists in the determination of a real object.
It should be understood that there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) because the locus of the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is non-different.

Although a difference in time is also logically established when there is a difference in place or state, the mention of "time" here is intended to indicate that some sort of temporal distinction is intended in this context, however slight it may be.
For instance, even after a lapse of time, there is no sublation of the cognition of a person regarding a post standing at a distance, as long as the cognizer does not come near;
or rather, [the cognition remains] until the object to be cognized is closest.
Thus, even when there is a difference in time, there is no contradiction in the cognition of an object during the dream state as long as there is no experience of the waking state.
Nor should it be argued that, this being the case, what is the use of apprehending a difference in time;

for even when there is no difference in place or state, contradiction is observed in some cases due to temporal sequence—for example, in the case of the cognition of a woman by one afflicted with passion, which arises from a sudden impulse despite very careful observation, where a difference [in the object] is perceived in some instances.
Because there is non-discrepancy at a later time, there is the apprehension of that [object].

By this, all the various auxiliary causes (*sahakāribheda*) of the sense organs and so forth, which arise in temporal succession and serve as the causes for a more vivid cognition, are fully included.

And although both discrepancy and non-discrepancy—characterized respectively by possibility and deviation—occur only with respect to the object of valid cognition (*pramā*), nevertheless, regarding non-discrepancy...

The mention of "essential nature" (svarūpa) is for the purpose of demonstrating that [the cognition] has a fixed object, because all cognition is non-erroneous with respect to its substratum (dharmin).

The phrase "due to the efficacy of activity" (*pravṛttisāmarthyāt*) is a reason with a different locus; therefore, he states its meaning as "because it produces an efficacious activity" (*samarthapravṛttijanakatvāt*).

Although it would have been more appropriate to say "because it is an efficacious activity" (*samarthapravṛttitvāt*), nevertheless, the genitive case is used in the sense of a relationship, namely "that of which there is activity.
And that [relationship] is precisely the relation of producer and produced between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the activity (*pravṛtti*); thus, that alone [is the intended meaning].
It has been shown [that there is no such relation].

Now, it is certainly not possible to grasp through perception the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between validity and the capacity to produce successful activity, because those two [properties] themselves are not perceptible.
For validity is indeed to be inferred from the fact that it generates successful activity;
and that [successful activity] is itself to be inferred solely through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
Nor can positive concomitance be grasped by means of inference.
Because validity is not established anywhere at all;
or, if it were established, what would be the use of inference?
But if it were established by a subsequent inference, there would be an infinite regress; therefore, he says: "If, however..."
Furthermore, since cognitions of equanimity (*upekṣājñāna*) are not included as part of the subject (*pakṣa*) here, there is no partial unestablishedness (*bhāgāsiddhi*).

And because a negative-only inference (*vyatirekin*) proceeds by assuming the absence of any similar instance (*sapakṣa*) everywhere, it does not suffer from the fallacy of being an uncommon inconclusive reason (*asādhāraṇānaikāntikatā*).

Nor should it be argued: "If the meaningfulness of this very inference is not established, how can the meaningfulness of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) be established? Or, if its meaningfulness is established, how can it be a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*)?
For the meaningfulness of an inference is indeed twofold.

[The definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists of] the characteristic of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) and the characteristic of producing valid cognition (*pramā*). In that regard, when its own object is to be determined, it requires only the ascertainment of invariable concomitance, not the ascertainment of being a cause of valid cognition. Thus, even by this [definition] whose validity has not yet been ascertained, the validity characterized as the fruit of the means of valid cognition is established for all means of valid cognition; therefore, everything is excellent.
By this, the following objection is also refuted: "If there is no ascertainment of validity (*prāmāṇya*), how can there be no ascertainment of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) either?
For that [invalidity] is ascertained through the ascertainment of validity;
but if that is not ascertained, how can there even be an ascertainment of its absence (*vyatireka*)?"
Is it because there is no ascertainment of the suchness of the counter-position?

For the establishment of the ascertainment of its own object occurs through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that exists even while its own nature and its ultimate reality (*dharmatā*) remain unascertained.
[Objection: But surely there is no such proponent who would dispute [the truth] even when the validity [of the means of knowledge] is not ascertained?
For there can be no disagreement regarding the ascertainment of validity once it has been accepted,
since acceptance is rooted in ascertainment; nor can there be such disagreement without having accepted it.

Because contradictory positions devoid of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) are easily found everywhere, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the total collapse of all conventional practice regarding the affirmation or negation of any doctrine.
Furthermore, as long as validity remains undetermined, even doubt as to whether a cognition has a certain form or not would be difficult to find anywhere,
because the recollection of specific features— which is the prerequisite for all doubts— is absent.

Nor can it be argued that this results in a universal lack of authority for all means of knowledge, because the same logic applies to the rejection of the means for apprehending authority even if that [rejection] itself lacks authority.
Furthermore, even by resorting to an authority and so forth that is constructed by conceptual thought and is charming only when unexamined, this flawed inquiry cannot be sustained.
If validity were not admitted, even the construction of conceptual thought would be unestablished;
moreover, no linguistic usage such as doubt exists regarding what is constructed by conceptual thought—
for no one ever doubts whether a horse's horn exists or not.
Nor is there anyone for whom the notion "a human horn does not exist" constitutes a misconception.
Therefore, validity and so forth do exist, as does the ascertainment thereof;
however, the means for that [ascertainment] deserves consideration.
In this way, positive concomitance (anvaya) certainly exists.

Anticipating the objection, "How then can there be a purely negative inference (kevalavyatireki-anumāna)?", the response given in agreement is: "Or it is both positive and negative (anvayavyatireki). The intention is that the doctrine of the purely negative inference is established by not admitting positive concomitance.
The mention of "of inference" (*anumānasya*) is illustrative;
the term "intrinsically" (*svataḥ*) also applies to its opposite,
since the establishment of validity occurs both intrinsically and extrinsically.

Now, one might object: since the probandum is established by the mere statement "because it generates purposeful activity," the qualification "through the apprehension of an object by means of a valid instrument of knowledge" is redundant and its locus is different [from that of the probandum]. To this, he says: "But as for the generation of purposeful activity... For it is through the exposition of validity and so forth that the treatise is connected with the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
But not by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*).

Therefore, just as the knowledge of the reality of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth is proposed as the purpose (*prayojana*) because it is that which is to be accomplished, so too it must be proposed as the subject matter (*abhidheya*) because the means of valid cognition and so forth are what is to be expressed.
For example: "Now, therefore, we shall explain Dharma" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.1).

Thus, while it is established that *dharma* alone is the subject to be explained (*vyākhyeya*), there is no formal proposition (*pratijñā*) here that it is the subject matter (*abhidheya*). Therefore, since its status as the subject matter has not been formally proposed, one might suspect—either out of deference to the listener's intellect or in accordance with the intention of the author of the Sūtras—that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth are not being taught by this treatise. Anticipating this doubt, the Vārttika author offers the following reply: "It might be argued... For this treatise was composed in accordance with the sequence of the student's inquiries.
For if one were to speak without regard [to the audience's needs], it would follow that the discourse would not be worthy of attention.
Furthermore, the student’s inquiry is not "What will you say?
but rather, "From what is the supreme good (niḥśreyasa) attained?"
The answer to that is: "From the knowledge of the reality of the categories beginning with the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), there is the attainment of the supreme good (niḥśreyasa).
To this [question], "How so?", [the reply is:
"Whence, how many," and so forth.
"What are the characteristics of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the others?
To this, [it is replied]: "They have the characteristics of enumeration (*uddeśa*), classification (*vibhāga*), and definition (*lakṣaṇa*).
Then, one asks: "How so?"
Regarding the phrase "there, at the beginning of the second chapter":
all of this is established by direct experience;
even here, there is no dependence upon verbal testimony.
However, commentators provide explanations for those who do not understand, saying, "For this reason, he said this.

The meaning is that even though it is established by experience that [the treatise] expresses means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, the commentator says "he said this" because the treatise expresses the ultimate human good (*puruṣaśreya*), for the sake of one who, due to some delusion, does not comprehend this.
But surely, the exposition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth is not established by the mere mention of "the highest good" (*śreyaḥ*).
For the categories such as the means of valid cognition are not themselves the highest good.
[The opponent replies: But he will explain it himself—that the categories beginning with the means of valid cognition are indeed that [highest good].
Nevertheless, what is the point of saying that this treatise teaches what is beneficial (*śreyaḥ*)?

If the meaning of the word *śreyaḥ* is simply the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, then why say "benefit, moreover, is happiness and the cessation of the harmful"? To this he says: "Even though... (*yadyapi*).
Although the treatise provides a clear exposition by taking up each word— such as "puruṣa," "punaḥ," "śreyaḥ," and "punar"—
up to the end of the section with "prakṣayeṇa," there is no suspicion that the passage beginning with "na ca puruṣā rāgādimantaḥ" is also merely an explanatory gloss (*vivaraṇa*).
Because there is no connection with the subject at hand;
for the scripture does not fail to declare the highest good along with its means to one who possesses passion and so forth,
nor does that [scripture] fail to be the highest good for him by whom it might be grasped through discernment once he has become free from passion.

Nevertheless, in order that there be no confusion regarding the interruption of the commentary— lest one think that the intermediate summary "therefore that treatise teaches the highest good of man" (tasmāt tac chāstraṃ puruṣaśreyo 'bhidhatte) stands alone— he demarcates it with the phrase ending in "by means of exhaustion through experience" (upabhogāt prakṣayeṇa).
Now, one might object that it is inconsistent to say "the collection is distinguished by its arrangement" because the two terms are synonyms; to this he says: "arrangement" (*vyūha*).
Since these collections depend either on the will of the person who composes them or on their own inherent meaning, he says: "by a single recollection" (*eka-smṛti*).

Although the definition of a word (*pada*) is simply that it consists of phonemes delimited by the communication of a single meaning, it was nevertheless stated— "those [phonemes] mounted upon a single recollection"— to explain how this very definition applies to phonemes that are momentary and perishable. The remainder of the definition, "the collection [of phonemes] is the word," is found in the *Vārttika*.
The statement that "a collection of words is a sūtra" is a Vārttika;
however, that is untenable,
for a sūtra is indeed a specific type of sentence.

Nor is a sentence merely a collection of words in general, for that would lead to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that even "cow," "horse," "man," and "elephant" would constitute sentences. Therefore, he says: "In this way, the collection [of words] regarding its own meaning..."—the remainder being that it is to be understood as a *sūtra*.
A collection of *sūtras* is a *prakaraṇa*, according to the *Vārttika*.

In that regard, since there is no reason for a distinction between intermediate groups [of sūtras], it would follow that the entire treatise (*śāstra*), being a collection of sūtras, constitutes a single topical section (*prakaraṇa*). To this he says: "In some cases, however... For example, with reference to a single purpose—namely, the exposition of the purpose, the subject matter, and their relationship—the collection of the first and second sūtras constitutes a topical section.
Thus [ends] the section on the means of valid cognition (pramāṇaprakaraṇa), the section on the objects of valid cognition (prameyaprakaraṇa),
and the section on the preliminary members of reasoning (nyāyapūrvāṅgaprakaraṇa).
The section on the basis of reasoning, the section on the basis of reasoning,
and the section on the nature of reasoning.
The section on the subsequent members of the syllogism (*nyāyottarāṅga*) and so forth should be inferred accordingly.

The Vārttika states that a collection of topics (*prakaraṇa*) constitutes a daily lesson (*āhnika*). This [designation] would not be established if there were no intermediate syntactic unity among these topics; therefore, he says: "of the topics.
For these topics possess a single common characteristic: they define the principles (*nyāya*) along with their ancillaries (*saparikara*).
A collection of those [topics] constitutes an *āhnika*.
In the subsequent *āhnika*, there is one section concerning the definition of the means for discriminating between valid reasoning (*nyāya*) and fallacious reasoning (*nyāyābhāsa*);
therein also is the section on formal debate (*kathā*).
The section on fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*),
the section on quibbles (*chala*), and the section on the signs of human incapacity (*puruṣāśaktiliṅga*): such is the meaning of the first chapter regarding its definitions.
In the second [chapter], there is an examination of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
in the third, an examination of the six objects of cognition (*prameya*) in their causal form;
and in the fourth, an examination of the six objects of cognition in their resultant form.
"In the fifth [book], there is the definition of the specific characteristics of the marks of human incapacity.
Thus, we shall demonstrate right there the connections between the chapters, daily lessons, and sections at the beginning of the second book.
This has been stated: "In this manner, it should be understood in each respective case."
The phrase "in each case" (tatra tatra) means in each instance, such as in the daily ritual (āhnika) and so forth.
Now, one might object: since not even a single variety has been shown therein, how is it to be understood "in each case"? To this he says: "And these... (etāśca).

Now, one might ask: "Having already promised that the treatise (śāstra) expounds the supreme human good along with its means, what is the use of demonstrating the nature of the treatise itself? To this, he says: "Thus, in this way.
The intention is that by first describing the nature of the treatise, the exposition of its meaning becomes easy to understand.

Now, one might ask: "Why is the number sixteen of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and so forth, which is already established by common experience, being merely restated? To this, he states the doubt that must be refuted with the word "nanu" ("now, surely"). "Sāmānyaviśeṣaḥ" means a specific similarity.
"Yato 'sya" refers to this collection of words, namely the treatise (śāstra).
The "categories" (padārthāḥ) are the objects of the words taken collectively, namely, the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and so forth.

Therefore, the treatise, in the form of sentences, expresses the human good (puruṣaśreyaḥ), which is the meaning of the sentence; the word "resolution" (samādhāna) is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the verb].
"How do they conduce to the supreme good?"—this is the initial [objection].
From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), since those [means] are conceptual (*kālpanika*), the supreme good itself would also be conceptual.
Consequently, effort for that purpose is fruitless, because [the supreme good] is established without effort; such is the intention [of the objection].

Because the treasury of conceptual construction (*kalpanākośa*) extends infinitely, [the self] appears to be infinite in nature; however, the underlying intention is that from the perspective of ultimate reality (*parārthataḥ*), it is selfless (*nirātmāna*).

He states—"the means of valid cognition and so forth"—pointing out that the presentation of only two means of valid cognition, perception and inference, by the author of the *Vārttika* contradicts his own established tenets.
"They are not within the scope of comparison.
Although comparison— which has as its result the determination of the relationship between a name and the named— does indeed have utility regarding the word as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
because a word whose convention (*samaya*) has not been grasped does not produce valid knowledge.

Furthermore, because the *samaya* (convention) is generally determined through analogy (*upamāna*), even so, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth are not directly made objects by it; this is the meaning.
Now, if it is argued that analogy is not mentioned because it is not directly applicable to the subject at hand, [the response follows].
"In that case, let the word itself be denoted;
for it is directly useful. To this he says: "Even though...
Here, the phrase "even there" refers back to the subject matter of the scripture (*āgama*).

For wherever scripture (āgama) operates, it depends upon either perception (pratyakṣa) or inference (anumāna) regarding that very object. However, those two [perception and inference], even when accompanied by their roots, do not depend on a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) operating within their own respective domains. Therefore, the meaning is that only those two are shown, because their objects are not contaminated by a root [source].
"Vainayika" means those who lack the intellect produced by a specific method (*naya*)—that is, the treatise on logic (*nyāya-śāstra*);
the sense is that they do not discern these [objects] from their superimposed form. This is the completion of the sentence.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" in the phrase "service and so forth," proficiency in listening and other such activities is intended.

Furthermore, even one who is in doubt does not necessarily lack the desire to know [the truth] regarding liberation (apavarga), which is not something undesirable; therefore, it is said, "of the disciple.
By the term "disciple," he indicates the possession of qualities such as the desire for liberation (mumukṣutā).

Even one who has fallen into error, though initiating a debate, does not become dependent [on worldly things] once the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) has dissolved, provided he does not desire liberation; therefore, the undertaking of *jalpa* (disputation) and *vitaṇḍā* (cavil) is fruitless. Hence, he says:
"of one remaining [in the world]," which means even for one desiring liberation out of delusion.
The construction is: "when the ego-sense has dissolved through *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā*."
"The state of being an object to be established belongs to that which exists as dependent" is the completion of the sentence [found] later.
"By some means of valid cognition" (pramāṇena) means by the manner of reciting the first sūtra.
Now, one might ask: "What is the purpose of making even that which is not doubtful into something doubtful? To this he says: "Even though it is not doubtful...
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "...for cognizers who are dependent [on others]."
If those ill-behaved disciples depend even upon liberation and so forth on the senses and other such factors,
then how can they be instructed? For this reason,
he completes the *vārttika* with the words "some [disciple]" (*kañcit*).
The meaning is "that which is perceived through direct perception and is useful for a seen purpose.
He says, "so too the subsequent [passage]," implying that one should supply the phrase "those desiring to know only that which is inferable and useful for a seen purpose" in what follows as well.
He says, "In this way, the subsequent [passage] also," meaning that even with this much, the word "those who desire to know" (jijñāsavaḥ) must be supplied in what follows.

Now, one might object: "Even with this much, it is mutually contradictory to say that those who are dependent [on scripture] are to be taught by this very scripture, and yet [also] by perception and inference. To this he says: "This is the intended meaning" (ayam abhisandhiḥ).
The phrase "those who desire to know" [is used] because it is the means for attaining the supreme human goal; this is the sense according to the rule of ellipsis (*śeṣe nyāya*).

Here, although it is possible to correlate them respectively—since pleasure, which is directly perceived, is indeed within the scope of prescriptive authority (*vidhāyaka-pramāṇa*), while the cessation of harm, which is not directly perceived, is indeed within the scope of prohibitive authority (*niṣedhaka-pramāṇa*)—nevertheless, since "the good" (*śreyaḥ*) consists of both pleasure and the cessation of harm, nothing further has been stated beyond this. Therefore, the primary purpose is merely to describe the connection with the specific authorities (*pramāṇa*).
And there is no purpose for that [definition] at present;

furthermore, when it is necessary to determine the specific excellence of the desired welfare (*śreyas*), the description of its being within the scope of injunctions and prohibitions is not useful. With this intention, he explains it otherwise, saying "even there" (*tatrāpi*).

The meaning is that by the word "that" (*tat*) in the phrase "that welfare is happiness and the cessation of the harmful," both [happiness and the cessation of harm] are referred to as being of the nature of welfare (*śreyas*).
He dispels doubt by means of their respective enumeration, stating "it does not pervade.
He clarifies the meaning of the words *dṛṣṭa* (seen) and *adṛṣṭa* (unseen) in the phrase "pleasure is seen" by way of an illustration: "garlands, sandalwood," and so forth.
"Aihika" means pertaining to this world;
"svargādi" means pertaining to the hereafter. He indicates that this has been stated elsewhere as well by saying "in this way."
The meaning is that the cessation of what is harmful is also twofold: pertaining to this world and pertaining to the next.
Since this is not how it appears in the Vārttika, he says: "due to the elision of the letter *ca*.
This means due to the elision of two *ca*s.
By that [elision], [the compound] becomes *dṛṣṭam adṛṣṭam ca* (seen and unseen happiness).
Likewise, "the cessation of the harmful" is the meaning of the *vārttika*.
Thus, this is the summary: the visible good.
And that consists of happiness and the cessation of what is harmful;
happiness is both of this world and of the next,
and the cessation of suffering is likewise both of this world and of the next.
In that regard, the characteristic of happiness is the highest good, whether seen or unseen;
this is not to be accomplished by scripture,
because it is accomplished by means of garlands and the like, or sacrifices and the like.
And because that [cessation] is not absolute;
furthermore, the cessation of what is harmful, even if it is not absolute and distinguished as pertaining to the seen or the unseen, is not to be accomplished by this treatise,
since it is accomplished by the removal of immediate harms such as thorns and the like.

But since that [non-existence] is not applicable here, it would not be something to be accomplished (*asādhya*). Therefore, he says "of the cessation of the harmful" (*ahitanivṛtteḥ*) to specify that it is an absolute cessation of the harmful.
Now, one might object: if "cessation" (*nivṛtti*) refers to the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of suffering, [how can it be accomplished?]
How is that absolute?
For absoluteness consists in the non-interruption of the future limit;
and if prior non-existence were likewise [absolute], it could not even be called "prior."

Now, if cessation (*nivṛtti*) is destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*), and that is entirely absolute (*ātyantika*) in every case, then from where does the demonstration of the absoluteness of cessation come? To this he says:
"Absoluteness" means the non-arising again of that which has ceased—that is, of what belongs to the same class as that which has ceased.
The ellipsis "in that very self" is to be supplied.
But surely, the absolute cessation of suffering is simply the removal of the twenty-one-fold divisions of suffering;
so how can it be called "removal" (*hāni*)? To this, he says: "And that [cessation]...
It is characterized by cessation, that is, by its very nature as cessation.
And here, by the word "effect" (kārya), suffering is meant;
by the word "cause" (kāraṇa), the body, the senses, the objects, and the intellects are meant;
and pleasure is included as a secondary consequence because it shares the same causes as suffering.
Now, even if the body and so forth have ceased, why would suffering not still occur?
Let there be no suffering;
why would happiness not occur? It is not so.
For when one thing has absolutely ceased, another does not come into being.

Thus, since there is the cessation of the pleasure associated with the secondary afflictions (*anuṣaṅga*), what remains to be described? To this he says: "Not indeed," for an effect that exists without its cause would forfeit its very status as an effect.
Therefore, when the body and so forth are absent, pleasure does not exist, just as suffering does not, because pleasure too is an effect of those [factors].
Or, if it were to exist, it could only exist when the body and so forth are present.
And thus, suffering would also exist because of the presence of its cause; this is the meaning.
To this very point, he applies the *Vārttika*, saying "this has been stated.
By this very [statement], ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) are the causes.

The commentary’s explanation—that dharma and adharma are concomitants of the engagement in action—is set aside, because the suffering nature of the body and so forth is contradicted by experience; therefore, he says: "in a secondary sense" (gauṇa).
Since the five sense organs are well-established in the *Ghrāṇādi-sūtra* (1.1.12),
and they are not [explicitly] stated to be six even in other passages, he says: "the sixth."
The intended meaning is "by means of the method of the treatise" (*tantrayuktyā*).

Now, one might object: "Are not the objects of cognition also established as only five in both their classification and examination, rather than six, since they are neither mutually the means nor mutually the ends? To this, he says: "Of that... (*tasya*).
Although cognition, pleasure, and pain are also objects of the mind, nevertheless,
by virtue of being its very object, they are metaphorically designated as "suffering," provided that when they are made objects [of the mind], they produce suffering.
For he will say: "Objects [are causes of suffering] because they are objects of cognition.
And it is not the cognition itself, while being cognized, that is the cause of suffering.
For he will say: "But cognitions [are causes of suffering] directly."
However, pleasure and pain do not possess the status of being causes of suffering in the same way;
for although pleasure initiates a dissimilar effect, it initiates only attachment (*rāga*),
whereas suffering initiates a dissimilar effect precisely because it is [itself] suffering.

Desire, aversion, and effort, however, produce suffering directly as soon as they are perceived. For instance, one seeking liberation becomes distressed simply by perceiving, "I desire [something other than yoga], I feel aversion [toward it], and I exert effort toward something other than the practice of yoga," because he has determined that these desires, aversions, and efforts are means for achieving what is harmful.
Even another person, upon failing to obtain what he desires, becomes miserable by perceiving, "I am hungry," or "I am thirsty.
Having perceived what is actually beneficial as harmful, one who has ceased his delusion yet still hates that which is beneficial suffers, thinking, "Shame on me!"— this is suffering.

Thus, for one who exerts effort with the notion that an undesirable object is desirable, once the delusion has ceased, suffering arises simply from perceiving the effort itself; it is for this reason alone that these [objects] are designated as objects of the mind.
