[Objection: Is it not the case that for one whose body is afflicted by old age, leprosy, and so forth, the very body being perceived is the cause of suffering?
In that case as well, the status of being suffering would be merely a figurative designation based on its being an object [of cognition]. To this, he says: "Even though...
The remainder of the sense is: otherwise, its status as a cause of suffering would be unique [to it alone].
In its capacity as an object, this [cognition] is not distinct from the six [consciousnesses];
however, it is distinguished by its connection with a specific sense faculty,
but not by way of its own intrinsic nature.
The meaning is: "because objects are infinite.

Although the author of the Vārttika will state here that "concomitance" (*anuṣaṅga*) means "inseparable connection" (*avinābhāva*), and for the sake of establishing that, [he will mention] having the same cause, having the same locus, and being perceived together; nevertheless, that is not [the case here].
In that much alone, the inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) is established;

for even when the cause is common to both, if one of the two specific causes is absent, the absence of the other follows, and thus the non-occurrence of the second is possible upon the absence of the first.

For this very reason, even when the substratum and the means of perception are identical, if one of them is absent due to the lack of its cause while the other remains present, the inseparable relation still holds.

Anticipating this objection, [the author] states that pleasure is indeed accompanied by the cause of suffering in order to establish that pleasure is associated with suffering—namely, "by means of its instruments" (*sādhanair*).
Therefore, there is no contradiction with the Vārttika and Ṭīkā on the second Sūtra;
for dependence upon instruments arises from the fact of being an effect (*kāryatvāt*).
And because there is no pleasure that is not produced by action,
dependence is a cause of suffering. As it has been said:
"All that is dependent on another is suffering";
and pleasure is subject to decay because it possesses a constitutive cause.
That too is a cause of suffering,
for separation from what is desired indeed gives rise to suffering.
However, the interpretation that "perishability exists when there is desire" contradicts the use of the plural form in the phrase "causes of suffering."
Therefore, these three reasons are indeed independent.
Desire (*kāma*) is longing (*icchā*);
and it pervades both pleasure and its means,
for there is no such thing as pleasure or a means to pleasure for one who lacks desire for them.
That [desire] is both easy to obtain and difficult to obtain.
Among these, the desire for what is difficult to obtain has exclusively suffering as its fruit.

As for the desire for what is easy to obtain, it is twofold: that which has for its object a means of accomplishment that is not prohibited, and that which has for its object a means of accomplishment that is prohibited.

In that regard, even an object of pursuit that is prohibited and difficult to obtain necessarily results in suffering as its fruit, either by way of its own nature, through its consequences, or by generating demerit (*adharma*).
Likewise, even an object of pursuit that is not prohibited and is easily obtained [results in suffering] provided there is physical vigor;
in the absence of such vigor, it is simply a cause of suffering.
Even when there is proficiency regarding the body and so forth, [rebirth] may be obstructed or unobstructed.
Among these, the obstructed brings about nothing but suffering;
the unobstructed, moreover, is either associated with undesirable objects or the opposite thereof.
Among these, the first is necessarily a cause of suffering;
the second, however, is both fruitless and fruitful.
Among these, the first is exclusively a cause of suffering;
the second, however, yields results either with delay or without delay.
Of these, the first is necessarily a cause of suffering.
The second [type of craving] is also either pure in its future course or the opposite thereof.
Among these, the first is solely a cause of suffering;
the second, however, gives rise to suffering precisely because the transformation of sensory objects is inherently distasteful.
Whether one is submerged in sense objects due to extreme delusion, or whether it is merely another form of desire,
in both cases it is the root of misfortune;
thus, even desire attached to pleasure is a cause of suffering.

In this context, although the activities of passion, hatred, and delusion are also appropriately enumerated as suffering— since they are the means for attaining that suffering, just like the sense faculties and so forth— nevertheless, these do not acquire their own existence, nor do they function toward suffering, apart from the body, the sense faculties, and the rest.
Furthermore, even though there is no engagement in vice (*doṣa*) on the part of the senses and so forth, the liberated one while living (*jīvanmukta*) still possesses activity toward suffering.

Although merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), which are the fruits of such activity, are the causes of pleasure and pain, they are not enumerated here because they serve as the foundational pillars for the twenty-one-fold hall of the dance of *saṃsāra*, which consists of nothing but suffering.
For in a future birth, the body, senses, objects, intellect, pleasure, and pain do not function by directly acting upon [the self] in the same way that merit and demerit do.

Intending precisely this, the author of the *Vārttika* has demonstrated that the cessation of the twenty-one kinds of suffering, which constitute the effect, occurs through the sequential elimination of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), which constitute the cause; he introduces the *Vārttika* accordingly with the words "in the manner described. Here, the means for the cessation of future merit and demerit is the abandonment of engagement in their causes, whereas the means for the cessation of what has already arisen is experience.
This has been shown;
yet both of these [arguments] are untenable,
because it is impossible to live while completely abandoning speech, intellect, body, and breath.
Even after death, because the internal coating of impurities such as semen and blood is difficult to remove,
its consumption is impossible; furthermore,
it is impossible due to the uncertainty of the timing of its maturation.
Because they are infinite and because their fruit is infinite;
for even in the state of enjoyment, there is no cessation of the production of further infinite karmas.
Now, if it were somehow possible through enjoyment and non-production to exhaust what has been produced and what has not yet been produced, [then karma might be exhausted].

In that case, there would be the undesirable consequence of the treatise being useless, since [the truth] would be established by that very [perception]. Anticipating this objection, he supplements the *Vārttika* with the words "doubt and so forth" (*saṃśayādi*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), all fourteen [categories] are included as the auxiliary components (*parikara*) of the Nyāya system.
By the phrase "supreme logic" (paramanyāya), all four means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) are established as being related to one another as root and rooted.
Logic is like a path— a "path of logic"—
because it is the cause for attaining the ground of ultimate liberation (niḥśreyasa).

The object of knowledge (*prameya*) consists of twelve types, beginning with the self (*ātman*). By this, the [relevance] and utility of the treatise (*śāstra*) at this juncture are shown; by the phrase "cultivation of reality" (*tattvaparibhāvanā*), the utility of practice (*abhyāsa*) is shown.
Thus, by the reasoning previously stated, one who seeks liberation engages with the treatise;
from that comes the thorough knowledge of the preliminary requisites;
and from that, the purification of the path of reason.
Then follows the attainment of the twelvefold objects of knowledge by means of that [discrimination], then practice,
and then discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*).
From that follows liberation from the persistence of faults along with their roots; from that follows non-activity;
and from that follows the non-accumulation of future merit and demerit.
In this way, the future stream has been obstructed.

And although activity persists as long as the body and so forth exist, nevertheless, due to the absence of the accompaniment of defects (*doṣa*) as its auxiliary cause, that activity is incapable of producing its effect;
thus he establishes the arising of experience [by stating]: "beginningless," and so on.
Although, just as in the beginningless succession of existences (*bhāvaparamparā*) karma is accumulated, it is likewise diminished;
for the beginninglessness of existence does not pertain to its commencement.
But surely, the commencement of karma occurs only when there is a body that possesses the capacity for experience (*adhikārin*).
And that [result] falls within the range of a single body among the millions of bodies;
it occurs only at some time, in some place, and for some [being].
Indeed, there is no enjoyment whatsoever where that body does not exist.
Because enjoyment has that as its basis,
therefore, through a careful consideration of income and expenditure, one's action is indeed limited;
for this very reason, the time of its ripening is also fixed.
Furthermore, its exhaustion through even a limited number of sequentially occurring bodies for the sake of experience is not difficult to establish.

Nevertheless, this has been resolved by accepting that— on the basis of the authority of scripture (*āgama*)— the simultaneity of bodies is established as a result of meditative discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*), and by acknowledging that [karmic fruits] possess infinite and indefinite times of ripening.

Regarding the point that even that which is to be enjoyed over many periods of time may be enjoyed all at once by one possessed of supernatural power (*vibhūti*), the drinking of the ocean is cited as the example.

Regarding the point that one endowed with the power of yogic mastery (*yogardhi*) can, by mere wish, emanate many bodies of diverse natures that simultaneously enjoy various fruits, the creation of the Daṇḍaka forest is cited as the example; thus some here say.
The cessation of suffering is not an end in itself (*svarūpataḥ*) as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), because it is conditioned by something else.
Since pleasure occurs only when suffering is absent, the absence of suffering is pursued just like any other means to pleasure.
One might object: "But is that not precisely what the person desires?"
As it has been said:
"It is better to desire the state of a jackal in the forest of Vrindavana than for Gautama to seek the specific liberation of the Vaiśeṣikas."
Thus [it is said]. That is untenable,
because error is also possible.
For it is only when pleasure such as that from food exists that suffering such as hunger ceases; thus, pleasure from food and so forth is sought solely for the purpose of ending suffering.
Why, then, do you not assume that this [pleasure] itself is what is desired?
If you argue that pleasure is desired even when some suffering is present, we say: no.
This is because even the cessation of suffering is desired in some cases despite the absence of pleasure.

If it is argued that there is at least the intention that "when suffering ceases, pleasure itself will come to be," we say no; for in that case as well, the intention that "in the state of pleasure, the separation from suffering will necessarily occur" is equally possible.

Therefore, although the cessation of suffering is necessarily accompanied by happiness, and the cessation of happiness is necessarily accompanied by suffering, nevertheless, these two desires possess the status of human goals independently of one another, because their respective objects are distinct and unmixed.
But another says: "The cessation of suffering is indeed the goal of human endeavor, but it must be one that is being experienced.
For the cessation of suffering does not occur during a state of delusion produced by poison and the like; therefore, discerning people do not exert themselves for its sake [in such cases]."
Therefore, since the cessation of suffering is not experienced in liberation, it cannot be considered the goal of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*).
As it has been said:
"Even the absence of suffering is not accepted as a goal of human endeavor if it is not cognized."
For a wise person is never seen to engage in an action for the sake of a state such as fainting.
This too is untenable,
because we observe that some people, desiring to eliminate the suffering born from separation from their sons and others, engage even in poison, weapons, hanging, or fire.
If it is argued that "wise people do not act in this way," we say no,
because there is no contradiction with the fact that [such acts] serve human ends.
For it is not the case that wise people refrain from engaging with another's wife simply because they are restrained by the goad of scriptural prohibitions.
In that case, desire is not the human goal; rather, because a small pleasure results in great harm, there is desisting from it.
Likewise, even for one engaged in poison and the like, because such action is censured by the scriptures, a small amount of harm is averted through desisting.

"It proceeds as something greater" and "they do not proceed"—this indeed is the very scrutiny [of the wise]: that even when something serves the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), one must consider whether it contradicts worldly convention or scripture.
For the status of being a human goal does not depend solely on being a non-goal [otherwise], but rather on the mere fact of being desired by its own nature.

Therefore, where there is no contradiction with worldly custom or scripture, discerning people are seen abandoning their bodies even by means of leaping from the banyan tree at Prayāga, falling down precipices, or fasting, when afflicted by diseases and other ailments.
For no one engages in the means for such ends thinking, "I shall experience the cessation of suffering."
Rather, [it means] "I shall abandon suffering.
Furthermore, is it intended merely that the cessation of suffering is being experienced, or is it limited to the actual existence of the cessation of suffering?

If it is the first [alternative], let the wicked man be satisfied; for in the final birth, the absolute cessation of suffering is indeed experienced through the power of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), whether it pertains to the future or even the present, being experienced before long. But in the second case, there follows the undesirable consequence that the cessation of suffering caused by thorns and such—which is already occurring—would not be a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*).
Because it would be experienced at all times;
or else, if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence of no transition to other objects,
since cessation would remain in that same state forever.

Therefore, just as the cessation of suffering produced by thorns and the like, though not being experienced at all times, impels a person toward action because it is a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), so too does that which constitutes the subject matter of the treatise [impel one].

Thus, having disregarded these two extremely weak positions—that this cessation of suffering is not a human goal, and that its status as a non-human goal is due solely to its not being experienced—one raises the third objection, saying: "It might be thus."
As it has been said:
"A wise person should not undertake tasks that are unreal, fraught with calamity, yielding results equal to the effort expended, or simply impossible."
Thus [it is said].
He illuminates the Siddhāntavārttika with the words "Even though" (*yadyapi*).
By this, through the analogy of eating food mixed with honey and poison, the notion that liberation (*apavarga*) results in an equal expenditure of effort and result is refuted.
For just as in this [worldly] state there is an abundance of what is harmful and only a meagerness of what is beneficial, it is not so in the case of liberation (apavarga).
By this, that which was stated is also refuted: [that liberation is undesirable].
Just as the pleasure of saṃsāra, being interspersed with suffering,
is not to be accepted, why should suffering— which is likewise interspersed with pleasure— not also be acceptable?
For those who seek pleasure are indeed seen to experience the suffering of sacrifice and the like.
For one for whom suffering is something to be taken up or abandoned, what could be said? For one who lacks anything to be abandoned, what liberation could there be, or by whom could it be taught?
Thus,

for one who fears even the flickering fireflies of pleasure while within the wilderness of saṃsāra— a place of incessant darkness caused by the thickest suffering— this path, which dispels all gloom, is taught as being easy to traverse.
This has been stated: "Therefore, let it not be 'not that' (atad), etc.
[Objection: If this is so, then it does not have all things as its object;
and thus there is a contradiction with the statement "for the sake of the peace of the world. To this, he says: "even for those who lack discrimination."

Although it was explained above that even if someone does not engage [with this work], its universal purpose is not diminished, nevertheless, the meaning is that those of dull intellect, who do not grasp what is to be abandoned as something to be abandoned, must be made to understand it by one who is compassionate.

Now, one might object that there is a circularity of mutual dependence—namely, that dispassion (*vairāgya*) arises from the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) through the scripture, and engagement with the scripture arises from dispassion; this is difficult to answer. To this, he says: "In engagement with the scripture...
Here, what is intended by "dispassion" is merely a turning away from enjoyment due to being repelled by suffering.
The meaning is not that there is merely an absence of passion (*rāga*).
He dispels the doubt regarding its twofold nature—namely, "uniformity" and "duality"—by stating that it serves the purpose of attaining the desired and avoiding the undesired.
[Objection: But even if there is a difference between persons, activity itself remains twofold.

For no one exerts themselves to attain suffering as they do to attain happiness, nor does anyone exert themselves solely for the abandonment of suffering as they do for the abandonment of happiness; therefore, he says: "The distinction between persons is due to passion and dispassion.
Now, from what [reason] does the fact that happiness is to be abandoned follow? To this he says: "Of that which is to be attained..."
It has been stated by the author of the Vārttika—that the activity of those lacking discrimination is of two kinds; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

While concluding the subject at hand, he recites what has been said and what is about to be said—namely, "Therefore, by this"—in order to dispel even the suspicion that something irrelevant might have intervened.
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "for the purpose of clarifying the intended meaning" in order to explain its constituent parts.
This is because [the subject] is not worldly (alaukika).
Because the world, including those such as ourselves, is eternally beyond direct perception [to them],
it is improper, lacking authoritative evidence, contradictory,
and mutually incompatible with their pervading [attributes].
"For the sake of activity" means for the sake of unshakable activity.
What then? "It is a valid means of knowledge" (pramāṇa).
The word "grasped" (gṛhīta) is understood to follow [from the previous context].
"This cognition of silver" means a cognition in the form "this substance, possessing a white and brilliant color, is silver.
"It determines" means that, having taken the aforementioned object as its support, it arises in the form of a definitive determination (*pariccheda*).
"The cognition of mother-of-pearl as well" [is to be understood in the same way].
The meaning is that this cognition—"this white, shining form, which is the substance of mother-of-pearl, is not silver"—is what is intended.

If this is so, one might ask: how can there be a relationship of sublated and sublator between these two? To this he says: "merely," [meaning] "by means of the imposition and subsequent negation of silver."
The meaning is: by way of having superimposition and denial as its intrinsic nature.
Thus, since the determiner is inferred by means of the determination, it has been shown that determination itself constitutes both the general and the particular aspects of determination.
Furthermore, there is no conjunction of contradictory properties within a single cognition;
for cognition consists of both direct experience and recollection by way of its generic nature.
In this context, recollection (*smṛti*) is indeed invalid (*apramā*).
Experience (*anubhava*), however, is twofold: experience of the thing-in-itself (*svarūpānubhava*) and experience of what is not the thing-in-itself (*asvarūpānubhava*).
This distinction is produced by the object.
Indeed, a single cognition can have various objects.

Consequently, that very cognition is a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*) when it is determined by an object existing in its own form; however, when determined by an object not existing in its own form, it is invalid (*apramā*). Thus, the nature of being a means of valid knowledge consists precisely in being an experience delimited by such [an object].
However, since invalidity is delimited by that which is not as it appears (*atathābhūta*), even an invalid cognition possesses the capacity to delimit a universal (*sāmānya*).
Thus the ground has been established.
To the question, "Is this all? he says: There exists, indeed, a unique cause for an ineffective activity, which is inferred in exactly that manner.
And its function is exclusively the determination of an object contrary [to reality], which is its unique characteristic;
and that which possesses such a function as its instrument is designated as "invalid" (apramāṇa).
Thus, even when there is doubt regarding the efficacy or inefficacy of the resulting activity, if that which produces it is invalid, then that activity is indeed ineffective.

Now, if that [cognition] were not a means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇa*), then the activity produced by it would also not be efficacious; thus, there is a necessary exclusion of efficacious activity from what is not a means of valid knowledge. And here, the proof for this exclusion of both is the logical mark (*liṅga*) consisting in the fact of being the effect of something incompatible (*viruddhakāryatva*).

The meaning is that perception, which apprehends the absence of that [cause] in the case of the effect under discussion, is what must be determined; therefore, it does not follow from a non-authoritative means of knowledge, nor from a cognition that deviates from the object, through its operation as a cognition that deviates from the object.
The negative concomitance (vyatireka) is established;
as to what follows from this, he says: "And thus," meaning that [the word] possesses meaningfulness, which is the non-deviation from the object.
The meaning is: "the state of being that which produces an experience that does not deviate from the object.

Now, one might ask: in the phrase "of that" (*tasyāḥ*), why is the immediately preceding [term], though relevant (*prakṛta*) but incapable (*asamarthā*), set aside in favor of the remote [term], though irrelevant (*aprakṛta*) yet capable (*samarthā*), which is what is referred to? To this he says: "But the incapable... and so forth.
The term *prakṛta* refers specifically to that which was previously introduced as being relevant, and not merely to what has been mentioned immediately prior; this is the meaning.
To the objection, "Of what use is the restatement (*anuvāda*) of something that has not yet been set forth? he says: "Presently" (*saṃprati*).
The meaning is that what was previously explained is now being challenged.

Although the challenge (*ākṣepa*) and its resolution (*samādhāna*) are clearly manifest, he says "he challenges" (*ākṣipati*) in order to avoid the charge of redundancy between the summary and the detailed exposition.
Since it is observed in various places that activity proceeds even from doubt, he revives the challenge with full confidence, saying: "Not yet," and so forth.

He corroborates this very point with the commentary, saying "This [is] that," the ellipsis being "stated by the author of the commentary. To the question "What follows if it is so?", he says: "And not..."
The determination of the meaning (*arthaviniścaya*) is of the nature already described; that is to say, it is accompanied by the inference of its being a cause of the highest good (*śreyas*).
The meaning is that the ascertainment of its validity cannot occur without the production of the consideration of the mark (*liṅga-parāmarśa*) which indicates its being a cause of the highest good.
And such is its form.

He also gathers the seed for that [determination of validity], which is precisely its association with the recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti*), stating: "and the apprehension of pervasion, which is the cause for the inference of being a means to the highest good (*śreyas*).
"Without those two" means without both the ascertainment of the essential nature [of the cognition] and the inference of being a means to the highest good.
Even though it follows immediately after the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), it is inference itself—the fruit of that [apprehension]—that has been introduced as the subject at hand.
Clarifying this very meaning of the *Vārttika*, he states: "This is what was said.
In the case of inferential certainty, there can be no determination of validity without both the apprehension of pervasion, which serves as the seed of inference, and the inference itself.
And those [two] do not exist without activity;
nor does activity exist without certainty and inference—this is the summary of the objection.
And here, activity is of two kinds:
[Knowledge] has results pertaining to this life and results pertaining to the next life.
Among these, that which has results pertaining to the next life is necessarily preceded by the ascertainment of its validity.
However, that which has results pertaining to this life depends merely on the knowledge that something is a desired means; it does not even require the ascertainment of the object [itself].
How much less, then, could there be knowledge of the nature of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
let alone its definitive ascertainment?
Even in cases where the definitive ascertainment of the true nature of the means of valid cognition occurs prior to the activity [of the subject], [it remains impossible].

Even in that case, this [defect] does not, by the force of its own cause, act as an instigator toward the engagement [in debate]; otherwise, if there were no certainty of an absolute victory, the seeker of victory would not engage in debate at all, as it would merely cast doubt upon his own authority.
For there is no necessary or absolute victory for one who merely prattles or engages in cavil.
Therefore, keeping in mind that activity proceeds even when the matter is not certain—a point established by both disputants—he begins the formal doctrine with the words, "In this regard, we say.
The phrase "in matters of perceived objects" (dṛṣṭārtheṣu) serves to exclude scriptures and other means of knowledge concerning unperceived objects (adṛṣṭa).
In that context, because there is no certainty regarding the connection between activity and its result,
the phrase "in those who have not reached the stage of practice" excludes the words of a father and so forth for one who has reached the stage of practice;
for those are ascertained as valid means of knowledge even prior to engaging in activity.
The intended practice is one that is non-erroneous.
Therefore, even when the practice concerns its own nature, the certainty regarding it arises precisely from the capacity for successful activity, because of the absence of erroneous practice.

And that [certainty]—whether it has as its object the [perceived] thing itself or an object necessarily concomitant with it—is the means for determining the belongingness to that class; where even the intrinsic form [of the object] is not present, there [certainty arises] solely from the capacity for successful activity regarding that object.
Just as one who, relying on a physician’s word, expects the cessation of a disease regarding roots located in an unfamiliar region [does so based on trust],

but where there is indeed a repeated practice of the thing's own nature— and where the means to the good has been practiced— there the validity of the cognition grasping its status as a means is established by the capacity for successful action (*pravṛtti-sāmarthya*).
Just as one who has perceived fire to be capable of cooking and so forth through the word of a trustworthy person—and having thus inferred its capacity—proceeds to cook for oneself;

likewise, even in cases where there is repeated practice regarding the fact that something is a means to the highest good (*śreyas*), but no such practice regarding its specific nature (*svarūpa*), the validity of the cognition whose object is that specific nature is nonetheless determined by the efficacy of the resulting activity.
This is just as for one who is certain that "fire is indeed capable of cooking," yet has never previously experienced forest fire.

In every case, there is an abundance of benefit; however, for one who considers that in the opposite case there might be a slight degree of harm, activity occurs even when there is certainty regarding its being a means to one's own ultimate good, just as if there were a doubt regarding the result. Thus he says: "Indeed not," and so forth.
Therefore, even those who are doubtful proceed [toward action], as if [they were certain] regarding both the nature [of the means] and its being a means to the highest good (*śreyas*).
This is the sense: it refers to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the nature [of an object] and that which apprehends its being a means to the highest good.
"Reality" (*tattva*) here means the state of being a valid means of cognition (*prāmāṇya*).
This means: "the state of being a means for producing a valid cognition that does not deviate from the object.
The phrase "having ascertained" implies "by way of ascertaining a valid cognition that does not deviate from the object.

The mention of "one who has reached the stage of mastery" is intended to include those cases where another instance of the same class is capable by virtue of this much alone, thereby encompassing all valid cognitions of perceived objects.
"Because of the capacity for activity" means even prior to activity, that is, before the activity itself occurs.
By this, the meaning is as follows:
although there is a capacity for activity even in those cases where the object is perceived and which have reached the stage of repeated practice, [non-perception still exists].
Moreover, although it is possible for that [cognition] to determine its own validity,

nevertheless, since activity occurs only after validity has been determined by the very mark characterized as belonging to that same class, the cognizer has no further desire to know [the validity] at a later time.
Furthermore, this is because the operation of inference is dependent upon that [prior determination].
If, on the other hand, the capacity to produce successful activity is considered independently of any desire to know [the truth],
then what harm is there?
By that alone, let validity be inferred.
This is because the convergence of multiple means of valid cognition (pramāṇa-saṃplava) has also been established.
Now, what is this "belonging to that same class"?
It cannot be "belonging to the class of valid means of knowledge," for that would result in the fallacy of the probans being non-different from the probandum.
Nor can it be the state of belonging to the same class as that which produces an efficacious activity; for would that consist in a relation to efficacious activity,
or in a restricted prior non-existence conditioned by it?
Not the first, because of the statement "precisely before the activity [begins]";
nor the latter, either.
Since that which transcends the senses cannot be apprehended without a logical mark (*liṅga*),

and since a logical mark for it exists only as being invariably concomitant with validity (*prāmāṇya*), then if such a mark exists, let validity itself be inferred by means of it; what is the use of inferring its belonging to the same class (*tajjātīyatva*)?
But what is the use of inference for that [validity] which is not already established?
Nor is there any property established by perception such that it could belong to the same class as that [validity].
For if it were perceptible, it would follow that it would be cognized even in the case of a means of knowledge that has not yet reached a state of familiarization.
And likewise,
in that case as well, the determination of validity would have to occur prior to the actual engagement [with the object],
because the pervasion (vyāpti) must already be cognized beforehand.
For it is not the case that this [cognition] has not inferred validity anywhere on the grounds of its belonging to that same class.
If it is argued, "In that case, there is no such class-membership at all; why then should it be perceived by perception?"—we say: no.

When validity is being inferred on the basis of belonging to that same class (*tajjātīyatva*) in the case of those cognitions that have reached the stage of practice, there arises the undesirable consequence that the example would be fallacious due to a deficiency in its probans (*sādhanavikalatā*), because the validity [of the example] is itself inferred from the capacity for successful action (*pravṛttisāmarthya*).
Therefore, we do not perceive "belonging to that same class" as anything distinct [from the property of being produced by a defectless cause].

True; nevertheless, since cognition is dependent upon its objects, those various objects themselves serve as the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of that cognition. Cognition, being conditioned by those respective adjuncts, becomes of that particular class; its state of being so is its "nature" (*tattva*).
Furthermore, because those adjuncts cannot be designated by their own specific names for every individual instance, they are indicated by this figurative expression: "belonging to that same class."
Therefore, a distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) should be understood here in the sense of "belonging to each respective class.
For instance, experience (*anubhava*) takes on both its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) and its specific qualifier (*prakāra*).

In that regard, an experience presented as the very nature of the subject (*dharmin*) is indeed valid cognition (*pramā*); therefore, when that [subject] is experienced in that form, its status as valid cognition is itself experienced—this will become clear later.
However, an experience whose object is a qualifier (*prakāra*) is of two kinds:
some [experiences] are presented by way of their own essential form (*svarūpa-prakāra*).
Since some [objects] may also exist through a mode other than their own essential nature (*svarūpa*), there arises in certain cases doubt.
In that context, specific limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) serve as modes to distinguish the qualified object from the experience as it is presented through its own essential nature.
And these, being invariably opposed to the objects of error, are precisely qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, whose distinct natures have been determined.

Thus, in general, the way [the universal] is apprehended in perception is that the very cognition whose object is the definiendum (lakṣya) as accompanied by the definition (lakṣaṇa) constitutes the "belonging to that class" (tajjātīyatva) residing in the cognition.
However, when a cognition is produced by means of a definition regarding a definiendum that is not perceptible, then that is inference; thus, its apprehension will occur in a different manner.
In that regard, the cognition of "earth" in a substance possessing odor, and so forth, is the general case.
Specifically, there is the cognition of a body possessing hands, feet, and so forth; among qualities,
there is the cognition of fragrance in things such as the *ketakī* flower, the cognition of whiteness in things such as a conch shell, and so on.

In the case of action (*karman*), however, when one stands without intoxication, with intense momentum yet unconditioned by it, and devoid of the perception of clear water and so forth that are moving, that substance which is perceived as "moving" is [itself] such [i.e., characterized by motion].
Thus, regarding those various particularities (*viśeṣa*), those respective particulars—which are neither deviant (*vyabhicārin*) nor contradictory (*viruddha*)—cannot be enumerated word for word.

Therefore, it should be understood that the nature of belonging to that class (*tajjātīyatva*) consists precisely in the experience of those respective objects as qualified by their respective limiting conditions (*upādhi*).

Thus, for such knowledge, the state of having reached the stage of cultivation consists precisely in the repeated practice of the adjunct (*upādhi*), since that adjunct is inseparable from its object.
However, where that very same object is practiced again and again, its being of that same class consists simply in its being consistent.
Thus, for now, external perception has been established.

He establishes the validity of scripture (*āgama*) by means of its sharing the same logical principles as perception—thus [he says] "and so" (*evam ca*). Here too, "belonging to that class" (*tajjātīyatvam*) consists in having a trustworthy author (*āptapraṇetṛkatvam*).

Furthermore, its state of having reached the stage of repeated practice (*abhyāsadaśāpannatvam*) is established through frequent observation (*bhūyodarśanena*) in the case of mantras and Ayurveda, whereby the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) between belonging to that class and possessing validity is proven.

The state of being in a phase of non-practice regarding mantras and Āyurveda constitutes their lack of established validity (*asiddhi*), which will be explained by the author of the Sūtras in the second chapter.

Just as validity is determined through the efficacy of successful action (*pravṛtti-sāmarthya*) in cases where one is in a phase of non-practice, so too is invalidity determined through the failure of such action.
And just as [validity is known] prior to action in cases where one is in a phase of practice...
It should be understood that validity is determined by belonging to that class (*tajjātīyatva*), and the same applies to invalidity;
furthermore, belonging to that class consists in the absence of any contradictory adjunct (*upādhi*).
The state of having reached the stage of practice is simply the repeated cultivation of that [cognition],
such as the cognition of two moons in the moon or the cognition of yellow in a conch shell.
"Knowledge of bitterness in molasses," and so forth.
Therefore, when there is doubt, the capacity for successful action must be ascertained.
This might be so:
its capacity (*sāmarthya*) is indeed its connection with the result.
Now, regarding how the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of the cognition of that very result is to be ascertained, he states the opinion of some [scholars] with the words "And not... (*na ca*).
Furthermore, it is not the case that even the cessation of thirst is examined; the meaning is "even the cessation of thirst.
This [objection] is untenable.

For knowledge of the result would not be examined because the result, being in a state of completion, is no longer a purposeful object since it is incapable of further means (*sādhana*); or rather, because knowledge of that specific class [of objects] is non-deviant from its object in all states.
Or [is it] because of the absence of doubt?

Not the first, because if the result were already in a state of accomplishment, then its means of attainment would likewise have become purposeless, leading to the undesirable consequence that it need not be examined.
If you argue that its means are examined by way of intending to obtain each subsequent [result],
then let it be the same for the result as well;
for only when the result has been established through examination will there be an intention to obtain each subsequent result once the nature of its means has been proven.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable,
because even the cognition of the result is seen to be fallible on many occasions during states such as dreaming.
If it is argued that the cognition of the result for one in a healthy state is not fallible, then in that case, the cognition of the result must itself be something already examined.

For instance, since the pervasion (vyāpti) is established that the cognition of a result in one who is in a healthy state is non-erroneous, one determines its non-erroneousness precisely where one perceives such a nature of cognition; with this intention, he says, "We, however...

The state of having reached the stage of practice for this [cognition] consists in the perception of a mark invariably concomitant with validity, and likewise, being of that same class means nothing other than the cognition of a result in one who is in a healthy state.
By this, desire, aversion, effort, and cognition are also explained.
Now, one might object: "How is the validity of that very cognition which is to be used as an example to be established?

And likewise, how is it established for each subsequent member of the series of examples used to prove those? To this, he says: "And not... (na ca). The phrase "of the resultant cognition" (*phalajñānasya*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*).

It should be understood that whatever is employed as an example when validity is to be established by means of the mark (liṅga) of being of that same class (tajjātīyatva), it applies to each and every such case.
If this were so, the efficacy of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti-sāmarthya*) would have no scope at all;
for there is no cognition whatsoever whose object is entirely unprecedented.

Thus, since the author of the *Vārttika* speaks of the beginninglessness of both the comprehension of an object through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the efficacy of purposeful activity, he says: "And among these... [to address this objection].
The remainder of the argument is that it is "susceptible to doubt and deviation" because there is no recollection of its belonging to that same class (*tajjātīyatva*).

Although the fruit itself is not the object of purposeful action (*pravṛtti*), nevertheless, since the action has as its domain either the means to that fruit or the continuum (*saṃtāna*) of that fruit,
it is either connected with another fruit of that same class, or connected with a fruit of a different class that is invariably concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*) with it.
The capacity for action, whether one's own or that of another person, is to be observed as the result of the knowledge of the fruit.

Thus, by means of this same principle (*samānanyāyatā*), immediately after establishing the validity of the perception of external objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, the validity of verbal testimony (*śabda*) was established; and for the sake of proving both of those, by that very same principle, the validity of the resultant cognition (*phalajñāna*) among the internal perceptual cognitions was established. By that same principle, [the validity] of that which is the object of desire, aversion, and effort was also [established].

It has been indicated that the establishment of the validity of knowledge (*jñāna*) remains; however, since this determination (*niścaya*) follows the same logical principles as inference (*anumāna*), its establishment will be carried out immediately after the establishment of the validity of inference. With this intention, he says: "Of inference.
For doubt regarding deviation (*vyabhicāra-śaṅkā*) is twofold: by way of the cause and by way of the essential nature (*svarūpa*).

And since that [inconsistency] is removed by the very same means of valid cognition that grasp pervasion and the presence of the reason in the subject, the inferential cognition becomes one in which all suspicion of deviation has been eliminated.
The implication is that the validity of such a cognition is ascertained intrinsically (svataḥ).

Now, one might ask: "Even though there is no difference in their being means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), why is it that only inference (*anumiti*) is [valid] by itself (*svataḥ*), and not perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the rest? To this, he says: "The object of inference" (*anumeya*). For inferential knowledge arises precisely by delimiting the state of the object as it is—for instance, "this very thing possesses fire."
And likewise, this [cognition] being determined by a subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) is itself determined to consist in the ascertainment of its own object.
Nor can its nature as an ascertainment be established without one determining that the experience possesses an non-erroneous object;
thus, that must necessarily be determined.
And that very [cognition] is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Even when there is such a subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), the suspicion that it might be erroneous remains;
however, that suspicion does not exist precisely because [the cognition] arises from a logical mark (*liṅga*).
For indeed, when [the cognition] has arisen as seized by the perception of a specific characteristic (viśeṣadarśana), there is no room for doubt.
This is what he says with the words "for indeed" (na hi).
The remainder of the sense is that the cognition having the form of the inferential mark (liṅga) is certain and non-deviant.

However, perceptual and verbal cognitions do not consist in the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*); rather, they manifest merely the object as it appears, common to both superimposition (*āropa*) and non-superimposition (*anāropa*).
And thus, they are experienced in that very same way by the subsequent reflective cognition (*anuvyavasāya*).
However, because they do not consist of the nature of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), there is no grasping of their own validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) by those two.
Now, if by chance they arise and are subsequently cognized (*anuvyavasīyete*) as consisting precisely in the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*),
then [their validity] is grasped only by including a restrictive factor (*niyāmaka*).

But in the absence of that [specific cause], since there would be no distinction, the nature of being a determinative cognition would be set aside, and it would remain common to both that which possesses the form of the object and that which does not. Bearing this intention in mind, he states the lack of a restrictive factor: "Perceptual cognition, however... For even in the case of the cognition of a fire or the like associated with smoke and the like, although there is an invariable concomitance of the object with its object, and although that cognition arises from such an object as well, [there is still no restriction].
Even so, is it non-deviation or the apprehension thereof?
In that case, the former is simply ineffective.

Because, by the mere contact of the sense organs, both [the object and the cognition] appear simultaneously in a single cognition, there is no dependence on the time of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*);
and because that which is not reflected upon lacks determinative power.
Thus it has been said: "but rather, from that which exists merely by its own presence."

The phrase "even for those that are non-deviant" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. By this, the claim made by some—that doubt is merely removed by other cognitions—is refuted; for "doubt" (śaṅkā) is indeed synonymous with "uncertainty" (saṃśaya).
And since that [error] cannot be removed except through the determination of reality (tattvanirṇaya), one must follow the means for the determination of reality.

Thus, when there is an absence of other means such as perception because of the deficiency of that which grasps the nature of cognition, inference alone is the means; therefore he says: "The efficacy of purposeful activity" (pravṛttisāmarthya).

It might be argued: "If the validity of perceptual and verbal cognitions is extrinsic (*parataḥ*), then is the validity of reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) also extrinsic? And if so, then by the principle that 'only a determined sign (*liṅga*) is a determiner,' one would introduce an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) through a succession of further signs. To this, he says: "Residing in the cognition... (*jñānagateti*).
In this case as well, the same reasoning applies:
because it arises by apprehending its own object precisely through the exclusion of what is not that form, there is experience exactly in that way.
Furthermore, from the very moment of its arising, it is occupied with the grasping of a specific object; thus, there is no room for doubt.
And the specific distinction [of this cognition] is precisely its nature as an *anuvyavasāya* (subsequent reflective awareness).
For no one, even while not knowing [an object], reflects by thinking "I know.
Nor would it be the case that in a cognition whose form is that of mother-of-pearl, one would think "I know silver"; thus it was said: "of such a kind."
This is also an elliptical indication:

even perception, whose object is merely the dharmin— including both the external and the internal— is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by its very nature, because it is impossible for there to be error that is entirely without a basis (*nirālambana*).
Keeping the aforementioned reasoning in mind, he extends [the argument] by saying "by this" (*etena*).
The meaning is that comparison (*upamāna*) is the act of comparing (*upamiti*);
thus it has been explained.
The phrase "having ascertained by itself" implies "as being valid.

For it is not the case that when the validity of both the cognition of the meaning of the analogical transfer statement (*atideśavākya*) and the cognition of similarity has been determined, the resulting analogy (*upamiti*) becomes a mere fallacy.

And although the validity of inferential cognition, analogical cognition, the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), and the cognition of the subject (*dharmin*) can indeed be apprehended extrinsically (*parataḥ*), [the point remains as stated].

For even there, there exist inferential marks (*liṅga*) of that same class, such as "arising from the cognition of similarity to a mark" (*liṅgasādṛśyajñānasamutthatva*) and so forth, according to the circumstances; nevertheless, it has been shown that here the apprehension of validity occurs spontaneously through its own internal state (*koṣṭhagati*), and not by itself [as an external act]. However, for one who is in disagreement, that must be established through something else (*parataḥ*); this is the ultimate point.

Therefore, the restriction "from itself alone" (svata eva) applies neither to the exclusion of non-connection (nāyogavyavaccheda) nor to the exclusion of connection with another (nānyayogavyavaccheda).
What then? It is the exclusion of absolute non-connection (atyantāyogavyavaccheda).
But even by this much, how is the validity of the sense organs and other instruments of cognition established?

For it is not the case that their validity consists merely in the result being true to the object. To this he says: "And of the enjoyer... [and so forth]. Now, if the sense organs and others deviate from the object, how could they produce a non-deviating cognition of the object?
Or, if that were the case, even a donkey might produce an infallible cognition of fire because there is no distinction [between it and firewood]; therefore, he says: "And not...
Just as wet fuel, although not invariably concomitant with burning, [is still indicative] due to its connection with fire...

The meaning is this: just as smoke, which by its very nature as a cause does not deviate from fire, is not subject to commands or inquiries when it produces that [fire], so too the sense organ and other factors—when augmented by such auxiliary conditions and connected with their respective objects—produce a cognition that does not deviate from those objects.
Furthermore, this validity is not necessarily determined in all cases.
For at that time, there would be no ascertainment anywhere of the very consciousness that serves as the support;
and if that were the case, due to the resulting infinite regress, there would be no transition to other objects.
Therefore, that consciousness which, by virtue of its intense momentum, must necessarily be experienced—

With the intention that validity must be determined by the aforementioned method wherever another person specifically or generally disagrees or desires to know, and thus there is no infinite regress, he summarizes the stated point under the guise of a conclusion, saying: "Therefore, because of doubt regarding the object."
Now, one might object: even if one acts despite uncertainty regarding the object, one cannot act by inferring that it is a means to that [desired end], because there would be no desire for it;

nor can there be an inference of its being a means to that end without the apprehension of pervasion (vyāpti); and that [apprehension of pervasion] likewise does not exist without action—thus, the fault of mutual dependence (itaretarāśrayatva) remains exactly as before. To this, he says: "of the object" (arthasya).

Although one acts in various instances even by means of a certainty regarding being a required means—just as one acts through a certainty regarding validity—nevertheless, action proceeds by accepting even a merely possible status as a required means.
Furthermore, that doubt would not arise in this case any more than it would in another case where [the object] has not been perceived;
therefore, perception once again follows.
Therefore, it has been refuted precisely by taking recourse to beginninglessness.
In the Vārttika, although the word "object" (*artha*) refers specifically to the means that is required, because that alone is the object of engagement and because it is what is being sought.

Nevertheless, because the cognition of the mere locus (*dharmimātra*) and the cognition of the object to be inferred (*anumeya*) occur at different times and are mutually dependent, he explains it in that very way: "the cognition of the object" (*arthapratipatti*).
Now, is the purposefulness of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) being resolved as something previously challenged, or is it being made known as something already sought after?
It cannot be the first;
for there is no person who would say that a means of valid cognition is devoid of purpose.
Because the accomplishment of all human goals is rooted in that [knowledge].
However, one for whom there is no human goal would simply perish, breathless.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable.
Since it is appropriate to make this known immediately after the recitation of the aphorism, just as one makes known doubt and so forth, he says: "In this regard, the following...

This is not an inquiry into the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or its purpose; rather, by one who considers the supreme Nyāya—which constitutes the subject matter of the treatise—to be the principal means for attaining the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*), the very commencement of the treatise is challenged while a simpler means for engaging [with it] exists.
And the meaning is that he began to concentrate.
The cultivation of the perception of suffering regarding the ten [objects] is for the sake of strengthening the desire for liberation.
The true nature of the self is its state of being entirely free from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
The cultivation of that is meditation (*dhyāna*).

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the activities that serve as its means—characterized by restraint (*yama*), observance (*niyama*), posture (*āsana*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and concentration (*dhāraṇā*)—are included.
The direct realization of the reality of the self (*ātmatattva-sākṣātkāra*) is meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Dispassion is supreme mastery;
ripening is liberation from the afflictions along with their latent predispositions.

By this, Yoga, along with its six ancillaries (ṣaḍ-aṅga), has been shown. Having stated the doubt, he offers the commentary: "In that regard, this is the final resort. Nevertheless, the fact that logic is a cumbersome means has not been avoided, because even an object determined by logic requires [further] engagement [in practice].
Since one who is already engaged in activity does not depend upon logic, he says: "The following is what is meant.
Now, if both are equal, why is it that only the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is explained and not the activity? To this he says: "Nevertheless.

Because the activity characterized by hearing, reflection, meditative absorption, and direct realization is included within the means of valid cognition both in its essential nature and in its result, the explanation of that [means of valid cognition] itself is the explanation of the activity.
Nor does the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) become explained merely by explaining [the subject's] engagement (*pravṛtti*).
For the meaning is that neither the fruit of engagement nor the nature of that [fruit] constitutes the means of valid cognition.
[Objection: But at the occasion of explaining the purpose of the treatise’s subject matter, it was said that "the means of valid cognition is purposeful"; from where [does this follow]?
For the meaning of a treatise is not the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but rather the logical principle (*nyāya*); therefore, he says: "and because it is a general designation."

By this continuous exposition, the objections regarding the lack of purpose, the impossibility of the purpose, the undesirability of the purpose, and the suspicion of excessive difficulty in the means have been refuted.

What else remains for which the conduct of the world (*lokavṛtta*) is restated? Therefore, while first reminding [the reader] of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), he introduces the *Vārttika* with the words "by means of authority" (*prāmāṇya*).

Regarding the phrase "not by what is non-authoritative" (*apramāṇena*), although there is a discrepancy between speech and mind, authority (*pramāṇa*) indeed consists precisely in the means for prohibitions and injunctions.

Therefore, even for one who knows that [the cognition] is a means of negation, the statement "I negate by means of a valid means of knowledge" (*pramāṇena*) is a contradiction of the mind. Nevertheless, since such a statement can be justified even through delusion, there is no harm to us even if such an intention persists; it is with this in mind that permission has been granted. [The point is: when there is a discrepancy between speech and mind, one cannot say "by means of a valid means of knowledge" (*pramāṇena*) while maintaining a grasp of its validity.

Therefore, for one who says "by means of a valid cognition" (*pramāṇena*), validity necessarily revolves in the mind; thus, the statement "without having grasped validity" is contradictory to the mind. The meaning of "worldly practice" (*lokavṛtta*) is uncontradicted worldly transaction (*avyāhata-vyavahāra*).

Now, as for the objection that the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "Indeed, this [object] is known by a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇena khalvayam jñātaḥ*) might be a mere restatement of worldly usage,
and as to how the subsequent phrase "by means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇataḥ*) is to be understood, he says: "By way of demonstrating the cause."
For worldly conduct is not useful in its own right;

rather, since that [conduct] must necessarily be accepted, the means for it must also necessarily be accepted. It is with this intention that it is restated together with its means—this is the meaning.

Lest one should suspect that because the points concerning what is to be abandoned (*heya*) and so forth will be clear in the upcoming commentary (*bhāṣya*), the literal meaning (*akṣarārtha*) of that [commentary] is now being explained, he says: "of this very [work].
This means: of the work connected to the *Vārttika*, which consists of words and phrases [forming] the form of the *Vārttika* text;
and of that very same kind [is] the work contained in the *Bhāṣya*, which is connected to the *Bhāṣya*. This is the meaning.

When the relationship of subordinate and principal among the topics to be denoted is being investigated for the sake of establishing their sequential order, one might ask: what occasion is there for the treatise (*śāstra*), which consists of the act of denotation? To this he says: "The word 'treatise'.
If that is so, then since the things to be abandoned (*heya*) and so forth constitute the very content of the treatise, they do not form separate categories.
And thus, since there is only a single category, with reference to what could there be an inquiry into the relationship of subordinate and principal? To this he says: "And here..."

But how is the fourfold group beginning with the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) obtained here by this [text]? Lest there be the reproach that the Vārttika has failed to state [this], he says: "By that," because the establishment of the others is rooted in that.
"Establishment" (siddhi) means both comprehension (pratīti) and accomplishment (niṣpatti).
In that regard, there is indeed the cognition of both what is to be abandoned and the means [to its abandonment];
however, for that which is to be realized, there is both cognition and actualization.
And although there is certainly also the cognition of the abandonment itself, which takes the form of valid cognition, [it is not the same as the realization].
Nevertheless, it was stated that [the cessation] occurs "only from valid cognition" (pramāṇāt) and "from something other than that.
The sense is: since the accomplishment of abandonment arises precisely from the absence of ignorance, what is the use of knowledge?
For, as for knowledge, its occurrence is entirely dependent upon valid cognition.
Regarding the fourfold group beginning with the knower (*pramātṛ*), the establishment of both the knower and the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is indeed their cognition;
it is also the accomplishment of the valid cognition (*pramā*) itself.
This is what was stated: "And because [the object] is the effect of that [valid cognition]."

Now, one might object: "Since the knower and the other factors are also purposeful, what additional quality has been imparted to the means of knowledge by the term *arthavat*? To this, he says: "The suffix *matup* is used in the sense of excellence (*atiśāyane*)."
Now, regarding these two groups of fourfold categories, is there an option (*vikalpa*) or a combination (*samuccaya*) with respect to the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*)?

Both are untenable because they are non-different. For instance, that very object which is the knower (*pramātṛ*), the knowable (*prameya*), and the knowledge (*pramiti*), is itself that which is to be abandoned (*heya*) and that which is to be attained (*adhigantavya*); likewise, that very object which consists of the means of abandonment (*hānopāya*) is [the same].
Thus, [it is] indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Since doubt (*saṃśaya*) and the others also constitute the body of reasoning (*nyāyaśarīra*) by virtue of being its auxiliary members (*parikara*), and since that [reasoning] is a means of valid cognition, there is no distinction [between them] because they are non-different; it is not a case of mere conceptual differentiation based on a difference in the phrasing of the words.

Nor is there a conjunction [of meanings], for it does not occur that "this is to be accomplished by a tree (taru) or by a plant (vṛkṣa)," or "by both the tree and the plant. Therefore, he says: "due to a difference in intended meaning" (*vivakṣābhedeneti*).
By the phrase "because that is untenable," he intends a difference in the underlying cause (*nimittabheda*).

Therefore, the meaning is this: although in both cases exactly sixteen categories are subsumed, nevertheless, just as the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is to be known as a means of valid cognition, so too is it to be known as an object of avoidance (hāna);
otherwise, another [separate] act of avoidance would have to be resorted to.
Furthermore, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be purposeless;
and if its status as a means of valid cognition were unknown, the act of avoidance (*hāna*) could not be accomplished.
Just as doubt and the like are to be known in their own nature as adjuncts to the means of valid cognition, so too are they to be known as means for avoidance.
Otherwise, one would have to resort to another means;
furthermore, these [preparations] would be purposeless.
Moreover, if their status as preparatory equipment (*parikara*) were not understood, their nature as a means (*upāyatā*) would not be established.
Just as the body and the other nine are to be known as objects of cognition (*prameya*), so too must they be understood as things to be abandoned (*heya*);
otherwise, they would not be abandoned, and one would continue to rely upon other things that ought to be abandoned.
Furthermore, if knowability (*prameyatva*) itself were unknown, the state of being something to be abandoned (*heyatā*) could not be established.
Just as liberation (*apavarga*) is to be known as an object of knowledge, so too is it to be realized as something to be attained.
Otherwise, one would have to rely on another means of apprehension, and [the object] would become something that cannot be apprehended;
furthermore, if it were unknown as an object of cognition (*prameya*), its status as something to be apprehended could not be established.
Just as the self is to be apprehended as an object of cognition (*prameya*), so too it is to be apprehended as a cognizer (*pramātṛ*);
otherwise, one would have to rely upon another cognizer.

Furthermore, there would be an infinite regress; and if the object of cognition were itself unknown, then the states of being with or without limiting conditions, as well as the processes of rejection and acceptance, could not be accomplished.
And just as cognition is such by virtue of being cognition, so too is its distinction [from itself] by virtue of being a valid cognition (*pramiti*);
otherwise, one would have to resort to another valid cognition, or the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) would be fruitless.
Furthermore, if the status of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) were unknown, the fact that [the four noble truths] are to be abandoned would not be established.

Therefore, the meaning is that both sets of four categories have been included with the intention that those very things—starting with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth—should be known in both ways.

As for what has been said by some— that the human goal (puruṣārtha) is fully encompassed within these four alone: that which is to be abandoned, the means of abandoning it, and that which is to be attained— just as in the world, the thorn is that which is to be abandoned,
and the shoe is the means of abandoning it.
The means for that [cessation] is the path consisting of the Noble Eightfold Way; the cessation to be attained is the absence of suffering;
and in the treatise, the disease is that which is to be abandoned, and the treatment is the abandonment itself.
The knowledge of the cause (*nidāna-jñāna*) is the means for that [health].

Since health is what is to be attained, one might object: "What is the use of describing sixteen categories when only four [topics] need to be stated? This objection is also refuted, because those very four goals are expressed as being sixteenfold through a distinction in the manner of presentation.
The commentator himself will demonstrate at every step the justification for the difference in intended meaning;
having understood this very point, he refutes the view of him who raised an objection regarding what was "additional," using the words "by this."
The meaning is that when the qualification "is explained part by part" (*avayavaśaḥ*) is used, the emphasis lies on the action (*kriyā*), and not on the object qualified (*viśeṣya*).
He clarifies this very point later with the words: "In that regard, among its parts... (*tatrāsyāvayaveṣu*).
Why was it not stated "from what means of valid cognition" (*kasmāt pramāṇāt*)?

The meaning is that in this way, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) would indeed be beyond doubt. [An objection is raised: If "of this" (*asya*) refers back to the ablative case under discussion, there is a grammatical inconsistency of gender (*liṅga*); therefore, he says "of this" (*asyeti*).

Having shown the use of the ablative case (*pañcamyāḥ*) with the suffix *tasi*, he introduces the following by explaining the objection that the employment of *tasi* apart from the ablative is inconsistent, stating: "For the sake of pervading the statement" (*vacanavyāptyartham*).

Now, [one might object]: "Surely there is a convergence (*saṃplava*) of two means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhyām*) or of many means of knowledge (*pramāṇaiḥ*), but how can there be a convergence of a single means of knowledge (*pramāṇena*)? To this he says: "Where there are two," etc. (*yatra dvayor iti*).
There is merely a merging into the unity of the object,
but not a conjunction of the causes;
for if that were the case, there would be no difference in the result.
Nor do they function as instruments when combined;
the meaning is that this is for the purpose of making it known that, were that the case, there would be no distinction in their respective operations.
"For this very reason" means: [as stated above].
The particle *eva*, while excluding other most efficient causes (*sādhakatama*), excludes both its operation and its result;
however, it does not indicate a mutual independence between its own operation and these two, because such [independence] is possible even when they coexist (*saṃplava*). This is the meaning.
Why, then, is it understood as having the sense of "instrument"?
The meaning is: from which of the two, the base (prakṛti) or the suffix (pratyaya)?
This is the intended point.

If the instrumentality is expressed by the third case ending, what is the purpose of the suffix *lyuṭ* residing in the base? Or, if it is expressed by that suffix alone, what is the purpose of the third case ending?
Lest there be any suspicion that the indicator (*jñāpaka*) might be a causal factor (*kāraka*), he says: "the object, namely the apprehension of the object.
Now, one might ask: "Is it not for the purpose of making known the relationship between cause and instrument that the pervasion by case-endings is adopted in the term *pramāṇam*?

Since the status of being an instrument is directly understood from the nominal stem itself, and the status of being a cause is understood through the sense of the matter, what is the use of the pervasion by case-endings? To this, he replies: "And here... (*atra ca*).
Nor should it be said that identity between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its fruit (*phala*) cannot be denied even on the grounds of their being related as instrument and result;

for if that were so, why would the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) be used to express the existence of a cause that is inseparable from it? This is because the suffix *tamap* (expressing the superlative) lacks the capacity [to convey] anything other than mere instrumentality (*sādhakatva*).
In that regard, with the intention of asking "Why? concerning the existence of misconception (*vipratipatti*), he says: "Because it is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Thus, [the scripture] possesses the character of being a restatement (*anuvādakatva*).

By providing this justification, the redundancy between the suffix *lyuṭ* and the third case ending is resolved. Furthermore, since the repetitive nature of the word cannot be established as mere restatement (*anuvādakatva*) without a specific purpose, he demonstrates that purpose by stating: "from among the other causal factors of valid cognition" (*pramākārakāntarebhyaḥ*).
In ordinary usage, however, one should understand that the case-ending possesses a meaningful function because it expresses number (*saṃkhyā*).

The objection that there must be a convergence (saṃplava) [of means of knowledge] because they have a qualified object is indeed irrelevant, since perception and inference do converge regarding a mountain or the like as qualified by fire and so forth; therefore, he says: "the qualified is distinct.
The singular number is used with the intention of referring to the generality of being an object.
Since perception arises from the causal efficacy of an object, it therefore has the object as its domain.
Is being a cause the sole definition of an object? No, he says: "And that very [cause] is the object."
To the question "What follows from this if it is so?", he says: "And there is no universal."

But is it not the case that even the conventional (*sāṃvyavahārika*) particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is exactly like this? To this he says: "the particular characteristic. This means that which does not extend across space and time, and which withstands analytical inquiry. Now, although perception does not grasp an object in the form of a universal (*sāmānya*), if inference were also to grasp the particular characteristic, then by that much alone there would be a convergence (*saṃplava*) [of the two means of knowledge]. To this he says: "no..."
And so it is said: "But surely, let inference be restricted to the universal alone; for perception will also operate here."

And since even a universal (sāmānya), by virtue of its existence, must be capable of imparting a form [to cognition], the convergence [of means of knowledge] is established from this as well; therefore, he says "not" (na ca).
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "it ought to exist as ultimately real" (paramārthasat);
the intention is that it cannot so exist because it cannot withstand critical analysis (vicārāsahatvāt).

Is it then the case that inference is entirely without an object because the universal does not exist and because it is impossible to grasp a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with respect to the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)? To this he says: "This [inference]... Is it then the case that inference is simply invalid because its domain is not the ultimate reality (*aparamārtha*)?
If so, how can it, having delineated one thing, cause one to act toward another?
And how is that non-contradictory? And how is that which has a sublated form conventionally designated as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)? To this he says: "Therefore..."

[Objection: But will there not be a convergence (*saṃplava*) of these two with another means of valid cognition? To this he says: "And not... [Objection: But does it not exist as verbal testimony (*śabda*) and so forth? To this he says: "Of the means of valid cognition... [Objection:
But surely it is not included at all, because its object is not a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) and because it is not bound to an object. To this he says: "And if there is no inclusion..."

[Objection: "But even if there is a fixed distinction between the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), will there not still be an overlap (*saṃplava*) between these two—perception and inference—with respect to another object?
For there is indeed another object [namely] that which 'possesses it' (*tadvat*). [The author] says: "And not so" (*na ca*).
For a particular characteristic, which is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*), cannot become "possessing it" by means of a universal that is non-existent.
The meaning is that there is no relationship between existence and non-existence.
Intending to show that "this path is difficult," he says: "And how this is so...
[and] "if, in the word *viśeṣa*, there is not an object-kāraka..."

Then, because there is another [type of] name similar to that, he says: "The specific" (*viśeṣa*). The word "investigating" (*mīmāṃsaha*) is to be supplied as the subject who cannot tolerate the confusion (*saṃplava*).

Desiring to state that the Vārttika beginning with "and the object already apprehended" (*adhigataṃ cārtham*) has a meaning distinct from the Vārttika beginning with "because it is already apprehended" (*adhigatatvāt*), he says: "It might be so," and so forth.
When an object has already been apprehended, another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*) has no utility whatsoever regarding the apprehension of that object.
This is because its prior existence is established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);

nor is it for the sake of sustaining the flow of successive linguistic conventions, since that too is established by a continuous stream of memories arising from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by those very conventions.
Nor should it be argued that whether there be a continuum of memory or a continuum of realization, there is no difference in their capacity to initiate worldly discourse;

for, like memory, they would have as their object only the thing already presented [to consciousness], and thus, being non-valid cognitions (*apramā*), the means of achieving them would result in being non-authoritative (*apramāṇa*).
Furthermore, for that very reason, those [realizations] would consequently be nothing other than memory.

Since the continuity of memory is necessarily established, and since the conventional usage [of objects] is already proven by that alone, the postulation of a continuity of cognition would result in the fault of conceptual over-elaboration (*kalpanā-gaurava*). Bearing this intention in mind, he concludes with what is already ground, saying "it is understood" (*adhigatam*).

Now, regarding the *Vārttika* passage "otherwise" (*nanu anyathā*): if one intends to refer to a difference in the mode of the cause itself, then even if there were a difference in the mode belonging to the cause, no distinction belonging to the object (*viṣaya*) would have been shown that is useful for avoiding the fault of grinding what is already ground.

Now, if it is shown that the distinction between means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) pertains solely to the object, then how can there be a convergence (*saṃplava*) based on the criterion of "cognizing an object not yet cognized"?

Furthermore, even when the object is non-different, no distinction in the type of result (*phala*) arises from the difference in the means of valid cognition that is relevant to the present context; therefore, he says: "This is the underlying intention."
