There would either be futility in grinding what is already ground, or a lack of distinction in the result,
or a result that is not desired.

Regarding the question, "Even when an object has been apprehended, why does the means of apprehension produce that apprehension?"—is this merely a question, or is it a denial of the possibility of such a means?
In that regard, he refutes the denial of the possibility of the means by saying, "For not... (na hi).
For there would be no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the obstruction of its own cause;
nor is the apprehension of the object contrary to the cause of valid cognition, such that [the latter] would [be absent] when the former is present.
The very causes of valid cognition would become non-causes;
therefore, they would have to withdraw of their own accord after having perceived [the object], provided they were capable of intending [to do so].
But this is not the case—this is the meaning.
He refutes the mere question with the words "nor even" (nāpi).
Having raised the objection that [the inquiry] lacks a desired fruit, he refutes it with the words "of the knower" (pramātuḥ).
He refutes the charge of fruitlessness with the words "therefore" (tasmāt).
"Being produced by a collection of present causes" means being produced by a collection distinguished by its own specific, contemporaneous causes;
by this, the nature of experience (*anubhavatva*) is demonstrated.
For the specific cause of memory (*smṛti*) is the mental impression (*saṃskāra*).
Because the self, the internal organ, and so forth are common to other cognitions; moreover,
that [impression] has arisen long ago and is not present,
whereas that which is present— namely, the auxiliary cause known by the name "awakening"— is not common [to other cognitions].
However, for experience, that which is uncommon [to other means of knowledge] is the fourfold contact (*catuṣṭayasannikarṣa*) and so forth;
and that is "present," meaning it has arisen freshly.
The remainder [of the definition] is that such a cognition is uncontradicted (*abādhita*).
Having accepted the premise that the result is non-distinct, he refutes the opponent's intention with the words "those which produce it.
If there were pointlessness because the result is non-distinct even from the result of the first means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
then, just like the second [cognition], the first means of valid cognition would also be pointless due to its having a result non-distinct from the second.

If it is argued that [the first cognition] is purposeful because it is independent [of another], then by the same logic, the second [cognition] would likewise be independent with respect to its own result. Consequently, that result would not be of the nature of valid cognition (*pramā*).

The argument that [perception] is like memory because it has as its object only what has already been grasped is also not tenable; for if the probandum is the negation of being a direct experience of an object as it truly is, the reason is "mistimed" (kālātīta).
Furthermore, if the probandum is merely the absence of an additional object, it results in proving what is already established (siddhasādhana).
And because it is equivalent to the probandum (*sādhyasama*);
and because, in the case of the negation of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), it is conditioned by the absence of its cause, and because it is sublated (*bādhita*).
The meaning is that we shall explain the cause for the conventional usage of "valid cognition" (*pramā*).
If this is so, what then is the meaning of the *Vārttika*? To this he says: "And that very [cognition]...
Now, one might object: even for the result (*phala*), there is indeed a distinction of modes consisting of being direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) or not being direct perception.
"Why is that very point not demonstrated by this [text]? To this he says: "Even though...
By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), the various distinctions of the means residing in the cause—such as the sense-faculties, logical marks (*liṅga*), and so forth—are also subsumed.
For it is precisely for the purpose of refuting the opponent's objection regarding the confluence of different causes that the other party has raised the counter-argument.
How, then, is he to be awakened by that very [means], given that awakening by another is the subject at hand?
This is why it was said: "because it is not applicable to the subject at hand."
Having thus established the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the heart and having examined the theories of convergence (*saṃplava*) and distinctness (*vyavasthā*),
he now states— "for the sake of distinguishing the categories" and "ascertainment"— in order to define the essential nature of the means of valid cognition.

If certainty were intended [as the goal], it would not necessarily be preceded by doubt; thus, a question regarding that which is doubted would be appropriate. Therefore, he says: "It is determined. The sense is that since investigation (*vicāra*) or examination (*parīkṣā*) must necessarily be preceded by doubt, it is logical that a question concerning what is doubted should come first.
He states the conflicting views regarding the cause of doubt, beginning with "some [say]":
for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is a specific kind of instrument (*karaṇa*), and an instrument is that which is most effective in accomplishing an action (*sādhakatama*).

Furthermore, once the object to be established has been accomplished, there is no longer the status of being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*) for anything of that same class, just as an axe is no longer such once the tree has been cut.

Therefore, just as an axe is an instrument of cutting while it is operating upon an uncut object, so too the sense organs and other factors are valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) while they are operating upon an object not yet cognized; thus say the Mīmāṃsakas.
He states another opinion: "conformity with the object" (*viṣayasārūpya*).
First of all, the result of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is simply the cognition of the object, because it consists in the nature of valid knowledge (*pramā*).
Indeed, there is nothing further that the means of valid cognition must perform regarding the object beyond the production of valid knowledge.
Attainment (*prāpti*) is indeed activity (*pravṛtti*);
activity, too, is simply the apprehension of an object suitable for action.
Therefore, there is nothing in the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) other than the determination of the object (*arthapramiti*).

Regarding the statement "the result is something [distinct]," it is said: "That very perceptual cognition is the fruit of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because its nature consists in the apprehension of the object.
Furthermore, that alone is the means of knowledge which establishes the object.
It establishes that very object which it restricts to its own specific cognition;
for if that cognition were not restricted in such a manner,
that cognition would belong neither to anyone in particular nor to everyone, and thus the cognition would not be restricted by the object.
And how can that which produces a cognition of an indefinite object be called a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
Furthermore, by means of the instruments of knowledge such as the sense faculties, the specific nature of that [object] is not determined;
for it is not the case that the cognition of blue arises from blue simply because it was produced by the eye.
Otherwise, it would follow that even the cognition of yellow would be [the cognition] of blue.
Rather, it is precisely because of its having the form of blue that the cognition of blue belongs to the blue.
Therefore, the very form of the object as it has entered into the cognition establishes the cognition as belonging to that [object], and it likewise establishes the object itself as such.

Therefore, because it is the cause for the determination of the object, that alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as he said: "Its conformity with the object is its means of valid cognition, because the establishment of the cognition of the object occurs by virtue of that. "Because of the establishment of the cognition of the object" means because of the determination of the cognition of the object.
And thus, it amounts to saying that the determination of objects [occurs] in such a manner;
nor is the relationship between instrument and result contradicted within a non-different self, for in that case, it is only the state of being a cause that is contradicted.

For indeed, either the relationship between the operation and the agent of the operation, or the relationship between the signified and the signifier, is certainly accepted [in this case]. For in common worldly usage, it is only when an axe is in contact with a tree or similar object that it is designated as an instrument by virtue of its operation, namely conjunction.
Furthermore, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) does not exist as some other distinct entity with a physical form apart from the things being conjoined, such as an axe.

Moreover, the relationship of indicator and indicated (*gamyagamakabhāva*) is indeed observed both in the case of self-luminous cognition and in the case of an external tree when it is indicated by its being a *śiṃśapā* tree;
for there is no tree other than the *śiṃśapā*, nor is there a *śiṃśapā* other than the tree.

The Sautrāntikas maintain that in conventional discourse based on conceptual alternatives, just as there is a distinction between exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) here, so too is there one between the form and its possessor; thus, there is no difference whatsoever.
He states another opinion: "of consciousness alone. For that which has the operation of manifesting an object is itself the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And manifestation, which consists of the nature of sentience (*caitanya*), belongs only to that which perceives.
Nor are the sense organs and so forth [the agents], even though they are instruments, because they are insentient by nature;
for there is no such thing as a conscious being apart from cognition.
Therefore, consciousness alone, by virtue of its sentience, performs the function of seeing;
and thus it is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, there is no difference between the function and the agent of the function, just as in the case of an axe being applied [to wood]. Thus argue the Vaibhāṣikas and others who maintain the theory of formlessness (*nirākāravāda*).
He states another opinion: "upalabdhi" etc. The "elders" (vṛddhāḥ) are those who are elders in terms of [their mastery of] the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
By this, he indicates that the former [opinion] belongs to children.

Some explain [the passage] by supplying the word "together" (*saha*), saying: "By the explanation of the question concerning the state (*bhāva-praśna-vyākhyānena*), the question concerning the possessor of the state (*bhavitṛ-praśna*) is explained.

Others, however, say: "The explanation of the question concerning the state is to be understood; by this, the question concerning the possessor of the state is explained. Still others say: "By means of the explanation of the question concerning the state as the reason (*hetu*), the question concerning the possessor of the state is explained; the question concerning the possessor of the state was explained in order to explain the question concerning the state."
"Because that [inference] would be untenable without it.
Those learned in the tradition maintain that this is a scribal error;
"vyabhicāra" means inconsistency or contradiction.
"Being devoid of meaning" means having a contrary meaning;
therefore, there is no lack of distinction from the probandum (*sādhyāviśiṣṭatā*).
[Objection: But in the case of "Is it a post or a person?", a difference is indeed perceived between the two things presented.
How, then, is there non-correspondence, and how is there meaningfulness? To this he says: "Indeed not," because it is not attained.
For this very reason, it is not employed for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*);
the meaning is that because it is neither attained nor functional, it does not exist.

Even if "perception" (*upalabdhi*) were explained with the intention of referring to experience (*anubhava*), there would be no undesirable consequence regarding its being a cause of memory (*smṛti*).
Since memory is not itself an experience, nevertheless— the sūtras stating "intellect (buddhi), apprehension (upalabdhi), and knowledge (jñāna) are synonymous"—
accept that the term *upalabdhi* is a synonym for knowledge (*jñāna*).
And with the intention that memory also possesses the nature of cognition, it was said: "For this [memory] is not...
Even in the case of a past object, there exists a connection between the word or the logical mark (liṅga) and the object through a causal chain;
however, in the case of a future object, even that [connection] does not exist. Therefore, it was suspected [by the opponent] that [the word] functions as a cognizer (*jñāpaka*).
"Of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) as well" means that its being an effect of the object and its being a communicator of the object through a causal chain are equally direct [in their nature].
"The cause of the apprehension of the form of memory" means the cause of the cognition of the form of memory.
He refutes this, saying: "It is not so."
Now, one might object that there is no dispute regarding the point that memory is not a valid cognition (*pramā*); to this he says: "In the world," etc.
By this, he indicates the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) which apprehends the ground for the application of the term "valid cognition."

For instance, its being a memory (*smṛti*) cannot be the basis for its application [as a valid means of knowledge], because that would entail the consequence that direct experience (*anubhava*) is not a valid cognition (*apramātva*).
Nor can the property of being a cognition (*jñānatva*) and so forth, which is inherent in the same object as that [memory], be the basis for it.
By this [definition], even memory would be a valid cognition (*pramā*), because it would follow that error (*viparyaya*) would likewise be so.
Nor does there exist a specific universal (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) called "validity" (*pramātva*); for a specific universal residing in cognition is grasped by the mind alone.
Furthermore, since it has already been established that validity (*prāmāṇya*) is something to be inferred;
moreover, if validity were a specific universal (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*),
then it could not inhere in a subversive cognition (*viparyayajñāna*), which either lacks that [validity] or possesses a universal contrary to it.
And likewise, erroneous cognition would not be a valid means of knowledge even with respect to its own subject;
thus, it would follow that such cognition is without a real objective basis (*nirālambana*).
Furthermore, a universal would enter into a single individual instance along with another universal through a relationship of higher and lower inclusion.
In that case, is it experience (*anubhūtatva*) or validity (*prāmāṇya*) that constitutes the highest [criterion]? In the first case, how can memory be valid knowledge (*pramā*)?
In the second case, however, experience would not deviate from validity.
And in that case, even error would be deprived of its very foundation.
Furthermore, if [the nature of cognition] were exclusively direct perception (*sākṣātkāritva*), then inference and the like, which lack direct perception, would not be valid cognitions (*pramā*).
On the other hand, if it were otherwise, erroneous cognition would not possess direct perception, because it lacks validity.
Therefore, being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*) is not a specific universal (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*).
If it is argued that [validity] consists merely in "correspondence with reality" (*yathārthatva*), we say no;
for then the consequence would follow that even in the case of "I remember," there would arise the cognition and designation "I am cognizing" (*pramiṇomi*).
If it is argued that this [usage] is indeed desired— no,
for it is impossible to restrict worldly usage and non-usage by mere desire alone.
If it is argued that this word "pramāṇa" has been restricted by that very [desire] to denote merely knowledge that accords with reality (yathārthajñāna)— no.
It has not been enumerated by the great sages as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is the fruit of memory.
If it is argued that it was not enumerated because it is included within those [already] mentioned, we say no;
for it is impossible for perception to have a fruit that is not direct intuition (*asākṣātkārin*).
And because words such as "linga" (inferential mark) do not establish cognition by their mere existence.
Furthermore, on what basis is memory considered to correspond to reality? For when an object is remembered, it is not exactly as it was at that time,
because its previous state has ceased to exist in the present.
For if there were no cessation [of the previous state], there would be no "previousness" at all.
Nor does memory take that object as its support by way of the previous state having ceased,
because the cessation of the previous state has not been experienced.
And with respect to an object not previously experienced, [recollection] is non-experiential because of the absence of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*).
Now, even though recollection and experience have the same object, why is it that experience is in accordance with reality while recollection is not?
Because that object remains in its very same state at the time of experience, whereas it is no longer in that state at the time of recollection.
[Objection: But surely, previously, it was indeed in that very state.
"Let knowledge be considered valid (*yathārtha*) by this much alone.
No, for it would follow that even in the case of a red object, the cognition of its being black would be valid. [Objection:
But the cognition "it was black" in that case is indeed valid.
True; for at that time, the object of that [cognition] is indeed in that state.
However, the object being remembered is not in that state at that time.
Therefore, memory is simply non-correspondent with reality (*ayathārtha*).
However, it should be according to the experience.
In that case, because the experience is in accordance with reality (*yathārthatva*), the memory which has that same object is also said to be in accordance with reality.
For this very reason, when the experience is not in accordance with reality, the memory—even if it is contrary [to the object]—is indeed not in accordance with reality.

Just as one who has fled after perceiving a rope as a snake possesses such a memory, so too is the nature of recollection (smṛti). Therefore, the validity of memory is merely like borrowed ornaments; it is not innate.
This very state of dependence is what some, whose etymological skills are blunted, have erroneously misconstrued.

Therefore, in both ways, the world has determined that the basis for the application of the term *pramā* (valid cognition) is precisely its being "true-to-reality" (*yathārthatva*), which is restricted solely to experience other than memory.
Otherwise, how could it be that the word *pramā* is employed only in that case and not elsewhere?

Nevertheless, with the intention that memory should not possess validity even with respect to its object (*dharmin*), [the author] has relied upon the worldly usage supported by the reasoning stated previously.

This has been stated: "and the world [accepts it as such]. Thus, first of all, it has been resolved that the definition of valid cognition (*pramā*) as "an experience that accords with its object" and the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as "the instrument for that [experience]" are faultless, having dispelled the suspicion of over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
Nor is this unacceptable even to the Mīmāṃsaka;
for he, too, cannot possibly charge it with the fallacies of under-extension (*avyāpti*) or over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
Indeed, there is no possibility that even for the Mīmāṃsaka, a cognition that is a veridical experience (*yathārthānubhava*) would not be a means of valid cognition (*pramā*).
But as for our definition of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) as that which apprehends an object not previously known, how could there be any disagreement? To this he says:

"And [it is] the apprehension of an object not yet cognized. This is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); for in the case of eternal entities, the state of being "not yet cognized" simply does not exist.
If [the object] is not apprehended in this life, nor even in another birth;

if it is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), nor even through inference (*anumāna*) or authoritative instruction (*upadeśa*); and because, even among things generally considered impermanent, we perceive only those very things previously perceived—otherwise, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) would be as good as abandoned.
Furthermore, the fact that [the object] is not apprehended even in its own nature would cause great confusion;
and as for its specific modes, when pillars and other such objects are being experienced again and again, no particular mode of quality is perceived that is born at every moment and then perishes.
Furthermore, even that which is produced by karma perishes very quickly and does not remain as something new at every moment;

nor, while persisting for four or five moments, does it— having produced a single cognition— remain indifferent toward the sense faculties and so forth, waiting for the birth of future karma and the like.

And therefore, the meaning is that other cognitions occurring at subsequent times—whether by way of a continuous stream or with interruptions—would not be valid means of knowledge, because [the object] has already been perceived throughout all previous births.
He raises an objection with the words "And not... (na ca):

although the essential nature or the mode [of the object] remains in that same state, nevertheless, it is only the object existing at the very moment of the stream of perceptual cognition that appears clearly.
Nor is a single present time the object for things that occur sequentially, because that would entail the simultaneous occurrence of cognitions— as in the case of multiple knowers—
and because recognition would be impossible.

Even though there is a plurality of cognitions, because they are not perceived as existing simultaneously, the meaning of the present object—which has not been apprehended by each preceding cognition—is determined by each succeeding one; thus, the meaning is that even in this case, there is indeed the apprehension of an object not previously known. He offers a rebuttal with the words "parama" (the ultimate).

First of all, for the Mīmāṃsakas, the production of the very nature of an entity is not its existence at every moment, as the Buddhists maintain; nor is it merely a difference in transformation despite the stability of the entity's form, as the Sāṃkhyas hold;
nor is it some kind of difference in attributes (*dharma*).
There exists [a time] that is new at every moment, which has "presentness" as another name for it;
yet this is not accepted by them,
nor is time an object of direct perception.
Nor is it of a different intrinsic nature.

Therefore, the distinctions of time are merely the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) that differentiate temporal portions; the direct perception of those [adjuncts] is itself the direct perception of the distinction of time—this is the ultimate truth.
In this regard, it has already been stated that limiting adjuncts (upādhis) conjoined with the post and so forth cannot possibly exist as they appear [in cognition]; furthermore,
because "cognizedness" (jñātatā) will be refuted later, and because such appearances do not occur in cognitions involving a continuous stream of consciousness.
But as for the adjuncts (*upādhi*) that are either perceived or otherwise associated with [the object], would they be associated with the cognition of that [object], or otherwise?

First of all, in the case of pillars and the like, there are no momentary things whatsoever that are associated with something other than that [pillar] which necessarily become associated with its cognition.
If it is argued that "they do so in some cases," [we reply:]...
In that case alone would there be validity for those cognitions;
however, where there are no adventitious conditions (*upādhi*) associated with that same single cognition, there the stream-like cognitions (*dhārāvāhika-buddhi*) would indeed lack validity.

And it is precisely such [cognitions]—which have as their objects other things within the scope of another cognition and are associated with other objects—that are intended as the subject matter of this investigation.

If it is argued that there will be limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), then in that case, there would be no such thing as a continuous stream of cognitions (*dhārāvāhana-buddhi*); thus, one who has gone for the sake of gain has lost even the root.

Indeed, when an object other than that [intended] subject is being experienced by another means of knowledge, by another sense organ, or by that very same one—due to the abandonment of that subject—a continuous stream of cognitions regarding the intended single object is impossible.
If it is argued that this matter is indeed accepted [by us], we say no;
for there is no evidence for a rule regarding the occurrence of various adventitious adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the *apūrva*.
Furthermore, those adjuncts that do not occur cannot be apprehended even by another cognition.
For this very reason, even in the case of a thousand cognitions such as "this is a jar" and "this is a jar," we do not perceive any distinction based on the object.
However, if one were to postulate that something which is not so perceived is nonetheless an object, it would follow that everyone would be omniscient.

Therefore, it is the pillar and so forth itself—existing in the form of the cessation of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), the absence of destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), and non-arising—that is the present.
The time delimited by that [pillar] is also the present.
And such a [present] is indeed common to multiple cognitions.
Nor does this entail the consequence of simultaneity of cognitions, because succession is possible in relation to subtle intervals of time.
Nor is it the case that, if these subtle adjuncts are not perceived, they are therefore impossible.
This is because [the object] is established precisely through its causal sequence.
Nor is there any impossibility of recognition;
for recognition is simply the synthesis of the object of a previous cognition with the present one.
And that is established precisely through the sequence of cognitions;
therefore, even when time and its limiting adjuncts are perceived, there is no contact with subtle adjuncts in every case,
nor is there cognition of them.
This is what was stated: "of those that are supremely subtle."

By this, the following [objection] is refuted: "Because there is an absence of being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*) when [the result] is already established. For the status of being the most effective means does not depend on another more effective means, but rather on other factors (*kāraka*) involved in the primary action.

Otherwise, where there is a collection of instruments (*karaṇa*), since they would not be distinguished from one another due to their mutual dependence, they would fail to qualify as instruments; thus, a collection of instruments could never occur anywhere.
However, in relation to other causal factors (*kāraka*), the instrument indeed possesses a state of excellence even in the case of continuous streams of cognition (*dhārāvāhika-buddhi*).
As for the claim that an axe is no longer an instrument once the wood has been cut: [this is not so].
Because there is no cutting of that [already cut], as there is no result characterized by cutting;
nor is there an absence of another cutting once it has been cut.
Furthermore, even when something is known, there is no impossibility of another cognition, such that—in this case too—there would be non-performance simply due to the absence of a result.
This is because of the arising of a continuous stream of cognitions (*dhārāvāhika-jñāna*).

Therefore, the meaning is that for one who maintains that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the apprehension of an object not previously known, it would follow as an absurd consequence (*prasajyeta*) that such successive cognitions are not valid.
He raises an objection with the words "If not," etc.:
a cognition is a valid means of knowledge (pramā) only when it produces activity (pravṛtti) and attainment (prāpti),
for it is precisely for that purpose that one pursues the means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
And likewise for the first [cognition];
therefore, that alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramā*).
Furthermore, subsequent cognitions do not serve as causes for the attainment of purposeful activity.
Therefore, these are not of the nature of valid cognition;
consequently, those which produce them are also not means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). This is precisely what is accepted—this is the meaning. He refutes [this objection] with: "No."
For consciousness does not cause one to attain an object without itself engaging [with it],
nor does it engage [with it] by force; rather,
it does so by way of having the form of the perception of the object.
And that [capacity] is common to all; this is the meaning.
This is what was stated by the words "and as an illustration.

Now, one might object: even so, since the required [result] is established from the very first [instance], what is the use of a second instance and so forth for the person? To this, he says: "The person... and so on.
It might be argued:
the author of the Vārttika has not refuted the conflicting views of other disputants,
nor has he established the principle that "the prescription of a specific rule implies the prohibition of everything else," because there is no contradiction [between his view and those others].

For it is not contradictory for that which makes known an object not yet cognized—which establishes the object through its similarity [to it] or through its capacity, and which reveals both itself and the non-self—to be the cause of apprehension (upalabdhi-hetutva). Therefore, he says: "apprehension" (upalabdhi).

Since that which is pervasive is incompatible with that which is non-pervasive, the status of being a means of valid cognition (pramāṇatva) in that form is effectively negated for that which does not make known an object not yet cognized; this is the meaning.
He refutes the [theories of] similarity (*sārūpya*) and capacity (*śakti*) with the words "hetu" (cause), etc.
For what is the meaning of the claim that the form (*ākāra*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it establishes the cognition of the object by virtue of belonging to it?
It cannot mean that [the form is the means of cognition] because it produces a determined cognition as belonging to that [object].

Because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself; nor does it cause [itself] to be known, because it does not produce another cognition with respect to the cognition that constitutes its own nature.

Nor does it ascertain [the object], because since the form and its possessor are one, and the two exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) are the domain of a single ascertainment, the rule that the ascertained and the ascertainer must be distinct is untenable;
for the ascertainment of the form is indeed "I know blue."
Nor is there any other determination of "belonging to that" [the object] besides this.

If it is argued that first there is the determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*) in the form "this is blue," and then there is the subsequent cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) which is a cognition of the object and its action in the form "I know the blue"— then, is the form determined while the cognition itself remains undetermined?
And this is not possible, because when the universal is not ascertained, the particular is not ascertained;
yet it is indeed ascertained.
If it is argued that [the cognition] does not possess that [form] as its own, then what is this so-called "belongingness" (tadīyatā) other than the form of the object itself?

If it is argued that it is "arising from that" (tadudbhavatva)—well then, the form which brings about an inference is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). If you say "yes," then alas! [this leads to our conclusion].

In that case, the perception of common folk (*pāmarapratyakṣa*) is destroyed, because [the object] is established by means of a mental aspect (*ākāra*) which, by inferring an object distinct [from the cognition], posits it as such. Moreover, it is well-established in the world that whatever action is intended to be the fruit of a particular instrument, that instrument produces that very action.

For indeed, the eyes and other such [senses], even though they do not produce the act of cutting, are not conventionally designated as "cutting instruments" merely by virtue of being determiners thereof;
rather, it is axes and the like which, even without determining [the object], are so designated precisely because they produce [the act].
Therefore, in this case as well, let that which produces valid cognition—even if it does not determine it—be conventionally designated as a "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*).
However, even the determinative aspect does not produce that [cognition];
and thus there is conformity with the world.
Otherwise, by one who composes a technical convention (paribhāṣā), the world would be disregarded.
And there is not even a scent of identity between the produced and the producer.

By this, the claim that "capacity is the means of valid cognition" is refuted, because capacity resides in that which possesses the capacity; and that which possesses the capacity is said to be the effect.
And because manifestation is its very nature, it is not an effect of that [nature].
This is what was stated: "of the relationship between cause and effect.
Now, if it is established by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),...

What is to be accomplished there by the knower and so forth? For that which is already established is not established by what is already established; nor does that which has fulfilled its purpose elsewhere possess causal efficacy elsewhere.
Now, if it is unestablished, how can it be a means of valid cognition?
For that which is unestablished cannot indeed be called a causal factor (*kāraka*).
Nor is an instrument something that lacks an agent, nor is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) something that lacks an instrument; therefore, he says: "This is the meaning.
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "of the conjunction of the axe, which has become the instrument and which constitutes the operation."

The specific transformation is the convergence of auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-samavadhāna*). Once the instrument has been employed or produced for the sake of the result, the agent’s purpose is fulfilled because there is no further action to be performed.
The meaning is that an instrument does not reach its conclusion without a result; it is not fulfilled [without one].
Now, how is it that the object of cognition (*prameya*) fulfills its purpose through the instrument of cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
For, unlike the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), the object does not produce or employ the instrument of cognition; to this he says: "But of the object...
This is the underlying intention.

For in all cases, [an object] is established as the domain (*viṣaya*) of both the action (*kriyā*)— comprising the agent (*kartṛ*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the result (*phala*) along with their respective operations (*vyāpāra*). In that regard, its status as the domain of the result is not the determinant for its being an "object" (*karman*),
because even that which is not a factor of action (*akāraka*) due to its non-existence can still be the domain of the result.
As it is said: "Only," and so forth.

However, it possesses the status of an object (*karman*) because it is the domain of the operation of the instrument (*karaṇa*); for it is not possible that something is both [an instrument and] an object.
Nor is it the object of the operation of the instrument (*karaṇa*).

Since the instrument lacks an object for its operation in that case, the operation itself would not be established; therefore, the very establishment of that [operation] constitutes the fulfillment of its purpose.
This is what was stated: "In that case as well, there is merely a connection with the sense-faculty (*indriya*)."
Furthermore, the instrument (karaṇa) does not have the agent's operation as its object, for it fulfills its purpose by that alone and possesses no further operation;
nor is the instrument the object of the object's (karman) operation;
nor is it the object of the result (phala).
Because the agent has not instigated the action for the sake of that [result],

and because the determination of the result is dependent upon the determination of that [action], by which means one could postulate that this [result] fulfills its purpose like the object (*karman*).
Therefore, even though the agent and the object have already fulfilled their purpose, the instrument has not yet fulfilled its purpose;

thus, he dispels the misconception that [the instrument] is a direct auxiliary (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*)—a misconception based on [its] being an inherent cause (*samavāyin*) or its being the object (*viṣaya*)—by means of the two applications [of the term]; this is established.

Although the object of inference and so forth is indeed not a cause for things such as the past, nevertheless, the negation of the universal necessarily implies the negation of the particular mode as well; it is by this much alone that it serves as an example.
Therefore:
That very [condition] is the cause of the fruit; "assembles" is the ellipsis to be supplied. "In some way" means:
The meaning is "without disregarding.

By this, while demonstrating that the definition of the instrument (*karaṇa*) is simply the state of being a cause for that which has not already fulfilled its purpose through another causal factor (*kāraka*), the definition of the instrument as "that which is the object of the agent's operation" is also indicated; this is exactly how the author of the *Ṭīkā* has explained it.
And this will become clear in the Vārttika beginning with "yadvān.

[The opponent objects: "It would follow that the production of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) occurs without an instrument (*akaraṇa*), because the agent (*kartṛ*) has fulfilled his purpose through the instrument; thus, what is connected with what? To this he says: "not without an instrument" (*nākaraṇa*).

This is said by one whose intention is that words denoting *kārakas* (factors of action) are based on their connection with a primary action that brings about a real entity (*vastusad-dhi-pradhāna-kriyā-sambandha-nibandhana*).

The objection beginning with "yadi" (if) and so forth, and the response intended by one who holds that words denoting grammatical factors (*kāraka*) function based on their connection with the primary action established by the intellect—this is the summary of the purport of the *Vārttika* scattered throughout the *Ṭīkā*, starting from "not like the word 'cook' (*pācaka*)" and so forth.
The term "equally" (*tulyavat*) means as if measured by a scale; that is, neither deficient nor excessive.

Lest there be the delusion that by this elaboration it has been shown that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not at all the cause of the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the object of cognition (*prameya*), he says by way of a conclusion: "That is the means of valid cognition. Even though it is a means for apprehension, the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
"Cognition" (*saṃpratyaya*) refers to an immediate and clear conviction.
The reason for this is: "because it possesses excellence" (sātiśayatvāt).

He asks regarding the meaning of "the most effective means" (*sādhakatama*): first of all, there can be no distinction between superiority and non-superiority among the various means with respect to the production of the result, because that single [result] is indistinguishable with respect to all [the means].
Nor can it be based on the production of the operation (*vyāpāra*).

The underlying intention is that since the mere possession of an operation distinct from the operations of others is common to all [causes], the conformity of the operation to its result (*phalānuguṇatva*) remains indeed undifferentiated; this is the remainder of the heart’s thought. Even though excellence (*atiśaya*) consists precisely in the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), [the result is still not differentiated].
Nevertheless, even though they are equal, it is precisely that [subject] whose excellence (*atiśaya*) and non-excellence (*anatiśaya*) are considered;

it is not intended that mere difference (*vaidharmya*) constitutes excellence. With this in mind, the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayoga-vyavaccheda*) has also been shown by means of both the exclusion of non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*) and the exclusion of connection with another.
And he will clarify this very point immediately thereafter.
Now, one might object: just as a result is not necessary even when an agent (kartṛ) and so forth exist,
so too it might sometimes not occur even when an instrument (karaṇa) exists, since there is no difference in their status as causal factors (kāraka).
And it is observed that when an axe exists, a cut does not necessarily occur; therefore, he says: "For [only] when there is the subject and the object...
By the phrase "whose function has been exhausted," he intends to convey that agency belongs to that which possesses activity.
Therefore, even an axe is an instrument only insofar as it possesses an operation;

and by such [an instrument], there is only the exclusion of non-connection with the result, but not [the exclusion of connection] by an agent or other factor, even though that too possesses an operation.

The meaning is that because the operation of the instrument is delayed by the operation of that [cognition], there is nothing further for the instrument—which possesses that operation—to accomplish. This is what was stated: "But when the operation of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) exists, [the result] indeed comes to be."
Thus, by this it is shown that the state of being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*) consists in the non-deviation from the result for one who possesses the activity.
Another interpretation is: "that which possesses [the suffix] -vat.
Regarding the phrase "by means of another's dependence" (*paratantra*), the meaning is that it is resorted to or depended upon by that which is to be operated upon by another.
He reminds us that this very point was stated previously with the words "and dependent upon the agent.
Although the definition of an instrument as "that which is set in motion by the agent" is never subject to deviation,

nevertheless, fearing that there might be an over-extension [of the term] to the object (*karman*)— which is also set in motion, albeit through a mediated succession— he has made this restriction in the present context because of the abundance of such possibilities.
He precludes the possibility that the forthcoming *vārttika* might be a different *kalpa* by stating "of this very [work].
Regarding the phrase "a different *kalpa*":
it was somehow understood as a different *kalpa* out of fear of redundancy with the exposition of the previous *kalpa*.
He provides the justification with the words "by the preceding [verse]":
independence of action is impossible;
therefore, the negation of a specific [quality] would be untenable. To this he says: "the state of being a non-agent."
Another alternative is: "like conjunction.
Here too, the definition is that the instrument is the final operation among the various causal factors (*kāraka*). Another alternative is: "by means of comprehension" (*pratipatti*).
In this case as well, the definition is that the immediate result is the instrument (*karaṇa*),
because there is no possibility of either alternative or combination— the word "ca" (and) is used here for emphasis.
In this view, the meaning is that this very excellence is [the instrument].

Regarding the other alternative—namely, that [the definition] is "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*)—since it would be useless to establish uncommonness with respect to all instruments of knowledge (*karaṇa*), he connects it to the specific instrument under discussion: "the four.
Here too, the definition is that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which designates the specific class intended for the valid cognition (*pramā*).

When the commonality and non-commonality of the causes of valid cognition (*pramā*) are being examined, one might ask: what relevance does the commonality regarding the person have? To this he says: "entirety" (*aśeṣa*). Another interpretation is: "the causes of valid cognition.
Here too—

The definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which distinguishes the non-inherent cause of a valid cognition (*pramiti*) by virtue of its utility for bringing about the specific class of valid cognitions intended to be expressed.

The definition of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is established from its own nature, from its effect, from the agent, from the prior and subsequent relation between the agent and the effect, from the arising of the valid cognition, and from the specific cause of that valid cognition.
Thus is the summary verse.

Thus, when these causes are established as the basis for the conventional usage of "instrument," if the conventional usage of [the other factors] such as "object" (karman) also occurs due to the presence of the same causes that serve as the basis for those usages, let it be so,
since that is what we intend. However,
by means of these specific causes, the conventional usage of "object" and so forth is not intended.

But that [action] does not exist at all; for in every case, the conventional usage of "object" (karman) consists in being the domain of the operation of an instrument (karaṇa), and the conventional usage of "instrument" consists in being the domain of the operation of an agent (kartṛ).
And since there is indeed a distinction between those signs (*nimitta*), there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
He explains this according to the intended meaning (*tātparya*): the sense is that [the sign] is not explicit within the sentence.
This being the case, it should be understood that even the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "that which is sought (*arthyate*) further on" is likewise directed toward the intended meaning alone.
"Why, again?"—

this is the seed of the doubt that it is not at all necessary to demonstrate the purposefulness (*arthavattva*) of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which is the object of [that] means of valid cognition.
"Another intended meaning" (*tātparyāntara*).
Since the result—the avoidance of the fallacy of partial unestablishedness (*bhāgāsiddhatā*)—is in some way one and the same, [the opponent asks]:

"In that case, is it not simply non-authoritative (*apramāṇa*) because it lacks the capacity for purposeful action (*pravṛtti-sāmarthya*)? To this he replies: "And not... [i.e., it is not non-authoritative]. [The opponent asks again]: "How then is its authority to be determined? To this he replies: "Of that too... [i.e., its authority is established].
Not every object is to be disregarded by everyone at all times and in every place, for that would entail the absurdity of making emanations (nirmāṇa) pointless.

Thus, when an object is not being disregarded, one determines the validity of the cognition of that object through its capacity for purposeful action; and having grasped that it belongs to the same class [as previously validated cognitions], one likewise ascertains the validity [of the cognition] even during a state of disregard.
It is indeed easy to grasp.

Even in cases where no direct operation has occurred, one should ascertain—whether through perception, inference, or scripture—that there is a conformity with non-contradiction and that the instance belongs to the same class; such is the literal meaning.
Since this is insufficient for dispelling doubt, he says: "This is the underlying intention."

Having grasped [the definition] as direct causality (*sākṣāj-janakatva*), one might suspect that [the cause] resides in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇatva*); therefore, this must necessarily be shown.
And that is impossible without stating that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) produces a cognition; such is the meaning.
To the question, "How is this meaning obtained from the *Vārttika*? he says: "[It is stated as] the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa*) of the means of valid cognition."

To the question, "What is meant by this much?", he says: "This is what is being said. [An objection: "But surely this is your own intention, not that of the author of the Vārttika. To this he says: "This has been stated. This is another aphorism concerning the purposeless.
For there is no relationship of "the one to be understood" and "the one who understands" between the act of practice and its capacity; therefore, he says: "This is the meaning.
One might object: "Why is it considered improper to include everything by the mention of the word *artha* (meaning) alone?"
Because such a doubt would lead to an infinite regress, he says: "a partial proponent" (*ekadeśin*). Regarding "contradiction" (*vyāghāta*):
although liberation (*apavarga*) does not possess the nature of pleasure, pain, or their causes, [the opponent's position is nonetheless contradictory].
For this very reason, because it is being sought as suchness (*tathātva*), it is impossible to encompass everything with the term "object" (*artha*);
nevertheless, since a clear contradiction would arise if that were accepted, that [contradiction] alone was stated.

And that [contradiction] occurs through the introduction of the treatise: for if liberation (*apavarga*) is accepted as something to be abandoned by virtue of being pleasure, pain, or their causes, [then the following ensues].
In that case, the treatise (*śāstra*) as well would not be worth undertaking, because its purpose is contrary [to one's welfare].
Although both the treatise and the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are generally causes of suffering,

nevertheless, since they have as their object the intended supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*), they must be accepted precisely because they overcome the state of being a cause of suffering by virtue of being the cause of that [supreme goal].
Otherwise, however, there would again be that same contradiction:
first, the other [object] is abandoned by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
but since the valid cognition itself must be abandoned by another valid cognition, this opens the door to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
And consequently, that very same individual instance of a means of valid cognition would have to be abandoned by that very same means of valid cognition;
and that is impossible.

Now, one might ask: "If it is not to be abandoned because it is impossible [to do so], how can it be accepted as something to be attained by virtue of being happiness and its cause? To this he says: "Nor [can it be abandoned] from this...

Therefore, since there is a contradiction in performing an action upon oneself in either way (as something to be abandoned or accepted), and since it is the cause of the supreme human goal, the means of knowledge cannot be abandoned. And this being so, it does not follow that it would simply cease to exist.
The meaning is that even that which is to be abandoned—which cannot be eliminated by human effort due to the force of its own cause of destruction—is nonetheless destroyed, just like pleasure.
[An objection is raised: "Because it follows from the context" is untenable, since this is the opening statement; therefore, he says: "By the efficacy of activity."

"Adhikāra" means fitness (*yogyatā*). And here, because it is the subject under discussion, it refers to the purpose for engaging [in the practice]. For in this treatise, the intended reason is the capacity to produce effective engagement.

And that [cognition] exists only as a comprehension whose object is the forms of pleasure, pain, and their causes; therefore, when the word "object" (artha) denotes the objective domain (viṣaya), it must be understood as being of precisely that nature. Thus, the meaning is that the scope [of the definition] is restricted by the specific context of the treatise.
To show the combination of this further reason with the previous reasons when criticizing the partisan view (ekadeśin), he says: "Not only... (na kevalam).
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "also because of the impossibility [of such a cognition], due to the non-establishment of the two reasons regarding consciousness.
Now, one might object: if consciousness is not being cognized, how can there be the existence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for it?
And if that [means] is absent, how can there be the conventional usage of its existence? To this, he says: "Not, first of all... and so forth.

By demonstrating the reasoning (*tarka*) characterized by the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā-prasaṅga*), mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) itself is shown to be the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding its opposite.
However, in the conventional usage of knowledge that has ceased after being unknown, recollection (*smaraṇa*) of that object at a later time is the sole cause.
And thus, in accordance with the desire to know (*jijñāsā*), there certainly exists a cognition in its general form;
for that which is unknown cannot be the object of conventional discourse regarding injunctions or prohibitions.
Consequently, the investigation proceeds by taking as its basis that which is already established in its general form.
If cognition were necessarily known as an object of cognition,
or if it were necessarily cognized, then there would be an infinite regress characterized by a succession of cognitions;
and that [regress] is sublated by non-perception— this is the meaning.
This has been stated by the words "of someone" (kasyāścit).
By saying this refers to the text of the Bhāṣya, it should be understood that he demonstrates not only a contradiction in meaning, but also a contradiction with the text itself.
Warding off the contradiction regarding the fourfold nature of both [cause and effect], he says: "by means of cause and effect.

Now, even if the word *artha* signifies "purposefulness," the contradictions and the lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vyadhikaraṇatva*) remain as they were; therefore, he says: "such as sandalwood, etc.
By stating that [the purpose] is "to be enumerated" (*parisaṃkhyātum*) and "to be regulated" (*niyantum*), he avoids the objection by not accepting the sense of "counting" (*gaṇanīya*).
Now, with what intention does the author of the Commentary introduce this which is indeed irrelevant? To this he says: "It is said as follows.
The sense is that they cannot serve as the purpose of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because a means of valid cognition has as its object an already existent thing (*bhūtārtha*).
And thus, even though the objects of the means of valid cognition and so forth are capable of being known, the treatise (*śāstra*) that expounds them is certainly not to be commenced.
The underlying intention is that [the causal relation] lacks an ultimate purpose.
In this regard, the remainder of the sentence is that the *Nirākaraṇabhāṣya* (the Refutation Commentary) applies here.

For, by demonstrating through the contrast with common [objects] such as blue that the causal relation is merely conceptual, one must necessarily accept that blue and so forth are indeed ultimately real.
If that [causal relationship] were not ultimately real, then precisely the desired [thesis] would not be established.
Furthermore, if the causal relationship were not ultimately real, it would be impossible for blue and so forth to be ultimately real,
because that would entail their being eternal.
Therefore, whoever maintains that blue and so forth are ultimately real must also maintain that the causal relationship is itself ultimately real;
yet neither of these two is [ultimately real].
And thus, this [objection] is equal even in that case.
However, this remains to be addressed: how could one [cause] produce many mutually contradictory effects?

If it is argued that it does so because that is its very nature (*tatsvabhāvatvāt*), then it would have to produce them from the very moment of its arising, since there is no difference [in its nature] at that time; to this he says: "For it will be explained... (*nivedayiṣyate hi*).
"Not by birth" means not being dependent on co-factors from the moment of birth.
Regarding "birth and place":
birth is that which determines intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
"By way of non-fixity" means by way of the variety of the arrangement of auxiliary causes (*sahakārī*).
The object of valid cognition (*pramāṇārtha*), characterized as pleasure and pain,
is "undetermined," meaning it is devoid of a fixed rule such that sandalwood produces only pleasure and a thorn produces only pain.
This is because the causes are indeterminate;
that is to say, because the auxiliary causes, such as sandalwood and so forth, are indeterminate.
The term "living being" (*prāṇabhṛt*) is used to indicate the diversity of these auxiliary causes.
For this very reason, the example is given as "at an indefinite time.
Just as "at an indefinite time" is an illustration, it should be understood that there is likewise an indefiniteness regarding place, state, and auxiliary causes.
This is what is meant:
just as clouds discharge water when certain times, places, conditions, and auxiliary factors are present, yet those very same clouds drink up water when other such factors are present.
Likewise, sandalwood and other such things produce pleasure for some people and pain for others.
A *viṣṭi* is a laborer dragged along by force.
Now, when the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) possesses an object, the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the other factors also become possessed of objects and are known as such.
This is what is intended,
but not that they are actually born;
and yet, such is not the case.

Since the non-deviation of other [means of knowledge] is determined precisely through the non-deviation of valid cognition (*pramiti*), he says: "Even though... Nor should it be argued that the Vedic comprehension is non-deviant with respect to its object because it is a comprehension born from the instruction of a trustworthy person (*āpta*); for such a doubt is indeed possible.
For it is impossible to determine this without first ascertaining that the instruction of a reliable person (āpta) produces a cognition of an object that is indeed non-erroneous.
Furthermore, it has already been stated that the very purposefulness of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) consists in nothing other than their capacity to produce non-erroneous comprehension.
If it is argued that, nevertheless, such a thing exists in the world:
Therefore, he says: "having an unseen purpose."

Although the inherence of that [action]—namely, the inherence of the valid cognition (*pramā*)—might indeed be useful for the present topic as "the state of being a knower" (*pramātṛtva*), nevertheless, the author of the *Vārttika* introduced independence (*svātantrya*) by means of both questioning and illustration. With the intention that a specific case may be understood through the general rule, he explains it accordingly: "by the mention of the *kāraka*";
that is, the inherence of that [action] consists precisely in the connection with the operation denoted by the verbal root and the suffix, primarily.
And by "predominance," what is intended is merely the state of being distinct from other causal factors (*kāraka*).
Consequently, in cases such as *pacati* ("he cooks"), agency is established for Devadatta and others alone, who possess an activity such as cooking that is distinct [from other factors].

However, in cases such as *pācayati* ("he causes to cook"), although there is a cognition of the activity of the prompted agent (*prayojya*), that activity is not distinct [from the activity of the prompter]; therefore, the one who possesses it (the prompted agent) does not have agency.
What is its name? It belongs to the instigator alone, because that person's activity is transverse [to the action].
If that is so, then:

For, according to the principle that "agency exists in every factor of action (kāraka) with respect to its own specific operation," there would follow the undesirable consequence of abolishing the conventional designations of 'instrument' (karaṇa) and so forth; therefore, he says: "by way of predominance.
The conventional designation of 'instrument' and so on does not depend on the [factor's] own operation.
However, the intention is that this is with respect to the primary action.

But one might ask: even though there is no difference in their being accomplished by a *kāraka*, why is it that the conventional designations such as "instrument" (*karaṇa*) and so forth are applied only with respect to the principal action? To this, he says: "intermediate... [repeated].
"Intermediate... [repeated].
For there is indeed a connection with intermediate operations for the factors of action (*kārakas*) who are engaged in activity directed toward some primary action;
however, the meaning is that their engagement is not for the sake of the intermediate operation alone.
Now, it may be objected that not every operation or primary action depends upon a person.
To the question, "How then does he say 'the person' (puruṣa)? he replies: "The term 'person' (puruṣa) refers back to what has been previously mentioned. This is the definition of the Grammarians;
however, that is untenable.
Because the mere employment of a word does not establish [the object],
and because a definition must be the cause of such establishment.
If it is argued that the definition is "fitness for denotation"— no.
Because that very [intention] is what is being investigated.
If it is argued that it is merely a matter of intention (*vivakṣāmātra*), we say no;
for even that is not established without a cause. Bearing this in mind, he says: "another definition."

The term "puruṣa" (the person) continues [to apply]. And thus, with the intention that there should be no suspicion regarding the analysis of the compound *tatprayoktṛtva* as *tasya prayoktā* (its agent), he says: "of that conscious one."
The meaning of the analysis is that "sa" (he) and "asau prayoktā" (that agent) form a compound, or else that the property of being an agent belongs to that conscious being.
And here, the phrase "all causes" intends to refer to many causal factors that are distinct from one another and mutually dissimilar to each other.
Therefore, even for a potter who does not preside over the unseen force (adṛṣṭa), his status as an agent remains entirely unimpaired.

Since the definition is completed by this much alone, the phrase "not being employed by another" excludes the independence of other [factors] with respect to the instigation of a conscious agent; thereby, their mutual causality is also excluded. It has been stated that even for the conscious agent, agency belongs only to one who sets those [factors] into operation.
And thus, just as an effect depends upon an agent, so too does it depend upon other causal factors; since it is pervaded by both, it has been shown that when one is absent, the other is also absent.
Therefore, the definition is not over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*).
What remains is the question of how the designation "agent" (*kartṛ*) applies to insentient things; regarding this, he says: "But of the insentient... (*acetanasya tu*).
The primary [meaning] is the essential nature (*svābhāvika*).

For one who asserts that reality (*tattva*) is the state of being pervaded by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or the state of being the object of the operation of a means of valid cognition, it is accepted that the definition of an object (*karman*) is "that which is the object of the operation of an instrument" (*karaṇa*);
in that definition, the intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) is to be understood.
And in the present context, the distinction is that the primary operation is characterized as valid cognition (*pramiti*).
By the term "fitness for application" (*viniyojyatā*),
it is shown that while the application mentioned in the *Vārttika* resides in the object, one must also understand that fitness itself resides in the object.
The meaning is that the fitness for application resides solely within the object itself;
furthermore, this refers to knowledge.
Therefore, the sense is that either the application residing in the object, or the knowledge of its fitness, constitutes the culmination of the fourfold aims of human life.
"Five" refers to form, perception, mental formations, feeling, and consciousness.
Among these, visible form, taste, odor, tangible objects, and sound constitute the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
Discriminative consciousness is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*);
the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*);
pleasure and pain are the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*).
Non-conceptual cognition is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*). "Living being" (*jīva*) means the conscious one (*cetana*).
That which is other than that is the non-living (ajīva). They are called *āsravas* because they flow (*āsravanti*); the sense-faculties (*indriya*) are the streams (*srotas*).
The meaning is that this living being (jīva) is filled by those [channels] as if by streams through merit and demerit (dharma-adharma).
Restraint (saṃvara) is the act of covering;
it is the misconception of non-difference regarding the objects of the living and the non-living (jīva-ajīva).
Enveloped by that [karma], this soul (jīva) is indeed non-omniscient. "Nirjarā" means the wearing away; "nirjara" refers to the practice of austerity (tapaścaraṇa).
The meaning is that this soul is bound and lacks independence, as if by shackles and fetters.
Liberation means the removal of all obscurations;
in every case, such a restriction lacks authoritative basis.
Now, it might be objected that non-existence does not follow from the cessation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). To this he says: "That" (*tat*).

It is indeed intended that existence and non-existence are identical insofar as they are objects of a means of valid cognition—that is, they are the objects of indistinguishable linguistic usage; therefore, the objection is baseless.
To this he says: "In respect of all causal capacity" (*sarvasāmarthya*).
For the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) is indeed the defining characteristic of existence.

If that [capacity] were present even in the non-existence (*abhāva*) favored by you, it would follow that even that [non-existence] would be an object of the conventional usage of "existent" (*sadvyavahāraviṣaya*); such is the meaning of the *Ṭīkā*.
By the words "And we do not," etc., the capacity of non-existence is accepted; however, the conventional usage of "existent" does not follow from that capacity,
because even that which has its capacity unperceived remains an object of the conventional usage of "existent."
Rather, it is by virtue of being the object of the cognition "it exists" or "it does not exist.
For it is impossible that something could be conventionally designated as "existent" while not being the object of the cognition "it exists."
The meaning of the context is that while something is conventionally designated as "non-existent," it is not the case that it is not the object of the cognition "it does not exist."
It might be argued as follows:

just as there is a distinction among objects of cognition (*prameya*), so too, by virtue of a distinction among the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), a difference in apprehension is possible—just as in the case of direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) and the like. Consequently, this apprehension that "it does not exist" must be a distinct entity [from the object itself].
Anticipating the doubt that this might sometimes be the case, he says: "In the present" (*saṃprati*).
The meaning is that when something is uncontradicted and more widely established, a disagreement regarding it does not cause any harm.
[Objection: But let a different entity (*bhāvāntara*) be negated!
Even so, what follows regarding the prescription of what has not yet come into being?

For it is not necessarily the case that when blue is negated, the prescription of yellow and so forth must follow. To this he says: "For blue and yellow... [and so on]. Now, one might object: since perception—which is capable of dispelling all doubts—is already operative, what room is there for reasoning (tarka)?
To the question, "What is the logical justification for this?", he says: "If someone...

This means that there are indeed certain disputants who, failing to see the punishment for opposing their views, deny what is established by direct perception and raise doubts; it is toward such people as the Sāṃkhyas and others that this method is directed.
This is to be explained as before;
the meaning is that it is included within the tarka (reductio ad absurdum) concerning the capacity for simultaneous perception.
[An objection is raised: "But surely there are many seeds of disagreement regarding non-existence and its perceptibility. To this, he says: "And all this... [is as stated].
Now, if these varieties of non-existence are irrelevant to the present context, then let it be said that they are not mentioned precisely because they are irrelevant.
On the other hand, if they are relevant, then they must certainly be stated.
Since they appear as dependent [on something else], what is the use of saying that they are not [independently] stated? To this he says: "The object to be negated," etc.
For those [terms] must be stated for the sake of demonstration;

however, since that [demonstration] is already accomplished by implication through the very demonstration of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and its locus (*adhikaraṇa*), what is the point of the effort to state them? This is the meaning.
This is what was meant by the statement that they are "comprehended" and thus not "stated.

Now, if it is argued that because they are established merely through the presentation of the means [of knowledge], they are not "stated," then objects of cognition (*prameya*) and so forth are also established merely through the presentation of the means of knowledge; why, then, would there be any need to state them as well?
Now, even though they are already well-known, they are presented here because they are highly esteemed for their specific utility;
and as for the various types of *han* (the act of killing), why are they not likewise employed when they are useful? To this he says: "Or rather... (*atha vā*).

[Objection: Since it was asserted that "just as the manifoldness of existence (bhāvaprapañca), the manifoldness of non-existence (abhāvaprapañca) must also be understood as having been mentioned," the reason—"because it is not included within the four aims of life (caturvarga)"—is both partially unestablished (bhāgāsiddha) and contradictory (viruddha). To this, [the author] replies: "With regard to the supreme good (niḥśreyasa).
By this, the reason—that it is not included within the four aims of life—is based on its being the locus of the manifoldness of non-existence which is unfit for the supreme good.
The probandum is that the manifoldness of existence, being of such a nature as to be the locus of that [supreme good], is not cited as the example.
However, that which is conducive to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) should be understood as what has been indicated [here], because it is included within the four aims of human life (*caturvarga*).
The meaning of the *Vārttika* is that it is like the detailed exposition of things already employed [in the sūtras]. This is the sense.

Precisely for this reason, considering that [the self] must be known as that which has been pointed out, [the author], thinking it to be sublated by non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), introduces the subsequent text with the word "Now" (*atha*).
By means of the non-perception of the cause, all varieties of non-perception are indicated.
Emancipation (*apavarga*) alone is the consecrated sovereign, preeminent like a king.
This is also an illustration: the object [of the action] includes the non-existence of an enemy's son and so forth,
and the activity includes non-violence and so forth.

It should be understood that "post-mortem existence" (*pretyabhāva*) also consists in the abandonment of a previous body and so forth, and "result" (*phala*) likewise consists in the cessation of diseases that have arisen and other such varieties of non-existence (*asat*).

Since doubt (*saṃśaya*), being of the nature of cognition, cannot possibly be of the nature of non-existence, [the author] bypasses it and extends the application [of the definition] by saying: "In the same way, purpose (*prayojana*)," and so on.
For instance, in cases such as the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyāvandana*) or expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*), the very purpose is the cessation of what is harmful.
There is also an example that consists of a non-entity (*abhāva*), such as when the state of deep sleep will be cited as an illustration for liberation (*apavarga*).
Furthermore, the established tenet (*siddhānta*) for others [the opponents] is the absence of self (*nairātmya*) and so forth.
And for us, there are such [definitions] as "light and darkness" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.2.19) and so forth.
For all [schools], liberation is the absence of suffering.
However, the categories of members of a syllogism, reasoning, determination, discussion, wrangling, and cavil are merely varieties of the existent.
Fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) are of two kinds,
such as: "Sound is impermanent because it lacks existence," or "because it is visible," and so forth.
Quibbles (*chala*) and fallacies (*jāti*) are indeed only varieties of the existent (*sat*).
Among the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), those consisting of types of misconception (*vipratipatti*) are varieties of the existent;
those consisting of types of non-comprehension (*apratipatti*) are varieties of the non-existent (*asat*).
This has been stated: "In this manner, it should be inferred in each respective case.
Now, one might object that even the mention of the distinction between the real and the unreal does not exist in the Bhāṣya; therefore, he says: "In this regard.
It is impossible for both mutually contradictory positions—that [the difference] is expressed and that it is not expressed—to be ultimately real.

To the question, "Which among these is the ultimate (pāramārthika)? he says: "But in the second alternative, [the reality] is the ultimate. The detailed purport of the Sūtra is as follows: the elaboration beginning with "by means of valid cognition" (pramāṇataḥ) and so forth;
and the purport is that this [reality], which is indeed sixteenfold in its manifestation, will be taught.
Its purport is as follows:
it refers to the introductory commentary beginning with "tāsāṃ khalvāsām," and not to the wording of the sūtra itself.
Because the intended meaning (*tātparya*) has already been made clear by the very phrase "desiring to explain the meaning of the individual members."
An Explanation of the Introduction, the Preface, and Other Sections.

The phrase "he states the nature of the *dvandva* compound" is to be understood as "in order to declare its intended meaning (*tattātparya*). The *dvigu* and *avyayībhāva* compounds are not introduced here because their usage has already been refuted.

He now refutes the *bahuvrīhi*, *karmadhāraya*, and *tatpuruṣa* compounds, which might otherwise be considered possible usages—stating "in the case of *bahuvrīhi*"—on account of impossibility, that is, the impossibility of the [required] meaning.
The phrase "a genitive compound" (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is intended as an illustration for any possible *tatpuruṣa* compound.
The word "iti" in the expression "iti hi," and so forth, has the sense of "for" (*hi*).
Therefore, having taken up the indication of the meaning, the plural number should be understood even when there is doubt.

The intended meaning here is that even in that case, doubts arising from similarity (*sādharmya*), dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), and misconception (*vipratipatti*) function as the instigators of formal reasoning (*nyāya*) only when they are mutually independent.
Furthermore, in the instance of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the dual number is used precisely at the point of defining its specific characteristics;
the purpose of that [dual number] is likewise the mutual agreement regarding the examples, which are themselves independent of one another. Thus...
Even among established doctrines (*siddhāntas*), there is likewise mutual independence regarding their own respective purposes;
and this is expressed by a term denoting number that has the same sense as the plural suffix.
However, although the members (*avayavas*) of a syllogism are mutually dependent when a single meaning of a sentence is to be established, [they differ from doctrines].
Nevertheless, the purpose of employing the plural number is precisely to indicate that those expressing a matter that is not mutually agreed upon are indeed many.

Even in the case of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), the intent of the plural number is solely to demonstrate their mutual independence in their respective functions; the same applies to quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
However, where there is no specific instruction, the analysis (vigraha) follows the literal wording regarding the definition;
the point is that the mere general form alone is what is operative.

Since the *kāraka* (participant in an action) is of the nature of an object (*artha*), it has nothing further to be expressed; therefore, he says: "The meaning of the *kāraka* is the principal action (*pradhānakriyā*).

Since the word *artha* is not seen anywhere used to denote the principal action, he says: "With reference to which [the subordinate actions occur]. Since the matter is well-established by the mere fact that there is no intention to express the *kārakas*, for what purpose is the non-intention to express the principal action stated? To this, he says: "By the mention of the *kāraka*s."

Now, one might object: "The non-intentional expression (*avivakṣā*) of the factors of action (*kāraka*) would constitute the definition of the 'remainder' (*śeṣa*) only if the status of being a *kāraka* were possible there; but that very status does not exist. To this he says: "Even though" (*yadyapi*).
