Here, an objection is raised regarding the genitive case used in the sense of the remainder (*śaiṣikī ṣaṣṭhī*).
Furthermore, the genitive case would be meaningless and purposeless;
for since there is no distinction [between the two], that [genitive] is untenable, as the relation denoted by the genitive is impossible.
Regarding the point that it is a partial position, the proponent of non-restriction [states]: "The seed..."
Since that [reality] is not independent, what connection could there be between it and the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth? To this he says: "of the entity" (*bhāvasya*).

It is not merely the means of valid cognition and so forth that is expressed by the word *tattva*, yet it is also contradictory to say that reality (*tattva*) is not something other than those; therefore, he illuminates a certain partial view with the words "even though there is non-difference.

The meaning is that the term *tattva* was employed even though its referent is not distinct, for the purpose of making it understood that the means of valid cognition and so forth are perceived in their own nature as non-superimposed forms.
Considering the example to be unestablished, he explains it with reasoning: "of duality and unity.

For one who considers the practical application (*vyavahāra*) and the ontological reality (*vastugati*) to share the same status of security and failure (*samānayogakṣema*), is simply unable to deny non-existence, since the practical application of non-existence is established for all disputants.

With the intention that the opinion of one who believes there exists a conventional usage even independent of real entities remains to be addressed, he says: "The refutation of the theory of momentary destruction" (*kṣaṇabhaṅgabhaṅga*). The words "will be explained by the author of the Vārttika" are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

With respect to the production of knowledge that accords with reality, the power characterized by its own nature (*svarūpalakṣaṇā śakti*) is precisely the state of being free from superimposition, while the sense organs and so forth—being devoid of defects characterized as adventitious conditions—are the auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).
Now, one might ask: what is the purpose of refuting the [notion of] liberation as something perceptible?

For it is not as if that [liberation] cannot be established for us. To this he says: "This is what is meant. The remainder of the sense is that the unseen (adṛṣṭa) alone is intended as liberation by virtue of being the fruit of the scripture.

Otherwise, he would not have undertaken the exposition of specific objects of knowledge such as the self (*ātman*), because the attainment of the visible supreme good (*dṛṣṭaniḥśreyasa*) can be accomplished even without the knowledge of their true nature (*tattvajñāna*); this is the underlying sense.

[Objection: How can there be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that is unestablished by authority, since it is inferred solely from its result, namely perception (*darśana*), given the absence of such perception?
The sense is that [the property] exists even in its absence.
Scripture and inference act as auxiliaries by way of establishing the subject (*pakṣa*) and so forth.
Among these, scripture serves to establish the locus (*dharmin*) characterized as the self (*ātman*).
"This Self is free from evil" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.3), "free from sin" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.2.9), "undecaying and immortal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.25).
This very [Self] is described as "not this, not this" (neti neti) and so forth [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26].
And inference arises from desire and the like [Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.10];
however, when the probans consisting of the absence of birth is established, [the conclusion follows].
The scriptural authority is such as "Indeed, being bodiless... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.1),
while the inference is the absence of purposeful activity.
Even in the absence of worldly activity,
for that person who is self-satisfied, who is contented in the Self alone,
and who finds fulfillment in the Self alone, there is no duty to be performed.
"Thus it begins, and so forth.
As for inference, however, it is the absence of defects;
even when there is an absence of defects, [the following applies].
"Even his taste for action ceases upon seeing the Supreme," as stated in Gītā 2.49, and so forth.
Inference, however, is the absence of false knowledge.
"Even here,
the knot of the heart is severed and all doubts are cut asunder," and so forth [Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8].
Inference, however, is the existence of the knowledge of reality;
even regarding the knowledge of the reality of the self, it is said:
"The self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen."
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.8] and so forth;
inference, however, refers to the excellence of the practice of means and so forth.
The mention of scripture and inference is, moreover, an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa).
Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) must also be considered;
the same should be inferred for the body and so forth.

The remainder [of the thought] is that this is intended for those who, being in disagreement, wish to establish that inference alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding this matter—even by means of the *Upaniṣads*.
On account of the authority of such passages as "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8),

and because the inference of a continuum (santāna) is taught separately from the objects of knowledge (prameya) such as the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and so forth, and because this is explained in the first sūtra, the author introduces the very beginning of his own work with the words "If, however... (yadi ca).
"Because it is enjoined by the first sūtra"— the phrase "by both scripture and meaning" is to be supplied as the remainder. Thus far [is the explanation].
To the question, "What has been accomplished by the author of the Vārttika through this treatise?", he says: "By this, therefore..."

He first explains the Bhāṣya which forms the subject matter of the *Uttara-vārttika*, beginning with the words "Now, what [is the purpose]? (atha kim iti). An objection is raised: "But surely the meaning of the second sūtra has not been stated here; so how can it be restated there? To this he replies: "Regarding the supreme good" (*niḥśreyasa*).

And in this regard, it should not be suspected that there is no *Tātparya-ṭīkā* commentary on the restatement of the reasons (*hetu*) and so forth, because the author of the *Ṭīkā* has raised [the discussion] as if [the text] were already established;
furthermore, the absence of [certain parts] in some manuscripts can be accounted for by the error of the scribe.
Otherwise, [the commentary] would merely be a restatement of the intended meaning of the Bhāṣya.

As for what was explained by the word "he explains" (*vyācaṣṭe*), that was done with a specific intention; therefore, even if there is no further explanation immediately after that restatement—since that very point is restated by the subsequent sūtra—there is no fault.

The meaning is that this point has not been explained here because it was already explained previously by the passage beginning with "And thus the meaning [is established] in the second sūtra," and so forth.

Now, one might ask: "Is aversion (dveṣa) indeed to be abandoned, or is it not the cause of worldly activity? To this he says: "It is an indicator" (upalakṣaṇam). Furthermore, one might ask: "Since the word 'abandonment' (hāna) occurs in close conjunction with the word 'final state' (ātyantikapada), it refers to liberation (apavarga);
so how can it be said that [the means] is the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna)? To this he says: "For [by it] is abandoned" (hīyate hi).
Relying on the instrumental derivation (*karaṇavyutpatti*), what is intended by this [term] is the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
However, by relying on the abstract derivation (*bhāvavyutpatti*), because of its co-occurrence with the term "final state" (*atyantikapada*), the meaning is liberation (*apavarga*).
Dispelling any doubt regarding the derivation of the term "knowledge of reality," he says: "of that means of valid cognition" (*tasya pramāṇasya*).
By this, the contradiction with the opening statement is resolved.
Regarding what was said—that the word *artha* in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) will have a different meaning—he says: "The stations of the goals of human life" (*puruṣārthasthānāni*).
This means the intended purport (*tātparya*).
The word "of the Vārttika" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

Although it is indeed intended that "prasthāna" means "mode," "manner," or "suchness"—as in the phrase "because the Ānvīkṣikī is thus"—nevertheless, such a manner might be [conceived] without rational justification; therefore, he says: "prasthāna" means "activity.
By this, the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*) for the word "prasthāna" occurring in the Bhāṣya has been stated.
However, the commentator himself has shown that the meaning of the suffix (pratyaya) is established separately from the word-meanings such as doubt and so forth.
This is what is meant:
this science of Ānvīkṣikī is distinguished from other sciences by its possessing the function of investigating the principles of reasoning (nyāya).
And that [science] is indeed elucidated by the very elucidation of its primary and secondary members, beginning with doubt (*saṃśaya*).
Therefore, for this [science], doubt and the others also become its objects; for without them, it would lack an object and thus would not even be a science.
Or else, by virtue of having different objects, it would simply be a different science altogether.
Right here, he raises an objection: "Nor should it be said...

He refutes this with the thought that other branches of knowledge, even while establishing their own respective objects, are not capable of removing the stain of doubt—such as "How can this be?"—without this science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī); thus he replies: "Of this very [science] alone..."

He shows that the Bhāṣya—"And that [object] is perceived," etc.—has as its subject matter another Vārttika. [The objection that] "it illuminates a baseless local [usage]" refers to knowledge (*jñāna*).

Furthermore, the contradiction between being "perceived" and being "not determined" is entirely untenable, because it was just demonstrated that "perception" (*upalabdhi*) is a synonym for "ascertainment" (*nirṇaya*).

Nor is it the case that what is apprehended as an object of the operation of a means of valid cognition must necessarily be determined; therefore, he shows another intention of the objector by saying "possessing five forms.
Just as perception or scripture applies even to what is unknown, so too do they apply to what is beyond doubt.
The meaning is that inference, just as it does not operate when [the object] is unknown, likewise does not operate when it is beyond doubt; therefore, its method is entirely different.
"Having the same object" means having one and the same object.
You do not establish co-referentiality.
The meaning is that there is no identity (*tādātmya*).

Intending to explain the resolution by considering that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is merely a relationship with a common substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) shared by both [terms], and not identity, he clarifies the response: "of the universal and the particular."
He shows that the phrase "one should act toward what is doubtful" has the sense of being fit [for inquiry], by stating "not doubtful.
And there are two ways in which something is unfit for doubt:
either because it is entirely unknown, or because it is specifically determined.
But that which is the opposite of this is "doubtful" (saṃdigdha), meaning it is fit for doubt;
the intended meaning is that in such a case, the *nyāya* (logical method) proceeds.
For this very reason, he cites one type [of example] as an illustration, primarily characterized by negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), saying: "For not... [etc.].

To the question, "What, then, is the purpose? the answer given—"that by which one is impelled to act"—is due to audacity; therefore, he says, "This is indeed even more evident. The phrase "Now, we [say]" is intended to demonstrate his own preferred view, while indicating dissatisfaction with the position of the partial school (ekadeśimatam).

And since we do not perceive any seed of dissatisfaction [with this view], he first demonstrates that very seed by means of a question, beginning with the word "tatra" (therein). [The phrase] "because all [objects], such as dharma and the rest, are desirable" means that desire—
whether directed toward objects like dharma or toward the means for attaining them— is the motivator even in that case.
Nor is it the case that dharma and the rest are apprehended as having that [pleasure] as their object,
for if that were so, it would follow that garlands, sandalwood, and the like would also be apprehended as such;
"saraka" refers to a drink.
[Objection: Even so, does this not undermine their status as purposes? To this he says: "Of dharma and mokṣa.
This is also an elliptical indication;
it should be understood that for those who are dispassionate, even the objects of the senses (kāma) and wealth (artha) do not function as purposes.
Therefore, this is what is meant:
it is not the very quality of being a dharma (dharmaness) and so forth that is the motivator for engagement with respect to dharmas and the like;
what then? It is the state of being desired.
"Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that everything would arise everywhere without distinction.

Now, one might ask: "What fault is there in the literal reading [of the sūtra], such that it must be explained as 'that by which the object characterizes the subjective cognition'? To this he replies: "Asatyoḥ" (when they are non-existent), and "satyor vā" (or when they are existent)—this is a locative case.
This is for the purpose of taking up the *Uttaravārttika*.
He refutes [the opponent's] position as it was stated: "Even so" (*tathāpi*).

Although it would be appropriate to raise the following objection here—"In this case, the cognition of the result causes one to engage with that which accomplishes it elsewhere; therefore, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)"—nevertheless...
Since there can be no activity at all if its status as a means [to a desired end] is unknown, he raises an objection by including that knowledge— namely, "from the knowledge of its being a means.

The meaning is that the causal relationship is established through co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), that is, by having a single object, because there is no contradiction due to their mutual agreement.

If that is so, why is the *Vārttika* statement "by the attainment and loss of pleasure and pain" irrelevant? To this he says: "The following is what is meant. He sets aside the intended [objection] by means of that [explanation].
Desirability (*upādeyatā*) consists in being desired as an object of activity; desirability as an end-in-itself (*uddeśyatā*) consists in being desired in its own nature.
Since the knowledge of both induces action, both are indeed purposes (*prayojana*).

However, this is the distinction: the cognition of what is to be acquired (upādeya) directly impels one to action. And its very nature as a direct impeller consists in its producing a desire capable of generating immediate effort;
that [desire] is called the primary impulse (pravṛtti).

The meaning is that the cognition of the object to be enjoined (uddeśyajñāna), by generating a desire for that object as its content, does so through the mediation of generating a cognition of the means for achieving it in such a manner.
He states "nyāya" [etc. to address the objection of one who does not perceive that the words *nyāya* and *parīkṣā* have the same meaning:
"But surely, if the word *parīkṣā* means 'investigation' (*vicāraṇā*), its dependence on a purpose might sometimes be appropriate;
however, if it means *nyāya*, then by the force of its etymology, its meaning is merely 'means of valid cognition' (*pramāṇa*)."
And since there is no purpose for that [Nyāya], everything becomes confused; such is the meaning of the commentary on the introduction of the objection.

Now, one might object: "Even by this much, the challenge remains exactly as it was. To this, he provides the resolution by analyzing [the term] with the words "perception and so forth" (*pratyakṣādīti*).
But surely, if Nyāya is the investigation and comprehension of an object through its constituent parts (*avayava*), [then...]
Then, what is its fruit? To this he says: "of the object, which is the mark" (*liṅga*).
Now, if reasoning—whose other name is "examination"—does not have the inferable object as its domain, [then...]
To the question, "From where will the comprehension of that [object] arise?", he says: "But it has been examined. Now, one might ask:

why is it not the case that the inferable object itself is established in the same way as the mark (liṅga) is established by means of the members of the syllogism rooted in the instruments of valid cognition (pramāṇa)? To this he says: "But not... [the object]. One might further ask: even though there is no difference in their being equally doubtful, from what does this distinction arise? To this he says: "Of that... [the mark].

The meaning is that, because it cannot be the object of examination (*parīkṣā*), it is impossible to establish [the object] by setting aside those who depend upon it without first presenting the logical mark (*liṅga*).
[Objection: "In that case, [the result of the means of knowledge] would not be by means of the *pramāṇas*.
[Response: And thus, the comprehension of the object—the logical mark—through examination would not be the fruit of the *pramāṇas*.

Now, if [it is argued that] the members [of the syllogism] are indeed [redundant] because they are accomplished by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) alone, then the intention [of the opponent] is that the members are fruitless.

By the passage beginning with "not directly," the author, while refuting the independence of the members in the apprehension of the logical mark (*liṅga*), has also rejected the notion that the apprehension is not the fruit of a means of valid cognition.
By demonstrating that the members [of the syllogism] possess intermediate functions (*avāntaravyāpāra*), the charge of their pointlessness (*ānarthakya*) has been refuted.

Furthermore, since the opponent will ask for the reason why—despite there being no difference in their status as means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—only this [inference] brings about understanding in a person who is in disagreement and not any other, he says "the whole" (*samasta*) for that very reason. Thus, this is the meaning of the *Vārttika*: because this [inference], which consists of all such auxiliary instruments of valid cognition, brings about understanding in a person who is in disagreement, it is therefore "supreme" (*parama*).
The meaning is that it is so designated in common usage.
Now, one might object: "Being non-contradictory is not the same as being dependent, because that which is dependent may be non-contradictory, yet even that which is contradictory can be dependent;
for this very reason, there is no necessary concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between these two."
How then can he say that "being dependent" is not contradictory? Nor is that the subject under discussion; therefore, he says: "in the five-membered [syllogism].
In reality, there is a single objective domain for both the Nyāya system and its fruit.
And that [explanation] succeeds only when there is no contradiction, and not otherwise;
thus, what was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya in terms of its meaning has been elucidated word-for-word by the author of the Vārttika—this is the sense.
Although the word *agni* denotes a specific kind of fire, since the conventional usage of "fire" is not observed in the case of sunlight and the like, [it is nevertheless applied].
Nevertheless, since the term *tejas* (fire) is sometimes employed even for that which possesses only [the quality of] heat,
he says— "fire is a composite whole"— with the intention that, by this [specification], there should be no "partial unestablishedness" (*bhāgāsiddhatā*) on account of atoms.

[Objection: Is it not the case that contradiction of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇavirodha*) consists precisely in the determination of contradictory objects, and since that is quite evident here through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), for what purpose is the question "What, moreover..."? To this he says: "This [is] here.
Precisely because of that, namely, because of the non-attainment of the three forms [of the syllogism].
The remainder [of the sentence] is that such an inference must be designated as a fallacy;
for it does not possess all three characteristics [of a valid reason],
otherwise it would follow that the probandum is already established.
Here an objection is raised with "Now" (atha):

"But if the presence of the three-fold form alone constitutes inseparable connection (avinābhāva), then how can it coexist with sublation (bādhā)? For they cannot coexist in this very same case. To this he replies: "In the case of sublation" (bādhāyām).
Having accepted the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), the demonstration of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) follows;
therefore, the objection beginning with "and not [present] in the similar instance" (*sapakṣa*) does not lack scope.

The "universal inclusion" (*sarvopasaṃhāra*) consists in the cognition of the similarity of the subject—which possesses the probans—with the form: "wherever this [probans] is, there this [probandum] is."

And this [reason] is invalidated merely by the fact that even where this probandum (*sādhya*) does not exist, this probans (*sādhana*) is nonetheless accepted as being present. The meaning is that this mode of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) cannot be prevented even in the case of the subject (*pakṣa*).

Sublation (*bādha*) does not constitute a flaw independently, because it is absent in cases where there is deviation and the reason lacks the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
And where sublation is possible, since those two [reasons] themselves exist elsewhere with their independence already established, the inference has become fallacious;
however, contradiction (virodha) fulfills its purpose by giving rise to [other defects] such as deviation (vyabhicāra).
This is the meaning of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa).

Regarding the statement "the application [of a reason] is in a domain other than that of inference," if taken according to the literal reading of the *Vārttika*, it clearly implies the opponent's objection that [the reason] lacks the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*apakṣadharmatva*), because that which is not a subject (*apakṣa*) is precisely what is not within the scope of inference.
Therefore, wishing to explain it otherwise, he prepares the ground, saying: "For it will be stated.
The construction is: "For it will be stated in the section on inference that [this definition] leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), i.e., an over-pervasion (*ativyāpti*)."
To the question, "What follows if this is so?", he says: "And that [fire]," etc.
Moist fuel is a single limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) because it is invariably concomitant with only one [of the two]; study is a double limiting adjunct because it is invariably concomitant with both.
By the passage beginning with "so 'yam" and ending with "nāsti," the form of perception is shown;
by "yadi bhaviṣyat," that of reasoning (tarka);
and by "nāstyeva," that of the resulting certainty (niścaya).

Now, one might object: "In the case of produced fire, because of its reversal [in the counter-example], a universal generalization—that whatever is produced is entirely non-hot—is simply not possible; and when that [fire] does not manifest [as non-hot], it is even less so. For that which does not manifest within a certain domain cannot be an object of that [cognition]. To this, he says: "In a general sense, whatever is produced... [and so on].

In this manner, that [fire] indeed revolves within the intellect (*buddhi*), but it has not entered the domain of the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) in its specific form; therefore, he says: "But not having distinguished [it], i.e., not having known it specifically, the relation was determined only with respect to the composite substance of fire (*tejo-'vayavin*).

Now, why should space be granted even to the composite substance of fire in its general form, when the pervasion could be determined with respect to earth and the other elements alone? To this, he says: "For not... [and so on].

For when pervasion is apprehended by way of a general form (*sāmānyākāra*), there is no justification whatsoever for abandoning the composite whole of light (*tejo 'vayavin*) prior to the sublation by perception,
since it is not observed elsewhere.
And thus, not only is that [composite] itself not seen, [but its parts are also not seen].
Even some things such as the earth and so forth are simply not seen; therefore, they too would have to be excluded.

And if pervasion (*vyāpti*) were to be grasped by repeatedly taking up [only those cases] in this manner, then—whether one accepts that there might be a suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding unobserved cases or whether one does not—the result in either case is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the total abolition of all inference. This is the meaning.
With the intention that the opponent himself might take up the opposing position, he states the matter in a gentle manner: "Not, first of all," and so forth.
The underlying thought is that as long as there is no sublation of the pervasion (vyāpti), there is simply no room for deviation (vyabhicāra).
Then, anticipating the objection that the reason (hetu) might indeed be inconclusive (anaikāntika) only when that pervasion is sublated, he raises the following doubt: "By perception," and so forth.
In this context, does the sublation of pervasion occur without disregarding the status of being a subject (*pakṣatā*), or by disregarding it?
First, he refutes the former alternative with the word "no."
If there is no obstruction to the inference that has proceeded, how can there be a refutation of the pervasion (*vyāpti*)?
The intention is: if contrary perception does not effect its obstruction, who else will?

Now, one might object: "If deviation (*vyabhicāra*) can occur even within the subject (*pakṣa*), why should it not be pointed out? Who is being punished by this [restriction]? To this he says: "Otherwise" (*anyathā*).
It is not the case that deviation can be apprehended through perception without disregarding the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).

For it is impossible that a property whose probandum is doubtful could be ascertained in its absence; thus, the meaning is that this is a counter-argument directed against one who is empty-hearted [in their reasoning].

He raises the objection that there might be a deviation (vyabhicāra) because the presence of the reason in the subject (pakṣadharmatā) is overridden by perception—this being expressed by "by perception. He refutes this with "then... (tahi).

For just as the occurrence of that which is contrary to the probandum (sādhya) is itself the cessation of the probandum, so too the occurrence of a contrary means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is itself the cessation of the proof (sādhana).
Otherwise, if the proof were not to cease even when a contrary pramāṇa occurs, then the probandum dependent upon it would likewise not cease.

The meaning is that, since that [qualification] is not excluded, there is no impairment of the status of being the subject (*pakṣatva*), and thus there is no opportunity for a deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
He presents the established point in the Vārttika, saying: "This has been stated.

Now, one might object: even if it is true that before the cessation of inference it is impossible to demonstrate the absence of the reason from the subject (*apakṣadharmatva*) or its deviation (*vyabhicāra*), nevertheless, those two can certainly be demonstrated after that time; therefore, let those two alone suffice.
It has already been refuted by the fact that its object has been removed; therefore, he says: "And thus.
For as long as an inference is not undermined by contradiction with perception, there is simply no room for fallacies such as deviation (vyabhicāra).
Therefore, these two [scriptures],
having scope for other interpretations, rely upon direct perception;
if the inference has already been refuted by that [perception], what is the use of these two?
For even one who is dead is not killed; such is the summary of the established doctrine.
Now, one who says "sound is inaudible"— how could he intend to express the non-existence of sound,
when he might just as well intend that it is perceivable by another sense organ? Or is there a contradiction in that case?
In that case, does it not exist when its own nature is denied?

Therefore, since the intention of the opponent cannot be restrained, he says: "For not..."—for, on the position that it is determined to be ungraspable by that [sense] due to the deviation in the operation of other senses, the denial of its very nature is precisely what is intended.
The meaning is that this is the illustrative example for that very point.

He prepares the foundation to establish the *vārttika*—which is firmly fixed because it crushes the previously stated prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)—with the words "for when there is a qualified [subject]" (*saviśeṣaṇe hi*).

The phrase "even in the case of a qualified injunction" (*viśiṣṭavidhāne 'pi*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); one should understand that the same applies to a qualified prohibition (*viśiṣṭaniṣedha*) as well.
Non-attainment means not being obtained through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
A turban qualified by redness is what is enjoined.
What is prohibited is clothing distinguished by being worn-out and soiled; the Vedic revelation (Śruti) does not enjoin the mere hearing of the words "even" and "dyed saffron.
A sentence is a collection of words arranged in the relationship of qualifier and qualified.
This is due to the force of those two [words].
What is meant is this:
in a compound, the purpose is not for the negation of the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*).
Its capacity, that is, its denotative power, resides in that very [word] alone;
for even in the case of non-compound construction, between two co-referential qualifiers and the qualified, it is connected with the qualifier alone,
since its capacity— that is, its fitness for syntactic connection— resides in that very [qualifier].
Therefore, in this case, whether by the power of convention or by the power of suitability for positive concomitance, there is no connection for us with the word "term."
It might be argued: "Let the connection of that which is being heard be with the word 'inaudible' itself; however, the negation of sound follows by implication. To this, he says: "Nor even... (nāpi).

For when a stated meaning cannot be established without something else, that [latter] thing, being implied by the former, is said to be "attained through implication" (arthāpatti). Furthermore, that which establishes [the meaning] is not called a "contradiction";
for its nature is precisely that of a non-contradictory establisher. This is the meaning.
He highlights the very contradiction [in the opponent's position] with the words "śrāvaṇatva" (the state of being audible) and so forth.
Now, one might object: even by means of a conceptual locus (*kalpitam adhikaraṇam*), the determination of a negation is possible, because that [locus] is insubstantial (*tucchatvāt*).
And thus, since there is no contradiction between non-existence and being the locus [of a property], he says: "Nor...
Having established this, he illuminates the meaning of the Vārttika: "Nor is audibility..."
The connection between sound and the auditory organ is the means for the apprehension of sound.
Now, if there is a connection [between the Veda and human authorship], how is it that the author of the Vārttika says "the Vṛtti"? To this he replies: "The Vṛtti.
But surely, human heads are not explicitly mentioned in the Veda.
The impurity of carrying a skull is heard in scripture; on the contrary, it is said:
"Rudra indeed performed the Great Vow."

"The very same [Manu] held together the human head"—this scriptural statement is indeed contradictory. To the question, "How then can there be no conflict with the scriptures? he says: "By Manu and others.
Although in this matter the direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*) is not explicitly perceived, [it is nonetheless supported by tradition].
Nevertheless, the Smṛti itself, being rooted in that [Veda], is the clearer authority.
As for passages such as "Rudra is the oblation," these are merely explanatory statements (arthavāda) intended to establish the excellence of human sacrifice and the like;
they do not serve as an authority for its purity—this is the meaning.
Now, one might ask: even having seen the scripture that has been presented, why does he ask? To this he replies: "Not for us.
The meaning here is that regarding this matter, which falls within the scope of means of knowledge other than verbal testimony (śabda), other scriptures lack authority.
Furthermore, as to why this pitiless man has the conceit of purifying a skull, he says: "For [the practice] is uncontradicted," and so forth.
For the determination of dharma and so forth does not arise from scripture alone, but rather also from uncontradicted worldly convention (*vyavahāra*);
and such convention exists for us as well. Nor should it be said that universal convention is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Just as there is a custom among matrons during the rite of a maiden's marriage, this [custom] might be suspected of being merely local; therefore, the example was given—"as among the Southerners."
He states the seed for the ridicule: "Śruti-smṛti...

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: the rites such as the *aiṇeya* sacrifice are rooted in the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*), because they are practiced by those who perform the uncontradicted meaning of the Vedas, just like the *agnihotra* and other such rites.
Now, why is it not concluded that this [practice] is itself a cause of the highest good (*śreyaḥ*)? To this he says: "Certainly not... and so forth.
Although this may indeed be possible at first glance,
nevertheless, because it is tainted by the suspicion of being rootless, it would not reach the stage of actual practice.
Therefore, the meaning is that inference of a source (mūla) alone is more appropriate.
The meaning is that inference does not have the Veda as its basis (*mūla*), because there is no inferential mark (*liṅga*).
What is being said? Avoiding the charge of tautology with the word "pure" (*śuci*), he says: "Moreover" (*api ca*).
Then [he says]: "due to hatred for the Triple Veda" (*trayīvidveṣāt*).
Nor should it be argued that "the subject (pakṣa) is only that extent of an object over which there is dispute;
since the purity of cow-dung and the like is established for both disputants, only that much shall be used as the example."
He raises an objection, stating "Now" (*atha*), that its purity cannot be accepted without accepting the authority of the Āgamas.
The meaning is that this is a question from one whose underlying intention (*abhisandhi*) has been set aside.
He states that intention: "Indeed not," and so forth.

[Objection: Surely, the coexistence of two inferences in a single instance is indeed a contradiction; so how can it be said that [the former] is due to non-existence? To this, he says: "This is the underlying intention.
For it is not the case that whatever was previously engaged is necessarily sublated by the latter, as that would lead to the undesirable consequence of total lack of restriction.
Therefore it is said: "dependent on that" (*tad-avalambī*).
The meaning is that it depends on that for its own establishment, for the establishment of its own substratum, and for the establishment of its own pervader.
He provides an example of what is sublated by the prover of its own pervader, beginning with "in this way."

This should also be understood as being refuted by one's own [logical] means: just as cognitions falling within a single continuum are capable of forming a synthesis even in the absence of a single perceiver, because they stand in a relationship of cause and effect.
For here, the relationship of cause and effect is not established in the absence of a single cognizer.
Where, then, is there non-coexistence, with reference to which it was said—"due to the absence of coexistence"? To this he says: "Therefore.
Capacity is the occurrence of all [necessary] forms.
In the case of co-inherence (*samāveśa*), there must necessarily be, at the very least, the loss of one of the two of its respective forms;
otherwise, that single entity would have to be both dual-natured or neither-natured. Therefore...
In reality, there is no coexistence of two contradictory things of equal strength;
and when they do coexist, their equality of strength is not real—this is the meaning.
Therefore, does this mean that *satpratipakṣatā* (the state of having a counter-balanced reason) does not exist at all? To this he says: "Not indeed.
Thus, while in reality *satpratipakṣatā* does not exist at all, nevertheless, in a state where no distinction is perceived, there is a failure to produce valid cognition due to mutual exclusion.
Therefore, the meaning is that the Sage has formulated that very [fallacy] as a defect.
He demonstrates this very point by means of the Vārttika, beginning with "But why?

Since one observes the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of two inferences—even those possessing the stated forms and endowed with positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—the Vārttika as it stands would appear inconsistent; therefore, he says "here" (*iha*).
There would also be no coexistence of perception and the other means of knowledge with that which has an uncontradicted object;
consequently, no distinction of inference from them would have been stated.
Therefore, it is characterized by the exclusion of that nature.

Now, just as two inferences may stand in a state of counter-thesis (*satpratipakṣatva*) when their specific differences are not apprehended, let it be the same for perception and inference; in that case, where would the relationship of the sublated and the sublator (*bādhya-bādhaka-bhāva*) exist?
Or, if it is maintained that perception is the sublater of inference once its specific [object] is apprehended, then let inference likewise be maintained [as the sublater of perception].

And thus, with the intention that there might also be a relationship of sublation and sublated between two inferences that are mutually independent, he states the purport of the objection: "Even perception...
He states the purport of the rebuttal: "...for they are of equal strength.
For perception does not wait for the inference's being established otherwise or not being established otherwise.

However, that which is itself independently established (ananyathāsiddha) indeed subverts the inference; just as the inference of non-heat is subverted by the independently established perception grasping heat, even though the inference was itself independently established prior to the subverting cognition due to its lack of adventitious conditions (anaupādhikatva).
This, then, is the superior force of these two [perception and inference].
Inference, however, even though it is itself not otherwise established, awaits the "otherwise-establishment" of the counter-inference (satpratipakṣa).
For that which is not otherwise established cannot be sublated in its true nature, as there would be no distinction [between them]. Thus, these two possess equal strength.

Nor is it logical to claim that what is established otherwise (anyathāsiddha) should be sublated by what is not established otherwise (ananyathāsiddha), because the latter is already refuted by its very status as being established otherwise.
Furthermore, it is not the case that wherever perception is established otherwise, there inference must necessarily also be established otherwise.
If neither [of the two] is established as non-different from the other, the entity would encounter an insurmountable predicament;
therefore, that [entity] too is sublated by that very [predicament].
It should be asked: what is the point of sublation by perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*) in that case? The distinction is that such sublation arises because [the inference] is established otherwise.
Therefore, as long as the non-otherwise-establishment (*ananyathāsiddhatva*) of the perception has not been determined, [the inference remains unestablished].
The non-arising of a definitive conclusion at that very time represents the nature of the "counter-balanced" (satpratipakṣa) state;
however, the meaning is that after that time, what is the poor thing— namely, inference?
This is what was stated: "perception is established as non-otherwise-proven" (*ananyathāsiddha*).
The meaning is that it cannot be established by any means other than the manner already demonstrated.
Furthermore, an establishment by another means—even if it involves a mere partial restriction of the object—is not [conclusively] subverting, except in the case of error.
For if that were so, it would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
Now, with the words "athopamānena" and so forth, he anticipates the following objection: [the word] "gosadṛśaḥ" (resembling a cow).

One might argue that there is no contradiction with the means of knowledge known as comparison (*upamāna*), because a misconception is itself accepted as a correct cognition according to the tradition of cultured people (*nāgarika*). To this he says: "it does not exist"—this is to be supplied.
The remainder is: "that which is found in the *Yogavārttika*."

If analogy, which is produced by perception and scripture that are otherwise established, were sublated or countered by inference, then those very perceptions and scriptures would likewise be either unsublated or countered.
And this being the case, everything would fall into total confusion.

Therefore, the meaning of the Vārttika as augmented by the Ṭīkā is that just as inference is refuted by those two [perception and verbal testimony], so too is it refuted by analogy (*upamāna*), which has its fruit and body produced from them.

The result of the commentary (*vivaraṇa*) is that it refutes the misconception of one who thinks [the *prayojana*] is the very nature of the purpose; thus, it is an auxiliary member (*aṅga*) for the explanation of the *prayojana*.

Although the *prayojana* is heard as an auxiliary member in the *Bhāṣya* passage beginning with "Debate (*vāda*) and sophistry (*jalpa*) have a purpose," nevertheless, it must be understood as the primary member (*aṅgin*).
Therefore, this is the meaning of the *Bhāṣya*:

The purpose [of this discussion] is as follows: it is intended to determine whether the *prayojana* (purpose) pervades both *vāda* (formal debate) and *jalpa* (wrangling), or whether it pervades *vitaṇḍā* (cavil) as well.
Now, one might object: "Surely, the consideration of the *prayojana* of *vitaṇḍā* should only be undertaken once the fact that *vāda* and *jalpa* possess a *prayojana* has been established."
To the question, "By which statement in the Bhāṣya is it established that these two alone possess purposefulness? he says: "In that regard, the meaning of the word [is as follows].
For he will state later: "That which is taught separately is for the sake of indication;
by means of what is thus indicated, worldly transaction (vyavahāra) will take place for the sake of the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna)."

And that conventional practice, characterized by the discrimination of valid reasons from fallacious reasons, is intended here by the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) through the word "therein" (*tatra*) as the specific intermediate purpose due to its unique nature; therefore, it is precisely this that has been explained by the author of the Vārttika—this is the meaning.
[Objection: Even so, it would be more appropriate to say, "therein, in the *Nyāya* [system], they are to be discriminated."
For it is not the case that a mere semblance of reasoning alone is primary in discernment; therefore, he says: "But [the term] 'semblance of reasoning' [is used] because of proximity."

Thus, by this, the object of investigation has been distinguished and shown. To demonstrate doubt, which is the precursor to critical examination (*parīkṣā*), he states the disagreement among commentators (*vyākhyātṛ-vipratipatti*) as its cause, beginning with the words "pratipakṣa" (opposing views).
He states the purpose of the investigation: "In that regard, if...
This is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*): "In that regard, some...
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "By means of the proof of the opponent's position..."

Although the *vitaṇḍā* (destructive criticism) is established as having a purpose even by the purpose of refuting the opponent's position— according to the statement: "That object with reference to which one proceeds is its purpose"— [nevertheless...]
Furthermore, if one were not even to engage in the refutation of the opponent's position, then one would not be a *vaitaṇḍika* (a caviller) at all.

Nevertheless, since this very [refutation] would be impossible for one who does not personally accept anything whatsoever, the intention is that activity is only appropriate for one who, by the method of exhaustion (*pāriśeṣya*), intends to establish their own position.
There is simply no such disputant who would not accept anything at all.
For in the end, one necessarily accepts the very thing that is not desired; however, if one did not accept that, one would not even say, "I do not accept anything at all."
Therefore, one might ask: "What is the point of this pointing out of what is non-existent? To this he says: "For the nihilist," and so forth. A "nihilist" (nāstika) refers to a Mādhyamika and others.
The meaning is that by this [method], the opponent's position is not accepted, nor is the refutation of the opponent's position accepted.
Thus it has been said: "It proceeds as being employed solely for the purpose of refuting the opponent's position.
For instance: "This world does not exist, because it is subject to sublation."
Nor is it non-existent, because it is being perceived;
nor is it of the nature of both existent and non-existent, because of contradiction; nor is it of the nature of neither.
"Because of contradiction and because it is not even perceived. [Objection:
But surely one does not accept that which one perceives.

If that were the case, then if the meaning of the opponent's statement is understood, it would be accepted, resulting in the defeat-ground (*nigrahasthāna*) of "conceding the point" (*matānujñā*); if it is not understood, it results in the defeat-ground of "ignorance" (*ajñāna*). Therefore, he says: "Acceptance is comprehension.
The remainder [of the definition] is: "as intended here."

Nevertheless, since it is precisely the object of acceptance (*abhyupagama*), it is not the *pakṣa* (the thesis), because that [acceptance] is what is to be made known; thus he says, "even though" (*yadyapi*).
"Because it is inseparable from that" (*tannāntarīyakatvāt*) means because it is inseparable from the act of acceptance.
The meaning is that by the word *pakṣa*, what is intended here is the established tenet (*siddhānta*), which is the state of being what is to be made known.
The deficiency, such as being unestablished (asiddha) or contradictory (viruddha), pertains to the proof (sādhana) stated by the proponent; this is the remainder [of the sentence].
There is over-extension (ativyāpti) because even that which lacks an example, such as a probans deficient in its properties, is an object of perception.
There is under-extension (avyāpti) because even that which is the object of scripture and the like, being within the scope of grasping pervasion, serves as an example.
To the objection that "even so, there is still over-extension," he says: "And here... [etc.].
He clarifies the ambiguous statement—"that which [is perceived] in those various [cases]"—by asking:
why then does this not result in a contradiction with the definition-sūtra, given that even that [definition] is common to both the perceptible and the imperceptible? To this, he replies:
He says: "But not as an illustration.
The meaning is that what is common can also be explained as having a specific scope.
Now, one might ask: "Is the Bhāṣya then entirely disconnected [from reason]? To this he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

But surely, what other logic (*nyāya*) is there besides inference (*anumāna*), such that the author of the Bhāṣya, having already stated that [the example] is based on inference, should separately state that it is based on logic?
The author of the Vārttika likewise approves of this very point. Therefore—

He says: "Of the syllogism consisting of five members. Even so, the status of being a substratum for the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) through either conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*) is not tenable, because the sentence has space (*ākāśa*) as its substratum; therefore, it is said: "the root" (*mūla*).

Nevertheless, it is inconsistent for the example to be the basis of inference, because the logical mark (liṅga) resides in the subject (pakṣa), and the cognition thereof does not reside in the example. Therefore, it was said: "Inference states its status as the instrumental cause."
Since the phrase "previously seen through direct perception" causes great confusion when taken literally as it was heard, he says: "by way of an example.
And this being so, there is no objection to the fact that the subject (pakṣa) is also mentioned separately because it serves as the basis for inference;
for its purpose is already fulfilled by the very mention of the established tenet (siddhānta).

Now, one might object: "In the case of verbal testimony, there is indeed no dependence upon an example, because in such cases as 'One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma,' the meaning of the sentence is understood even without it. To this, he says: "Regarding the object of the apprehension of the relation."

The intention here is that this was stated with the desire to indicate that [the Veda] serves as an example merely by being an object of the apprehension of a relationship (*saṃbandhagrahaṇa*), and not, however, by being an object of the apprehension of a specific relationship characterized by pervasion (*vyāpti*).

As for the explanation given by some— that even scripture requires an example with the intention of inferring its validity regarding its own subject matter— that refers to the case where one explains to another a matter already previously known.
This has been refuted by the author of the Vārttika himself when he spoke thus;
therefore, [the opponent] disregarded that [position].

In this context, since the relationship of primary and secondary importance between the object (*artha*) and the acceptance (*abhyupagama*) depends on the speaker's intention, the "accepted object" (*abhyupagamyamāna artha*), whether it be the object itself or its acceptance, constitutes the *siddhānta*.
Consequently, there is no mutual contradiction among the Sūtra, Bhāṣya, Vārttika, and Ṭīkā.
The phrase "idam iti" (this, as such) serves to dispel the misconception that the words "this" (*idam*) and "of such a nature" (*itthaṃbhūta*) stand in a relationship of qualifier and qualified.
But it does not establish [the property] in a particular person.

The word "establishment" (vyavasthā) does not denote a restriction of acceptance regarding a particular person; rather, its meaning is a restriction of the essential nature itself, by way of excluding the possibility of non-acceptance and of combining [contradictory] positions.
[Objection: Surely, it is only the *pratitantrasiddhānta* (tenet established within a specific system) that is useful for engaging in debate and so forth;
what, then, is the use of the others? To this he says: "In the same way" (*tathā*).
[Objection continued: But since the *sarvatantrasiddhānta* (tenet established in all systems) is not a subject of disagreement, why is it mentioned at all?
For this very reason, it is not the cause for engaging in debate and so forth; therefore, he says: "For instance" (*tathā hi*).
Although the universally established tenet (*sarvatantra-siddhānta*) is not, in its own nature, a constituent part of engaging in debate and so forth, [it serves as such indirectly].
Nevertheless, the meaning is that it would be useful by way of establishing the tenets of one's own specific system (*pratitantra*) and so forth, and by serving as the basis for logic (*nyāya*).
By this very [statement], the purpose of the tenets of one's own specific system has been revealed indirectly.
And what, then, would be the basis of logic?
The phrase "there is no established conclusion for all systems" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
He states the purpose of the *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* with the word "thus": the construction is as follows:

since the general property of the means of proof (*sādhana*) is pervaded by the general property of the probandum (*sādhya*), how could a specific probandum be understood from a specific means of proof?
This is the meaning:

for, by means of the *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (the established conclusion of the context), the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) becomes either fruitful or possesses a [valid] object;
in its absence, however, it is fruitless or lacks an object.
And likewise, how could pervasion (*vyāpti*), being itself concerned with universals (*sāmānya*) and presenting only a universal, establish it within the subject (*pakṣa*) by itself?
And without establishing it, how could it fulfill its purpose?
In that case, inference as a whole would be destroyed.
And thus, where is the logic, or where is the scope for debate?

Therefore, even the *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (the established conclusion based on the context) must necessarily be explained as having the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) as its fruit, so that even the pervasion (*vyāpti*), when assisted by it, may become fruitful.
Taking the primary sense, he raises an objection with "But surely" (*nanu*). He resolves it through the secondary sense (*bhakti*) with "like the parts" (*avayavā iva*).
He states that secondary sense with "For just as" (*yathā hi*).
The illustration of an action (kriyā) is "with soma" (somena);
this is because the word *soma* is the name of a ritual act (*karmanāmadheya*).
Furthermore, it is expressed separately from the word denoting the instrument (*kāraka*) because there is a desire to express merely the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).
In reality, however, even *soma* possesses the status of a *kāraka*.
The example "by means of the *godohana*" (*godohanena*) is an illustration of a *kāraka*, because the fetching of water (*apaḥ praṇayana*) is already established by another statement.

An example of the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is [the word] *vrātya* in the phrase "of whom" (*yasya*), because it possesses a meaning and is not of the nature of a verbal root or an affix. Nevertheless, since the collective sense has not been derived [from its parts], he says: "By this... [and so on].
Now, with the intention that there are indeed elements that cause the cognition of specific meanings even though they do not constitute a sentence, he asks: "Which?"
While refuting the primacy of the condition (*pratyaya*), he states the purpose for employing the word "condition" as follows: "And not that...
He states "and cognition" (*pratītiśca*) in order to avoid the objection that the qualification is unestablished (*viśeṣaṇāsiddhi*).
Now, why does it not become an experience itself?
For it is not the case that the final term is never experienced at all.
If that were so, one might ask how it could even be remembered; therefore, he says: "For not... [and so on].
Nevertheless, even for one who is in such a state, memory of this [object] could not occur without a prior experience; therefore, he says: "But they are possible.
Let it be, then, that the experience of that [object] itself is the factor for the cognition of the object; to this he replies: "And these are not...
By this, the view that experience alone is the factor for the communication of the object is refuted.

He refutes the conjunction of experience and memory with the words "nor [is there] the previous... It should be understood that the phrase "there might be a coexistence of memory and experience" is to be supplied.
And this is to be seen in light of the admission of memory occurring in the interval between the experiences of the penultimate and final phonemes.

If, however, the experiences of the phonemes—which arise in immediate succession—are themselves uninterrupted, then one might suspect a coexistence only between the penultimate and final experiences, namely those in the states of perishing and not yet perishing; yet this must be rejected by the reasoning already stated.
Therefore, it was not raised as a separate doubt by the author of the *Ṭīkā*.

He raises an objection—accepting as his own the synthesis of the nature of the cognition which, due to the synthesis of its causes, possesses a non-synthetic object—by saying, "And not the previous...
He refutes it by saying, "The relation..."
Although there is no so-called "awakening" (udbodha) of a latent impression (saṃskāra) other than the acquisition of auxiliary conditions (sahakārin),

nevertheless, not just any condition serves as its auxiliary; for if that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of all latent impressions being awakened at all times, which would result in the recollection of everything.
Nor is the experience of the phonemes that constitute a portion of a word the auxiliary cause for the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) that brings about the recollection of a specific convention;
for if that were the case, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Therefore, it is the very recognition [of the word] as a word (*padatvena pratisandhāna*) that serves as the cause for the latent impression which triggers the memory of the convention.
It must be accepted that [the letters] act as co-operating causes (*sahakārī*).

Thus, even when the phonemes are made the object of a single, variegated cognition by a single stroke, they are to be recollected as parts in the form of words, and they are to be remembered as being connected with the meaning; therefore, how could there be any deficiency in experience? This is the meaning.

The process is as follows: the arising of the experience of the final phoneme and the simultaneous production of its latent impression (saṃskāra) and the recognition of the word-meaning occur at one and the same time.
Now, their arising:

that very [arising], which consists in the production of the connection of words, is the awakening of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*); it is the state of the recollection of the relation being produced, while the diverse cognition is in the process of perishing due to the awakening of the latent impression—this is one moment.
Then, the arising of the recollection of the relation is the destruction of the diverse cognition, while the connection of the word-ness is in the process of perishing—this is another moment.
And he says that this is not an unobserved assumption, stating: "For this very reason."
But surely, through a single continuous flow, there will be a cognition itself that is manifold in nature,
and it will likewise produce such a recollection of the convention.
Even so—
Since only one prior memory that encompasses all words must be accepted, he says: "And thus," etc.
For it is that which has been experienced that is recollected, not [the object] at the very first moment.

And thus, although it is possible to synthesize the status of a word based on the preceding phonemes because they have been experienced, there is no possibility of synthesizing the final word because the final phoneme has not been experienced.
Furthermore, experience and synthesis do not exist at the same time, because they stand in a cause-and-effect relationship.

Therefore, it is rightly said that immediately following that [the cognition of the word-meaning], there is the synthesis of the words as a sentence; for while experience is not the cause in the communication of the word-meanings themselves, it is indeed the cause in the arising of the memory that serves as their means.
In the phrase "determination and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) is intended to signify the recollection of those [word-meanings].

The intention is that since context and the other factors are included within that very [capacity] because they are specific types of fitness (yogyatā), the cognition of the sentence-meaning is thereby established; however, if there is no such establishment, the definition fails, which constitutes its defect.
Now, one might object: "Is it not possible for even things experienced sequentially to ascend into a single memory?
However, words are not experienced even in sequence. To this it is said: "without interval" (*nirantara*).
This means they are made objects of uninterrupted memories, and consequently, they are consolidated within a single memory.

The uninterrupted succession of the cognitions must be understood as resulting from their contiguity. Now, even with this much, the definition remains unestablished; for even if the final term were of such a nature, it would not be the cause for the apprehension of the specific object. Bearing this intention in mind, he says: "It might be so."
Now, it might be argued that if there were deviation in each individual case, there would indeed be mutual dependence;

and since the recollection of the word-meanings—unlike the mental coordination of the collection of words—is not itself subject to such deviation with respect to the production of the cognition of the sentence-meaning, he says: "This is what is meant," the intention being as follows:
To begin with, those very word-meanings are not the means of valid cognition for the sentence-meaning, because that would entail the consequence of its being cognized at all times;
nor are they [the means] when merely remembered.
Furthermore, it would follow that even things merely remembered [by words] would exist in that same manner;
nor are those very objects [the cause], for if words were useful only for the remembrance of word-meanings, the same consequence as before would apply regarding the lack of actual cognition.
But if they are useful for the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, how is it that they do not have the status of being its cause?

If it is asked, "Even so, what is the reason for the distinction between subordinate and primary status? the answer is: the words possess the quality of being uncommon causes [for their own specific meanings].
However, since those objects— being past, future, and so forth— lack causal efficacy altogether,
how could they possess a unique [causal] nature?
For this very reason, memory is not their operation.
However, [this applies] only to those words that have become the cause.
And thus, by taking into account the non-deviation of the operation, the admission that those which deviate in their state devoid of operation are not causes creates great confusion.
With the words "being reconnected" (*pratisandhīyamāna*), he shows the over-extension (*ativyāpakatva*) that is to be refuted by the Vārttika— introducing it with "If" (*yadi*).
To demonstrate the difference from [the previous] accomplishment (*niṣpatti*), he restates the explanation of "establishment" (*siddhi*) as being "real" (*vāstava*).
For the statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*) alone is not determinative of the specific [object], as is understood from the ellipsis;
because it would otherwise entail the consequence of futility, namely, the uselessness of stating the reason (*hetu*) and so forth.
The "method" (*nyāya*) of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) refers to its mode of operation;
and this has been shown in the *Bhāṣya* in the passage beginning with "it is not [known] through non-apprehension" (*nānupalabdha*).
Its "transgression" (*atipāta*) is simply its absence.
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "one should explain that very [system] primarily.
And the meaning is that this refers to that specific system of reasoning which has the self (*ātman*) and so forth as its object.
He states the purpose—namely, "of the application of scripture"—because it involves a non-worldly figurative usage (*alaukikopacāra*).
In the phrase "by correspondence with the object" (*arthasaṃvādena*), the third case ending denotes the instrument (*karaṇe tṛtīyā*).
"Benefit" (*anugraha*) refers to the removal of the suspicion of contradiction with scripture (*āgamavirodha*).
Furthermore, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) possesses a firm foundation because its sole domain is scripture (*āgamaikaviṣayatvāt*).
And it possesses a purpose; that is to say, it becomes known as having a purpose by means of the purpose that is the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
Why?
Because [this applies] to the knowledge of the meaning of the scripture (*āgama*).
The meaning is "because it is firmly established" or "because it is well-known.

Now, if that statement of the reason were to be a presentation of inference (*anumāna*)— that is, if it were to present the probans (*liṅga*) as it is being referred to— then it would have to be supported by the probans as it is being referred to by the inference through its being the object [of that inference].
And the sense is that the mark (liṅga) being reflected upon is not its object.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the very visible mark (*liṅga*) which is the object of the statement of the reason (*hetuvacana*) is precisely what brings about the inferential cognition? To this, he says: "And not merely the perception of the mark," meaning "not merely the visible mark itself."
Rather, the meaning is that the "mark" (liṅga) is that which is being reflected upon as assisted by the recollection of its relationship [to the probandum].
This is what was stated: "Therefore, the verbal expression of the mark is not the means of establishing inference.
The meaning is that it is the mark as it exists in the object of the second [inferential] cognition that is the establisher, not the mark as it is being reflected upon.
Intending to show that the explanation [provided] is unclear due to its adherence to the literal text of the treatise, he says: "This is what is meant.
And thus, the meaning is: "of that which establishes it," i.e., of that which establishes its object.
First of all, the consideration of the mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*) is inference.
And since that [first perception of the mark] has the recollection of pervasion as its auxiliary in producing an inference,

and the second perception of the mark also has the recollection of pervasion as its auxiliary solely for the purpose of generating the cognition of reflective awareness (parāmarśa), both possess the same status of having the recollection of the relation as their auxiliary; therefore, both are inference.

The meaning is: "thereafter [the validity] of the mark (liṅga) which has that as its object, and thereafter also of the statement supported by that. To the question, "What is the purpose of this figurative designation (upacāra)?", he says: "And thus... (evam ca).

Now, one might ask: "Since it should have been stated that [the object] is shown again through memory because it was previously the object of perception, why has the opposite been said? To this he replies with the words "yatra" (where).

Although the object of the previous perception is the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), nevertheless, at the time of the formal citation (*udāharaṇa*), it functions precisely as it has ascended into that memory; it is for this reason alone that it was stated in that manner. This is the meaning.

The seed for the metaphorical usage [of "example"] is not only its having the same object as perception, but also its having a similar function; thus he says: "from the repeated showing" means from the recollection.
For even perception, having set aside any contradiction, recalls the example by way of being the locus of the pervasion—this refers to the statement "that too."
He states another seed as well: "That which is the root," etc.
Now, one might object: "If there is not even a mention of the application (*upanaya*) regarding the word and its meaning, then why did he say 'just as so' (*yathā tathā*)?
To this, he says: "For the application... and so forth.

Although even in the conclusion (*nigamana*) there is indeed the inclusion of specific means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), nevertheless, this [statement] is intended with reference to the general class (*jāti*);

and since there is no means of valid cognition there that is of a different class from the fourfold set, he states the application of all the means of valid cognition immediately before its explanation, in order to establish its status as the supreme, saying: "This very... (*so 'yam*).

It might be argued that since there is no fundamental inherence (*samavāya*), inherence will exist only in a figurative sense; therefore, it is said: "or of the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇānām*).
Since superimposition (*adhyāropa*), imposition (*viniveśana*), or error (*bhrānti*) are not possible, he says: "superimposition" (*adhyāropa*).
[This is] because of the capacity [of the means of cognition].

Dharma is characterized by causality. By this, the intention of the questioner—who asks "What, then, is its capacity?"—is revealed. He states the intention of the answer with the words "But here... (iha tu).

The meaning is that, because capacity (*sāmarthya*) and expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) are mutually pervasive, it is precisely expectancy that is intended here by the term "capacity. By demonstrating these two—co-occurrence (*samavāya*) and capacity—in this manner, he shows the result with the words "In that case" (*tadatra*).
Even though the purpose is not different, there is no status as a single sentence within a larger sentence complex (*vākyaikavākyatva*) because of the absence of expectancy.
For example:
"May Bhaga divide for you two; may Pūṣan divide for you two."
"May Aryaman divide for you," and so forth.
Therefore it is said, "while being divided. Even when there is an expectation [of completion], if there is no single purpose, there is no syntactic unity (*vākyaikavākyatva*) between the sentences.
For example:
"I prepare a pleasant seat for you; I fashion it well-seated with a stream of clarified butter," and so forth.
Therefore, it has been stated that there is a single purpose.
Therefore, by this [sūtra],

the definition of the unity of a sentence according to Jaimini— namely, "therefore, because of the unity of purpose, it is a single sentence, provided that there would be expectancy if it were divided"— is intended.
Now, if one who is in disagreement can indeed be enlightened by means of a sentence alone, then by what means should one who disagrees regarding either the sentence or its meaning be enlightened?
If it is by another sentence, there would be an infinite regress; therefore, he says: "Even though... (yadyapi).
The meaning is that this refers to the domain of perception and scripture that cannot be established otherwise.
A conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is a specific type of restatement (*anuvāda*).
What is its purpose: an injunction (*vidhi*) or a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*)?

And here, at this juncture of the objection, by stating that it "possesses the quality of establishing a distinction," the author has clarified its status as the basis for the determination of reality;
in this context, "reality" (tattva) refers to the specific distinction.
Its establishment is its practice;
its causality is its basis.
To the question "What is the distinction therein?", it is said: "the dharma is distinguished by the dharma."

For from the statement, the subject qualified by the property that serves as the means (sādhana) is directly perceived, whereas the subject qualified by the property in the form of the probandum (sādhya) is perceived through that [means]; thus, intending both of these, it was stated in a general manner.

But surely, even if *tarka* is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is indeed included under the term "means of valid cognition" because a general category encompasses its particular instances;
so why does he say, "it is not a distinct means of valid cognition"?

Therefore, he says: "For by the word *pramāṇa*... The intention is that it is indeed observed that even by means of a general term (*sāmānya-śabda*), there may be a non-inclusion of something for some reason.

For this very reason, when there is a suspicion that [this cognition] might be a separate means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*), after stating its difference from those specific types [of cognitions] already included, the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is adduced as an example;
because [the suspicion] is not certain.
The word "independently" is to be understood as the ellipsis;
however, [it is so] by virtue of being the cause for the distinction between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and their objects (*viṣaya*). Of which...
The meaning is that this is the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it depends upon its object;
this is what is being said:
for reasoning (*tarka*) would indeed be a means of valid cognition in the form of a valid cognition, just like the perception of a logical mark (*liṅga*).
Or [it might be argued that] it has the form of a non-cognition, like the sense faculties and so forth.
First of all, it cannot be the former,
because that consists of an imputation that is removable.
For this very reason, its instrument (the cognition) cannot possess validity either, because it results in an invalid [cognition].
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable,
for its validity is established only when its object pervades the negation of its own object.
And for that reason, there is no restrictive relationship between them;
if that which is unrelated were a signifier, it would lead to over-extension.
However, its opposite does have an intrinsic relationship with it.
Therefore, since the activity is conjoined with that [cognition], it is precisely that which constitutes its *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance).
For we do not observe anywhere a contingency that, failing to culminate in a reversal [of error], has already achieved its purpose.
But if that is so, then even a solitary means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would never achieve its purpose;
and this being the case, validity would ultimately reside only in the aggregate of the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) and its contrapositive (*viparyaya*).
This is indeed so, because in all instances it is only that which possesses the auxiliary procedures (*itikartavyatā*) that functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*).
However, regarding the conceptualization of the "way of acting" (itikartavyatā) and its possessor, this is the distinction.
This he will state: "Because, by virtue of being a consequence (prasaṅga), it is dependent and not itself a prover.
The "undesirability" (aniṣṭatva) and "impropriety" (ayuktatva) of that which is to be entailed consist in its being contradicted by valid cognition (pramāṇa).
The "reasonableness" (*yuktatva*) of that which is to be proven consists in its being intended as not contradicted by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, this is the meaning of the *Vārttika*: if it were not thus, then such reasonableness would not have been stated.
And since this would entail an inconsistency, he says: "by means of the particle *iti*.
Consequently, there is no contradiction with the Vārttika which provides an exposition in the form of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*).
The commentary, however, is clear in this context.

Now, if it were already ascertained even before the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that "it is," then *tarka* would itself be a *pramāṇa*; therefore, he says: "it is possible" (*saṃbhavati*).
And here, "possibility" (saṃbhāvanā) means merely the absence of contradiction, not doubt;
for even that which is untenable may be a locus of doubt.

And this very "permission" (anujñā) consists in remaining in conformity with the currently operating means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus he says: "This is what is meant. "Granting permission" means not contradicting [the object], by way of excluding those properties that are contrary to it.
"It favors" means it renders [the object] active.

Anticipating the misconception that inference (tarka) also has that as its object because it conforms to the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) regarding that object, he refutes it with the words "but not," meaning "not by way of dependence," that is,
not by way of dependence on error.
While demonstrating that [the reason] has the nature of a superimposition (āroparūpa), he refutes its validity by way of its own object, stating: "For there exists...
The meaning is: the reason is not a prasanga, nor is the prasajyamāna a logical mark (liṅga), because it is unestablished (asiddha).

Now, is it not the case that there is no such rule that whatever exists must necessarily be perceived? To this he says: "together with that. Therefore, by means of the result, the supporting proof for the logical reasoning (*tarka*) has been shown, namely, that [the object] does not exist.
Being authorized by that [reasoning], the proof proceeds and establishes the result.
He states the result: "This is indeed absolute" (*kevalam eva idam*).
Because there is a disagreement regarding the nature of absoluteness (*kaivalya*), he explains it by saying: "Not here" (*na iha*).

Thus, by demonstrating that even perception regarding non-existence requires *tarka* (reasoning), the Buddhist position— that non-existence is the object to be proven (*sādhya*) by an inference based on the mark of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi-liṅgaka*)—
is refuted; for since non-apprehension itself is of the nature of a negation, it would require proof by another inference, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*),
and because what is unestablished cannot serve as a means of proof (*agamaka*).
If that [existence] is established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there is no room for inference (*anumāna*),
because even conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) functions by following conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and thus its establishment occurs through direct perception alone.
Otherwise, even for the sake of positive conventional usage, one would have to rely on an inference based on the mark of apprehension (*upalabdhi*).
