Moreover, there would likewise be an infinite regress;
for even a logical mark (*liṅga*) cannot produce an inference if it itself is not conventionally established as such.
Therefore, just like affirmative conventional usage, negative conventional usage is also established by perception (*pratyakṣa*).
However, it is reasonable that for one who is mistaken, the investigator should employ reasoning (*tarka*) as an auxiliary means.
He states the reasoning supported by scripture (*āgama*) as follows: "In this way, [regarding] heaven...

In the injunction "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), let the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) be the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*), because it is expressed by the same word and because it is the nature of an action to be brought about.
Let it be so;
however, since there is a doubt—namely, that heaven [is the goal] because it serves human purpose—the application of reasoning (tarka) occurs:
if the meaning of the verbal root were the thing to be accomplished (sādhya),...

In that case, the reliability of the instructor, the fact that the injunction is a means to a desired end, the fact that the sentence expresses that [injunction], and the activity of a discerning person would not occur.
Yet all of this is established by means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); such is the meaning. He states the valid cognition by which this is authorized: "by means of identical words," etc.

For there is no contradiction whatsoever between the fact that the fruit of the heaven (svarga) belongs to the efficient force (bhāvanā) of the sacrifice and the fact that the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) does not have that as its fruit, given that both are expressed by the same word and [the former] is the goal to be accomplished (bhāvya).
Therefore, it is logical that the fruit of heaven belongs [to the bhāvanā] without contradicting that [fact];
whereas it is illogical for the meaning of the verbal root to be the goal to be accomplished, because that would involve a contradiction. This is the meaning.

One might ask: "Since reasoning (*tarka*) distinguishes between what is logical and what is illogical for the sake of assisting the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but does not determine [the truth], on what basis is this distinction made? To this, he says: "And not... [The term] *kriyātipatti* refers to the non-occurrence of an action;

it is intended by the word *kriyātipatti* specifically when the state of being accomplished (*sādhyatva*)—which is the meaning of the verbal root—is presented by the suffix as the existence of the jar.
The meaning is that neither a jar nor the meaning of a verbal root (dhātvartha) exists as something to be established (sādhya) when it is not an object of such a [valid] cognition.
To the question, "What follows if this is so?", he says: "That which is based on...

Reasoning (tarka), which is established upon a certain basis—either by way of being equally perceptible or by way of suffering—as a cause that brings about an undesirable consequence, is the means for determining what is logical and what is illogical.
The meaning is that he who will exist does not exist.
By this, the non-establishment of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) and the non-establishment of the proof (*sādhanāsiddhi*) for the [proposition] being negated are indicated;
previously, however, the non-establishment of its own nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*) was shown.

Therefore, because it is a superimposition (āropa), it is not a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) with respect to its own object; nor is it so because there is no restrictive factor (niyāmaka) for its deviation from what is pervaded by its own object.

The meaning is that if it were dependent upon a deviation regarding its own object—which is invariably connected—it would not be a means of valid cognition due to its dependence on another (pāratantrya).
To the question, "In that case, where is its utility?", he says: "But for the sake of ascertainment (niścaya)."

[Objection: But does not the doctrine of the non-difference of Mīmāṃsā from the Veda contradict the accepted distinction between reasoning (*tarka*) and valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? To this he says: "valid cognition... [and so on]. [Objection: Why then should the meaning of the *Vārttika* not be exactly as it is heard in the text? To this he says: "And the state of being a procedure (*itikartavyatātva*)," and so forth.
The purport of this commentary, which distinguishes between the various schools (nikāya),
is that since the body, the sense organs, semen, blood, and so forth are effects of the primary elements (bhūta) such as food,
and since cognition (buddhi) and feeling (vedanā) are likewise their effects, there is no evidence for any other cause [for these mental states].

If "having diverse causes" is what is to be proven, then the reason "because of having differentiation" (*bhedavatvāt*) would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) if intended in its literal sense; for even things like jars, which possess differentiation in their own nature (*svarūpa*), do not have diverse causes. Therefore, he explains it with the intention of referring to the *mode* (*prakāra*)—the meaning being "because of diversity" (*vicitratvāt*).
This means "because of arising through variety."
[Objection: Is it not the case that if you are merely establishing the diversity of causes, you are proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*)?
For the establishment of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) does not follow simply from the fact that there is some diverse cause;

rather, by establishing a diverse cause characterized as merit and demerit, there is neither positive concomitance (*anvaya*) nor negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). To this, he says: "Having stated the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇam uktvā*).
If the cause were manifold, it would follow that birth is manifold; if the cause were not manifold, it would follow that birth is not manifold.
If sacrifices and the like alone were the cause, it would follow that an effect could arise from something that has perished without leaving a trace.
If the cause were eternal, it would follow that the effect would be eternal.
If it consisted of multiple substances, there would be the consequence of its being common to all [beings] who experience prosperity;

if it were a single substance common [to all], the same fault would apply. Thus, the inference of diversity—which proceeds by the force of universal concomitance and is supported by these reasonings operating on the basis of the property of the subject (pakṣadharmatā)—overcomes the contradiction regarding particulars and establishes the intended particular.
The meaning is that it accomplishes [it].

[Objection: Is it not the case that there is no determination of the fruit based on the mere class [of action], such that one asks about a specific time, "But when? To this, he states the intention: "It might be so. [Objection:

Since the purpose for employing a definitive conclusion (nirṇaya) ought to be stated, what is the intent behind the recurrence of *tarka*—which has already served its purpose of providing a conclusion? To this, he says: "Having synthesized... (saṃkalayya).
The meaning is that, by way of synthesis, the inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) of both is intended.
They state the proof and the refutation in accordance with their own respective tenets; thus, [the terms] "one's own" and "the other's goal" correspond respectively.

Now, although it is true that in every instance of debate (*jalpa*) there is no finality in reaching a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*), because even when a conclusion is not reached, the discussion may be interrupted due to human error, nevertheless, in those cases where there is finality in reaching a definitive conclusion—
Therefore, debate cannot be delimited by the mere verbal discourse, because it culminates in the determination of one of the two positions; nor does it encompass all forms of debate,
since determination is the fruit of debate.
And because the fruit is not pervaded by the means [of debate], he says: "For in debate...
For its fitness consists in its culminating in a definitive conclusion (nirṇaya);
and that [fitness] is the engagement of two disputants directed toward that [conclusion] with the desire to know the truth.
This has been stated:
"Because those who desire to know reality have the qualification for debate.
This is the meaning:
Vāda is the formal arrangement of statements consisting of proof and refutation by those two [opponents] with a view toward the determination of truth;
thus, there is neither under-extension nor over-extension.
To explain what kind of *jalpa* (disputation) it is, he says: "In *jalpa*, however...
He states the objective as "the power of the person.
This is the meaning:
Granted that a determination of reality might occasionally occur even for one who prattles;
nevertheless, such a person is neither to be sought out nor trusted,
for their sole purpose is merely to display their own power and the lack of power in others.
"Therefore, by way of terminating in one of the two determinations" means with the intention of terminating in a definitive conclusion (nirṇaya).
Now, one might object: "If *jalpa* (wrangling) and *vitaṇḍā* (cavil) are specific types of *vāda* (discussion), how can there be a mention of both the general and the particular together?
And how can there be a relationship of general and particular between two things that are mutually contradictory? To this, he says: "They are distinguished.
He states another reason for their distinction: "from *vāda*," with the words "*of jalpa and vitaṇḍā*" being understood as the remainder.

Previously, during the occasion of explaining *vāda*, the cause for the distinction was stated to be the intention regarding a specific objective; with reference to that, [the author] says "another [cause] as well. The meaning is that those two who employ *vāda* and *jalpa* are distinguished from each other by being qualified respectively by the absence of the desire for victory in one case and the presence of the desire for victory in the other. Thus, *vāda* and *jalpa* exclude one another.
One should connect this as follows: "He explains according to the opinion of the *ekadeśin* (partialist) commentator in order to refute him.

[The phrase] "because it is inconclusive in both ways" means that even if no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is observed, the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is not established, because the separate mention [of the reason] depends upon the whim of the person [who states it].
Since the fact of being subject to censure in debate is due to its causing an obstruction to the realization of truth when it is not pointed out,
nevertheless, because the deviation (vyabhicāra) is manifest, that alone has been shown.
Therefore, by the statement "they will be subject to censure in debate," only the purpose for their separate mention is established.
Furthermore, the meaning is that the status of being a cause was merely superimposed by a partisan who considers himself a logician, without even considering [the matter].
Now, one might ask: "How is such a purpose achieved?
For it is not possible to establish [the point] here by the mere fact of a separate mention. To this, he says: "In general."
The author of the Sūtras, by stating the general [purpose] while specifying the particular, has indicated a specific purpose;
this very point is what the author of the Bhāṣya has demonstrated—this is the meaning.
Now, if this alone is what the author of the Sūtras intended to express, [then...]

To the question, "Why then did he not show this himself in some part of the treatise? he says: "It is only this much. To the question, "How was this inferred by the author of the Commentary (Bhāṣyakāra)? he says: "Therein. And:
"Even so, what [of it]?"
The meaning is: "What is the purpose achieved by establishing this?
Now, [one might object that] in the case of Agni and so forth, it is precisely their status as being subject to injunction (*codanīyatva*) that is established;
however, here [the author] describes it as being for the purpose of making known the difference in the systems of knowledge (*vidyā-prasthāna-bheda*).
To the question, "Why then is there no contradiction? he says: "Vāda, jalpa, vitaṇḍā," and so forth.
Regarding this very point, he cites the Vārttika as an indicator: "For this very reason.
This is the meaning.

If by the word "knowledge" (vidyā) his [three] forms of debate and so forth were not intended, how could he later, after demonstrating the operation of formal debate (vāda), state that all points of defeat (nigrahasthāna) constitute the operation of both contentious debate (jalpa) and destructive debate (vitaṇḍā)? Therefore, since he himself says this, it is certain that this is the meaning he intends.
Thus, this is the summary of the intended purport:
To begin with, words and the like cannot be presided over by a conscious agent if their own nature, as well as the distinctions between their functions and results, are unknown;
nor can a result be accomplished by means of those that are not so presided over.
Therefore, just like their own nature, these distinctions of function and result must also be made known.
For this very reason, the author of the Sūtra will also demonstrate the fruit in the fourth chapter.
[The words] "they would be applied" or "they would be possible" mean that there is no possibility of their being applied; for indeed,
the true nature of a thing is not established by a definition.
Rather, it is that which is established [as the object] that is made known;
how then can it be said that the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is dependent on that? To this he says: "It is called a *lakṣaṇa* because it is characterized (*lakṣyate*).
Now, if it is argued that the state of being subject to censure in debate is established solely by means of a separate designation, [we reply:]...
How is it understood that deficiency (*nyūna*), excess (*adhika*), and failure to establish a thesis (*apasiddhānta*) are to be censured there, given that they are not mentioned separately?

If it is argued that even otherwise their status as such is indeed understood, then the same principle applies to fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) as well; what is the use of mentioning them separately? To this, he says: "And of the fallacious reasons... (*hetvābhāsānāṃ ca*).
This is the intended meaning:
it is not understood that fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) must be pointed out in debate simply because they have been mentioned separately;
rather, this is because debate is a discourse aimed at the desire to realize the truth.
Furthermore, because the realization of reality is obstructed if fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are not pointed out, those who seek to know reality must necessarily point them out;
otherwise, the debate would forfeit its status as a debate.
Thus, the failure to point out fallacious reasons constitutes an obstruction to the realization of reality.
And this very principle has been indicated by the author of the Sūtras through specific separate mention;
and that principle is the same in the case of [the categories] beginning with "deficiency" (nyūna).
This being the case, the question posed by the author of the Vārttika is not irrelevant; thus he says: "In that regard, he asks.

Now, if the introduction of *jalpa* (disputation) and *vitaṇḍā* (cavil) is for the purpose of establishing the truth (*tattva*), what is the point of pointing out [defeats] such as *apratibhā* (lack of ingenuity)?
Or, if those two do not have that as their purpose, [how can they be introduced]?
What is the purpose of that descent?
Nor can it be argued that, if they serve another purpose, they are not to be explained by this treatise; therefore, he says: "For [the world] with ego," etc.
[referring to] that which is characterized by ego (ahaṅkṛta).
Since the realization of reality is impossible [otherwise], the very purpose of these two [objections] is the destruction of the conceit [of victory];

and that would not occur without the pointing out of "aprati-bhā" (lack of ingenuity) and so forth. Therefore, the meaning is that this must certainly be performed by one who desires to establish the truth.
Now, an objection: the thorough knowledge of quibbles (*chala*) and the like does not directly contribute to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), as do the self (*ātman*) and so forth;
nor does it do so by way of establishing those [categories], as do the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
nor does it do so as a constituent part of reasoning (*nyāya*), as do doubt (*saṃśaya*) and the rest.

Furthermore, thorough knowledge (*parijñāna*) alone is not the fruit, because it would not constitute a human goal (*puruṣārtha*); therefore, he says: "And the fruit of thorough knowledge has been stated.

The meaning is that thorough knowledge is conducive to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) by means of the purification of the three types of discourse, which serve as the means for attaining reality (*tattva*).

Since the application [of the treatise] is easy for oneself and because the text is established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the question regarding its essential nature—asking "what is being said?"—is inappropriate; therefore, he completes the sense by saying, "by this commentary.

Intending that the statement of another purpose in the commentary does not contradict the purpose stated by the author of the Sūtras, but rather is entirely consistent with it, he restates the purpose mentioned in the Sūtra: "by the author of the Sūtras."
Consistency, however, is established by demonstrating pervasion (*vyāpti*);
for it is impossible that there could be a human goal that is not caused by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, this is the meaning of the commentary:
since every purposeful undertaking of a discerning person is rooted in the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) expounded by Ānvīkṣikī,
there can be no doubt whatsoever regarding its being the foundation for *niḥśreyasa*, the supreme human goal.
Because if it were not rooted in that [ultimate reality], there would be the undesirable consequence of losing its status as being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*).
Thus it has been said: "That does not exist at all.
Now, is it not the case that...?

In that case, there would be no practice of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-vyavahāra*) regarding other things at all, because it would follow that the practice of everything else would also be abolished; but if the practice of valid cognition does exist, what then is there for Ānvīkṣikī to illuminate therein?
Because they are illuminated by those very means of valid cognition (pramāṇas), he says: "Even though" (yadyapi).

The meaning is that the practical usage (vyavahāra) of the means of valid cognition and so forth occurs therein [in the treatise] by means of what has been explained; however, the explanation of those [means of valid cognition] arises from this very [treatise], and not from them.

[Objection: But surely, the reliance upon the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) belonging to the author and the listener is common even to Ānvīkṣikī; therefore, there is no distinction from the other sciences. To this, he says: "But not [relying] on the means of valid cognition and so forth.

Although the reliance on the means of valid cognition is the same, the meaning is that while those [other sciences] rely on what is established by this [Ānvīkṣikī], this [Ānvīkṣikī] does not likewise rely on what is established by them.

Now, one might ask: even though the state of being dependent is common to both, where indeed has such a mutual relationship of the supported and the supporter been observed? To this he says: "Just as...
For even perception and the other means of knowledge depend upon another means of knowledge for the establishment of their own validity;
and inference likewise depends upon another for its own production.
Nevertheless, inference proceeds toward its own object by depending solely on perception and the like;
however, perception and the like do not depend on an inference that is dependent [on them],
whereas another inference does depend on that which establishes its own validity.

That too does not occur at that very moment, but rather even earlier; with this intention, in order to refute the dependence on something of the same class as that which is to be defined, it was stated: "Even the object of perception and so forth does not [arise] at that very time.
An object consisting of perception and so forth is called "the object of perception and so forth."
The "accessory to knowledge" (*vidyopakaraṇa*) refers to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth.
Its "comprehension" (*grahaṇa*) is explained by the *Vārttika* as follows: other branches of knowledge (*vidyā*) establish their objects as illuminated by the means of valid cognition and the rest.
What is meant is this:
The mention of "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) and so forth in the *Vārttika* is for the purpose of establishing that it illuminates the types of knowledge (*vidyā*) mentioned in the *Bhāṣya*,
and not independently;
therefore, there is no contradiction.
Thus, having shown dependence in its own nature (*svarūpa*), the author of the Bhāṣya has shown dependence as it pertains to the object (*viṣaya*) by the word "means" (*upāya*).
He explains this in order to apply that Vārttika, beginning with the words "now" (*saṃprati*).

[Objection: But since other forms of knowledge (*vidyā*) are authoritative because they consist of words, and since those [words] are independent regarding their own objects to be conveyed, [how can there be dependence?]
To the question, "What will *anvīkṣikī* do there?", he says: "For not...
When a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) exists, there is no dependence on another means of valid cognition regarding its own object of comprehension;
however, this does not mean there is no dependence on *tarka*, which constitutes its own procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
And the meaning is that this [knowledge] is to be attained through *anvīkṣikī*.
Now, [the author] says "let it not be" in response to the question: what would happen for one who disregards reasoning?
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), the sacrificer is [included as] the sacrificial grass-bundle (prastara).
Such passages are to be understood.
Furthermore, since reasoning (*tarka*) does not arise without doubt, it too has been shown in the conclusion.
Although investigation (*parīkṣā*) is indeed the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) accompanied by reasoning, [it is defined as such].

Nevertheless, here, according to the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*), since *pramāṇa* (the means of valid cognition) is already included by its own term, only the inquiry into the purpose (*prayojana*), the desire to know (*jijñāsā*), and reasoning (*tarka*) are intended [to be mentioned].
The application (*niveśa*) of the *pramāṇa* is its operation (*pravṛtti*); the gateway (*dvāra*) for that is non-contradiction (*avirodha*).

Having ascertained the reality of the matter— whether it be the reality of the word-meaning or the reality of the sentence-meaning— from another means of valid cognition or from an explanatory passage (arthavāda) itself,
the threefold Veda, consisting of injunctions and prohibitions, is to be applied therein; this is the meaning.

And thus, in the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*), [statements] such as "King Yama or Kubera reigns" and so forth, or in the science of economics (*vārttā*), [statements] such as "the earth, when ploughed in the month of Māgha, yields fruit made of gold," become fruitless if they do not depend on reasoning (*tarka*).
Therefore, he extends [this principle] by saying "in this way" (*evam*), indicating that there too a dependence on that [reasoning] exists.
In the phrase "the object is the remainder," the word "remainder" also implies [the distinction] between being that which is enjoined and that which is prohibited.
Now, he states the expectation regarding the activity according to the opinion of the Bhāṣya, beginning with "api ca" (furthermore):
just as in the case of a substance,
[as in] "one offers oblation with curd."
And so forth;
as for a quality, for example:
"One purchases the Soma with a red [cow]."
And so forth; as in the case of the action:
"He threshes the rice grains."
And so forth;
even in the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*), as in the case of the ownership of property by the sovereign and the minister—
And so forth;
as in the case of the division of the *sāman* chant according to its quality (*guṇa*).
And so forth;
just as training with weapons, riding elephants, or mounting horses [are results] of karma.
And so forth;
even in the case of trade, one should collect seeds for a substance according to the season.
And so forth;
just as one might flood or dry up the earth by means of water.
And so forth. Desiring to lead the tree immediately after the ritual action, one should consecrate it with the mantra.
And so forth.
Having shown the subject matter, he states the doubt: "In that regard, what [is the case]?
And the cause of the doubt is the co-occurrence of that word with an injunctive term.
For the qualified person (*adhikārī*), being mentioned in grammatical coordination with the injunctive word (*vidhipada*), is not the object of the injunction;
rather, it is the *agnihotra* sacrifice, existing in that very state, which is its object.

Therefore, since there is doubt regarding the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*), one presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) as follows: "Should heaven be the object of the injunction—like the *agnihotra* and so forth—because it is mentioned in coordination with the injunctive word, or should it be like the qualified person, and thus not? Thus he shows the prima facie position.
Regarding this, he states the undesirable consequence: "In that case, if...
One should not argue that since the violence accomplished by the Śyena sacrifice and others is prescribed, it must simply be considered a beneficial purpose (*artha*), for what harm would there be?
For an injunction (*vidhi*) is that which impels; its meaning is that, through its own cognition, it produces an effort by generating a desire even in the absence of [any other] desire.
Furthermore, that effort cannot be made to have the goal as its object;
for the means is the object of effort, not the result.
Therefore, because they are the objects of effort, it is the means and the procedure that are enjoined, but not the goal.
Because that is not its object;
for being a mere indicator does not constitute being an injunction (vidhi),
but rather it is the state of being an indicator of an object of desire and effort.

Therefore, it has been rightly stated that if the violence accomplished by the Śyena sacrifice and others were the object of an injunction, it would indeed be an undesirable end (anartha) despite being [formally] an "object" (artha).

While demonstrating the authoritative means for the established conclusion (siddhānta), he dispels the doubt—namely, "In that case, what is the use of the co-occurrence with the word 'to be accomplished' (sādhya)'?"—by saying: "Now, as for the factor of being accomplished...
For the status of being a means to a desired end cannot be cognized without first cognizing the desired end itself.
Nor does that [cognition] which has not yet arisen cause [the object] to arise;
therefore, the meaning is that this is a restatement of what is desired in order to qualify it.
Is it then the case that a fault arises merely because something is not enjoined?
No, he says: "One shall not harm. But surely, let that be so for now; what, however, does this have to do with *ānvīkṣikī* (the science of inquiry)? To this he says: "In this regard... (*tad iheti*).
He states another point regarding the subject matter with the word "evam" (thus):

just as the *ābhikhyā* (the specific name) is the efficient cause because it is substituted for the milk-oblation due to the similarity of its taste and other qualities, so too the *vājina* (the whey) is not the efficient cause because its production is unavoidable.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), the omission of the remaining portions of the oblation and other such matters are included.
There is no contradiction with the commentary's explanation because the word "knowledge" (vidyā) indicates its constituent properties (dharmas).
However, the Vārttikakāra intends to express that these properties are dependent upon knowledge; this is the remainder [of the interpretation].
"The consequence of confusion" refers to the result.
Thus, the meaning is that its possession of a result occurs solely by virtue of being rooted in knowledge (vidyā), and it does not possess a unique result of its own.
In order to demonstrate their non-confusion, he first states the unique fruit of these very [sciences] with the words "other sciences" (*vidyāntarāṇi*).
He states the unique fruit of this [present science] with the words "but here" (*iha tu*).
With the intention that there should be no contradiction regarding the utility established for this [science] elsewhere, he says "the means of valid cognition, etc. (*pramāṇādi*).
"Even though it is common to all"— by this it is meant that even when the branches of other sciences depend upon the science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī), this constitutes its "proof by heat" (ūṣmasiddhi).
As for its principal fruit, that is indeed unmixed, because it is not possible [to obtain it] through other forms of knowledge.

The phrase "of debate and so forth" (*vādādīnām*) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the qualities of the members are not included in the referent (*atadguṇasaṃvijñāna*), because debate does not function for the purpose of overcoming others.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: "For frivolous talk (*jalpa*) and the rest are causes of pride and so forth, because they are means for overcoming others, just like the acquisition of wealth or a physical body."
Regarding that, he first states its contradictory nature: "In that regard, of the disputation (*jalpa*) and so forth.
This is the intended meaning:
first of all, the person to be instructed has no entitlement to engage in disputation (*jalpa*) or cavil (*vitaṇḍā*).

However, those two have the authority [to speak] for the sake of preserving the realization of reality by one who has already entered upon the path, and for the sake of instructing those who are difficult to subdue.
Furthermore, the crushing of the pride of others is indeed contrary to intoxication, arrogance, and the like, because these are specific defects.
Furthermore, because the destruction of egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) consists in its cessation,
there can be no inference based merely on the fact that it is denotable by a word that serves as a means for overcoming others;
otherwise, it would follow that even speech and other such faculties possess horns.
It might be argued:
"Let it not be established that [wealth] is a cause of intoxication, pride, and so forth, on the grounds of its being a means for overcoming others;

rather, let it be established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) alone. To this, he says: "And the reason—that it is a cause of intoxication, pride, and so forth—is unestablished (asiddha)."

Furthermore, by asserting that [pride and the like] do not occur among those who know reality, it is also indicated that the status of "overcoming others" as a means [to liberation] for one who has merely heard the teachings is non-conclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Therefore, if pride and the other [afflictions] are observed even in those who possess knowledge of the reality of speech and so forth, [the aforementioned claim is undermined].
Those [cognitions] do not have that [object] as their cause;
rather, they are caused solely by powerful false cognition—this is the result of citing the examples of Sanaka and others.
With the intention that this is clear, he says: "He concludes. //1//
// Purity //
An examination of that whose own nature is not yet understood, and which lacks a connection to a purpose, is not appropriate, because it would lack a basis.
However, the first sūtra is intended solely for the purpose of enunciation (uddeśa); therefore, he says: "Thus, in this way..."
From that very [statement] which concerns the subject matter (*abhidheya*), the connection (*saṃbandha*), and the purpose (*prayojana*), the *uddeśa* (brief enumeration) is also understood;
and the meaning is that it is grasped because it is required.
By this, the object of investigation (*parīkṣā*) has been shown.
While demonstrating what is appropriate, he states the reason for its transgression with the words "of them" (teṣām).
By this, the purpose of the examination of the relationship has also been shown by way of a subtle argument.
The twofold nature of expression consists in its contact with both ends.
Following the principle of "it is correct," etc., the sequence of meaning should be understood as in the *Vārttika* and similar works.
Therefore, from the mere similarity of expression—meaning, from the observed commonality of expression alone, which is devoid of any decisive [evidence].
"And because it is seen in both ways" means that it arises from a memory produced by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) born from seeing both alternatives occurring together.
This should be understood as referring to what occurs prior to the ascertainment of the author of the Sūtra’s reliability.
Although in this case the statement itself directly presents the doubt, nevertheless, it should be understood that the doubt pertains to the meaning through that medium.

And when the purpose, which is the related object, is being examined as the effect of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), it is precisely the relationship—characterized by the nature of cause and effect—that becomes examined; therefore, that very [relationship] is pointed out as the object of examination with the words, "That indeed is the supreme good" (*niḥśreyasa*).
In reality, however, this is an examination of the relationship itself; thus, there is no lack of common locus (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between the proposition, the doubt, and the examination.
"In that regard" means when the Sūtra is to be explained;
"contrary to the Sūtra" means [in a manner that deviates from it].
The intention is that without a prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), there can be no introduction of a sūtra presenting the established conclusion (siddhānta).

Now, the objection that "in the case of liberation while living (jīvanmukti), there would be no abiding for those who possess such knowledge" is rendered groundless; therefore, he says: "That absolute... [etc.].
One might object: "Let it be that supreme beatitude (niḥśreyasa) does not occur immediately after the knowledge of reality; what loss is there to us?"
For we have not indeed made such a formal proposition; therefore, he says: "That being so.

Although this has not been explicitly stated as a proposition, nevertheless, the author of the Sūtras has demonstrated the causal relationship between the knowledge of reality and the supreme good (niḥśreyasa).
The meaning is that the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) considers that this must necessarily be an immediate succession (ānantarya-niyama) and not otherwise;
thus it is said: "it is false."

Now, even so, one might object: why is it asserted that "liberation (apavarga) is the absolute release from that" [NS 1.1.22] constitutes the highest good (niḥśreyasa), when liberation while living (jīvanmukti) is also indeed a form of the highest good? To this, he says: "And there is nothing else."

In this intended sense, the "seed" refers to the fact that once the knowledge of reality has arisen, there is no further requirement for anything else to be performed in order to achieve liberation; or, if something were required, it would be that very knowledge itself which is the means to liberation.
"It is not the knowledge of reality.

Regarding this, the author of the Vārttika has stated: "Even when the knowledge of reality exists, that other factor whose absence prevents one from being liberated is another matter"—this is the clear meaning of the Vārttika, according to the *Ṭīkā*.
In order to demonstrate that the *Vārttika* is derived from the *Sūtra*, he introduces the *Sūtra* with the words "In this regard, this... (*atredam iti*).

The *Vārttika* as it was heard [by him] does not cover the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), because there is no other supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) that arises directly from scriptural knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), and because that which arises directly is not scriptural; therefore, he establishes the ground [of his argument] with the words "For there are four... (*catasro hi iti*).
And that [science] depends upon, that is, is contingent on, Ānvīkṣikī.
He states its utility as an auxiliary to that [Arthaśāstra] with the words: "And Ānvīkṣikī... and so forth.
Now, it may be argued that hearing (*śravaṇa*) is useful by giving rise to expectancy,
and likewise for reflection (*manana*) by means of ascertainment;
so what else remains for the sake of which another mode of realization, namely meditation (*upāsana*), is required?
For the fruit of no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is anything other than certainty; therefore, he says: "And this is not... The intention is as follows:
for certainty is not delusion, and it cannot be sublated by either scriptural or inferential ascertainment of reality.
But through the practice of the means to that [knowledge], there is the union of those two.
Therefore, those Vedāntins who desire liberation from the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence alone should be questioned:
Do you engage in practice by accepting a relationship between means and ends that is substantially real (*vastusat*), or one that is conventionally real (*saṃvṛtisat*)?
In the first case, there is a destruction of the non-dual doctrine (*advaitasiddhānta*).
Since the relationship between cause and effect is based upon difference, if those two were ultimately real, it would follow that difference itself must also be ultimately real;
as for the second [alternative], does activity occur without distinction,
or according to the established order of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*)?
In the first case, even those who enjoy worldly pleasures would be liberated;
but in the second case, the removal of sensory delusion does not result from knowledge of reality derived from scripture or inference.

What then? It is observed that it results only from direct perception; therefore, it is logical that one who desires that [liberation] should apply themselves precisely toward that [direct perception].
Nor should it be said that the dawn of the direct realization of the Self arises from the mere statement [of scripture],
for the capacity of that alone is not observed.
If, however, it is argued that because its nature is self-cognized, what need is there for meditation (*dhyāna*) and so forth to produce something unprecedented therein?
In that case, even the Veda would be rendered futile by this very same reasoning.
As for the example cited regarding Bhūtadāśaka’s crossing of the river,
there too direct realization did not occur through the sentence alone, but rather through the eyes and other senses.
If it is argued that here too [the realization] will occur through the mind being assisted [by other means], we say no;
for even in one who has heard the scriptures many times and possesses a highly refined mind, there is still an absence of the direct realization of Brahman.
Why is this so?

For one who desires liberation, there is no such thing as the mental eye (mānasa) directed toward the Self, just as there is for ordinary beings directed toward their own bodies; this is because the practice of the visual [perception] is far more firmly established.
Therefore, for that purpose, practice alone is the refuge.
This is what is meant by the phrase "established in the world."
Whether the causal relationship established by worldly consensus be ultimately real or not, for everyone engaged in pursuit of human goals, that very relationship is their only refuge.
If it were disregarded, then even human goals would not be worthy of regard, as they share the same fate.

If it is argued that although there are four modes of apprehension regarding objects of knowledge such as the self, what relevance does this have to the present topic? To this he says: "Now" (*atha*).
What is meant is this: if the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is taken on the basis of either scriptural or inferential knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), [then the following applies].
In that case, non-acceptance itself is the answer;
for we do not assert that it is the direct cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). What then? It is the indirect cause, as shown by the passage beginning with "those four," and so forth.
Therefore, the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) takes direct realization as its basis,
for it is precisely that which is accepted as the cause of the supreme good (niḥśreyasa).
The sense is that, in order to avoid the objection raised therein, the demonstration of the twofold nature of the supreme good is presented.
Now, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) extends up to the words "atha idyucyate.
Each preceding reason possesses each succeeding one.
[Objection: But surely it is impossible for one who possesses direct realization (sākṣātkāra) to still possess a body and so forth;

for when the supreme good (niḥśreyasa) is to be accomplished, there is no further duty to be performed regarding direct realization, as there is in the case of hearing (śravaṇa) and the like. To this, he says: "And not thus. An example is given to raise the doubt: "And not as by means of expiation (prāyaścitta)," and so on.

To begin with, the attainment of eligibility for the penance is not its result, because there is no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for postulating a specific result for unseen actions in the absence of scriptural authority (*āgama*), and because it would entail the abandonment of the results that are actually heard in the texts.
If it is argued that this [abandonment] is not undesirable since there exists a powerful subverting factor (*bādhaka*), we say: no.
For a scripture that is established as non-erroneous cannot be subverted even by a thousand refutations;

otherwise, if such subversion were possible, then the inference that "the drinking of liquor is a duty" would also be difficult to prevent, and thus the logicians (haituka) would be handing the matter over to themselves.
For this very reason, the mere suffering resulting from the performance of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) is not the fruit of acts such as the killing of a Brahmin.
Because it is not heard as having that [sin] as its fruit, because it would follow that the injunction for expiation is futile,
and because no distinction [of result] is produced.

Since even one who does not desire it achieves that [result] solely through the power of karma, it is therefore correct to hold that only those karmas whose fruits have not yet been bestowed are exhausted by expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Likewise, in that very same way, the direct realization of reality (*tattvasākṣātkāra*) will also bring about this result; such is the meaning.

And here, with the intention that those who proceed by the force of scripture (āgama) should be enlightened by scripture alone, he says: "What has not been experienced does not perish. Now, [one might object]: *Note: The Sanskrit fragment "nābhuktaṃ kṣīyate" is part of the famous verse from the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "nābhuktaṃ kṣīyate karma kalpakoṭiśatair api" ("Karma is not exhausted until it has been experienced, even in hundreds of millions of eons").*

"The fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes" (Gītā 4.37); such a traditional teaching (smṛti) exists even regarding the contrary case. Therefore, how will a definitive conclusion be reached? To this, he says: "by the final pleasure," and so forth.
This might be so if there were no logical reasoning (nyāya) to support the Smṛti passage beginning with "If one has not experienced [the fruit]... and so forth;
yet such reasoning does exist.
And the formal argument (prayoga) is as follows:
The actions under dispute are exhausted through experience alone, because they are actions for which no expiation has been performed, like the karma that initiated the present body;
nor is there any contradiction with scripture in this regard.
The meaning is that it is not determinative because it contradicts other scriptural authorities (*āgama*).

With the intention that it is not logical for a *smṛti* established as a general rule (*utsarga*) to be otherwise when there is no sublation (*bādhaka*), he says: "of the general rule" (*autsargikasya*).
Now, [an objection]:...
The knot of the heart is loosened, all doubts are severed,
and one's karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen.

Since this Śruti passage from the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* (2.2.8) stands as an obstacle, how can it be said that "when there is no sublater," and how can Smṛti be determinative in opposition to it, as well as receive support from inference? To this, he says: "They are exhausted. For this Śruti does not state that only those actions whose fruits have not yet been given are destroyed by the knowledge of reality.
But it is merely a depletion; and since that occurs even through enjoyment, it does not cause any harm—this is the sense. "Enjoyment in bodies" means enjoyment within the bodies.
Moreover, he says "only so long" (tāvadeva) to show that even a contrary scriptural statement exists:
for one who has the direct realization of this reality, the delay is only so long as liberation from the accumulated mass of karma has not occurred through the exhaustion of its fruits.
The meaning is that when that [knowledge] exists, liberation (kaivalya) will be attained;
for it is stated in the supplementary portion of the sūtra: "But having exhausted the others through experience."

Now, one might object that the exhaustion [of karma] through experience is indeed untenable, because the mass of karma is infinite and its time of fruition is not fixed; to this he says: "by the power of yoga" (*yogarddhi*).
This was stated in the opening verse.
He raises an objection with the words "If not" (*na ceti*).

This is the underlying intention: if it is the very power of the karmas that, through various intermediate operations such as diverse bodies and so forth, simultaneously brings about experience by means of those respective [operations], [then there is no fault].
What is the use of imagining the power of yoga?
Or, even if this greatness does not belong to them, where would the power of yoga be of any use?
For even the Lord is not able to alter the inherent nature of karmas;
therefore, this must be postulated through one's own independent reasoning.
If that is the case, it would be simpler to postulate that these very karmas, without having yielded their fruits, are exhausted through the power of yoga.
He refutes [this objection] with the words "in accordance with what is observed," meaning in accordance with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For indeed, the exhaustion of karmas occurs only through experience; experience occurs only while the body and so forth exist;
and the production of the body and so forth occurs only through karmas that have attained their functional state.

The acquisition of their activity is precisely the acquisition of auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*); and those auxiliaries are, in some cases, inferred from the result, as in the simultaneous engagement of multiple sense organs; in other cases, they are known through scripture, as in the simultaneity of bodies among Vāsudeva, Saubhari, and others—thus, there is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for all such instances.
It is not so in the case of the exhaustion of karma that has not yet been experienced.

Just as the cessation of the activity of all karmas simultaneously at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) is accepted on the authority of scripture, so too must the simultaneous acquisition of activity by all [karmas] be accepted at the time of yogic power (*yogarddhi*) based on the authority of scripture alone; thus, nothing here is merely imagined through one's own fancy. And such a sage is one who possesses the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
To the question, "What follows if this is so?", he says: "Thus, it is not the doctrine of Vātaputrīya.
Then, to the question, "Of what nature is the supreme *niḥśreyasa* (final beatitude)? he says: "But the supreme... Thus, the twofold nature of *niḥśreyasa* is established.
The phrase "for the purpose of refuting the prima facie position" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
The meaning is that he does not perceive it as pleasure or pain, because it lacks the quality of being a cause for the arising of attachment and aversion.
For it is impossible that one should not be thirsty for that which is pleasure to an ignorant person, yet serves as a generator of thirst for him.
The meaning is that he does not hate that [object] which causes hatred in an ignorant person, even though it is a source of suffering for him.
Having stated the intended sense, the author proceeds to justify the literal meaning and raises an objection with the words "this might be so.
The remainder of the thought is that one who hastens toward liberation must still exert effort toward experience, such as the manifestation of multiple bodies (kāyavyūha) and so forth.

As for him who hastens, thinking, "When the exhaustion of karma occurs, then liberation will also occur—what is the use of haste? his heart is already satisfied by the thought that he has attained the stage free from danger; thus, the sense is that for such a person, there is not even a suspicion of the simultaneous occurrence of the two forms of the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*).

One might object: "If this much alone is sufficient for everything to be well-established, what is the use of the subsequent treatise? To this he says: "In this way, the comprehension of the meaning...
It should be understood that [this refers to] the flow-like nature of false cognition, defects, and activity (*pravṛtti*).
Furthermore, in this context, "activity" (*pravṛtti*) is to be taken in its causal sense.
Because that which has the nature of an effect is not severed;
there is no sequential process of severance for birth and suffering, which exist in the form of a continuous flow.
Why? Because of what was previously acquired.
The meaning is "because the root is not cut off. Anticipating the contradiction with a future Vārttika, he says: "And this..."

Although a connection characterized by inherence in a single substrate (*ekārthasamavāya*) is possible for [qualities] such as suffering and so forth, nevertheless, that [connection] does not exist for the birth of the body and so on.
However, since the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is precisely what must be understood even in that case, he says: "by way of fitness" (*yogyatayā*).
For it is logical that a cause exists prior [to its effect]; therefore, he says: "in this case..."

And [the word] "ca" (and): since that which follows immediately after the subsequent [word] would necessarily be the preceding one, yet the preceding cannot be the effect, he says: "and its immediate succession."
"Uninterrupted" means without interval; therefore, "reading at the beginning without interruption" refers to that initial recitation.
The implication is that the defects (doṣas), which are the effects of false cognition (mithyājñāna) as its cause, are recited at the very beginning without any interval.
Since this is so, it applies elsewhere as well; therefore, he says "in this way.
By this, the meaning is as follows:
there is a causal relationship between suffering and the other [factors].
"Upon the successive disappearance of those very [defilements], liberation occurs because of the non-existence of that which immediately follows them.
He refutes this, saying: "No, for..."

"Liberation (apavarga) is the sole goal" and "because upon the successive disappearance [of each], the one immediately following it ceases to exist"—these are two phrases. The phrase "of which? requires a complement, as does the phrase "of suffering and so forth. What is it that becomes [the goal]? It is liberation. And what is it that ceases? It is suffering and so forth. Thus, these two phrases are mutually expectant. Furthermore, since the cessation of suffering and so forth occurs through the successive disappearance of each preceding member, the statement "upon the successive disappearance... is intended to show that liberation is the sole goal. Therefore, these two phrases are not redundant. Alternatively, the word *eka* ("sole") is used to exclude other goals such as heaven (*svarga*) and the like; thus, the meaning is that liberation alone is the goal, and nothing else. Consequently, the two phrases are not redundant. Alternatively, the word *eka* is used to indicate that there is no second goal for those seeking liberation. For example, just as a person who desires water seeks only water and not fire or anything else, so too the seeker of liberation seeks only liberation and not heaven or anything else. Therefore, the word *eka* is employed to exclude other goals. Consequently, the two phrases are not redundant. Alternatively, the word *eka* is used to indicate that liberation is the primary goal among all goals. For example, just as when a king goes out on a hunt, although he may desire various things such as deer, women, and wealth, his primary objective is the deer; so too, although there are many goals such as heaven and the like, liberation is the primary one. Therefore, the word *eka* is employed to indicate its preeminence. Consequently, the two phrases are not redundant. Alternatively, the word *eka* is used to indicate that liberation is the ultimate goal. For example, just as when a person travels from one village to another, although there are intermediate stages, the ultimate destination is the final village; so too, although there are various goals such as heaven and the like, liberation is the ultimate one. Therefore, the word *eka* is employed to indicate its finality. Consequently, the two phrases are not redundant. Alternatively, the word *eka* is used to indicate that liberation is the goal for all beings. For example, just as when a person sets out on a journey, although they may have different destinations according to their respective purposes, the destination is common to all travelers; so too, although there are various goals such as heaven and the like, liberation is the common goal for all beings. Therefore, the word *eka* is employed to indicate its universality. Consequently, the two phrases are not redundant. Alternatively, the word *eka* is used to indicate that liberation is the goal for those who seek excellence. For example, just as when a person seeks excellence, although they may desire various things such as food, clothing, and ornaments, their goal is excellence itself; so too, although there are various goals such as heaven and the like, liberation is the goal for those seeking excellence. Therefore, the word *eka* is employed to indicate its status as the object of excellence. Consequently, the two phrases are not redundant. Alternatively, the word *eka* is used to indicate that liberation is the goal for those who seek happiness. For example, just as when a person seeks happiness, although they may desire various things such as food, clothing, and ornaments, their goal is happiness itself; so too, although there are various goals such as heaven and the like, liberation is the goal for those seeking happiness. Therefore, the word *eka* is employed to indicate its status as the object of happiness. Consequently, the two phrases are not redundant. Alternatively, the word *eka* is used to indicate that liberation is the goal for those who seek peace. For example, just as when a person seeks peace, although they may desire various things such as food, clothing, and ornaments, their goal is peace itself; so too, although there are various goals such as heaven and the like, liberation is the goal for those seeking peace. Therefore, the word *eka* is employed to indicate its status as the object of peace. Consequently, the two phrases are not redundant. Alternatively, the word *eka* is used to indicate that liberation is the goal for those who seek the cessation of suffering. For example, just as when a person seeks the cessation of suffering, although they may desire various things such as food, clothing, and ornaments, their goal is the cessation of suffering itself; so too, although there are various goals such as heaven and the like, liberation is the goal for those seeking the cessation of suffering. Therefore, the word *eka* is employed to indicate its status as the object of the cessation of suffering. Consequently, the two phrases are not redundant. Alternatively, the word *eka* is used to indicate that liberation is the goal for those who seek the end of transmigration. For example, just as when a person seeks the end of transmigration, although they may desire various things such as food, clothing, and ornaments, their goal is the end of transmigration itself; so too, although there are various goals such as heaven and the like, liberation is the goal for those seeking the end of transmigration. Therefore, the word *eka* is employed to indicate its status as the object of the end of transmigration. Consequently, the two phrases are not redundant. Alternatively, the word *eka* is used to indicate that liberation is the goal for those who seek the exhaustion of defilements. For example, just as when a person seeks the exhaustion of defilements, although they may desire various things such as food, clothing, and ornaments, their goal is the exhaustion of defilements itself; so too, although there are various goals such as heaven and the like, liberation is the goal for those seeking the exhaustion of defilements. Therefore, the word *eka* is employed to indicate its status as the object of the exhaustion of defilements. Consequently, the two phrases are not redundant. Alternatively, the word *eka* is used to indicate that liberation is the goal for those who seek the destruction of the afflictions. For example, just as when a person seeks the destruction of the afflictions, although they may desire various things such as food, clothing, and ornaments, their goal is the destruction of the afflictions itself; so too, although there are various goals such as heaven and the like, liberation is the goal for those seeking the destruction of the afflictions. Therefore, the word *eka* is employed to indicate its status as the object of the destruction of the afflictions. Consequently, the two phrases are not redundant. Alternatively, the word *eka* is used to indicate that liberation is the goal for those who seek the transcendence of existence. For example, just as when a person seeks the transcendence of existence, although they may desire various things such as food, clothing, and ornaments, their goal is the transcendence of existence itself; so too, although there are various goals such as heaven and the like, liberation is the goal for those seeking the transcendence of existence. Therefore, the word *eka* is employed to indicate its status as the object of the transcendence of existence. Consequently, the two phrases are not redundant. Alternatively, the word *eka* is used to indicate that liberation is the goal for those who seek the cessation of birth. For example, just as when a person seeks the cessation of birth, although they may desire various things such as food, clothing, and ornaments, their goal is the cessation of birth itself; so too, although there are various goals such as heaven and the like, liberation is the goal for those seeking the cessation of birth. Therefore, the word *eka* is employed to indicate its status as the object of the cessation of birth. Consequently, the two phrases are not redundant. Alternatively, the word *eka* is used to indicate that liberation is the goal for those who seek the end of rebirth. For example, just as when a person seeks the end of rebirth, although they may desire various things such as food, clothing, and ornaments, their goal is the end of rebirth itself; so too, although there are various goals such as heaven and the like, liberation is the goal for those seeking the end of rebirth. Therefore, the word *eka* is employed to indicate its status as the object of the end of rebirth. Consequently, the two phrases are not redundant. Alternatively, the word *eka* is used to indicate that liberation is the goal for those who seek the cessation of the cycle of existence. For example, just as when a person seeks the cessation of the cycle of existence, although they may desire various things such as food, clothing, and ornaments, their goal is the cessation of the cycle of existence itself; so too, although there are various goals such as heaven and the like, liberation is the goal for those seeking the cessation of the cycle of existence. Therefore, the word *eka* is employed to indicate its status as the object of the cessation of the cycle of existence. Consequently, the two phrases are not redundant. Alternatively, the word *eka* is used to indicate that liberation is the goal for those who seek the end of saṃsāra. For example, just as when a person seeks the end of saṃsāra, although they may desire various things such as food, clothing, and ornaments, their goal is the end of saṃsāra itself; so too, although there are various goals such as heaven and the like, liberation is the goal for those seeking the end of saṃsāra. Therefore, the word *eka* is employed to indicate its status as the object of the end of sa
Therefore, because it possesses the characteristic of being a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), the meaning is that this is indeed one sentence.
As for the claim that there is an increase in purpose due to a division of sentences,
he says "by the cessation of one" to show that even that does not exist.
Even though it faces all directions, there is no contradiction because its lack of ambiguity is established through the continuity of the context and other factors;
it is substantial (sāravat), meaning purposeful,
and irreproachable (anavadya), meaning it produces no unpleasant cognition for the learned.
He explains "without filler" (astobha) by virtue of its being the subject at hand—namely, "astobham.
To instruct one who might disagree with the explanation as it has been given, he provides another definition, saying: "For thus they say. Brevity in sentences consists in the arrangement of words.
The brevity of the words is due to the syllables, and thus there is no tautology.
This has been stated on the assumption that the relationship of cause and effect is being expressed through the analysis of the yoga;
however, in reality, it must indeed be indicated by that [yoga] as well.
For this is not the functional capacity of the *yogavibhāga* (the splitting of a rule);
rather, it is merely an indication of an additional meaning.
And since this [meaning] is obtainable even from the split [rule], he says: "mutually," and so forth.
Now, it may be objected: "In the Sūtra, only false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) is mentioned;
how then can he say 'therein, with respect to the Self and so forth'? To this he replies: "Even though that is not [explicitly] stated.
He shows that the Vārttika has the Bhāṣya as its subject matter by saying: "By this, therefore..."
The meaning is that it is certainly not like a jujube fruit in a bowl through conjunction (*saṃyoga*), or whiteness in a cloth through inherence (*samavāya*).

Now, similarity does not serve as the cause for error merely by its existence; for instance, in the case of a crystal and the like whose whiteness is overwhelmed by the proximity of a hibiscus flower or similar objects, even when there is no recollection of its specific qualities, [error occurs].
Therefore, it must be accepted that only perceived similarity is the cause of that [error].
That too is inconsistent;

since similarity (sārūpya) is the basis for difference, when that [similarity] appears, difference also appears, leaving no room for the superimposition of non-difference. Therefore, this doubt—that there is an absence of similarity between the existent and the non-existent—is itself untenable. To this, he says: "For in all cases... [sarvatra hi].
Indeed, O friend, we do not say that the apprehension of similarity occurs by taking [the object] to be "similar.

What then? If that very property—such as brilliance—which was previously perceived in silver and the like, or something of its same class, is perceived in the object present before one, then it is an error.
The meaning is that it cannot be otherwise than this.
Having shown the positive concomitance (anvaya), he states the negative concomitance (vyatireka) with the words "for not" (na hi).

Although some kind of similarity certainly exists even between elephants, mosquitoes, and so forth, nevertheless, what is intended here is a similarity that is not overwhelmed by a differentiating property.

Furthermore, since the state of not being overwhelmed by that which excludes [the object] does not exist there, it should be understood that [theories] such as "similarity in its entirety" or "similarity in one part" are thereby refuted.
He raises an objection: "Even in the case of what is dissimilar.
What is intended here is this:
For is the similarity of the superimposed object considered with respect to the locus of superimposition, or otherwise? In the latter case, there would be an over-extension [of the definition].
In the former case, however, it is not the case that the yellow quality is superimposed upon the white conch-shell which possesses the quality of whiteness.
Nor is there a yellow quality in the white quality, because the cognition "this is yellow *ciravilva*" does not arise,
and because the white quality itself does not appear [as yellow].

Nor can the quality of yellow reside in the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) of color which is the substratum of the universal "whiteness," because in visual perception, it is impossible for the unique particular of color— which is the substratum— to appear if the universal "whiteness" does not appear;
or, even if it were to appear, there would be no coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the universal "substantiality."
Nor can yellowness be a universal superimposed upon the substratum of the universal whiteness;
for would it be superimposed as being identical with that [substratum], or as being in contact with it?
In the first case, an individual entity that is the substratum of the universal "whiteness," appearing as the nature of the universal "yellowness," would not be restricted by space and time;
for it is the individual entity, and not the universal, that is restricted by space and time,
and yet that [individual] has not appeared at all.
Nor is it tenable that the universal of yellowness (*pītatvasāmānya*) alone is superimposed in the form of an individual instance of the quality white (*śuklaguṇavyakti*);
for if that were the case, yellowness would not be perceived.
Nor, again, could the universal of whiteness (*śuklatvasāmānya*) alone be superimposed as having the nature of the universal of yellowness.
If that were the case, whiteness would have to be perceived as whiteness;
for it possesses no other form whatsoever by which it could enter the path of cognition.
Furthermore, since that which is entirely unperceived cannot be the object of superimposition, this conceptual construction is indeed incoherent;

for if the universal were superimposed as something connected [to the substrate], the quality of whiteness would be perceived only as "whiteness," and there would be no gradation of intensity in the removal of the perception of yellowness.

Because a universal possesses a single form, it must be said that the yellow quality is superimposed upon the conch shell; and if that were so, what talk could there even be of similarity between a quality and its possessor? This is the meaning.

He explains: "Not even there," for in this case it is not merely the quality of yellowness that is superimposed; rather, both the yellow quality and the conch are the objects of superimposition, while what is superimposed is their state of being mixed together in nature.

And thus, in this case, what is the operative factor is the similarity between these two—which possess unmixed natures—on the one hand, and the quality and the possessor of qualities, which possess mixed natures, on the other.

Since that [similarity] has already been demonstrated, what is the use of an operative factor such as similarity with the possessor of qualities or similarity with the quality, whether it exists or does not exist? This is the meaning.

The non-apprehension of a relation (asaṃbandhāgraha) and the non-apprehension of a difference in substratum (vaiyadhikaraṇyāgraha) characterize the subject (viṣayin) by its object (viṣaya). Thus, it is stated that their similarity (sārūpya) consists in not being made the object of an apprehension of a difference in substratum,
just as yellowness [is the same] in both the *aci* fruit and the *bilva* fruit, and likewise in both the yellow substance and the conch shell.

Having established similarity (*sārūpya*) regarding two related objects presented to a single sense-faculty, he establishes similarity regarding two related objects presented to two sense-faculties with the words, "In the same way, by means of the sense of touch.
And this being so, one might argue that even in the case of an error of identity, let similarity be nothing other than the non-apprehension of difference (*bhedāgraha*).
And it must be stated that this is accomplished by means of glittering appearance and so forth,
because without those, there would be no arousal of the latent impression (saṃskāra), and without that, the rule governing the superimposition of silver would be untenable.
In this case, however, only that much is required for the awakening of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of a relation;
and the object of that relation is precisely the two things being related,
which are themselves being experienced.
"What is that [similarity] which depends on another similarity that leads [to the cognition]?"—thus everything is clarified.
Now, one might object: "But surely this sequence of experience is contradicted by actual experience"; to this he replies: "Because of extreme rapidity."

Now, if it has been established that similarity is the seed of error, then everything could be superimposed upon everything, for there exists some kind of similarity between one thing and another in some way; to this he says: "No."
Thus, regarding the "two moons":
in the illusion of two moons, there is the state of being an object of such a dependent cognition;
however, in the superimposition of mere difference, there is the connection with various directions, locations, and parts.
When there is a delusion of the west in what is actually the east, the nature of "direction" (dik-tva) remains present despite the difference between south and north.
Likewise, in other cases as well, such as in the delusion of a fire-brand's circle (alātacakra), when there is no connection with the center, there is a connection with all directions.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), it is understood that in the delusion of motion regarding one who is not moving, there is a reversal of the distinction [between the direction of motion and its opposite].
In the case of thick hair, the perception of thickness [occurs] because it covers that much space;

in the case of the illusion of a curved stick in water, it should be understood as the non-apprehension of the lack of contact between the stick and the curvature of the waves. Thus it is to be explained.
And in all cases, the non-apprehension of reality is what constitutes convergence.
In this regard, the Buddhists have established that the self (ātman) is indeed to be abandoned, just like the body, the sense faculties, and so forth, because it is a cause of suffering.
For just as the self is not capable of producing suffering without the sense faculties and the rest, so too the sense faculties and the rest are not capable [of doing so] without it.
For there is no such thing as suffering that is without a basis;
therefore, the self (*ātman*) must also be abandoned.
As Dharmakīrti has said:
If you claim that the self is the cause of suffering only in the absence of those [faculties], then they too must be of such a nature;
thus both are faultless, and from that, detachment arises toward both.
[Pravāraṇā 1.227] This, moreover, is not at all sound;

for, first of all, the abandonment of the self cannot be characterized by destruction, as in the case of a disease and so forth, because the self is eternal. Nor can it be characterized by disjunction, as in the case of a finger bitten by a venomous snake.
Nor does it have the characteristic of cessation of activity, like the death of a son and so forth, because it is self-cognized; thus say the Vedāntins.
We, however, say: that would indeed be so if suffering, while already known, were the cause of the self, as is the case with the death of a son and so forth;
but this is not the case.
What [is meant by] "merely by its existence"?
Therefore, the demonstration that the self (ātman) is to be abandoned is merely a display of impudence.
Anticipating the objection that the demonstration that the view of self (ātmadṛṣṭi) is to be abandoned is somewhat more substantial, he refutes it with the words "But not... (na tu).
The most worthy of veneration and the greatest beneficiary is the sentient being,
who is oneself.

Although the vision of selflessness (*nairātmya-darśana*) is the cause for the cessation of passion and other afflictions— this being a "sugar-coated pill" (*guḍajihvikā*)— [the Bodhisattva acts otherwise].
In reality, however, the mere vision of the absence of a permanent self is not the cause for the cessation of passion and the like,
because it would follow that the Cārvākas and others would likewise be free from passion. Rather, the vision of selflessness is the cause for the cessation of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).
If it is argued that the cessation of passion and so forth occurs from that very [knowledge],
is that [cessation] with respect to the body and such, or with respect to consciousness?
In the first case, it is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
Since the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) with respect to the body is false,
and since attachment and aversion are rooted in that [ego-sense], who indeed would not accept that when the latter ceases, the former two also cease?
Furthermore, the cessation of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) with respect to the body and so forth is not opposed to the perception of an eternal self; rather, it is actually conducive to it.
For the cognition of silver does not cease for one who has not established the distinction between mother-of-pearl and silver.
Now, if you intend to say that the cessation of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) removes passion and the like only when it has consciousness as its object,
then alas, it would follow that ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*) who do not employ the notion of "this-ness" (*idantā*) toward their own forms would be free from passion;
for they do not perceive themselves as "I" as something distinct from the body and so forth.
Now, is it intended that the cessation of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) occurs through the [realization of] external and internal objects?
And does that [cessation] occur either because of the total absence of cognition, or because even consciousness itself is merely the locus of "this-ness" (*idantā*)?
Is it because of the superimposition of non-existence upon that very [object]?
Not the first,
because it would follow that it is not a [correct] view.
And this is not accomplished even by a hundred efforts;
for in whatever way an effort is made to suppress views, in that very same way the views reassert themselves.
Furthermore, passion and the like do not cease merely through non-perception,
because we observe that even after sleeping for a thousand ages, passion and so forth reappear upon waking;
nor is the second alternative tenable.
Because when there is no "I," there is also no "this," for you yourself have stated that "the notion of another exists only when there is a self.
Nor is it the third [alternative].
Because neither grasping nor non-grasping is possible [in this case]:
for if the conscious self, which is the locus, were grasped, how could there be the superimposition of non-existence?
If it has not been apprehended, where could there be the superimposition of non-existence? Nor can you maintain that there is first an apprehension and only afterwards a superimposition.
Nor is the possibility of a negation [possible] unless it pervades that which is to be negated.

If you argue that this occurs merely through a cognition established in itself (*svapratiṣṭha*), we say no; for even though a cognition is necessarily established in itself, we observe passion and other such states [which do not negate their objects].
If you argue that [knowledge] exists when there is an absence of the surging of external forms,

then what wrong has been committed by the view that knowledge established in its own nature (*svātmapratiṣṭha*)— in the absence of the surging of external forms— is the cause for the cessation of passion and so forth?
Why, having rejected such a view, is the view of selflessness (*nairātmyadṛṣṭi*) adopted instead?
If it is argued that the view of equanimity is itself the view of selflessness,
what is this equanimity?
If it is claimed to be emptiness, [then...]
If that were the case, then even the view of one's own self would not be a "view," leading to the absurd consequence that it is not a view at all.

If you argue that its lack of connection— due to having no objective referent— is what constitutes neutrality, then why do you, like one who is asleep, prattle on about the "view of selflessness" while actually describing a view of the absence of anything belonging to a self?
In this way, the phrase "the ultimate cause" is supplied to the knowledge of the non-existence of rebirth;
and likewise,
the expression "it is also so" is a mere "sweetness on the tongue" (guḍajihvikā).
In reality, however, there is no karma,
there is no fruit of karma,
and there is no state after death.

Adopting the maxim, "One should live happily as long as one lives; there is no escape from death," he would proceed to commit the killing of living beings, the taking of what is not given, and so forth,
thinking that in this way his liberation (*kaivalya*) would be more effectively achieved.

Nor should it be said that the view of existence after death and so forth would be possible by taking the continuum as the basis; for it would indeed be possible [only] if one were to take that [continuum] as the basis.
