If that view were to turn one away from what is harmful and lead one toward what is beneficial, then it would be that very same view which performs engagement and withdrawal; yet it is not so, because those two are rooted in passion and hatred, which that view produces.
And likewise, such a view of a continuum (saṃtāna) must also be abandoned;
for if it were not such, it would simply result in nihilism (nāstikatva). This is what was said: "This is like the fear of a scorpion."

Therefore, for one who seeks the next world, effort toward heaven or liberation is possible only by accepting a self that persists into the next world; however, for one who does not admit a permanent self—such as the Cārvāka—heaven and liberation do not exist at all. How then could there be any activity for their sake? Bearing this intention in mind, he says: "This [is it]," etc.
As for what was said—"seeing oneself as worthy of honor"—to whom does this apply?
Is it to one who does not see the benefit of the cessation of all suffering, or to one who does see it?
If it is the former, then that is so.
For such a person, the view of selflessness is not tenable;
indeed, no one considers the mere annihilation of the self to be beneficial, but rather, desiring to abandon suffering, one abandons the self.

Thinking that suffering cannot be abandoned without abandoning the self, it follows that for one who does not wish to abandon suffering and desires to acquire happiness, the view of selflessness is simply impossible.
Thus, for such a person—whether they possess the view of selflessness or the view of a permanent self—saṃsāra remains the same.
The second alternative, however, is entirely untenable.
For one does not regard the mere eradication of all suffering as a benefit, yet strives for the sake of happiness and that benefit;
moreover, it is a contradiction to say that the eradication of all suffering is itself happiness.
Likewise, it is inconsistent to claim that while desiring the eradication of all suffering, one simultaneously causes harm to others.
For it is not by keeping in mind that "offending others is the cause for the eradication of all suffering" that he says, "and because of being more venerable."
The common property is the state of being the locus of the "I-notion" (*ahaṃkāra*).
This refers to being the object of the grammatical subject (*kartṛpada*) in the expression "I";
by this, it indicates a portion of agency (*kartṛtva*), which is the basis for the application of that term.
Therefore, the meaning is this:

having observed that [the self] is the instigator of other causal factors and yet is itself impelled by external causal factors, and failing to grasp the distinction between them, one superimposes agency upon the body and so forth, thereby mistaking them for the Self. This is what was stated: "Indeed, that... and so on.

Having thus established that the opposite [view] consists in the nature of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*), the remainder of the sense is "being particularly doubtful" at present. Now, one might object: "It is well known even to cowherd women that this cognition of a thief has arisen for me with respect to a post; therefore, there is no doubt here at all. To this, he says: "of the investigators" (*parīkṣakāṇām*).
The meaning is that there is no distinction—that is, no difference—between the cognizer and the object to be cognized.
Now, one might object: in the cognition "this is silver," two things appear.
The nature of cognition and the object present before one;
therein, when the silver-nature of the object present before one is negated,
By implication, it follows that this applies to knowledge; however, for others, there is no concern at all because they simply do not ascend to such realization.
Therefore, how can it be said [that this occurs] in places such as market streets?
Therefore, he says: "But how can its internal nature, which has never been perceived before, be established?

For when something has been known to belong to one thing at some time, it is understood to belong to that other thing through the method of elimination (pāriśeṣya) upon the negation of its presence elsewhere."

But this is not the case when two things have entered the path of cognition; for if one is negated, then by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the other would acquire [the property] even if it were impossible for it.

If that were so, then in the negation of "silver-ness" in mother-of-pearl through the judgment "this is not silver," the status of being silver would be attributed even to earth and other elements that are associated with it in the same single cognition.
Yet such is not the case.
For what reason?
Because its state of being silver has never been perceived at any time; for thus...
Even one's own self never becomes the object of anyone's perception as having the nature of silver, even in a dream.
Now, if your intention is that the nature of silver is indeed perceived as belonging to the self in the cognition of real silver,
then this is merely dreaming.
For even there, when silver standing before one is being experienced, what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has as its object the fact that the self possesses the form of silver?
By this, it is shown that there is an absence of any proving means of valid cognition for the externality of one's own form.
The subverting proof (*bādhaka*) has also been indicated:

for just as the negation of "silver-ness" in the object present before one occurs by the force of the subverting cognition "this is not silver," so too the cognition "I am not silver" is clearly a subverting proof as well.

If you say, "This very thing is the error," then the intention is this: in that case, silver-ness is not superimposed upon the external object; rather, externality is superimposed upon that very locus of the "I" (the internal self).
If that were the case, then that very [notion] would have to be removed by the subverting cognition;
and once it is removed, there would be the thought "I am silver.
This being so, what would be the meaning of "this is silver"?
"I am not silver.
What is the meaning of "this is not silver"?
[It means] "I am silver."

Furthermore, just as there can be no misconception of a synthesis between "this is not this" and "I am not I" due to their mutual contradiction, so too there could be no misconception of a synthesis between "this is not silver" and "I am not silver" because of their mutual contradiction. Yet such a misconception does exist; therefore, the negation of silverhood in both cases establishes silverhood in something else. This is like a line carved in stone, which cannot be removed merely by filling it with dust. It cannot be refuted by such a trivial means.
The excellence of capacity is an excellence of intrinsic nature;
however, this excellence is relative to the cognition produced by the object.
The phrase "as if existing" intends either true knowledge or the thing's own essential nature.
"Capacity of the object" (*viṣayasāmarthya*) means causal capacity (*kāraṇatva*), because its existence has not been established;
it is for this very reason that even certain followers of the Vedānta [hold this view].
The acceptance of the Buddhist doctrine of formlessness (nirākāravāda) has been demonstrated;
it is not conceptualized as "grasping by way of existence or non-existence" because that [position] is utterly refuted.
For in the present context, it is the object conducive to activity that appears.
But it is not possible for activity to occur by grasping [an object] as being either existent or non-existent; rather,
it is precisely the non-existent silver that appears, and because of the failure to grasp its difference from the thing present before one, [it is mistaken for mother-of-pearl].

The statement beginning with "activity does not occur elsewhere" is not subject to doubt, because it shares the same logical status as the Prābhākara position and because the theory of apoha will be refuted later.
He refutes the theory of the manifestation of the indefinable (*anirvacanīyakhyāti*) by pointing out its contradiction with experience, beginning with "And not...":
for instance, what is this "indefinability"? Is it simply the absence of a definition?
Or is it simply the absence of the cause for verbal designation?
It cannot be the first case,
because [the cognition] occurs as "this is silver" and "this is not silver."
Because verbal designation (*nirukti*) is being experienced.
Nor is the second [alternative] possible:
would the cause of verbal designation be a cognition or an object?
First of all, there is no absence of the first [type of manifestation], because manifestation itself is not admitted [by you]. Nor is there an absence of the second.
Is the object also of a positive nature or of a negative nature?

In the first case, there would be the undesirable consequence of accepting the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*). In the second case, however, it is simply the theory of the manifestation of the existent (*satkhyāti*).
If you say that neither exist,
then by the terms "existence" and "non-existence," do you intend those two things established by worldly consensus,
or their opposites? First, regarding the former:
Just as there is no affirmation of both, so too there is no negation,
because affirmation and negation are mutually inseparable from one another's affirmation and negation.
In the second case, however, there is no deficiency whatsoever;
for even if thousands of non-worldly objects cease to exist, there is neither the cessation of the object of true knowledge nor the cessation of its definition.
Or, is it that [the world] lacks intrinsic nature and is inexpressible?

Here too, since the prefix *nis-* has the sense of negation, if the word "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) also signifies either existence or non-existence, the same undesirable consequence follows as before.
If it is argued that "being beyond the scope of cognition" is what constitutes "lack of intrinsic nature," then there is a contradiction with one's own words here.
It is both the object of dependent origination and that which is dependently originated.
If you argue that "whatever is perceived in a certain way is not actually so," we do not disagree with this point.
Therefore, even by those who maintain the theory of the indefinable manifestation of forms (akhyāti-anirvacanīya-khyāti), the theory of misapprehension (anyathākhyāti) must necessarily be accepted.

Now, one might object: "If the world-appearance (prapañca) manifests in a certain way while being non-existent, then let the universal (jāti) and so forth also be exactly like that. To this he says: "But as for that which...
If it were non-existent, it would manifest merely as non-existence;
it would not be the object of purposeful activity (pravṛtti).
If you mean by "existence," then surely similarity must also be required;
yet that does not exist.
The meaning is that there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) even in the case of manifesting something dissimilar by means of its existence.
"Contrary to consciousness" means contrary to the consciousness under investigation;
it should also be understood as the consequence of [the subject] becoming omniscient regarding all things, and the consequence of attaining supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) of the past and future.
The meaning is that a cognition arises which bears the imprint of that which is appearing.
The seed of *śyāmāka* millet is cited with the intention of referring to auxiliary factors conducive to the production of the normal effect;

the seed of *kṛtaja* [millet] is cited with the intention of referring to the presence of other obstructing causes. In a case of doubt that is the subject of dispute, the cause for engagement [in action] would be either non-apprehension [of the object] or [the apprehension of its opposite].
Is it the cognition "this," or the cognition "silver" together with that, or both together with the non-apprehension of their difference?
Regarding that, the refutation begins with "First of all, not... for the first case;
with "Alas, O sir! for the second;
and with "Now, the cognition of silver... for the third.
But in the fourth case, when the attainment of equality occurs, is the qualifier the property of cognition— namely non-apprehension—
or is it the property of the object?
In the first alternative, there is no equality.
For it is not accepted that the cognition of both [aspects], when their difference is not grasped, serves as a cause for error.
In the second case, however, the properties of the object, if unknown, are of no use toward the activity [of the subject];
yet they certainly do exist for the sake of cognition.
Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "Not so, for the causes of knowledge," and so forth.

Alternatively, even when the visible causes are identical, an error may arise due to the influence of a specific invisible cause, because the causal complex (sāmagrī) must be inferred from its effect.
This is what was stated: "Not so," and so forth.
If it is argued that the same applies to me as well— no,
because that specific cause does not function independently;
this is what was stated by the word "intelligent" (cetana).
If it is argued that [the agent acts] by means of knowledge—no, because that [knowledge] is common to both engagement and withdrawal.
This very point has been stated: "But if [action] were preceded by cognition... and so forth.
Therefore, there is no parity [between the two cases].
The formulation beginning with "its establishment" (*tatsiddhi*) is directed toward one who holds a contrary view.

The terms "by necessity" (*niyamena*) and "with certainty" (*niścayena*) are intended to indicate the exclusion of the idea that a general cognition can lead to the engagement with a particular object.
Nor is there any inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) due to the knowledge of the result, precisely because that [knowledge] does not incite action;
rather, it is the knowledge of the means to achieve that which incites action,
and that [knowledge] has only that [means] as its object.
However, it will be refuted that the cognition of "being an effect" (kāryatva) is what prompts action.
Regarding the argument based on the reason "because it does not appear [as such]," the fault is either "unestablished" (asiddha) or "proving what is already established" (siddhasādhana).
But as for the description of perception, we also agree that its objective support is not in the form of "mother-of-pearl-ness."
The ultimate point is that it is contrary to experience for something to fail to appear simply because it lacks white luminosity.

Regarding the reason "because of being defective," the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) is pointed out; however, if one merely points to an example, things such as the seeds of the *vetra* reed may be cited.
The statement "this is not silver" is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).
The statement "this is mother-of-pearl," and so forth, should also be understood in this way.
Furthermore, would this lack of confidence consist in the absence of knowledge regarding the correspondence [of the cognition] to reality, or in doubt as to whether it corresponds to reality or not?
The first alternative is refuted by the very explanation of the means for determining validity.
But he says that the second [type of inference] is indeed accepted as being preceded by the perception of a specific property—namely, "And just as... and so forth.
Now, it may be objected: "Was it not already stated that the reversal of sequence was intended to establish beginninglessness?

What, then, is the purpose of establishing beginninglessness again? To this he says: "And because of beginninglessness," [meaning] "lest there be the consequence of that [reversal] also being sublated."

And thus, the sense is that there would follow the consequence of no distinction between true abandonment and false knowledge. "Demonstrating the falsity of the previous cognition" means that it arises by way of not being able to tolerate the mode [of reality] demonstrated by that [previous cognition].
"Obstructing the activity produced by that" intends the designation appropriate to it;
the meaning is "forming a contrary intention.
"It takes away its fruit" means from the object up to the final result.

This very "deprivation of the object" consists in the production of a nature that rejects that object; and since it extends to the rejection of the stream of its results, this is the collective meaning. [The phrase] "of two things whose properties consist in mutual non-existence" means: The collective meaning is as follows: this very deprivation of the object consists in the arising of a nature that rejects that object, and that [nature] culminates in the rejection of the flow of its results. Regarding the phrase "of two things whose properties consist in mutual non-existence":
The meaning is: "of those two properties belonging to the two subjects which are perceived as being mutually non-existent.
This is the reason for their sublation.
The meaning is that the definition of the inferential mark (*liṅga*) is its being characterized by the absence of the reason (*hetu*).
"A stream of cognitions whose object is reality" means meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).
A "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*) is an underlying single nature, which is a property that excludes [the subject] from both similar and dissimilar classes; this is what is meant. //2//
// Purity //
"Because it is easily accessible everywhere.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the scripture does not possess an inherent threefold nature, since it is dependent upon persons.
Regarding "the purpose":
The meaning is "of the intermediate [state].
The phrase "it becomes fourfold" implies "it becomes an object of cognition. This is because there would be a contradiction with what was stated regarding the reversal of the object.
This is a restatement of the means of valid cognition (pratyakṣa-pramāṇa).

Therefore, there is neither the fault of being non-different from the probandum (sādhyāviśiṣṭatva) nor the fault of having a different locus (vyadhikaraṇatva). Furthermore, in the case of a rabbit's horn and the like, which are being examined, there is no defining characteristic (alakṣaṇa).
However, when something exists but is useless—as in the case of the sands of the Ganges and the like—there is no definition [of it].
Therefore, because one perceives common properties while a distinction is absent, doubt arises; the undertaking of the [section on] distinction is for the purpose of removing that doubt.
But surely, if doubt regarding what is useless is not eliminated, what would happen?
Would it not be that the desire to know (*jijñāsā*)—as to how that [useless thing] is useless—would remain unextinguished?

Furthermore, there would be doubt even regarding *arthāpatti* and the others, which possess utility and whose definitions are proclaimed by others, because their definitions have not been formulated: "Are they non-existent because no definition has been formulated?"
Or are they useless?
Or are they included within those very same [categories]?
Therefore, for the sake of resolving these [questions], there is this classification.
Likewise, in comparison with the Buddhists, the Mīmāṃsakas state definitions for additional means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) even though there is no increase in the actual number of such means;
whereas for the Sāṃkhya, the statement of definitions for additional means of valid cognition occurs only when there is an actual increase.
Thus, here too, there arises a doubt regarding the mention of additional [means] in comparison with the Sāṃkhya.
Is there an excess of truth or not? To dispel that doubt, the statement of distinction is made.
For this very reason, having raised the suspicion of an excess, the author of the Sūtras undertook an examination of the distinction.
It should also be understood that the consistency between the preceding and subsequent sections of the text is clear in this regard as well.
The root of the non-acceptance of *śakti* (potency) is the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
because the presumption (*arthāpatti*) [of its existence] is exhausted once the production of an effect is accounted for by visible causes alone that lack a counteragent.
Furthermore, the status of being a counteragent belongs to mantras and the like, insofar as they consist in the absence of auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*).
And because their status as auxiliary causes is determined through the method of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) regarding their absence;
for there are indeed three types of entities that follow upon an effect.
These are its favorable factors, its unfavorable factors, and those that are neutral toward it.
Among these, wind and so forth are favorable to fire and the like;
likewise, there are also those that are unfavorable.
They are of two kinds: by way of their own nature and by way of being auxiliary causes.
By way of their own nature are the sprinkling of water and so forth;
by way of being auxiliary causes are those who employ mantras and the like.
For those who employ mantras and the like oppose a cooperative cause characterized by the absence of that [mantra],
whereas donkeys and the like remain indifferent in that very situation.
In this context, conformity is established through the pleasure of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*);
whereas opposition is understood through the absence of the effect when that [cause] is present,
which ultimately results from the presence of its opposite.
And indifference is to be understood through deviation.
This being the case, wherever, whenever, and for whomever there is evidence of favorability or unfavorability in a particular manner, it must be accepted as such at that time and in that way.

What is the point of postulating an additional capacity? Furthermore, for our opponents, the possibility of such an inquiry is equally applicable even regarding supersensible capacities; thus, setting aside *arthāpatti* (presumption), he considers another possible ground for accepting supersensible power by raising a doubt: "It might be so," and so forth.

The meaning of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is this: while the essential nature [of the cause] is perceptible and its totality is indicated solely through its effects, there remains a supersensible capacity that must be inferred.
The meaning is "the state of being connected with an effect" or "being characterized by an effect.
As it has been said: "the form qualified by an effect.
Now, is this qualification by an effect [of one thing] due to another effect, or indeed by its own effect?
In the first case, that which is not a cause would itself be the cause; in the second case, however, there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*),
for only when its status as the cause of that [other] is established could its status as the effect of that [other] be established.

And since causality would be characterized by that [effect] only if it were its effect, he says: "This very thing is its being conditioned by that (tadupadhāna), namely, its necessary existence prior to the production of that effect.
The meaning is: that which necessarily exists prior to the production of something is the cause, and the other is the effect.
Now, would such causality be inferred generally for that which belongs to that class, or for each individual instance? It cannot be for each individual instance,
because some [instances] are seen to perish even when their subsequent effect is absent.

However, [the opponent might argue] that since a member of that class has already been determined in a general sense, it is merely being remembered here; anticipating this objection, he says: "And not of a member of that class.
Just as, even though there is a general determination that "whatever is smoke possesses fire," it is not yet determined that "this particular smoke possesses fire."
The meaning is that this water is determined to be for the purpose of allaying thirst, even though it has not yet been definitively ascertained as such.
Nor is there any deviation [in the logical rule] when something perishes without having performed its effect anywhere,
because the probandum is "it would perform [the effect] provided there were a completeness of auxiliary causes."
And because that [state], which consists in the absence of the effect due to the deficiency of auxiliary causes, exists there as well.

Therefore, that which is not the cause for the production of either [pleasure or pain] through effort is the third, namely, the indifferent cognition (*upekṣābuddhi*). Thus, there is a distinction between cognitions due to a distinction in their objects;
and since that [indifferent cognition] is threefold—being the cause of pleasure, the cause of pain, or the cause of neither—it is very clearly established. This is the meaning.

Since the author of the Bhāṣya, while explaining the term *anumāna*, has incidentally stated its definition as well, the author of the Ṭīkā also demonstrates what is excluded by [the mention of] memory (*smṛti*) and so forth, beginning with the words "And thus" (*tathā ca*).

He says, "Having restated this very Bhāṣya," because the definition was indeed stated in the Bhāṣya; therefore, the objection raised against it in the Vārttika is not a criticism of what was not said.
Since that which possesses a fruit is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
and since inference is a specific form of it, it is not logical for it to be without a fruit.
Even if some other fruit were possible in some way, the consideration of the mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*) is the fruit of this [inference], just as it is the fruit of perception.
It should also be understood from the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) that well-established inference is pervaded by this [definition].
And this being the case, the connection with the resolution beginning with "therein" (*tatra*) and so forth is appropriate.
Thus, he states another resolution.
To the question "In what [context] is there an objection?", he says: "That which was stated previously."

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that when the validity of inference is said to have 'rejection' (*hāna*) and so forth as its object, it is stated only with respect to its own specific domain (*svagocara*), since its functional operation (*vyāpāra*) is necessarily connected only to rejection and the like? Therefore, this doubt is itself untenable; what need is there for a resolution here? Anticipating this objection, [the author] states: "Because its functional operation is necessarily connected [to them], rejection and the like constitute its domain."
However, because the cognition of fire is invariably connected with its opposite, fire alone is its object;
and with this intention, the [author] states "even though" (*yadyapi*), intending that the doubt and its resolution are made from that perspective.
The meaning is: that which appears in the cognition, by means of which the cognition is defined.
Nor is another object distinct from its own object possible for this [cognition], because it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga); such is the sense.
The words "of the opponent" (pūrvapakṣiṇaḥ) are to be supplied.
"Autpattika" means not dependent on [external] nature.

Now, by what distinction are the cognitions of what is to be abandoned and so forth the fruit of the second inference, and not of the second perception? He says: "By virtue of its penetration into an object that is beyond the senses."

Now, one might object: "When it is stated that 'the measure (māna) of proximity—that is, similarity—is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the determination of the name and the named,' how can there be any room for contradiction?
To this, he says: "Like the word 'inference' (anumāna)," and so forth.

Is it not the case that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is, by its very nature, a means of valid cognition insofar as it delimits its own object, since a specific cause possessing an operation is what constitutes a *pramāṇa*? Nor is the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence the fruit of this [cognition].
At that time, it [the word] has perished;

nor can the recollection of the word itself be its result, because even when there is a recollection of the word, that [result] is absent for those who have not grasped the linguistic convention (*samaya*) and for whom the object is not being remembered. Therefore, he says: "Indeed, as in the case of Caitra..."
[Objection: But surely inference and the other means of knowledge also possess primacy in the determination of their own respective objects;

so why [is it said] "because perception is primary"? To this, the proponent of the single-part (ekadeśin) says: "For [all means of knowledge] have perception as their ultimate goal. This means that, for the most part, they are directly preceded by perception alone.
The meaning is that, in an indirect sense, all inference is indeed of that nature.
As for analogy (*upamāna*), although it is preceded by perception, it is nonetheless preceded by verbal testimony (*śabda*);
for its being preceded by perception occurs only when it is already preceded by verbal testimony.
The meaning is that the state of being preceded by perception belongs exclusively to inference alone.

If this is so, one might object: "In that case, let analogy (upamāna) be mentioned immediately after verbal testimony (śabda). To this he replies: "Because it requires the assistance of recollection" (*smaraṇasahakāritā*).

Although even for the means of knowledge called verbal testimony—which consists of sentences—sentence-meaning is communicated only when the words are present in memory and thus assisted by the recollection of word-meanings, nevertheless, there is no instance where [analogy] functions as a sign (*liṅga*) for something currently being experienced. Furthermore, although the specific designation of verbal testimony is established by logic, the statement of its purpose here follows the view of a partial proponent (*ekadeśin*).

Although the view of the "Partialist" (ekadeśin) was already intended as faulty in order to demonstrate his lack of skill, the author of the *Vārttika* introduces the subsequent text without fully refuting it, merely to teach that even such a flawed argument can be countered with a fallacious refutation: "This, then, is the view of the Partialist.
Some [hold] that perception comes first because of its primacy.

If another person, being talkative, says that the teaching of verbal testimony (*śabda*) comes first because its scope is vast, and intends thereby to establish what was previously stated, then [the response is as follows]: the quality of having a vast scope is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For one who, while asserting that verbal testimony is primary due to its vast scope, also maintains that perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not primary, a different example must be cited.

Thus, since "having a vast scope" is found even in perception—which is a heterogeneous instance (*vipakṣa*) such as the cognition of a variegated [color]—the meaning is that the quality of having a vast scope is inconclusive.
This [is the case] in the context of a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga); however, in the case of an independent proof (svatantra-sādhana), the reason is "mistimed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa),
because the fact that sound is the last [of the sense objects] and that perception is the first [of the means of knowledge] are established by direct perception itself.
Furthermore, it should be observed that in the case of a negative concomitance (vyatireka), there is also the fault of being contradictory (viruddha).
Regarding the phrase "because of having a vast scope": the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) being taught previously is the subject (dharmin).

The common property [of being] "because of having a great object" gives rise to the doubt: "Is it perception or is it verbal testimony? The sense is that, due to this commonality, it cannot serve as a logical reason (*hetu*).

The purpose is to demonstrate its preeminence; the meaning is that if preeminence were not established without priority, then inference (*anumāna*) would also have to occupy the first position because of its own preeminence.

Now, if there is no overlap [between the objects of perception and inference], what loss is there for us? Or if there were such overlap, what would happen that the author of the Bhāṣya would have undertaken this investigation? To this he says: "This might be so.
Because perception has a fixed domain, its operation upon the domain of inference would then not occur.
If it were thought that inference (*anumāna*) also has a fixed object, he says: "And [the object] of inference is not of the nature of a universal.
Therefore, this is not a redundant statement.
The meaning of the phrase "the reason for not explaining" is the cause for removing the doubt as to why it was not explained.

Regarding the phrase "for [it is] by means of what is doubtful," one should understand that, given the authority of the instruction, this applies to fire as well at a later time through that same door; therefore, there is no contradiction with the statement "one for whom a cognition—a certainty—has been brought about or produced with respect to fire.

By mentioning a single part with the words "he considers it to be most venerable," he causes us to recall the previously stated justification for the convergence (*saṃplava*) of the means of knowledge.

But one might object: "Even though there is no difference in the fact that both result in certainty, why is it that the cessation of expectancy occurs through perception alone? To this he says: "In the first place, this...
The meaning is that such is the very nature of direct realization, which is the fruit of perception.
Now, since "limb" (*aṅga*) and "qualification" (*viśeṣaṇa*) have the same meaning, why is it explained as being "pervasive" (*vyāpakatvena*)?
And why is the path shown by the former teachers abandoned? To this he says: "Because that [latter interpretation] is irrelevant to the present context."
The essential characteristic of perception is its nature as a direct cause capable of terminating expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*); this quality does not exist in inference and the like.
For it is the established point that there is no termination of expectancy regarding an object determined by inference and so forth;
nor is the absence of that [quality] in inference and the like demonstrated merely by showing their capacity to grasp a qualified object.
The meaning is that even though perception grasps a qualified object, it does not [grasp] that [qualified nature as a whole];
this is because each of the established [constituents] is singular, which means its object is not mixed with a second [element].
Thus ends the first chapter consisting of three sūtras in the *Tātparya-pariśuddhi*.
// The Chapter on the Means of Valid Cognition //
// Purity //
The phrase "of the specific definitions of the means of valid cognition such as perception" is for the purpose of stating their essential nature (*svarūpa*).
As for the words beginning with "for a definition," and the term "implied by the object" (*arthākṣipta*), [they serve to show that a definition is not merely a verbal description].
This is for the purpose of explaining the connection with the nature of the subject under discussion.

For a definition (lakṣaṇa) is intended to instruct one who desires to know; and that [instruction] regarding a particular (viśeṣa) is not possible for one who has not yet ascertained the general (sāmānya).
General cognition is dependent upon its definition; therefore, that definition [is stated].
Having made a distinction between the general and the particular, and having aroused the student's desire to know, the introduction to the specific definition follows.

Thus, because the knowledge consisting of the general definition, its divisions, and its enumeration serves as a cause for the knowledge of the specific definition by way of generating the desire to know, it is said—intending to express a causal relationship even between their respective objects—that [the former] exists "by way of being a cause."

Since exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is not its denotation, he says: "the purpose" (*prayojana*). [In this context,] inference and so forth are of the same class (*samānajātīya*) insofar as they are means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whereas that which is non-perceptual (*apratyakṣa*) is indeed of a different class (*vijātīya*).
Therefore, the definition is not over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇya*).

The state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣakatva*) is a characteristic property (*lakṣaṇadharma*). Therefore, it is inconsistent [to say] that this is its purpose. Consequently, having extracted the action—which is the result—from the causal factor (*kāraka*), he shows: "the state of being a qualifier is the qualification (*viśeṣa*)."
The meaning is the demonstration of perception as excluded from its opposite.
To the question, "Who, then, will be demonstrated by this definition? he says: "He who indeed...
And not all people are deluded.
Otherwise, there would be no distinction between the object of instruction and the instructor;
nor would there be universal delusion, which would lead to an infinite regress; nor would all things be causes of delusion, which would result in a total lack of comprehension.
And it is not the case that there is no apprehension at all [of the subject], by which there would be the fallacy of the unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhi); such is the intended meaning.
Now, since the definiendum (lakṣya) is unestablished, how can it be the subject (dharmin)? Or, if it were established, what would be the use of a definition?
Furthermore, what is its denotation?
If it were asserted that [the definition] would be the primary object [of the statement], he says "therefore" (tasmāt).
Now, if the definition is already well-known, what is there to be enjoined?
For it is not well-known.

If it is [already] established, how can it be a definition, since it would not be something previously unknown? To this he says: "But from this [text], its definition is understood. Because it is not already known to the person to be instructed, it is something to be enjoined, like the Agnihotra and other such rites.
But it is not [unestablished] because the means of communication is unestablished.

And the meaning is that the object to be communicated, by the very cognition of the injunction, subsequently accomplishes the goal—just as one accomplishes a sacrifice after [cognizing its] definition.
This means that the cognition of the qualified object is conceptual (savikalpaka).

[Objection: Surely the contact between the sense organ and its object is not the sole cause of perception, because even when that contact exists, it is not established in the case of atoms and the like, nor in the case of jars and the like when they are separated from the sense organ by an intervening barrier; therefore, this definition is unproven. To this, he replies: "By the inclusion of the term 'object' (artha)."
Now, one might object: "But surely universals such as 'color-ness' (rūpatva) do not exist at all;
so for what purpose is the admission of inherence-in-the-inherent-in-the-conjoined (saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya)? To this, he says: "And not... (na ca).
Now, one might ask: even for those who find it acceptable that similarity (sādṛśya) is a distinct entity (arthāntara), why would there be a contradiction?
For nothing contrary to that has been accepted here. To this, he says: "Of them... (teṣām).

One might object: "Surely there will be either the apprehension of that which is not in contact, or the apprehension of that which has a substrate in contact; so how can there be a contradiction? To this he says: "Otherwise.

For if there were apprehension of that which is not in contact, there would be a contradiction with the accepted doctrine that the sense organs function by reaching their objects (*indriyaprāpyakāritā*).
However, if there is apprehension of that which has a proximate substratum, there is a contradiction with the accepted doctrine of "inherence in what is conjoined" (*saṃyuktasamavāya*).
And if there is no apprehension, there is a contradiction with that very doctrine, because there is a lack of evidence; such is the meaning.
To the objection—"Since a fourth contact is not experienced, how can there be a contradiction regarding it?"—he replies: "For they are indeed experienced.

The meaning is that since the experience of *rūpatva* (the nature of color) and so forth is the effect of a fourth contact, by accepting that [experience], one contradicts the denial of that [contact]. This is because a cognition of a qualified object (*upahita*) would otherwise be impossible.
The meaning is that the designation based upon that [root], being superimposed, would be untenable in its absence.

Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the perception of form and so forth as qualified by universals and particulars such as "form-ness" (*rūpatva*), apart from the perception of those very things. If the specific perception of the mutually distinct [objects] such as the eye and so forth were itself the means of valid cognition, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*parasparāśrayatva*). Nor can the mere sense-faculty, brought forward by a non-specific perception alone, be accepted as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for the designation of "form" and so on; for if that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of designating taste and other objects as "form" and so forth. Bearing this intention in mind, he says: "Nor are the sense-faculties... This [statement] is based on the conviction that [the designation of form] is dependent upon limiting adjuncts such as "being visible to the eye" (*cākṣuṣatva*).
The claim that there is no difference in the designation of "form" and so forth for another [object] has already been cited and refuted;
however, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), even that [designation] does not exist when there is no difference in the designations of "blue," "sweet," and so on.
"Even by that much, our desired objective is attained.
However, since the status of being a "sound" (śabdatva) has not been established, [the author] concludes with the general statement "therefore" (tasmāt), intending [to prove it] from that point.

[Objection: But surely there is no apprehension of anything as a qualification of the sense organ; if that [object] is apprehended as a qualification of something else, what does the contact with the sense organ have to do with it? To this he says: "And by way of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇabhāvena*).

Nor should it be argued that, since both [inherence and the relation of being a qualifier] are included by the term "being a qualifier," the fourfold [contact] should also be included by the term "inherence" (*samavāya*).

Because pure qualification (*viśe�ṣaṇabhāva*) is not a factor in perception, while qualified [qualification] is easily available as a factor therein; and because even pure inherence (*samavāya*), being a factor in perception, is the subject under discussion, the word "that" (*tat*) is exhausted by denoting only that much.
The Vārttika states: "Because of the qualifier-qualified relationship (viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva) both in the case of inherence (samavāya) and in the case of non-existence (abhāva).
But that is untenable, because the existence of inherence and its perceptibility are unestablished; therefore, he says: "the parts," and so forth.
But surely, only the parts and the whole are perceived, and not their relation as well; to this he says: "Not otherwise.
For it is of such a nature that...
The meaning is that practice, by turning away from things that are not mutually connected, comes to rest in those that are mutually connected.

Now, one might ask: "Are not 'sāmānādhikaraṇya' and 'connection with a common substratum' synonyms? So what has been stated by this [term]? Bearing this intention in mind, he asks: "But what [is meant] by..."?

For here, the substance does not manifest as a locus, like a bowl, nor do whiteness and clothness manifest as located therein, like jujube fruits; rather, the cognition occurs precisely through non-difference, such that "that which is white is the very same as the cloth. Bearing this intention in mind, he raises the objection: "If it is argued that there is identity (*tādātmya*)."
Tautology of the cognition consists in its having a meaning that is neither less nor more than that of the preceding [cognition].

For if there were indeed no difference between the quality and the possessor of the quality, then, because the two words expressing them would have the same referent, they could not be used together—just as in the case of the words *taru* and *vṛkṣa*.
When it is said, "Bring the cloth," one might bring anything whatsoever that is white.
Because that very thing is a cloth,
the statement "the cloth is non-white" would be as contradictory as saying "the cloth is non-cloth.
Furthermore, just as even a blind person has the cognition "this is a cloth," they would likewise have the cognition "this is white."

Alternatively, it might be argued that the cognition of the cloth would not occur just as the cognition of whiteness does not; for just as whiteness is concealed when combined with saffron dye and the like, the cloth too would be concealed and thus not perceived— this being the sense of the rebuttal, which holds that perception itself, aided by such reasoning, apprehends the difference between the cloth and its whiteness.
For all this criticism applies only if there were absolute non-difference; we, however, are proponents of non-absolutism (anekāntavāda).
Thus, by taking difference into account, there is no redundancy.
And because grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is based upon non-difference, he says: "Nor is there one single entity.
The meaning is that difference and non-difference are mutually contradictory;
for difference is well-established among both common people and investigators.

The opponent asserts that the cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for non-difference; however, it has already been considered below that such a cognition does not represent non-difference. Therefore, since difference and non-difference as established in common worldly experience are unmixed, they are indeed contradictory.
Alternatively, that which is called "difference-and-non-difference" might be *samavāya* (inherence), which is distinct from the worldly difference and non-difference.
Whether it be mere cognition or both [cognition and an object], in either case there is no loss of our position; with this intention, he concludes: "Therefore..."
Now, even if the cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) does not explicitly represent identity (*tādātmya*),
nevertheless, by being excluded from both difference and relation, it must establish either non-difference or a relation of non-difference.
For the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:
The whiteness and the cloth are neither distinct nor related, because they possess grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
On the other hand, those things which are both distinct and related do not possess coreferentiality, as in the case of "curd in a bowl."
But these [words] are not like that;
therefore, with the intention that they are "not thus," he raises the following objection: "Even if there is a connection..."
This would indeed be so, if its distinction from difference and relation were inherent;
however, [it is like] "the cloth is red."

He states that [the difference] is conditioned by a distinction in the function of words, as in the case of "The boy is fire," whereas the distinction in the function of words is itself conditioned by convention— by saying "not by the word" and so forth—
and [he provides the reason] "due to grammatical coreferentiality" (sāmānādhikaraṇyāt).
If it is argued that the reason is "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) because it is excluded from both difference and relation just as it is from non-difference and relation—

where the probandum is "that which is non-different and related," and there exists nothing accepted by both disputants that is of such a nature from which [the reason] could be excluded, thereby making the reason uncommon— the answer is no.
For the exclusion of both [alternatives] as the final conclusion is not established even by mere wishful thinking.
For how can that which is non-different be related,
since relation has difference as its basis?
And how can that which is related be non-different?
Because there is no relation between them by virtue of that very [identity].
If it is argued that they are distinct, even so, the relation is established only by taking their difference as the basis, and not by taking their non-difference as the basis.
And since relation is pervaded by difference alone,
while non-difference is pervaded by the absence of relation, how is the proposition "in a non-different relation" not contradicted?
If it is argued that this is by taking into account a distinction of modes— no, [it is not].
Because of its non-existence;
for a substance does not possess the nature of a quality, nor does a quality possess the nature of a substance.
By which there would be non-difference.
And according to the manner stated, there is indeed difference;
if it is argued that there is non-difference by virtue of existence (*sattva*), what is this "existence"— is it being (*sattā*)?
Or its own nature?
First, as for its own nature,
a quality is simply a quality.

Substance is indeed substance; but how can existence (*sattā*), which is common to those two [particular substances] while being distinct from them as something shared by many, be their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)? If it is argued that it is so in some respect, [we reply:]...
We do not perceive any unique form of *sattā* (existence) that is distinct from the common forms of substance, quality, and action, by which it might exist as such.

Likewise, we do not perceive any other intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) among those substances, qualities, and actions that is unmixed with one another; for if that which is perceived were said to be non-different, it has already been explained that either *sattā* would not exist, or those [substances, qualities, and actions] themselves would not exist.
Therefore, for substance and quality, existence (*sattā*) alone is their common nature, essence, property, and qualifier; this is the meaning.
For substance-ness and quality, substance alone is their essence, the possessor of properties (*dharmin*), and the qualified; this is the meaning, since there is only one qualified [entity].

Because both words and cognitions have as their objects two qualifiers, others—such as [the followers of] Guṇa and Guṇin—maintained either non-difference or both difference and non-difference; thus, he says by way of introduction: "But of words... (śabdānāṃ tu).
But surely, the cognition of distinction (*vivekakhyāti*) between things that are absolutely distinct, whether by time or by space, is observed;

and since that [cognition] is excluded from both the quality (*guṇa*) and the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*), it must also exclude the absolute difference (*aikāntika-bheda*) pervaded by it. To this he replies: "by way of non-separability" (*ayutasiddhyā*).
Indeed, such [non-separability] exists.
But it is not [perceived] more clearly by way of having its inner essence fully extracted;
nor does the cessation of that [quality] alone entail the cessation of the difference, for otherwise it would follow that iron and fire are non-different— this is the meaning.
This might be the case:

even if there is an experience of distinct relata, how can there be an experience of the relation? To this he says: "And that [relation] is not [perceived]. For indeed, when the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is not apprehended, there is no cognition of the qualified (*viśiṣṭa*).

The meaning is that the object of cognition (*bodhya*) is not inferred by the cognition (*buddhi*), for that would entail the undesirable consequence of the abolition of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Furthermore, the opponent must necessarily accept that the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—"whatever relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) exists, it is preceded by another relation"—is violated precisely in this case.
For one who accepts either inherence (*samavāya*) or non-existence (*abhāva*) cannot fail to accept its status as a qualifier.
Otherwise, one would not even accept the cognition characterized by the absence of inherence;
rather,
one might perhaps say that the qualifier-qualified relationship, being devoid of any other connection, does not constitute a factor for perception.
Therefore, he refutes that [position] by means of an analogous argument: "What then is here?"—
just as there is a cognition qualified by that [object] even without any other relation.
Likewise, the direct perception (sākṣātkāra) of that very [object] is understood as being inseparable from its being an object of the senses;
the meaning is that the logical argument (tarka), characterized by the consequence of infinite regress (anavasthā-prasaṅga), applies equally to the contrary case (vipakṣa).

Nor should it be argued that even in the case of qualities, actions, and universals, their apprehension should occur merely by virtue of being qualifiers [of a substance], rendering relations such as inherence (samavāya) unnecessary;
for a word is apprehended through inherence even when it is not a qualifier of its own substratum.

If it is argued that this [relation] may also be the third, we say no; for odor and taste, though not being of such a nature [i.e., not being qualities of the same substance], are perceived through inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*).
If it is argued that this may also be the fourth, we say no.
This is because both the nature of sound and [the nature of] form are being perceived.
If it is argued that [they appear] solely as qualifiers— no,
for in the absence of a relation between substance, quality, action, and universal, the very status of being a qualifier is untenable.
And the relation has already been established;
therefore, there is no sublation by perception as there is in the case of the non-existence of inherence (samavāya),
nor is there an infinite regress.
For it comes to rest in a relation that is independent of any other relation.
It might be argued as follows:
"The ground itself is the absence of the jar, and that is perceived precisely through conjunction;
therefore, what is the use of its being a qualifier? To this, he says: "And not..."
The remainder of the argument is that even when a jar or the like is present, because the bare ground exists there,
it would follow— just as there is the conventional usage of "ground"— that there would also be the conventional usage of "absence of a jar."
And as for "isolation" (*kaivalya*):
if isolation were said to be a property of the bare ground that is not in opposition to jars and the like, it could not coexist with jars and so forth;
and thus, that very same fault remains exactly as it was.
If it is contradictory,
then it cannot be any one of the categories such as substance (dravya) established by both disputants,
because those are compatible with the jar.

Furthermore, because certain things are impossible even at the time of the conventional usage of "non-existence," and because those properties of the ground are neither destroyed nor obscured by the jar; therefore,
[the absence] is a tenth substance distinct from those.
Or the twenty-fifth quality,
or the sixth action,
or generality, particularity, and inherence do not exist at all.

For it would follow that [the object] possesses a property invariably concomitant with being one of the categories such as substance; or, if such a consequence does not follow, then its status as such [an object] is untenable.
Could this indeed be a seventh category of existence?
In that case, would it take the form of a negation of being, or otherwise?
It cannot be otherwise.
If that were the case, it would follow that there is no contradiction;
furthermore, if even the form of negation does not cease despite being unarisen,
then conventional usage regarding jars and the like would never occur at any time.
If that which has arisen were to cease, then even a destroyed pot might sometimes be perceived.

Therefore, the seventh category of things, consisting of negation, is non-existence (*abhāva*); it is both the non-arising and non-perishing, as well as the arising and perishing, of the properties of the ground and so forth, and its sole meaning is absolute isolation (*kaivalya*).
This is what was stated: the meaning is that the absence of a jar is not something other than the absence of a jar itself.

It might be argued: "Even if there is no other reality in the form of an object of knowledge (*jñeya*), it may nevertheless exist in the form of knowledge (*jñāna*); and its object, when the visible counterpart [of the jar] is present, is simply the ground. To this, he says: "And not... (na ca).

The meaning is that just as there is the undesirable consequence [of perceiving absence] even when a jar is present on the side of the locus (the ground), so too there is the same consequence even when there is a cognition of the ground containing a jar, on the side of the cognition of the locus.

Now, it was stated that [the counter-positive] must be perceptible; however, in the cognition of a floor as "devoid of a jar," the jar is not merely perceptible but is actually being perceived. To this, he says: "Not indeed" (*na hi*).
The meaning is that what is unfit for perception cannot be perceived.
For since the jar is fit for perception, if it were not there, it would necessarily be apprehended just like the floor.
Or else, even the surface of the ground would not be perceived,
since they share the same logical status.
Therefore, even when the surface of the ground is perceived, its non-perception is only possible by taking its absence into account.
Even if an opponent can be made to accept the non-existence of the perceptible through the application of reasoning, nevertheless, one might ask:
"What is the use of that even for one who does not see the contradiction in their own words? Bearing this intention in mind, he says: "When [the object] is perceptible yet not perceived."
For non-perception must be either the absence of perception,
or the perception of the bare ground when the object visible is being remembered,
or the perception of the self alone when the perception of a jar is being remembered?
First of all, the second and third [definitions] are not tenable;

for when a jar is being remembered while a jar is actually being perceived, and the ground is apprehended, it would be impossible to avoid the undesirable consequence that the ground is empty even though the jar is present there.
Therefore, non-apprehension is simply the absence of apprehension.

Now, one might ask: "Since all worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*) are established by this alone, what is the use of the non-existence of the perceptible? To this he says: "What offense has been committed by the non-existence of the perceptible?

For, just as the non-existence of perception is established from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that negates perception, so too the non-existence of the perceptible is established precisely through the force of the means of valid cognition that negates the perceptible.
Indeed, there arises the cognition "the jar does not exist" just as there is the cognition "I do not perceive the jar."
Furthermore, these two do not have the same object;

for in one whose eyes are closed, there is a certainty regarding the absence of perception, yet there remains doubt and a desire to know regarding the absence of the perceivable object, even when the ground has been somehow ascertained.
Since this cannot occur in a single place at one time, the author concludes with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt), expressing this intention.
The meaning is that "non-existent" (asat) is a negation of existence (sat).

And some maintain that this [non-existence] is understood solely through the non-perception of the perceptible, because the operation of the sense organs is exhausted by the apprehension of the locus; however,
that is untenable.

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence that even a blind person would perceive the absence of color in a jar or similar object presented to the sense of touch; for in that case, there is indeed the apprehension of the locus,
and there is also the recollection of the counter-positive.
And there is both the absence and the non-perception of whiteness—which is otherwise suitable—in the blue.

If it is argued that this [objection] is equally applicable even to one who maintains the non-existence of the object of apprehension by means of the sense organ that apprehends the locus— [we reply: no,

because it is the core of our established doctrine (siddhānta) that the absence of that [object] is apprehended by the sense organ that apprehends its counter-positive (pratiyogin), since that [apprehension of absence] is dependent upon the existence [of the counter-positive].

If it is argued that the essence of our own tenet is this: "That which is my non-existence is to be understood through non-apprehension; when the locus is grasped by the sense organ that perceives that [locus], it (the non-existence) is also grasped"—this is not so, because it would follow as an absurd consequence that the cognition of the absence of color does not arise when air is presented to the tactile sense organ (*tvagindriya*).
For the locus has not been brought there by that which apprehends the form.
If it is argued that even in that case the visual faculty is connected [to the object], then, in that case, the faculty has no function regarding the apprehension of the locus.

Nor has it been established that [the cognition of absence] necessarily depends on both the recollection of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) and the perception of the locus (*rūpa*); for the perceptibility of absence is otherwise established (*ananyathāsiddha*). Disregarding this prattle regarding its being otherwise established by closing one's eyes like an elephant, he says: "Because that cognition occurs when the operation of the sense organ is present.
Anticipating the delusion that an intermediate operation acts as an obstacle, he says: "And not the counter-positive... [and so forth].

Having raised an opponent who argues through verbal quibble (*vākchala*) regarding the phrase "recollection of the counter-positive," [the author] instructs him: "Nor [is it due] to the recollection of words, etc.

He then raises an opponent who claims that sensory contact with an object is not the cause for the arising of the cognition of absence because of its deviation (*vyabhicāra*): "But [it arises from] the intrinsic nature...
and so on. "Therefore, this... [is the conclusion].
The meaning is that the opponent’s conceit is that another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) is possible by means of that [non-apprehension].
Now, would this non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) indicate absence by its mere existence, or by its own cognition?
Not the first, because at that time the house is remote and obstructed, such that its non-existence cannot be established through the non-perception of the perceptible.
Not the second, either.
Because it would lead to an infinite regress;
for since non-apprehension itself is of the nature of an absence, it too would require another apprehension to establish it.

If it is argued that there is indeed an absence of recollection of the counter-positive (pratiyogin), we say no; for if such an absence were the case, it would follow that there could be no error or doubt regarding it.
Indeed, even when both the counter-positive and its locus are recollected, there sometimes occurs a cognition of the presence of something that is actually non-existent.
The notion of non-existence arises from that which exists; otherwise, how could one, having said "it does not exist," suddenly experience a contradiction and say,
"No, no, I was mistaken"?
Having first said, "I saw him there," or "He exists," one later says,
"He does not exist," or "I cannot determine whether he was there or not."
For it is not the case that one remembers the counter-positive or the locus in a different form when they have not been perceived.
Nor is a reversal possible for a memory that is established by its own nature yet remains unperceived.
And this much is the causal complex: namely, the memory of the counter-positive and the locus, together with the memory of "that-ness" (tattā).
Nor is it the case that defects, without corrupting the common instrument of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), can be the causes of error, for that would entail a lack of confidence in all cases.
If you argue that this must also be maintained by you [the opponent], we say no.
This is because I accept the non-remembrance of one who is capable of remembering as the inferential mark (*liṅga*);
and because, through the reversal of that mark and through doubt regarding it, the resulting doubt and error concerning the object inferred from it are easily established.

However, when the mark characterized by non-remembrance is ascertained even while there is remembrance of Caitra’s house—Caitra being one whose capacity for grasping a single cognition with extreme precision is well known—[the inference proceeds].
At that time, the cognition of the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) is indeed non-erroneous;
for this very reason, he says, "having meditated for a moment. Otherwise, even meditation would be untenable.

Indeed, having observed the deviation of mere non-remembrance, one who desires to know [the absence of perception] disregards that and applies focused attention (*praṇidhāna*) toward qualified non-remembrance.
Therefore, non-remembrance is utilized precisely as a logical mark (*liṅga*).
However, it remains to be explained how even that itself is to be known.
Regarding this, he says: "Not so.
To avoid the fault of a lack of grammatical coordination (*vyadhikaraṇatā*), he shows the formal argument (*prayoga*) with the words: "For instance" (*tathā hi*).
Nor is it a defect for the delimited (avacchedya) and the delimiter (avacchedaka) to reside in different loci, because that rule applies only to qualifiers (viśeṣaṇa),
whereas in this case they function as indicators (upalakṣaṇa).

Even in the case of a lack of coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), there is no contradiction in its being a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), because it is useful for that purpose alone; however,
what is thus characterized is indeed coreferential with the probandum (*sādhyasamānādhikaraṇa*).

For this very reason, the author of the *Vārttika* demonstrated that [the epithets] "one whose feet have not yet arisen" (*anutpannapādavihāra*) and "one whose eye is immovable" (*acalacakṣus*), and so forth, are indeed in grammatical apposition (*vyadhikaraṇa*).
The author of the *Ṭīkā* also accepted it as such,
since he did not alter it otherwise.
Even by others, whenever something is capable of producing a cognition, this very point has been accepted;
for what reason?
Because the necessary connection (pratibandha) is established in exactly that way.
[Objection: But surely the deviation from the contact between the sense organ and its object remains as it was; to this he says: "And not that which...
For the direct perception of people like us does not deviate from the contact between the sense organ and its object.
This [cognition], however, is inferential and characterized by mediacy; therefore, there is no suspicion of error anywhere.
If non-existence is cognizable through inference, how can perception operate therein?
One might perhaps argue that "this is because the objects of these two [means of knowledge] are non-overlapping";
however, the meaning is that this has already been resolved by the very establishment of *saṃplava* (the convergence of means of knowledge).

He introduces the Vārttika with the words "Now, however" (*saṃprati*), while simultaneously dispelling the doubt as to which part of the Sūtra is being explained by the Bhāṣya beginning with "Not then" (*na tarhi*).
To the objection that even so the definition remains unimpeachable, he replies with the words "the cause of perception" (*pratyakṣakāraṇa*);
the meaning is that this is a challenge from one who prides himself on having determined the cause.

By stating that [the cause] consists of the eye, light, and contact with the object, it is asserted that the function of light occurs solely through contact with the object, and not through contact with the location of the tactile sense organ.

This can be inferred from the fact that even one situated in the midst of darkness perceives objects situated in the midst of light, while even one situated in the midst of light does not perceive those standing in the midst of darkness.

Now, since largeness (*mahattva*) and the state of being composed of multiple substances (*anekadravyavattva*) are invariably concomitant (*avinābhūta*) with one another and their specific distinctions are not perceived, both must be causes for visual perception (*cākṣuṣatva*); thus, there is simply a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of them.
Or else, if there were a distinction [in their efficacy], only one of them would be the cause.
Whence is there an option?
For an option regarding causal efficiency arises only among things that are mutually exclusive; however, these two are not such.
Therefore, when defining the substance perceived by the eye, an option between these two must be presented.
The meaning is that if both [the whole and its parts] were taken as the substratum, the definition would possess an ineffective qualification.

For this very reason, he states later, "even though it possesses such a characteristic," that even when the aforementioned causal complex is present, the eye as a composite whole (*avayavin*) is not perceptible;
therefore, the author of the *Vārttika* stated that "the result of the refinement is apprehension" (*upalabdhiphalaḥ saṃskāraḥ*).
And that [nature] is difficult to define;
for instance, would it be a property of the possessor of qualities (guṇin), or would it be a property of the quality (guṇa)?
In that case, if [color] were a property of the substance (*guṇin*), then color and touch would be perceived without distinction;
it would not be the case that one is perceived in some instances while the other is not.
If it is argued that there is indeed the perception of both as they are inherent in the same object (*ekārthasamaveta*), we say no.
At night during the summer season, although there is the perception of the touch of heat, there is no perception of its color;
and although there is the perception of the color of moonlight, there is no perception of its touch.
Thus, the property of a quality (guṇadharma) is certainly not non-eternal.

But that which is eternal and of the nature of a universal (*sāmānya*) is neither denotable by the word "disposition" (*saṃskāra*), nor is it the fruit of perception; for it serves as no cause for anything other than its own perception. Therefore, he says: "It is designated as arising with dharma and adharma as its cause. For some, that distinction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) arises from the very power of their own causes, such as color and so forth.
That wherein the general property-particularity called "manifestness" inheres is called a *saṃskāra* (impression) because it is produced by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*);
the meaning is that it also results in apprehension as its fruit.
It has been stated that it is the cause of perception by virtue of being the definition of perception,
but not solely by virtue of being a cause;
nor is "cause" and "definition" one and the same thing.

For a characteristic (lakṣaṇa) establishes the arising [of a thing], whereas a causal factor (kāraka) establishes the nature of the cause; it may be either a characteristic or a non-characteristic, and likewise either a causal factor or a non-causal factor.
However, light and so forth are not like this.
Because those [other definitions] fail to establish the true nature of perception due to being either over-extensive or under-extensive, [the author],
intending to show that these [five factors] are what establish its arising—
since perception would be impossible even if any one of them were absent— explains the rebuttal with the words: "The definition of perception..."

Now, although the non-difference of the contact between the sense organ and the mind may appropriately occur— whether by way of the identity of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) or the identity of the continuum (*saṃtāna*)—
nevertheless, the non-difference of the cognition must be either produced by the individual instance (*vyakti*) or produced by the universal class (*jāti*).
In the former case, even when there is no difference in the contact between the sense organ and the object, the successive cognitions (*dhārāvāhika-vijñāna*) are nonetheless distinct.

But later on, even though there is a difference in the contact between the sense organ and its object, there is indeed no difference [in the resulting cognition], because all such cognitions belong to the same genus of direct perception (*sākṣātkārijātīya*).
With the intention that the rebuttal offered by the "partialist" (ekadeśin) has already failed—like a miscarriage—and is therefore not even fit to be proposed, he says: "For when... (*yadā hi*).
For there exists a distinction among cognitions produced by the object, which is distinct from the differences created by their own nature or genus;

and that [distinction] is observed to arise solely from the difference in the contact between the sense organ and the object, not from the difference in the contact between the sense organ and the mind.
But where, in a continuous stream of cognition (*dhārāvāhijñāna*), the sense-object contact does not differ, there the cognition itself has no distinction based on its object; this is the meaning.
This is what was stated: "The cognitions of elephants, horses, and so forth, occur in succession."
In refuting this as well, he provides a corresponding example with the words "when" (*yadā*).

Just as in the case of that very cow, through conjunction with the eye, there first arises the cognition of the quality of whiteness by means of inherence in that same cow, and subsequently the cognition of the action of moving; thus, [the opponent's argument] regarding difference is [actually] non-difference.
The meaning is that it is the same.
Although "unestablishedness" (aprasiddhatva) is already implied by the term "non-designative" (avyapadeśakatva) because the latter pervades the former,

nevertheless, while contact between light and its object is well-known even though it is non-designative, contact between the sense organ and the mind is both non-designative and unestablished; it is on this basis that it constitutes a distinct category.
But surely, even the contact between a sense organ and its object has as its locus that which is beyond the senses for at least one of the two;
whereas the contact between the self and the mind does not have as its locus that which is beyond the senses for both. To this he says: "As for the self, although..."
Now, one might object: since they are produced by specific karma, there is no distinction between those who are clear-sighted and those blind men whose black pupils are blinded;

for surely, in the case of those who do not seek the enjoyment of forms, there can be no craving for the black pupil arising from such karma. And if that craving does not exist, how can its production occur?
Therefore, he states that even with respect to the effect, action possesses the status of a cooperative cause— this is what is meant by the phrase "it amounts to this.
The expression "from the destruction of karma" is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa), [including] from its obstruction as well.
It should also be observed that this is due to the absence of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).
For if the conjunctions of the chariot and other parts were all-pervading like space, then it would follow that their effect, sound, would be produced everywhere;
for [the production of sound] must conform to the localized nature of its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).
Pervasive qualities arise by means of a spatial limitation;
however, in this case, since that [limitation] is absent, there would necessarily be an absence of spatial restriction.

Consequently, chariots and the like, as well as their conjunctions, which are perceived through that [quality], would not be cognized as having a fixed location. Bearing this intention in mind, he says: "Let it not be everywhere."
He provides a rebuttal to the question, "Why was the position that space is perceptible not even suspected? with the words, "Not for us.
Regarding the phrase "by the skin and so forth," the example given there is the skin;
the example for the tongue, however, is molasses that is exceptionally sweet, characterized by the absence of bitterness.
Likewise, the example of the nose [perceiving fragrance] is not contradictory to the plural number, because musk is more fragrant than other scents, being distinguished by the absence of foul odors.

Furthermore, according to the Buddhist tenet, since there is no difference between a quality (*guṇa*) and that which possesses the quality (*guṇin*), the corporeality of the possessor of qualities is itself the corporeality of the qualities.
Thus, the sense organ that perceives the qualities is precisely that which perceives the possessor of qualities.
Furthermore, the absence of qualities is itself the absence of the possessor of qualities;

therefore, when the apprehension of that which is qualified by the absence of corporeality is to be cited as an example, he mentions the apprehension of that which is qualified by the absence of "smallness."
Now, it might be argued that the meaning of the reason is not the apprehension [of an object] together with an interval, nor the apprehension [of it] as "with an interval";
rather, the meaning will be the apprehension of the non-connection between the body, the sense organs, and their substratum.
For this [reason] is not established otherwise.
Because this very [connection] acts as the motivator by virtue of being a subsequent limiting condition (*upādhi*), he says: "Whether there be a connection with the sense-faculties or not.

There is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the claim that "whatever is connected to the body is necessarily connected to the sense-faculties," nor for the claim that "whatever is connected to the sense-faculties is necessarily connected to the body."
Because those two are distinct and have distinct substrata;

for there is no rule that whatever is connected with a lamp must necessarily be connected with a jasmine flower, nor that whatever is connected with a jasmine flower must necessarily be connected with a lamp.
