Therefore, the meaning is that there is indeed doubt in this case because of the absence of any proving or refuting evidence (*sādhaka-bādhaka-pramāṇa*).

Consequently, since its [the opponent's reason] is established otherwise (*anyathāsiddhi*), one must observe— even though it is contradictory— that the tactile sense-organ (*tvagindriya*), which functions by reaching its object (*prāpyakārin*) and perceives things such as cloth together with water and fire, also perceives them internally along with the intervening space, in order to exclude the fallacy of being unestablished (*asiddhi*).

Refining the reasoning (*tarka*) which consists in the impossibility of an obstruction, he states the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by means of a formal argument (*prayoga*): "The formal argument, however... and so forth.
In this context, there are two kinds of relationship: that characterized by reaching, as in the case of light and so forth with respect to a jar and so forth;
and its opposite, as follows:

Regarding the statement that "the designator, cognition, and so forth, [do not produce their effects] by reaching their respective objects, such as the designated, the knowable, and so on"—this is for the purpose of excluding the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

If one were to state simply "because of being a producer" (*janakatvāt*), the argument would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to sound and other factors which produce the cognition of their own objects without reaching them; therefore, it is specified "because they do not produce [their effects] without reaching [them]."
However, because [the reason] is in every way inconclusive due to non-producers, one must add "provided that it is a producer. This is another argument, another line of reasoning.
There would be the consequence of [the cognition] not conforming to distance and proximity;
this [argument] should also be understood by applying it in the reverse order.

Now, if there is no difference in terms of being reached [by the visual organ], one should likewise perceive the summit of Mount Meru and the light of a meteor at midday, just as one perceives the solar disc.

If it is argued that the abodes of the sun and so forth are not perceived because they are overwhelmed by what has been manifested [in consciousness], while the solar disc is perceived because it is manifested and not overwhelmed— then [the same logic must apply].
If that is the case, then one must simply accept that there is a certain object of such a nature which is perceived, and not any other;
what is the use of resorting to the apprehension of a deviation? To this he says: "But in the case of reaching" (*prāptau tu*).
For the greatness of the object itself is the auxiliary factor for reaching.
But it is not independent.
For touch, taste, and so forth are not grasped by the skin and other senses without having reached them, as they are not fit for apprehension [without contact];
or rather, because they function through contact (*prāpyakāritva*), even those [objects] that are experienced or overwhelmed are grasped merely by virtue of having been reached—this is the meaning.

Even according to the theories of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) and transformation (*pariṇāma*), it is only those factors that have attained mutual contact— namely the agent (*kartṛ*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the object (*karman*)— that produce an effect,
and not those that remain unattained;
for auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*) are never observed to produce an excellence in things unless they are in close proximity to one another.
Proximity, however, is precisely their arising without interval;
that alone constitutes their fitness regarding their own nature (*svarūpa-yogyatā*).
Thus, by one who asserts that the sense organ and the object possess fitness regarding their own nature, it must be stated that they arise without interval.
Furthermore, there is no such thing as "intrinsic fitness" (svarūpayogyatā) for things that have arisen separated by an interval or at a distance.
Therefore, one might disagree regarding "attainment" (prāpti) as something distinct from the intrinsic nature;
however, even in the case of uninterrupted arising, it is not necessary to posit an additional attainment there as a means of proof. With this intention, he says: "For these two will be refuted."
Thus, with his pride dispelled and seeing no means of valid cognition even in another philosophical system, he remains in a state of doubt.

One might object: "Since he perceives the reason for the determination that [the cause] must possess the quality of being a producer (*janakatva*), how can he possibly be in doubt? To this, he says: "This is the underlying intention. The meaning is that the opponent considers the reason to be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because it is observed even in the case of a magnet, which produces its effect despite the object not being in contact. Furthermore, seeing that skin and the like, as well as sticks and the like, produce their effects only when they have come into contact, why would one disagree in every instance? Therefore, he states the seed of that disagreement: "By means of capacity alone (*yogyatayaiva*)."

[Objection: But if the magnet acts without reaching its object (*aprāpyakāritva*), what remedy is there for other [causes] as well? To this he says: "Of the magnet-stone... [Objection: But a distinction in its operation (*vṛttibheda*) is contradicted by non-perception (*anupalambhabādhita*). To this he says: "Just like the eye.
The meaning is that they share the same status regarding proof and refutation (*tulyayogakṣematvāt*).
For "obstruction" and "distance" must consist either in non-contiguous arising, or in non-attainment, or in the lack of intrinsic capacity.
Among these, there is an absence of non-contiguous arising.
There would have to be an uninterrupted arising;
however, an uninterrupted arising of a gem with iron or of a magnet with iron is not possible.
Furthermore, the absence of non-attainment is itself attainment.
And thus, who is adverse that performs what is favorable?
Furthermore, the absence of incapacity is itself capacity;
and it has been stated that, according to the Buddhist system, this does not differ from the continuous arising of things belonging to the same causal class.

Therefore, in the theory of permanence, it remains that causes either produce an effect through mutual contact or else contact itself depends upon a pervasion (vyāpti) conditioned by intrinsic capability (svarūpayogyatā).
To this, he says: "Precisely because of contact."

Now, one might object: "If the object to be defined (lakṣya) is already established by another definition, how can there be the fault of mutual dependence (anyonyāśrayatva)? To this, he says: "Or else, there is no comprehension. For does that [definition] depend upon the object to be defined or not?
In the first case, there is simply no comprehension due to the very fault of mutual dependence.
But later on, once the object to be defined has been understood, there would be no way at all for the definition—which depends upon that object—to convey anything further; this is the meaning.
As for the phrase "for it exists":

if pleasure were of the same nature as consciousness because it arises from causes non-different from those of consciousness, then [consciousness] too would be of the same nature as pleasure because it arises from causes non-different from those of pleasure.
If it is argued that consciousness is not produced from causes identical to those of pleasure,
then how, in that case, can pleasure also be said to be produced from causes identical to those of consciousness?
Is it not the case that the conformity with the causes of cognition exists in pleasure as well?
But the pursuit of the cause of pleasure does not apply to cognition;
therefore, let that which follows from a cause exist only where there is similarity of kind (*tajjātīyatva*) with it.
Just as when one follows the causal sequence starting from a mere sprout, a barley sprout possesses the nature of being a sprout;

yet not everything [in that sequence] becomes a barley sprout, because the causal sequence for that specific [barley] is absent—bearing this intention in mind, he raises an objection with the words "avāntara" (intermediate).
For there is no rule that wherever there is a following of the causal cycle of a cause belonging to a certain class of effect, there must necessarily be the same class-nature [in the effect].

He states that even when following the cycle of causes and effects consisting of the same class as the seed, there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) in the general application because the sprout is not of the same class as the seed;
however, in the case of a specific application, there is a doubtful inconclusiveness, as he says: "not anything at all."
For, fearing the consequence of [causes] being accidental (*ākasmikatva*), you exert yourself in following every distinction among causes in order to account for the diversity of effects;

yet that diversity of effects, like that of the seed and the sprout, is not accidental even in the case of cognition, pleasure, and so forth, but arises from some specific distinction among their causes.
This is what is meant by the phrase "and because they have that as their purpose" (*tadarthatvāt*).

Now, is it not the case that for color, taste, smell, and touch, their belonging to that class or not belonging to that class is determined solely by whether their material cause (upādāna) is identical or different?
For there is no possibility that something could have color and so forth as its material cause and yet itself be devoid of color and so forth.
Therefore, if pleasure has cognition as its material cause, pleasure must necessarily belong to the same class as cognition.
If one objects that if [the cause] were ignorance, it could not have knowledge as its material cause (*upādāna*), he says in response: "And not...

For if being of the same genus (*ekajātīyatva*) were to result solely from having a material cause of the same genus, why should there not also be a more specific internal similarity of genus (*avāntaraikajātīya*)?
Furthermore, it would follow that from a single immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), cognitions of multiple intermediate types could not arise;
yet we observe that from a cognition of form arises another cognition of form, as well as cognitions of the type of taste-cognition and so forth,
and from a direct perception arise both further direct perceptions and non-direct perceptions, and so on.

Now, the meaning is as follows: just as the restriction on the production of a certain [effect] possessing the nature of producing various intermediate types of effects is established through the entry of multiple heterogeneous auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), so too—even when there is a single intended homogeneous material cause (*upādāna*)—the restriction on the production of a certain [effect] possessing the nature of producing multiple intended types of effects will be established through the entry of multiple heterogeneous auxiliary causes. Thus, just as the distinction between intermediate types of effects is established, the restriction on the production of a specific effect is likewise accounted for.

Thus, this admission by others of internal differences in genus despite having a single material cause has been set forth for the sake of providing an example; furthermore, what was set forth beginning with "api ca" was intended to clarify the fact that the exclusion [of the reason from the heterologous] is doubtful.
Therefore, it is not incoherent.
All of this has been stated by way of accepting the Buddhist tenets.

From the perspective of ultimate truth, however, the rule is this: whatever possesses a material cause (upādāna) belongs to the same genus as that cause; and whatever possesses a pervasive material cause belongs to the same genus as the qualities thereof.
This is the supreme rule.

Therefore, if it is sought to prove that pleasure (*sukha*) and cognition (*jñāna*) belong to the same genus either by virtue of their existence (*sattā*) or by virtue of being qualities (*guṇatva*), [then the following applies].
In that case, it would be a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhanam*).
To provide an unambiguous example for the alternative case where there is no such restriction, he says: "For this very reason.
Even though color-form (*rūpa*) and the other qualities share a single material cause (*upādāna*), there is no distinction between them produced by their individual manifestations (*vyakti*).

Nor is it produced by an intermediate genus, nor even by way of being a quality (*guṇa*), because action (*karman*), although having the pot as its material cause (*upādāna*), is not a quality. Here, by the power of the material cause alone, just as substances, qualities, and actions exist externally despite being non-existent [prior to manifestation],
so too do internal cognitions, pleasures, and so forth.
And just as for them, due to the difference in their respective ultimate causes (bhavāntara-kāraṇa), there is substantiality (dravyatva) for earth and the other [elements],
quality-ness (guṇatva) for color and the other [qualities],
and action-ness (karmatva) for upward motion and the other [actions].

Likewise, due to the difference in intermediate causes, there is the nature of cognition (*jñānatva*) in seeing, touching, remembering, and so forth; and there is the nature of pleasure (*sukhatva*) in that which is favorable, unfavorable, or more favorable, and so on, without any further limiting conditions.

Just as there is a distinction such as the jar and so forth for earth, and the distinction of white and so forth for color, [the unity of a single entity persists] despite the differences in its intermediate and specific causes.

The meaning is that just as there is a distinction such as proficiency and so forth in the case of throwing upwards, likewise there will be a distinction such as vision and so forth in the case of knowledge, and a distinction such as gradation and so forth in the case of pleasure.
It might be argued: "What, then, is the proof for its nature as ignorance? To this, he says by way of a conclusion: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

Although it is established by experience that consciousness, pleasure, and so forth belong to different categories—since in the cognition "I perceive sandalwood," pleasure does not manifest such that one would think "I am happy"—[it is nevertheless the case that they are non-distinct].
Nor does the cognition "I am happy" flash forth at that time such that one could say "I know";
yet this is not the case.

If it is argued that pleasure is a particular kind of cognition and thus the notion of pleasure arises toward such [an object]—well then, my friend, does that particular cognition also have a particular object, or not?
If it does not exist,
it follows that pleasure is a cognition devoid of an object;
yet this is neither observed, nor desired, nor can it be established.
If it exists, is it external or internal?
It cannot be external, for there is no distinction whatsoever among objects;
for that very same song which is experienced by one possessed of passion is experienced by one free from passion as well.
If it is argued that the song is the very same, yet it is favorable for one possessed of passion while it is the opposite for one free from passion?
Is this favorability toward him unconditional or conditional?
And in what way is it toward someone?
If it is argued that [the relation] is qualified (sopādhika), let that very qualification be stated.
If it is claimed that desire itself is the qualification, we say no,
because it would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (itaretarāśrayatva).
Being favorable consists in being desired;
and by that [favorableness], there is the state of being desired.
Therefore, for that specific cognition which is intended as pleasure, an internal object must be accepted as its cause—one whose nature is naturally favorable.
It is precisely because of this [internal] object that an external object becomes desired as something favorable; thus, that object of the aforementioned nature is called "pleasure.

Nevertheless, for the sake of the linguistic conventions of those with dull intellects, the properties that distinguish cognitions and the like from both similar and dissimilar classes have been stated.
In this context, "being directed toward an object" means that the determination of knowledge is dependent upon the determination of the object;
its lack of such direction is the definition of non-cognition (*ajñāna*).
Furthermore, in that regard, being experienced as agreeable is the definition of pleasure (*sukha*).
The meaning is that such points as "suffering is to be experienced as disagreeable" and so forth are to be understood in accordance with other treatises (samānatantra).
Surely, if pleasure and the like were non-cognitive by nature, they would not be necessarily cognized, as is the case with jars and other objects;
yet they are necessarily cognized, for [pleasure] is never experienced when it is not being known.
There is another criterion for pleasure;
this very point is most appropriately established in its nature as cognition because it is self-cognized (*svasaṃvedana*). Therefore, he says: "by virtue of its intense agitation.
For there are indeed certain objects which, despite the lack of distinction in their being acquired through their own karma, are directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*).
For example, one's own body and so forth;
however, some things are indeed imperceptible,
such as the configuration of the channels (nāḍī) situated within them.

The meaning is this: although there is no difference in their being objects of ignorance, certain things such as pleasure and so forth—possessing a specific nature acquired through their causes—are necessarily cognized, while others are not.
He raises a related objection: "It might be so.
Nevertheless, in the waking state, the contact between the sense organ and its object is necessary for the arising of pleasure by way of generating an experience;
otherwise, the experience [of pleasure] would occur even without it, just as pleasure itself does.
Moreover, the immediate cause alone is not the [sole] cause;
for if that were so, it would follow that those possessing an operation (vyāpārin) would be indifferent (udāsīna).
The argument that the operation does not constitute an intervention applies equally here as well; therefore, he says: "But of the contact between the sense-organ and the object..."
The meaning is that mere cognition, having become non-functional therein, [is the cause], because of its application.
This is the intention:

this would indeed be the case if the operation (*vyāpāra*) of the contact between the sense faculty and its object were cognition itself; for that [operation] must reside in the effect and cannot deviate from the agent of the operation.
Furthermore, knowledge—even when it culminates in its effect—certainly transcends the contact between the sense organ and the object in the case of dreaming;
otherwise, if one were to assume a [constant] operation, there would be the undesirable consequence of lack of restriction.
He refutes this, saying: "That is incorrect," because it is unestablished and not perceived.

The ellipsis is "due to the absence of a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇābhāvāt*). [Objection: But surely, in this case, mental experience (*mānasa-anubhava*) is the means of valid cognition. To this he says: "of that cognition" (*tajjñānasya*).
Why is there the realization of its falsity? To this he says: "For just as... (*yathā hi*).

The object of this misconception (*viparyāsa*), however, is precisely that pleasure which was previously experienced and is now worthy of being remembered—just as a beloved woman who was previously experienced and is now worthy of being remembered.

Its status as a misconception consists solely in this: that the beloved woman and the pleasure produced by her, though existing at a distant place and time, appear as if they were at a proximate place and time.
It does not mean, however, that a non-beloved woman or a non-pleasurable state appears as a beloved woman or as pleasure.
That being the case, the appearance of something else— by way of negating both "being a beloved woman" and "pleasure"— would constitute a sublation [of the claim].
Nor should it be argued that if pleasure were not produced in a dream, one would not desire a woman for its sake.
Because activity is observed even toward that which lacks a means [to achieve a goal] due to delusion—
just as monkeys act toward a heap of *guñjā* seeds to ward off the cold—
it has been said: "it is a distortion of memory."
When recollection occurs, its distortion is "distortion of recollection"; the meaning is that it has the very same object as the characteristic of the original experience.

Now, it might be argued that merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) have the production of pleasure and pain as their purpose; therefore, when they produce bodies and other things that do not consist of pleasure or pain, it is solely for the sake of those [pleasures and pains], and thus their status as the efficient cause (*nimitta*) of all produced things is maintained.
However, this dream-cognition is not of the nature of pleasure.
If even the means of attaining merit (*saṃkha-sādhana*) were not to exist,
then it would not have merit as its cause;
nor would it have demerit as its cause, because it is not suffering and does not have that [demerit] as its cause.
Furthermore, its arising independent of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) would cause great confusion; therefore, he says "pleasure" (*sukha*).
For the primary purpose of the unseen force is the enjoyment of pleasure and so forth.
Moreover, pleasure and the like are not enjoyment in their own nature (*svarūpataḥ*).
However, there is the experience of that [past object].
And since that experience arises by taking as its object what previously arose—even though it does not take a presently existing pleasure or the like as its object—it renders everything consistent.
Nor should one say that this must be the case everywhere, because of the diversity of causal complexes (*sāmagrī*).
Because of the establishment of the distinction between true and false cognitions.

For it is not appropriate to say that because a cognition of silver occurs even with respect to what is not silver due to the force of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) from a previously perceived object of silver, this must always be the case.

As for one who thinks that, at least in a dream, pleasure and so forth are experienced—of which there is no dispute—the sublation (*bādhaka*) occurring therein would be of two forms: either "this is not pleasure," or [the other form].
Nor is it the case that [the negation] "there was no pleasure" occurs; however,
in the waking state, the sublation "there was no beloved woman" is logical because of its stability.
Because even a sudden retreat is impossible,
and because his effects— such as tooth-marks, nail-scratches, and so forth— do not persist;
and although the emission of the final element and such may persist, they are not his effects.
For if it were to persist because of being its effect, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that other effects of that same cause would also have to persist.
Furthermore, the statement "there is no happiness now" is a negation of present happiness, not of past happiness,
because the latter is momentary (kṣaṇika).

Furthermore, because its effects—such as tears of joy and horripilation—are perceived as persisting [even after waking], whereas otherwise, things that perish very quickly would not be seen in the subsequent moment, those experiences would simply lack any basis in valid cognition (*prāmāṇikatva*).
Therefore, since it is established by uncontradicted experience, pleasure exists even in the state of dreaming; to this, he replies: "And it is not non-existent," etc.
Although there is no direct sublation (*bādhaka*) of the pleasure experienced in a dream while one is in the waking state,
Nevertheless, there is a sublation of sandalwood, women, and so forth— which are perceived as the causes [of pleasure]— precisely within the state of dreaming.
And when the cause is sublated, the effect is necessarily sublated as well, just as the flash of lightning supported by it is sublated when the mass of clouds seen in a dream is sublated.
However, tears of joy and the like are not effects of pleasure itself, but rather effects of the cognition of pleasure; therefore, its existence cannot be established by that alone.

Consequently, the argument that pleasure is established as having cognition as its sole effect by means of the example of dream-experiences has been refuted by citing the example of mental desires and the like.
Indeed, pleasure arises for those in saṃsāra in four ways:
some from habituation, as in hunting and the like;
some from conceit, as in [the enjoyment of] sandalwood and the like;
Some [pleasures] arise from the actual enjoyment of objects, such as fragrant, sweet, and pure *gāndhāra* notes and the like;
others arise from mere conceptual conviction, such as the contemplation of the great festival for the birth of a future son and so forth.
These various experiences are perceived as possessing distinct intrinsic natures.
For the happiness found in mental fantasies is not equal to that found in the enjoyment of sense objects;
if it were so, then the abandonment of the former and the acquisition of the latter would be pointless.
For a hungry person only fantasizes about sweetmeats for so long as they have not yet been obtained.
As long as these [objects] do not exist for him in an ultimate sense,
yet he nevertheless proceeds toward them with necessity, having abandoned the frustration of his desires—
if they were of the same nature [as the objects], then everything would be inconsistent.
The meaning is that, in the case of a difference in genus, a difference in cause must necessarily be admitted.
In this context, the proponent’s intended meaning is that the arising of pleasure conforms to the existence of the contact between the sense organ and its object.
Considering that this [conformity] is established otherwise, he recalls what was stated previously— "mere cognition itself"—
thinking that it is not merely the conformity to its existence that is intended here.
What is meant [by this]? A difference in genus implies a difference in cause;

and that difference in cause is established as being precisely that which conforms to the presence and absence [of the effect]. Wishing to demonstrate that this is what is intended here, he restates what has already been said.
No, because of the non-proximity of the object.
This has been stated: "because such a specific pleasure is not produced," the remainder being that [it is not produced] from the contact of the sense organ with its object.
He raises an objection with the words "viṣaya... (regarding the object).
For if there were no difference in the cognition, pleasure—which belongs to a different genus—would necessitate a distinct cause.
But here, it is the cognition itself that belongs to a different genus; this is the meaning.
He refutes this, saying: "Alas, even for the Lord...
[The opponent objects: "But surely the direct perception of an object, characterized by the attainment of what is desired, is a cause of happiness;
and such a thing does not exist in the Lord, because He is devoid of desire to enjoy."
How can there be the consequence of the arising of pleasure for such a person? To this he says: "for those endowed with the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of yoga.
But surely even they possess [the notion] that [objects] are sufficient; how then could they be partakers of pleasure? To this he says: "in the absence of...

For they do not always maintain the meditative cultivation of the antidote (*pratipakṣa-dhāraṇā*); otherwise, due to their constant lack of enjoyment, there would be the undesirable consequence (*mā bhūt*) of the persistence of the accumulation of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma-pracaya*) for them.
Therefore, the meaning is that when there is no cultivation of the antidote, pleasure would necessarily follow for them from the mere direct perception of the objects themselves.
Nor should it be argued: "If this were so, what fault would there be?
For [if it were so], it would follow that the manifestation of bodies and sense-faculties in the *kāyavyūha* would be rendered purposeless.
Because the direct perception of the desirable and the undesirable is accomplished by the mind alone within a single body;

and because it has never been observed that the sense organs and their objects possess the capacity to produce a quality of the self merely through their existence when they are not in mutual contact,

[the author] concludes with "Therefore," intending that for those possessing the supernatural power of yoga (*yogarddhi*), even though there is direct perception of objects, pleasure does not exist due to the absence of contact between the sense organs and their objects.
Therefore, this is the meaning of the proof:

the sense faculties, through their yogic powers, have the production of pleasure and pain as their purpose; for, while pleasure and pain are distinct from cognition, the faculties would otherwise be rendered purposeless elsewhere.
It is like the perception of the desirable and the undesirable;
nor is this [reason] unestablished,
for the fulfillment of its purpose could only be possible in the case of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*).
That [knowledge], however, is produced by the mind alone, assisted by the dharma born of yoga. Furthermore,

those pleasures and pains are produced by the sense-faculties themselves when they are in close proximity [to their objects], because, while being produced by external sense-faculties, they possess the nature of attributes of the self (*ātmadharma*).

"Just as [the cognition] of those beginning with ourselves has direct perception of its object"—this refers to the fact that when this contact (*sannikarṣa*) does not exist, even for them there is no pleasure and so forth.
This is what was stated: "And that... (*sa ca*).

[Objection: Surely, the direct perception of an object arising from the contact of the sense organs with their objects is the cause of pleasure and so forth; and since such [perception] does not exist for the Siddhas, there is no consequence of pleasure arising for them. To this, he says: "Moreover" (api ca).
There is no innate difference between the two types of direct perception— one produced by the sense organs and one not produced by them—

but rather, the distinction lies solely in the connection with the cause consisting of the contact between the sense organ and its object. And if that [distinction] is intended to apply to the effect, [then...]

How is it that he is not the cause with respect to pleasure and so forth? If it is argued that he is not intended [as the cause], then the undesirable consequence that pleasure and so forth would arise even for those who have attained perfection (siddhas) is difficult to avoid.
Because they share the same security and vulnerability (*tulyayogakṣematvāt*).
Therefore, the intention of the heartless opponent remains: "If direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) occurs only at the very final moment, what is the use of the sense faculty?
And in that case, there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); such is the meaning.
Regarding this very point, he states the consensus of the elders: "A garland and so forth.
Here, "a garland and so forth" is a statement regarding the causal cycle (*kāraṇacakra*).
"That which arises" refers to its essential nature (*svarūpa*), which is to be experienced as agreeable.
The effect consists of favor and so forth. Favor is a condition of happiness, another name for which is enjoyment.
Attachment, moreover, is the desire for the non-interruption of the flow of happiness again and again.
Clarity is the proficiency in grasping objects of pleasure.

[Objection: "Indeed, we see neither anything to be included nor anything to be excluded by the two terms *avyapadeśya* (non-verbal) and *vyavasāyātmaka* (determinate). On the contrary, since these two are mutually contradictory, they cannot possibly coexist in a single perception.
To this, [the author] says: "In this case, there are two kinds... [The opponent asks:
"Even if it is included, why is it mentioned by its own specific term? This is the remainder of the doubt.
The answer is: because there is disagreement (*vipratipatti*) regarding that [point]. The meaning is: since there is disagreement regarding it, [the author] proceeds in order to refute it.
"Designation" (*vyapadeśa*) means that by which something is designated, that is, distinguished (*vyavacchidyate*).
And since that exclusion—the cognition of differentiation—is produced by both [the qualifier and the qualified], he states that pair: "the qualifier" and so forth.

In this context, that which is coreferential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) and serves as a delimiter is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*); whereas that which is non-coreferential (*vyadhikaraṇa*) is a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).
For example: "Devadatta is a staff-bearer" and "He is my father by virtue of his matted locks."
But this is not a qualification of the essence itself, because it would be over-extensive and thus fail as a definition.
If it is argued that this is a qualification of the definition?
Now, what is the definition [of a qualifier]?
If it is said to be "the state of generating a cognition colored by itself," what would this mean— is it simply "delimiting" (avacchedakatva), or something else?
The first [alternative] is not tenable,
because even a secondary indicator (upalakṣaṇa) functions as a delimiting factor (avacchedaka).
If it is argued that for this very reason "existent" (sat) is a primary qualifier (viśeṣaṇa)— we say no.

Because even something existent may be intended as a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), whereas another [qualifier] is nothing other than that which excludes [the object] through co-referentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Therefore, whether existent or non-existent, a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is that which excludes [the object] while being co-referential; the opposite is a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*).
For this very reason, one cites only a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and not a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*);
for what reason is that?
Because that very [indicator] is a secondary indicator by virtue of being in a different grammatical relation (*vyadhikaraṇatayā*).
For [it is said]:
"That which is to be designated is the qualificand," meaning "that which is to be excluded. This is the sense.
The same applies in the subsequent cases as well.
"Endowed with a name" means having the nature of a name.
He demonstrates this very point through the method of exclusion (vyatireka) by stating, "it does not exist."
"It is separated from the name" means it is divided from it.
To prevent the misconception that "by them" refers to the cause, he completes the sentence with "upeta" and explains it as "for the objects," etc.
This, then, is the collective meaning.
The referents of names are identical in nature to the self [of the object], because they are perceived through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with it;
for whatever is not of the same nature as something else is not perceived through coreferentiality with it.

Just as a cow is perceived through its grammatical coreferentiality with a horse, so too are objects perceived through their coreferentiality with words; therefore, they have those [words] as their essence.

Now, one might wonder: regarding the exclusion of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in cases such as "cow" and "horse," does this result from the exclusion of non-difference, or from the exclusion of the relationship between means and end (*upāyopeyabhāva*) between their respective cognitions? To address this, he says: "And not... Furthermore, if the relationship between means and end were the limiting condition (*upādhi*) for the coreferentiality of word and object, then that [coreferentiality] would also cease precisely upon the cessation of the state of being a means.
And because it does not turn back, he says: "Moreover" (api ca).
He states another reason with the words "Furthermore" (*kiṃ ca*).
"Exaltation" (*utkarṣa*) means excellence;
"depreciation" (*apakarṣa*) means lack of excellence.
And this is not merely a matter of conventional usage;
for the conventional usage of superiority and inferiority based on words will arise precisely from the cognition of things as they actually exist.

The phrase "in the case of the ṣaḍja notes, etc. is stated for the purpose of providing an illustration: namely, that the conventional usage of superiority and inferiority regarding peacocks and so forth is based on the conventional usage of superiority and inferiority regarding the ṣaḍja notes and so forth.
Otherwise, what would be the point of this in the context of establishing identity with the name?
For this very reason, he states in the final conclusion: "it is the application of a designation."
The application (prayoga), however, consists of the name and the self, because it conforms to their increase and decrease;
for that which does not consist of something else does not conform to the increase and so forth of that thing,
just as a cow [does not conform] to a horse.
Now, one might object: "If the cognition of the object does not enjoin the extraction of the name and so forth, then let that [extraction] belong to the name itself;
what has come of the object? To this he says: "Of the cognition" (*pratyayasya*).

Even though there is no direct denotation, since the relationship between quality and qualified (*guṇa-guṇin*) and so forth is also a fit case by virtue of its suitability, it is impossible to manifest a contradiction through the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) residing therein; therefore, setting that aside, otherwise...
He raises an objection with the words "it exists" (*asti*).

For there is indeed a cognition of co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between silverness and that which is reached by reasoning—such as its white, radiant nature—and not a mutual identity (*tādātmya*) between the two substrates; this is the meaning.
To prevent the impression that this has already been stated, he says: "even though the designation has already been mentioned."
And this is the purpose of the explanation: namely, the indication of another reason; and thus follows the formal argument (prayoga).
Cognition whose object is a thing such as form has as its object the word "form" and so forth,
because it is invariably designated by that [word]; for that which does not have a certain thing as its object [is not so designated].
It is not designated by that [word] through such a necessary rule, as in the case of "consciousness of form" being designated by "taste.

Since consciousness does not possess even the state of being permeated—meaning the characteristic of being conjoined—with that [object], how much less could it exist with a word whose essence is that [object]? Therefore, it is said "as if" (iva).
The meaning is that just as an object, as it were, enters within cognition and manifests clearly as its objective content, so too does the word.
The meaning is that it has an object mixed with words, just like the "piercing by words" (śabdānuvyādha).
Nor is this without authoritative proof,
as stated in the remainder of the passage beginning with "that which is called a means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa).
The experience of sound, the mental impression, and the recollection.
the desire to utter,
effort,
and the impact upon the articulatory locations;
The manifestation of sound means that its own nature is understood sequentially;
therefore, even when a child first utters a word, this very sequence is inferred—this is the meaning.

In the first case, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), and the subject (*pakṣa*) has an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇa*), because the Śabda-Brahman itself is like the horn of a horse. Furthermore, it should be observed that the superimposition of contradictory properties characterized by visibility and invisibility entails difference, which results in the establishment of a contrary means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). In the second case, however, the meaning is that the reason is partially unestablished (*bhāgāsiddha*).
For there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) even for indistinct words such as those of children or the mute.

Neither the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) nor the memory produced by it can serve as a means of valid cognition regarding the existence of what was previously experienced, or its connection with what is being experienced now.
If that were the case, a destroyed jar would have to exist simply because it is being remembered.
The ground being experienced would not be conjoined with a jar; thus, the notion that "the ground is devoid of a jar" would be abolished.
Therefore, one must consider the doctrine of the superimposition of contradictory attributes to be accepted.
Is it not the case that the form being experienced by the fool is indeed quite clear?
Consequently, how could the word "form," which has that very form as its essence, be anything but clear?
Furthermore, how could it be non-authoritative, given that the form itself is authoritative?
It would follow that even one who is entirely unlearned could engage in linguistic usage [merely by hearing a word]; however, that is untenable.
For we do not maintain that the cognition of a word's own nature (śabdātmatā) is a constituent of linguistic usage.
But what is this "grasping of the relation"? To this he says: "And not... (na ca).
This too is merely a statement of one's own position (*abhyupagamavāda*).
For sound is perceived by the auditory organ as delimited by a portion of space enclosed by the mouth of the speaker, even when the object is not being perceived;
likewise, the object is perceived by the visual organ as being present before one, even when the word is not understood.
Therefore, this fool’s claim that the very form which one perceives is itself the word for "form" merely echoes the analogy of the clod of earth and the sweetmeat.
If he suspects that this cognition of difference is an error, the author says in response: "Not so.
This too is merely a statement made for the sake of argument (an *abhyupagamavāda*).
For there is no means of valid cognition for its being erroneous.

It might be argued as follows: let it be that for the cognitions of infants, the mute, and others, the commingling with words is indeed merely doubtful; however, let the conceptual cognitions (*savikalpa-dhī*) of those who are proficient [in language], which arise through co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words, establish that the object has the nature of the word.
If that were the case, then regarding the cognitions of infants, the mute, and others—
Because it has that as its object, it follows by implication that its object is mixed with words; therefore, he says: "for the purpose of refuting coreferentiality.
The intended meaning is: "[of that which has the form] possessing a dewlap and so forth," and not "[of that which has the form] of the letter *ga* and so forth."
The intended meaning is that this sound has the form of the letter *ga* and so forth, but not the form of a dewlap and so forth.

Now, one might ask: "When you utter the word 'Ḍittha' as 'this is Ḍittha,' you are not negating that very word 'Ḍittha' by saying 'this is not the word Ḍittha'; what then is this? To this he says: "For it is the general rule... (autsargikaṃ hi).
The meaning is that its orientation toward the goal (arthaparatā) is established precisely by the negation of its orientation toward itself, because there is no contradiction [between them].
Is it thus in every case? No; therefore he says: "But in some cases..."

In that case, where there exist words such as "eternal" (*nitya*) and so forth, which have no conventional designation (*asaṃbheda*) [for their objects], they cannot, because they lack a conventional designation, be directed toward an object; yet, if they were not even for one's own sake, their employment would be useless. Therefore, he says: "Even where... (*yatrāpi*).

For just as in the expression "the Vāhīka is an ox," the nature of being an ox (*gotva*) is an adventitious attribute (*upādhi*) of the Vāhīka by way of indicating the connection with the qualities of an ox, and not because of its inherence (*samavāya*) in him or because of identity (*tādātmya*) with him;

likewise, in the case of "this is Ḍittha" as well, the word "Ḍittha" is an adventitious attribute of the physical body by way of indicating its denotability, and not because of its inherence in it or because of identity with it.

And just as in this case the absence of the cognition "this is a cow" with respect to a Vāhīka is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), so too here, the absence of the cognition "this is Ḍittha" with respect to a particular tree is the means of valid cognition; such is the meaning of the whole passage.

Now, since conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is necessarily preceded by words, it must either have those [words] as its means (*upāya*) or have them as its object (*viṣaya*), because that necessity of being preceded by them excludes [the possibility] of not having them as a means or not having them as an object. In this regard, if the conceptual construction of the object has that word as its object, then our desired conclusion is established. But if it is the means, then is it known or unknown?
If it were unknown, its status as non-conceptual would be untenable;
therefore, being a means [of cognition], the word must be said to be known.
And there can be no knowledge of that which is not present.

Therefore, because of the identity between the object and the word, the proximity of the object is itself the proximity of the word; thus, even if one does not wish to admit it, one must accept that the observation of the object is itself the observation of that [word]. To this he says: "As for that which..."—the word does not necessarily precede conceptual construction.
What then? It is observed as a rule that for one who is proficient [in language], conceptual construction is preceded by the recollection of the word.
Nor does the cognition of a jar have the word "jar" as its object merely by this much;
for if that were the case, the cognition of the absence of a jar would also have the jar as its object,
since it is preceded by the recollection of it.
Therefore, when a jar is to be conceptualized, the remaining question is: why is the word "jar," which is neither the means nor the object [of the cognition], necessarily remembered?
In this regard, the following sequence of recollection has been explained;
the meaning is that it is preceded by the word—that is, preceded by the recollection of the word.

Right here, he states the consensus of the elders with the words "as they say": the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of fire in the kitchen generates a memory when assisted by the perception of the body of its correlative [the smoke], just as the impression arising from the experience of fire in the kitchen generates the memory of it when assisted by the experience of smoke.

Nor does it follow from this alone that there is a fixed relationship of means and end between the recollection of a word and the conceptualization of a particular object, nor is it established that the word itself is the object of conceptualization,
such that one might suspect an identity between the two.

If that were the case, then the same would apply to the memory of fire and the conceptualization of smoke, or else fire itself would become an object of the conceptualization of smoke; such is the meaning of the Vārttika.
It might be argued as follows:

"Every conventional transaction (vyavahāra), whether for one's own sake or for the sake of another, is accomplished by conceptual construction (vikalpa); there is no object whatsoever that must be established even by sensory perception (ālocana).
Therefore, this [perception] is purposeless; how then does it arise? To this, he says: "Therefore" (tasmāt).
We do not, for our part, directly perceive the purpose of every single thing that possesses an origin with our physical eyes;
nor do we refuse to accept an effect—though it has been determined by a most acute perception—merely because its purpose is not understood.
Therefore, this "non-apprehension of a purpose" is a false rejoinder.
Nevertheless, it has been demonstrated that its purpose is clearly nothing other than the production of conceptual cognition itself.
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of recollecting the name":
when a conceptual construction (vikalpa) delimited by a name is to be produced, it is not distinguished—that is, it is not grasped as a specific [qualifier].

Therefore, because the dissimilarity (vaidharmya) is sublated by the appropriate means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), the knowledge of that object becomes exactly like that; the meaning is that it becomes of the same genus as that [name].
Therefore, for one who avoids the redundancy of the commentary, the reason is not non-different from the probandum.

He clarifies the reason indicated by the Commentator through his explanatory gloss with the words "Now then" (*nanu*). "The form of the designation of the object" means having the designation of the object as its domain.
That the cognition which possesses the form of the object has both that form and that object as its domain is established for both disputants.
And its being the object of that designation would only occur if there were no difference between the form and its designation; such is the meaning.

If one thing were designated by means of another, there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) and the collapse of conventional usage (*vyavahāra-vilopa*), because of deception; in this regard, the restriction [of designation] occurs precisely because of its being that very name, as is clear in the *Bhāṣya* itself.

Anticipating the objection—"Why is cognition not designated by its own nature (*svarūpa*) or by its object (*viṣaya*)?"—he provides the following rebuttal, explaining: "It is only the form of the object (*arthākāra*).
First, with respect to itself, cognition is distinguished from non-cognition solely by its own nature.
Who indeed would not accept that [an object] is [known] by means of another cognition as well as by the object itself?
For the opponent, however, another's cognition is eternally beyond perception;
therefore, how could even its object be made known by something other than its own nature and its object?
Or how could one who does not understand engage in conventional discourse?
Therefore, this person is to be instructed by means of words that express that knowledge and words that express the object;
it cannot be done through what is unknown.
Since one must necessarily employ the expressive word in order to comprehend the expressed object, the communicator utters the expressive word;

yet, by this much alone, the identity of the object and the word is not established. For it is not the case that because the object of cognition cannot be apprehended apart from the means of cognition, the two must therefore be identical. This is what was meant by the statement: "because otherwise [the comprehension] would be impossible."

[Objection: Is it not the case that even at the time of the cognition of the object, the word indeed functions, when the prompted elder understands the object from the prompting elder? [Reply: He says: "By way of being perceived," which means "by way of being the object."
This might be the case: one may ask what kind of reason it is that [the property] conforms to increase and decrease. To this he says: "By this...

First of all, from the excellence of [qualities such as] degrees of intensity (*tāratamatva*) and so forth, an excellence of the cow and so forth is not perceived, as is the case with the peacock and so forth.

For when the word "cow" is whispered into the ear, or even when it is corrupted, one does not perceive a cow that is smaller, emaciated, deformed, or disfigured; nor, conversely, does one perceive it as the opposite when it is the opposite.
Nor is there any excellence or lack of excellence whatsoever in the word "cow," despite its distinctions such as grammatical correctness and so forth.

The deviation from auspiciousness and so forth in the assignment of names such as *Nandābhadrā* and the like is indeed quite evident, since even in the case of those who are inauspicious (*abhadrādi*), there is the designation of "Auspicious" (*bhadrādi*) and so on.

Therefore, the meaning is that the establishment of both [auspiciousness and inauspiciousness] cannot be achieved merely by the excellence or deficiency of worldly usage, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Since it is precisely this [perception], which is directly understood from the term "inexpressible" (*avyapadeśya*), that is established as being free from the association with words and free from the association with word-meanings, its refutation has been indicated; therefore, there is no contradiction with what was stated previously.

One might object: "Having begun with an exposition of the *Vārttika*, to provide an exposition of the *Bhāṣya* is like the incident of a pumpkin falling out of season. To this he says: "This very *Bhāṣya*... The meaning is: "This effort of ours in expounding the *Bhāṣya* is for the purpose of explaining this very *Vārttika*.

For [the author] intends to state: "Sound indeed has such an effect, such a cause, such an object of apprehension, such a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such an opponent, such properties, such a form, and such an object-domain."

That object—which is not its effect, not its cause, not its object of apprehension, not its means of valid cognition, not its correlate, and which possesses neither its properties nor its form, and which is distinct from its sphere—is determined by perception itself.
This very fact constitutes the conformity of this cognition of an object to the distinction of its object, as well as its capacity to apprehend the non-difference of words.
If, however, this cognition, even while delineating difference, were disregarded...
Therefore, when the properties as stated are not contradictory, there may be observations even through the transposition of the substratum (dharmin).
Regarding this, he states some examples for the sake of illustration: "For that which is visual," and so forth.
For that which is visual is produced by the eye alone;
it is restricted to form alone, and it is defined by form alone.
The meaning is that it does not function through words, nor is it defined by words alone;
the same applies to what follows.

Having stated the undesirable consequence of the lack of restriction regarding the subject and the object, he states the undesirable consequence of the lack of restriction regarding the action and the instrument with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*).
Now, one might object that this [person] sometimes lacks even the sense of hearing; to this he says, "For it exists.
What is the proof for this? To this he says, "And the cognition of sound."
[Objection: But surely, even in the absence of the eye, non-apprehension is possible; to this he says: "For there exists...
What is the proof for this? To this he says: "And the cognition of form...
This is also an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa).

Since the universal of an object (*arthasāmānya*) is perceivable by all the sense organs, the universal of sound (*śabdasāmānya*) would likewise be perceivable by all the sense organs; or, since the universal of sound is perceivable by the auditory organ alone, the universal of an object would also be perceivable by the auditory organ alone.
Furthermore, it should be observed that this would render the other sense organs useless.
He states the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that there would be no conventional usage regarding the possession of mutual non-existence (itaretarābhāva) with the words "aśabda" (non-sound).
This is also an illustration;

one should understand that in the case of the other three types of non-existence—namely, the unarisen, the destroyed, and the absolutely non-existent—the opposite of what is intended would likewise result.
He states the consequence of contradiction regarding the designation of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) with the words "non-existence" (*abhāva*).
Here too, it should be understood that non-arising (*anutpāda*), destruction (*vināśa*), and absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) would be contradictory;
for here, by the explanation that [an object] is being perceived (*īyamānatayā*), the word "object" (*artha*) is intended to mean precisely that which is graspable by the senses.
And that alone is the object of a sense-faculty which is the objective referent of the cognition produced by it;
therefore, even when these [objects] such as the eye are in contact with the faculty, they are not its objects from the perspective of a cognition whose objective referent is something else.
And if this is so, what occasion is there for the charge of perceptuality (*pratyakṣatā*) regarding the cognition of the sense-faculties and their objects?
For in relation to that [cognition], jars and the like are not its "objects" (*artha*).

Therefore, even though the application [of the term *artha*] was not actually entailed, the author of the Vārttika demonstrated an alternative solution by accepting that the word *artha* refers merely to the "referent" (*padārtha*) in general.
And he explains that this [perception] is the cognition of suffering with the words "not this":
"This [suffering] does not arise from the contact of the sense-organ with its object when [the object] is established as a mere existence.
For in the case of perception, it is intended that the contact of the sense-organ with the object is established as a mere existence even while remaining unperceived itself.
In the case of inference, however, it is the very state of being known that is intended for the logical mark (liṅga), and not its actual existence; such is the meaning.
Now, one might ask: "In inference as well, why is it not simply the non-existence of the mark (*liṅga*) that is intended? To this he says:
"For this very reason," meaning "from the mere recollection of that [the mark] alone.
The inclusion of the word "mere" (*mātra*) is intended with reference to its existence, and not with reference to its being a causal factor for the cognition of the object to be inferred (*anumeya*).
This is because it is the smoke itself, as it is being known, that serves as its cause;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of it not conforming to the time of that [smoke].
For in a case where cognition alone, independent of the object, is the cause, there is no conformity to the time of the object.
Just as in the case of the cognition of absence, which is produced by the cognition of the counter-positive, [the counter-positive itself is not the cause];

furthermore, if the cognition of a probans (*liṅga*)—which does not depend on a probans—were to produce the cognition of the probandum (*liṅgin*), then the doctrine of the "two-fold movement" regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth would not hold in various instances.
This is the meaning:

from the contact of the sense organ with its object—which is established as mere existence—knowledge arises; that which is the most effective instrument for that [knowledge] is perception (*pratyakṣa*). But from a mark (*liṅga*), however...
Inference is that knowledge which arises even from what is non-existent, provided it is known to be endowed with the five characteristics.

[Objection: "In that case, the words 'regarding the objects of the sense-faculties' must be supplied [as a supplement]. What, then, is the basis for the preceding [statement] in the Sūtra? To this he says: "And this...

For by one who says "not from the contact of the sense-faculty with the inferable object," it is effectively stated: that which arises as a cognition through contact of the sense-faculty with something is not its [the cognition's] object;
whereas that which is the object does not arise from contact of the sense-faculty with it.
Therefore, if the cognition arising from the contact of a sense faculty with its object has that very object as its domain, then it is perception;
yet this is not obtained from the sūtra.
Therefore, some have understood that this ellipsis was supplied by the author of the Vārttika itself;
yet this understanding is incorrect,
because the supply of the ellipsis is untenable in either case.
The meaning is that since that which is to be excluded has already been excluded in another way, there is no possibility [of its arising].

For although the qualification "non-erroneous" (*avyabhicārī*) is not logically untenable for a cognition produced from the contact of a sense-faculty with its object— since the possibility of error exists—
it is nevertheless purposeless, because that which it would exclude is already excluded by the general definition itself; and yet,
it must necessarily be included.

For by the word "yataḥ" (from which), which has been supplied as an ellipsis, not merely an instrument is referred to, since that is not the subject under discussion; rather, it is the instrument of valid cognition (*pramākaraṇa*).
And thus, this is the meaning:
Perception is that cognition which arises from the contact of a sense-organ with its object; it is produced by that means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Thus, what possibility is there for error? To this he says: "Even though... (*yadyapi*).

One might ask: "Is there some distinction between employing the term 'non-deviating' (*avyabhicāri*) or following the term 'means of valid cognition' (*pramāṇa*)? To this he says: "Otherwise" (*anyathā*).
The meaning is that the term "non-deviating" refers to the means of valid cognition itself, because only a means of valid cognition possesses non-deviation.
Although the exclusion of erroneous cognition (*vyabhicārin*) occurs simply by examining the definition-word "preceded by that" (*tatpūrvaka*),
for a cognition whose two preceding perceptions are of the nature described would not produce even an erroneous valid cognition (*pramā*);
therefore, the inclusion of the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) there for that purpose is indeed superfluous.

Nevertheless, even when the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) and the ascertainment (*nirṇaya*) are produced by such two types of perception, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that they would be forms of inference remains exactly as it was.
Therefore, the meaning is that if the term "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) were not employed to exclude those [two], it must necessarily be supplied.

If this is so, one might ask what the purpose of the term "non-deviant" (*avyabhicārin*) is; to this he says: "Even so... It should also be understood that [the term "non-deviant"] is neither useful nor possible [to supply] because of the consequence of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*).
Nevertheless, since the restriction has not yet become clear, he says: "Therein."

[Objection: "But surely, just as in the case of inference, the establishment of the result occurs through the establishment of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*), and not as it does in the case of perception, so it is also with regard to verbal testimony (*śabda*). Consequently, for the sake of making that [non-deviation] understood, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of introducing the term 'non-deviating' (*avyabhicāri*) even there. To this, he says: "But in the case of verbal testimony and so forth... (śabdādau tu).

The meaning is that the rule— that the determination of non-deviation [of a means of knowledge] occurs only through the determination of the non-deviation of its result in the case of perception— does not apply elsewhere.
The remainder [of the explanation] is that the inclusion of the term "non-deviating" (avyabhicāri) is as a qualifier of the result.
And this rule is perceived directly as being established by way of the result itself, even in terms of its own nature,
and not otherwise;
whereas inference and the like, once they have become known, serve for the sake of the result.

But since there is a restriction that "it would exist [only] in this way and not otherwise," this [restriction] has already been shown previously as being implied by the sense through the phrase "the two-fold.
Furthermore, he states another pair of restrictions connected with origination (*utpatti*) and manifestation (*jñapti*), beginning with "or else" (*athavā*).
The cause accomplishes both [functions]: it is productive and it is indicative—this is expressed by the words "for not...
The description of the assistance of *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum) is for the purpose of removing the suspicion of an *upādhi* (limiting condition).

Furthermore, since scripture also resides in the speaker and the listener, it depends upon perception both for its own production and for its cognition; therefore, he speaks vaguely with the word "thus" (*evam*).
Nevertheless, one might ask how this meaning is obtained merely by the inclusion of the term "non-deviating" (*avyabhicāri*); to this he says, "For not...
This, then, is the summary.

This specific effort by the author of the Sūtra here indicates that while there is no doubt whatsoever regarding the absence of deviation (vyabhicāra) in this [inference] which is non-deviant elsewhere,
one must therefore strive particularly here to grasp that [absence of deviation].

Even though, according to the view of "making known" (jñapti-pakṣa), the absence of deviation in worldly statements is grasped through the capacity for purposeful action (pravṛtti-sāmarthya) and so forth, [the author's effort here is directed toward a different point].
Nevertheless, the certainty regarding the non-deviation of scriptures concerning the world beyond is established solely by virtue of their being the words of a reliable authority (āpta);
and that, in turn, depends solely on the purity of the perception that constitutes their source.
Now, what is the status of the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika? For this meaning is not perceived from them.
What then? It is merely the exclusion of that which deviates. To this, he says: "Therefore, it has been well said."
The meaning is the same, but the intention is that it is [the object] as something to be restricted (niyamyatayā), and not as something to be enjoined (vidheyatayā).
The statement "it moves up and down" is a description of its similarity to water, serving as the seed for delusion;
this is due to the defect of impairment in the eye caused by sunlight and other factors.
This is what is meant.
Deviation (*vyabhicāra*) consists in the failure to bring about the object that was indicated.
Now, no object whatsoever has been indicated by [the cognition] such that, by failing to bring it about, the object would deviate.
Otherwise, there would be the arising of something whose very nature is the indication of an object, yet...
And its nature is the manifestation of the object, nor has it arisen otherwise.
Therefore, such a deviation belongs to the cognition itself and not to the object.
This is what was stated: "A mistaken cognition arises."
He states the consensus of the elders with the words "as they say.
The term "blind" refers merely to the absence of the means for correct perception;
likewise, the phrase "he does not see" is intended as an indicator of the mere absence of right knowledge.
Therefore, that constitutes a human error (*puruṣāparādha*).
In this context, "error" means either non-perception or contrary perception.
The intended meaning is that just as a post might remain unperceived, so too might it be perceived as a person.

Even though doubt is also excluded by the very persistence of the definition of a general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), since it is not the fruit of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), nevertheless, the term "non-deviant" (*avyabhicāri*) must necessarily be employed for the purpose of making known the restriction (*niyama*).
And by that term, the restriction must be demonstrated precisely through the exclusion of what is deviant.
Doubt, too, belongs to the same class as that which deviates [from the probandum];
therefore, its exclusion by that very term is appropriate. With this intention, he says: "by the word 'non-deviating' alone."
But how is it that this [cognition] is indeed inconstant?
For erroneous cognition has the form of a certainty (*niścaya*), whereas this does not; to this he says: "Certainly not," and so forth.
For it is not the state of being certain that is the determining factor here, but rather non-discrepancy; and that consists in the impossibility of [the object] being reached.
Furthermore, there is no connection with attainment for a thing possessing two forms, because it is not attained anywhere, at any time, or by anyone; such is the meaning.

Nor should it be argued that all this is inconsistent because error must have non-error as its counter-correlative, because an indeterminate object is never within the scope of any means of valid cognition, and because the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*) is not accepted.
For indeed, one who is wavering [in doubt] is neither distinct from a post nor from a person.
Some indeterminate object appears in a flash, wherein there would be an inconsistency.
Now, if both the post and the person are superimposed, then there ought to be a sublation consisting in the destruction of both.
On the other hand, if one of them is not superimposed, then because the other would be ultimately real, its cognition would necessarily be non-sublatable.
This is just as, when two things are joined, if the silver-portion is false, the determination of the white, shining quality and so forth remains true.

And thus, while there is certainty regarding the aspect of the post (*sthāṇu*), the error regarding the aspect of the person (*puruṣa*) consists merely in the presence of one alternative; consequently, the possibility of doubt—which requires the suspension of both alternatives—is rendered impossible. Therefore, it must be that this [cognition] consists merely of the recollection of both. This cannot be so; for in a case where there is a superimposition of both upon something that is neither—such as a stone pillar—the sublater (*bādhaka*) consists precisely in the annulment of both. What more need be said in this regard?

Even where there is the superimposition of one aspect, there is no certainty regarding the other aspect; for, due to the contradiction inherent in the simultaneous presence of mutual exclusion, only a cognition consisting of non-certainty arises.

For in a case where, despite the superimposition of "silver-ness," there is certainty regarding "whiteness" and so forth, there is an absence of mutual contradiction between what is superimposed and what is not superimposed.

Therefore, although there is no difference in terms of being superimposed or not superimposed, that case where the superimposed and the non-superimposed are mutually non-contradictory is error (*viparyaya*);
whereas that case where they are mutually contradictory is doubt (*saṃśaya*). Thus, everything is clear.
If this is so, then doubt is also included within error, and by the very refutation of the latter, it too is refuted.

For what purpose, then, did the author of the Sūtra include the word "of the nature of determination" (*vyavasāyātmaka*)? Or, if that noble meaning exists, why was it neglected by the commentators? And how can such a [meaning] be inferred by those who are inferior? To this, he says: "Therefore... (*tasmāt*).
"It might be so":
it might be for the sake of understanding that [object], if that were perceptible.
But this is not the case; such is the meaning.
He states the reason: "by means of expression" (*abhilāpa*).
For its nature is that of an objective form capable of being associated with the form of the denoting [word]; such is the meaning.

He states the exclusion from the contrary (*vipakṣa*) with the words "And not... For when there is a connection between the denoter and the denoted, there is a rule regarding the connection of their respective forms.

He says that this [connection] cannot possibly consist of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), or the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), stating: "For words do not exist in the object."
The ellipsis is "by way of conjunction (saṃyoga), inherence (samavāya), or being an effect (kāryatva). As for the phrase "or having that as their nature," the word "not" (na hi) is to be supplied.
He states the proof: "If that were so," and "Nor is it."
For that nature of cognition must it be of the form of the apprehended aspect,
or rather of the form of the apprehending aspect independent of that [apprehended]?
It cannot be the first [alternative].

The intention is that since it does not touch upon the object, and this non-contact with the object is due to its not occurring therein and not being produced from it, the same reasoning as before applies. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable.
Because it is applied to objects; that is,
because that expression is necessarily applied only to external objects being apprehended,
meaning it is cognized through necessary external grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya).

This is what is meant: for the nature of being a knower and so forth is indeed the form of cognition itself, and it is perceived as being in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [cognition].
Verbal expression, however, is connected with external objects and is [perceived] as being in coreferentiality with them; therefore, it is not a property of cognition.

Consequently, since its capacity for association with verbal expression is impossible—both from the perspective of its object and from the perspective of its own essential nature—the cognition arising from an object possessing a form would, by its very nature, manifest only the object in the form of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
This is an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*).
The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "not by way of being associated with a verbal expression (*abhilāpa*) in relation to an object (*artha*)."
It might be argued as follows:
"Whatever arises from its own causes has some particular object as its cause, or perhaps no cause at all.
And so, even if that which arises from an object were to have multiple expressions as its objects, what would be the fault? To this, he says: "For not... (na hi).
Visual consciousness, which arises from form as its object and from the eye, is accompanied by a taste that is not its object, thinking, "This is not that form."
This is what is meant:
first, for the sake of establishing the theory of cognition with aspects (sākāravāda), an object is a cognitive domain only insofar as it imparts an unimpaired aspect;
nor does it possess the fitness for association with words.
There is no object by which the cognition could possess that form;
nor is the auditory consciousness the independent depositor of the form,
because such an object is absent at the time of conceptualization.
Or even if it exists, it would appear independently, not as being conjoined with an object; this has already been stated.

Even in the view that [cognition] is formless (*nirākāra*), because cognition possesses the power to illuminate both itself and what is not itself, that alone is the object toward which the sense faculty has restricted efficacy.
Otherwise, there would be an over-extension [of the principle].
Furthermore, the visual faculty is not capable of apprehending the object of another sense-faculty;
nor has it been considered that there can be a conjunction of sound with the very object of vision.
Having stated the *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum), he says "therefore" (*tasmāt*) for the sake of the opposite case (*viparyaya*).

The meaning is that [conceptual cognition] does not arise from the power of the object itself, but rather—while presenting an object as associated with verbal expression—it determines an object that is produced by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of conceptualization and is independent of association with verbal expression.

To the question, "What is the subverting proof (bādhaka) in the case of the opposite [view]? he says: "Because it apprehends an indefinite object"; the meaning is that it lacks any restrictive determination regarding the objective form contained within conceptual construction (vikalpa).
This is what is meant:
for if even an object that is appearing were the producer of a conceptual construction, it would then determine its form.

But it does not restrict [the object], because even in the absence of that [object], such a form arises for it through the force of the latent impressions of conceptual construction (*vikalpavāsanā*).
[Objection: Let the sense faculty be its producer; however—
For it is not its status as an agent that determines its form; therefore, he says "mental" (mānasa).
The meaning is that it originates from the mind alone.
For even a sense faculty, in producing knowledge, does so only through contact with an object that determines its form, and not independently of it;
the point is that, as has already been stated, such a sense faculty lacks contact with an object of that kind.

Is it not the case that in a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) under dispute, the form of the object manifests precisely as something visible? Yet, in conceptual constructions that do not depend on the presence of an object established for both disputants, the object does not appear as something immediate; therefore, that specific type of conceptual construction which depends on the presence of an object is what is meant [by "visible"].

And likewise, since the object is the determiner of that [cognition’s] form, its status as the producer [of that cognition] must be accepted even by one who does not wish to admit it; otherwise, because conceptual construction would merely be a function of imagination, its capacity to motivate action could not be established. Therefore, he says: "its own... [i.e., *ātmīyam*].
Poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is the attribution of what is non-existent; since this necessarily occurs, there is the verbal expression, "I thus fancy it to be so.
Disregard (*tiraskāra*) is non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*).
Perception (*darśana*) is direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*).
It is either the apprehension of a distinction as being foremost,
or a superimposition caused by that [apprehension].
Thus it is established.
By means of the connection through a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*):
