if the conceptual constructions under dispute were produced by the causal efficacy of the object, then they would not be followed by verbal conceptualization; such is the meaning.
"Being followed by that" means being followed by the conceptualization of words (*śabdakalpanā*).
The remainder of the sense is that perception, by negating the state of being followed by verbal expression, excludes the state of being produced by the power of the object (*arthasāmarthyaja*).

Since the fallacies of the unestablished (*asiddha*) and the contradictory (*viruddha*) are impossible here, [the author], after first recalling what was stated previously, removes the suspicion of the doubtful-uncertain (*sandigdhānaikāntika*) by saying "not so" (*na ceti*).
The meaning is that it would "conform to the form of the object," i.e., it would possess a form similar to the form of the object.

For if there were no restrictive factor in conforming to a form that is unrelated through either identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*), then by conforming to all forms, the consequence would be that everyone would be omniscient.
The meaning is that [the cognition] has that as its object because it is merely a semblance of the form of that [object].
Indeed, a relationship characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*) is not established in its own nature;
rather, it is established by way of being a restrictive factor (*niyāmakatā*).
Thinking that there might be no fault if convention (*saṅketa*) alone were the regulator in this case, he raises an objection with the words "If [it were] convention" (*saṅketa*).
The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "That very [perceived object], being present, would necessarily cause these [words] to be remembered.
To the question "What about these two as well? he says: "And in that very [case]" (*tatraiva ca*).
It has as its objective domain that which is followed by [the cognition];

for this very reason, it is a universal (*sāmānya*) that follows across space and time, because it is easy to apply a linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) precisely therein— this is the intended meaning.
To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "And that [object] is not seen—that is, directly perceived—but rather the *svalakṣaṇa* (particular characteristic) is the object of perception.
The phrase "because of its possessing a form" (*sarūpakatvāt*) is to be supplied. To the question "Whence does it possess a form?", he says: "For that very [thing]... [and so on].
The ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is an uncontrived, non-superimposed nature; because it exists [in that sense], it is "ultimately existent" (*paramārthasat*).
Why is this so? To this he says: "It is the cause of consciousness.
Because of its relevance to the subject at hand, "of consciousness" means that it is the cause, insofar as it is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsamartha*).

Now, one might ask: "Is not the universal (*sāmānya*) also an object of perception? To this he says: "But not the universal. Why? Because that [universal] is devoid of all causal capacity (*sāmarthya*).
Every human goal (*puruṣārtha*), consisting of what is to be rejected or accepted, has its capacity—that is, its power—[in the particular].
Because that [universal] is devoid of that [causal efficiency];

for there is no purpose of man whatsoever that can be accomplished by a universal. Therefore, because it is incapable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), it is not ultimately real; and because it is not real, it does not produce a cognition of itself.
Because it does not produce [cognition], it is not similar [to its object];
because it is not similar [to its object], it is not within the range of perception—this is the meaning.
Now, it may be granted that because a universal lacks causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), it cannot be an object of perception;
however, let it be that only what is an object of perception is denotable. Furthermore, a linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) regarding it can still be established by some means or other.

Therefore, in that case, the instigating elders who intend to convey an object capable of causal efficiency, as well as the elders being prompted, are observed to possess the comprehension of such an object in verbal communication; hence he says, "Moreover" (*api ca*).
For in the Buddhist tenet, there is no such thing as "fire" distinct from heat (*auṣṇya*).
Nor is it ever the case that the heat commonly recognized by both parties is not perceived to remove cold;
for if it did not act at all, it would either be unperceived or merely superimposed.
Furthermore, it is not the case that fire is entirely unperceived from the word "fire."
Therefore,
the intended meaning is that what is delineated by the conceptualization of words is indeed a non-entity, appearing as if it were a real entity.
Having accepted that universals (*jāti*) and so forth are ultimately real, he says: "That is not so. "By way of distinction" means by way of spatial separation.
For the relation of qualifier and qualified consists in their mutual connection through the relationship of the delimited (*avacchedya*) and the delimiter (*avacchedaka*).
And that [the state of being a word] is pervaded by the condition of being situated in a distinct location.
When that [condition] is absent, it ceases to exist only by taking with it its own pervaded [consequence], namely the relationship between qualifier and qualified.
Consequently, since there is no mutual connection between universals and the like, it is not possible to easily establish a linguistic convention for them when they exist independently.
And thus, the meaning is that there is no perception of a mixture.
By this, it should be understood that even if the apprehension of distinction (*viveka*) regarding a word were possible, its application (*yojanā*) is refuted;
[the object] is one, not aggregated,
undivided, and partless.
The specific characteristic is distinct from the three worlds;
it is "thus and thus."
The meaning is that [the object] is conceptualized as being composed of qualities, actions, and so forth, or as being common [to many], but it is not actually perceived as such.
Moreover, even when there is cognition of the three things that exist in the ultimate sense, the word "by way of distinction" (vivekena) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

Now, it might be argued: "Indeed, two fingers that are objects of a single cognition at the same time are not related as cause and effect; therefore, even though they possess a fixed sequence of priority and posteriority, it is not logical to say that they are not likewise [related] when they are both within the scope of a single cognition of an omniscient being.
What fault would there be if this were asserted?"

For it is not the case that being a cause or a non-cause is determined by the difference or non-difference of perception; rather, that which is independent is the cause and that which is dependent is the effect—
this principle applies equally here as well.
Even though they share the same object of a single cognition, that which delimits is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), and that which is delimited is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).
As for that which is not thus, it is not like that; therefore he says: "The qualifier indeed... and "...not otherwise.
The phrase "because of over-extension" (atiprasaṅgāt) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
If it is argued that there must then be some benefit [to the agent], he says: "And not one...
Why should this not be the case? To this he says: "Of those two...
The word "consequence" (prasaṅgāt) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

The meaning is that the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is a restriction of priority and posteriority by way of intrinsic nature (*svarūpataḥ*), whereas the relationship between the signified and the signifier (*jñāpyajñāpakabhāva*) is by way of cognition (*jñaptitaḥ*). And this twofold [relationship] is not restricted for two things that are objects of a single cognition and exist at the same time; such is the sense.
It might be argued as follows:
even if the two kinds of assistance described above are not possible, there could still be a relationship of container and contained;
for that [relationship] is observed only between two things existing at the same time, such as a bowl and a jujube fruit.

"Since the doctrine of momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) must be established by you and refuted by me as well, he says 'Moreover' (api ca). Even though the non-Buddhists, due to their dullness born of faith in stability, do not accept that the production of the jujube fruit—which possesses the property of not falling—occurs because of the bowl as its substratum; nevertheless, the bowl is accepted as the substratum of the jujube only by producing a state of stability characterized either as the cessation of motion or as the conjunction that obstructs gravity, which is a property of that [fruit]."
By those [arguments]. And what follows from this? To this he says: "In the same way here too.
Even with this much, what is the point? To this he says: "And not by other powers."

Although the opponent does not indeed accept that there is any benefit to a property such as "universality" (jāti) and so forth, consisting in its arising or passing away— just as in the case of a jujube fruit—
nevertheless, this should be understood as a concessionary argument (abhyupagamavāda) made by the Buddhist.

And likewise: for by this conceptual construction "existent," that which is capable of benefiting sentient beings is made its object; and there exists nothing other than that—such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) or the like—which is capable of benefiting [inanimate] things or incapable of benefiting sentient beings, wherein conceptual constructions of substance and so forth would be meaningful.

"Therefore, since these [words]— operating upon an object that possesses substance and so forth, which is capable of providing assistance, and which is non-different from that which is capable of assisting the existence [of the object]— would result in being meaningless without touching the object that serves as their substratum, the Buddhist, perceiving his own excessive cleverness in reasoning and the extreme triviality of the objection, will suspect that it is our own lack of mental acuity [that is at fault]. Anticipating this, he writes that passage, beginning with "As he says," which is the meaning of the Vārttika.
In whose view, even when an object possesses manifold adjuncts (*nānopādhi*), the cognition that apprehends it as a distinct, qualified entity is a conceptual cognition (*vikalpadhī*).

Since that [object]—which is a single essence (*ekātman*)—possesses a power that constitutes the basis for the assistance of the various adjuncts, when there is an apprehension of that very object of qualification (*viśeṣya*) which is assisted by all its adjuncts in their entirety and in its unitary nature, what difference could there be? That is to say, how could it be differentiated such that it is called "distinct" (*bheda*) or "qualified" (*viśiṣṭa*)?
Would it be uncertain?
On the contrary, the meaning is that it would indeed be certain as qualified by all its adjuncts (*upādhi*).
When this adjunct, whose nature is to assist, is apprehended as being grasped, there are no assisting natures that do not assist.
Furthermore, there exist other distinct adjuncts (*upādhi*) which, even when that single nature which is the benefactor [of all] is perceived, would not themselves be perceived.

What does this mean? That single nature is the benefactor of all; therefore, when it is apprehended—that is, when it is apprehended as qualified by one particular adjunct—it follows that there must be an apprehension of the whole, meaning an apprehension of it as qualified by all its adjuncts. This is the sense.

Indeed, it would be better for our opponents to adopt the doctrine of the intrinsic nature of things (*vastusvabhāvavāda*), whereby they are able to establish the clearly observed relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) even between things that neither benefit nor harm one another;
and by means of the distinction between the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and that which is limited (*upādhimat*), they avoid tautology.
But this is not possible for the Buddhists, because they do not accept that the limiting adjuncts such as "existence" (*sattva*) and so forth possess the status of real entities (*vastutva*).
And since your arrows have thus fallen upon you yourself, he says: "But for us...
[referring to the verse beginning with] "that which they grasp as a mere generality" and "that which they determine as a continuum."
They do not grasp it even in the slightest degree, nor even in a general form; they do not take it as their object.
The meaning is that because it is false, it lacks the nature of a real entity (*vastudharma*).
If so, how are they non-contradictory and motivators? To this he says: "by way of a lineage" (*pāramparyeṇa*).
What follows from that? To this he says: "therefore" (*ataḥ*).
In that case where cognition is dependent upon the object...
The specific and the non-specific are dependent upon that [the object],
but here the reverse is the case, because the very appearance of existence of the object depends upon the intellect; thus,
in this context, the object of conceptual construction is the qualified.
The meaning is that even regarding whether [the self] is distinct or non-distinct by virtue of being qualified by this or that particular attribute, doubt alone is the witness, not inquiry.
[Objection: "Granted that an ultimately real object may not be the object of conceptual construction, it will nonetheless be its producer. To this, he says:
"Moreover... [and] "not even a conceptual one."
The particle *api* is displaced [in the sentence].
The meaning is that the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is neither its domain (*gocara*) nor its producer (*janaka*).
The application of the object is contact (*sannikarṣa*).
And [the phrase] "not that which alone," etc.,
is because of logic (*nyāya*).
The word "to be stated" (*vācyam*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

Indeed, it is not the case [that they are mutually dependent], because memory (*smaraṇa*) and the sense faculty (*indriya*) lack the capacity for a single object; therefore, there is no mutual dependence between them.

And therefore, the meaning is that this very [cognition] is equally useful for the purpose [of action]. To the question, "Why is it not the case that these two have the same object? he says: "And if they had that as their object," and so forth.
[This refers to] even objects never experienced before, by the mere operation of the eyes.
It should also be understood that there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of remembering one's former states.
By that [consequence], it would follow;
such is the meaning of "it would entail" (prasajyeta).
The phrase "even when the sense organ has ceased" is an illustration;
it should also be understood that "when the latent impression (*vāsanā*) is absent, there is no cognition of memory.
The meaning of *sahate* is "it awaits" or "it endures."
He introduces the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "herein" (*atre*).

First of all, it is established by experience that even a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), such as "this is a cow," possesses a direct perception of an object that has an appearance capable of being associated with verbal expression.
Furthermore, there exists a conformity with the presence and absence of the sense-faculties and their objects.
If it is argued that this [conceptualization] is established otherwise, because those two [the senses] have their purpose fulfilled by mere observation (*ālocana*) alone,
then does this now constitute the power of observation toward the production of conceptual construction?
If that were the case, then no *ālocana* (indeterminate perception) would ever arise from it.
If you argue that this is not so because of the absence of the maturation of latent impressions (*vāsanā-paripāka*),
then, since that maturation of latent impressions necessarily resides within the midst of the sense-faculty and the object, why is the effect not dependent upon them?
If you say it is like the "crow-and-palmyra-fruit" coincidence, [we reply:

even when the sense objects are present and close at hand, a conceptual cognition possessing direct manifestation (sākṣātkāravat) arises only occasionally due to a specific maturation of latent impressions (vāsanā).
Indeed, there is no such thing as a conceptual cognition that possesses direct manifestation.

If it is argued that, however, due to the non-apprehension of the difference from the indeterminate [perception], it appears as if it possesses that [object]— we say no, because there is a lack of evidence. For there is no perception to the effect that this operation of seeing, residing in the conceptual cognition under dispute, is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*).

Nor is it inference. If it is argued that the operation of perception is pervaded by being free from conceptual construction (kalpanāpoḍha), and therefore, when that [freedom from conceptual construction] is excluded from this [perception], it also excludes the operation of perception—[we reply: no.
For it is equally easy to state the opposite as well; that is to say,
the status of being the operation of seeing is pervaded by the accompaniment of conceptual construction.

And that state of being accompanied by conceptual construction (vikalpa), ceasing upon the occurrence of pure observation (ālocana), also causes the cessation of "the operation of seeing" (darśanavyāpāratva) which is pervaded by it.

Thus, why should this "operation of seeing" not be merely adventitious (aupādhika) due to the proximity of conceptual construction, such that it is called "observation"? You yourself have already rejected the notion of experience (anubhava) as a possible limiting adjunct (upādhi).
If it is asked, "How can that object appear in a non-conceptual cognition within a future conceptualization?", we say: no, because the difference in time is equal in both cases;
and the causal relationship between material cause and effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*) is likewise the same as a restrictive factor.
If it is argued that the attributes of the material cause (upādāna) follow the effect (upādeya), but the attributes of the effect do not follow the material cause— this is not so;
for in reality, there is no transfer of the attributes of a non-entity.
But regarding the transition into one characterized by conceit (*ābhimānika*), there is no such certainty.
If it is argued that the causal condition of the grasped (*upādeya*) arises in that manner through the power of the causal condition of grasping (*upādāna*),
then, alas, if direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) arises as something possessing direct realization, how could its suchness (*tathātva*) be merely adventitious (*aupādhika*)?
If it is argued that it is called "conditioned" (*aupādhika*) simply because it arises from that much alone, independent of the sense organs and so forth—this is not so;

for if direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) were produced by the power of the immediate antecedent condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), it would follow as an undesirable consequence that non-perception could never arise.
Moreover, a direct perception could never be produced from that which is itself non-perceptual.
If it is argued that this could still occur due to a particular auxiliary cause (*sahakāriviśeṣa*),
then one must accept that a thing serves as an auxiliary cause for a specific effect only insofar as its positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with that effect has been observed.

Moreover, it has already been stated that the causal capacity for direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) resides in both the sense faculty and the object as admitted by both parties, and not in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Thus, first of all, the direct realization of the object is intrinsic;
because it is inseparable from that, its status as arising from the capacity of the sense faculty and the object is established.
Furthermore, its non-erroneousness is also not adventitious.
For instance, if there were an ultimate contradiction regarding this [cognition],
then it might be conceivable that this non-contradiction, though being perceived, is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*); however,
that [non-contradiction] cannot be produced by place, time, or form.
If it is argued that [the conceptual cognition] shows that which is indeed not followed by [the object] as if it were followed by it—
no, because the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), being uncommon, cannot be touched by conceptual construction;
or, if it were touched, it would follow that [the conceptual cognition] is produced from that [particular].

But if that which is not a producer [of cognition] were indeed the object by virtue of being a real entity, then the claim that perceptuality is pervaded by arising through the power of the object would be mere prattle from one who is asleep.
For conceptual construction (vikalpa) functions only by delineating a common nature;
and that [nature] is devoid of all causal efficiency (sāmarthya).
Moreover, one who seeks purposeful action does not engage with that which is seen to be incapable;
therefore, it is precisely that which is incapable which is conceptualized as having superimposed capability.
And if it is asked, "In that case, how can there be such a thing as 'correspondence' for this [cognition], which consists in the superimposition of a contrary [nature]?"—we say: no;
for if it were to project only the capacity [of the object], it would delineate only the unique [specific characteristic].
For in your system, nothing other than the unique particular (asādhāraṇa-rūpa) can truly be called "efficient" (samartha).
Therefore, conceptual construction (vikalpa) merely displays that [particular] as if it were efficient; furthermore, the sense of "as if" (iva) is not something to be superimposed there.
Because the object of conceptual construction is not similar to that which possesses causal efficiency.
If it is argued: "But surely capacity (*sāmarthya*) is merely the exclusion of incapacity and not a distinct reality;
and since that [exclusion] does not contradict a common form, the manifestation of a single identity is therefore not contradictory"—we say no.
Because superimposition is impossible when there is no contradiction;
for that which is perceived in a certain place while being non-contradictory with respect to it cannot be said to be superimposed upon it.
Therefore, activity arises from the non-apprehension of difference.
Nor is that itself a contradiction;
for if that were the case, even non-conceptual perception would be contradictory,
since no distinction between conceptual and non-conceptual perception is indicated.
By this, the [position] that "one acts because of the determination of an object within one's own appearance, although it is not an object" is refuted.
For if there were non-reality [of the object], would the object of conceptualization be non-different from the conceptualization itself,
or different from that which is being observed?
First of all, it is not possible for that which is false— the domain of conceptual construction— to be non-different from the conceptualization.
By what means could there be an imposition (āropa) characterized by the delineation of difference?
Even if there were a difference from the object of perception, there is no imposition because there is no manifestation of non-difference.
This fault does not apply because it is stated that [the object] is "non-existent" with respect to its own manifestation.

If it is argued that this form (ākāra), although non-different from conceptual construction (vikalpa), is nevertheless superimposed as being different—provided that this is said with reference to the system of consciousness-only (vijñānanaya)—then [we reply]: [The argument continues: ...if this is indeed asserted on the basis of the system of consciousness-only...

The same principle applies to the reflection upon that [object] as well, since that too is of the nature of a superimposition. Regarding the form of the apprehended object, conceptual cognition lacks validity; yet, regarding its own self, it possesses the nature of self-awareness. Thus, both possess validity alone, and there is no distinction whatsoever between them.
Now, is this discussion undertaken with reference to an external object?
Even so, would an external object appear in exactly the same form as the conceptual construction?
Yet such a common form does not exist.
Therefore, that which appears as this common form does not adhere to the aspect of conceptual construction;
thus, it remains strictly external.
If it is argued that its "commonality" is merely superimposed upon it just like its "externality"—no, [that is not the case].
Because an ultimate unique particularity is never perceived anywhere, it is impossible to superimpose it;
for if there were a representation of what is non-existent, one would have to admit that conceptual construction has a purely false object,
and in that case, as has already been stated, there could be no possibility of superimposition at all.

If it is argued that the commonality [of the two cognitions] consists precisely in the synthesis of the non-difference between the two conceptual forms of the preceding and succeeding moments— [we reply: no,
because when the possessors of the forms (the cognitions) are perceived as distinct, it is impossible to synthesize their forms as one,
since those two [cognitions] are admitted to be identical with [their respective] forms.
If it is argued: "The very nature of conceptual construction (vikalpa) is its form (ākāra), which is projected as something external;
therefore, even when there is a determination of difference among the natures of conceptual constructions, there is no determination of difference among their forms;
thus, there is a synthesis [of them] as one."
Well then, if this mental form were perceived as being of the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*),
how could it be superimposed as something external?
Furthermore, the non-perception of identity [between the form and the external object] would occur in both cases alike.
Because conceptual construction is not self-cognized,
or because it is self-cognized [only by itself],
identity with that [object] is excluded due to their being distinct.
First, the initial [position] is untenable precisely because it is not accepted by the Buddhists.
As for the second, however, it is understood by everyone.
If it is argued that "it is understood but not ascertained"—no, [that is not so].
Because the occurrence of contradictory properties characterized by certainty and uncertainty would entail a difference [between the two].
If it is argued that the difference lies only between the exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) and not between the two real entities (*vastu*),
then what indeed is this so-called "exclusion"?
If you say, "There is nothing at all," let it be so; and in that case, there is not even a report of superimposition.
Consequently, there is not even a trace of contradiction with the object as it was presented.
If it is argued that "misrepresentation is simply the manifestation of a non-existent object," let that be for now;
what is intended here is merely the nature of the object itself.
Because it is applicable to the subject at hand;
and thus, because its object is non-erroneous, it possesses validity (*prāmāṇya*).
Being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) due to its nature of immediate realization.
Furthermore, because it is directly perceived by people such as ourselves, [conceptual cognition] arises from the capacity of the sense faculties and their objects.

This being the case, all the counter-arguments (pratipakṣahetu) employed by the Buddhist are rendered incapable of gaining a foothold, as they are shown to be "mistimed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa); this is true even more so in the case of attempting to prove that conceptualization is not perception.
Nevertheless, this remains: even by this much, the validity of the object as being ultimately real has not been established;
and since we disagree on that point, he says: "There may be a contradiction."

[Objection: But surely, because the world is momentary, it is impossible to demonstrate that an ultimately real entity possesses the capacity for association with verbal expression; therefore, it was said: "possessing stability. [Objection continued: Even if stability were established, since universals (*jāti*) and so forth are difficult to justify, how can an ultimately real entity possess the capacity for association with verbal expression? Therefore, it was said: "possessing universals and so forth," and likewise [the word] "tathā" (and so).

Even if this reductio argument (*prasaṅga-hetu*) were to be "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*) given the establishment of the object in the form described above, and if its observation were not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*),

there would still be no possibility [of such a thing], for it is impossible that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) could arise from the causal efficacy of an object while that object’s ultimate existence is both certain and uncertain.
Nevertheless, since the opponent has also raised an objection solely for the purpose of establishing its refutation, he is not to be dismissed by royal decree.
Therefore, the meaning is that, given the initial doubt regarding it, let there simply be the presence of the reason in a doubtful counter-example (vipakṣa).
By this, the contrary [fallacy] should also be understood as refuted.
[Objection: Granted that birth and the other [factors] are ultimately real; nevertheless, if they too were of the nature of a composite whole (*piṇḍātman*), how could they appear as distinct?
And if they do not so appear, how could they delimit the substantive by way of being qualifiers?
Furthermore, if they were not of the same nature [as the substance], how could they attain grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)? To this, he says: "And not... (*na ca*).
Nevertheless, how could a word, which is distinct in nature and does not reside in that [object], serve as its delimiter?

If it were to be a delimiter, then either the [property] residing in that [object] or the essence of that [object] itself would have to be cognized; yet, if delimitation occurred in this very manner, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
But he raises the objection that the cognition of limitation is an error, saying: "And not... (na ca).
The conceptualization of non-difference is the conceptualization of delimitation.
And is that [delimitation] by way of being identical with it (*tadātmatayā*) or by way of being in contact with it (*tatsaṃsargitayā*)?
This has already been stated; for there is no rule that contact with something must necessarily consist in subsisting in it.
Rather, the meaning is that there is no contradiction between the knower and the knowable, or between the designator and the designated, even when they are situated as separate entities.
But surely this delimiting factor, even though it is external, does not function by its mere existence, but rather as something known;
yet at that time, the ear has no operation in the cognition of the word.
Because of the separation from the object,
and because the mind is distracted elsewhere while the eye is occupied with its function;

therefore, just as in the state of dreaming, even when the sense organs have ceased their activity, non-existent objects are made the objects of cognition by the mind alone due to the strength of prior latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).

Likewise, since even a sound is made an object by the eye alone—or by the mind—made potent by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) produced by the conceptual exclusion of non-sound (*aśabdavyāvṛtti-vikalpa*), it is nothing but an error because its objective support (*ālambana*) is a non-existent sound; therefore, he says:
"And [there is no] [simultaneous apprehension] of word and meaning.
The ellipsis to be supplied here is: "in the case of being grasped by a single sense-organ (*ekendriyagrāhyatā*)."
The meaning is this:

if it follows that [sound] is perceptible by a single sense-organ by virtue of being intended by the mind (*manas*), there is nothing undesirable, because the mind has all things as its object. Or, if...

With reference to the external sense-faculty, even there, what kind of conceptual construction is intended— is it one consisting of the joining [of names], or rather one consisting of the joining of universals (*jāti*) and so forth?
In this regard, the position that the name functions as a qualifier has already been refuted by its very non-acceptance.
Furthermore, it has already been established that its function is merely as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), and that this applies precisely to something standing apart [from the object].

Since this [functioning as an indicator] is possible even for that which is presented by another sense faculty, the manifestation of the name is not required for a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) based on a sensory perception.

But in the case of the association with universals (jāti) and so forth, there is no utility even for the recollection of the word, much less for its apprehension, because that [recollection] does not serve as a differentiator.
Only this remains to be addressed: why is it that sound is necessarily remembered?
To this, it is said: "But rather... (kiṃ tu).

One might ask: "In that case, does the recollection of the word have no utility whatsoever? To this he says: "[It has utility] with respect to the production of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising from the sense-faculties.
The meaning is that it certainly does have utility with respect to linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*).
The phrase "at the time of the convention" (*saṅketasamaye*) is intended as an indicator for either of the two: the recollection of a prior state or the grasping [of the object].
The word, however, does not establish itself [in the cognition], whether it has been grasped or even if it is recollected; this is the remainder of the sense.
The meaning is that this very [object] is seen even with the eye, but the sound residing previously in the heart is not;
having explained this very point, he confirms it with another verse beginning with "for by this... and so forth.
"But not even the application of a word" means that even the form of the word is an object [of cognition].

Although in the verse beginning with "saṃjñā hi," only the phrase "it is external" (sā taṭasthā) is relevant to the present subject, nevertheless, wishing to provide a remedy for what is yet to come, he explains another component: "not [arising] from object and sense-organ" (nārthendriya).
"Object and sense-organ" (arthendriya) means the sense-organ together with its object.

Even if [the cause] is momentary, even in the case of being a constituent part, those things which are individually incapable may possess causality when combined, provided that a quality is possible in them.

Thus, by this principle, it is the very same sense organ—which, through the production of a succession of intensifications, occupies the midst of auxiliary factors such as the recollection of the previous state—that generates the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and not any other; therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

Nevertheless, considering that because a conceptual construction has a stable object, if momentariness were accepted, it would result in the consequence of being objectless (*nirviṣayatva*)—and thus [the effort] would be fruitless—he offers a rebuttal while relying precisely on stability: "No..."
And [the phrase] "and as a producer" means:
it might be argued that this [is the case], namely,
that the conditioning factor (saṃskāra) acts as a cooperative cause (sahakāritva) with respect to the sense faculty.
The meaning is: "If there were no difference in the objects of these two.
To this [he asks]: "Why is that? [The answer is:

Due to the difference in their objects, how could there not be a mutual influence between the refinement of the sense organ and [the cognition]? Is it because [the object] is not connected to the apprehension?
Or [is it] connected with activity?
Not the first,
because even when there is such a difference in objects, one observes the arising of a cognition of form through the mutual influence of the olfactory cognition and the visual faculty.
The second [reason], however, is unestablished (*asiddha*),
because it is inferred merely from its being subject to the influence of the effect;
the meaning is that both of these [points] are established for both disputants.
Now, if the object present before one were the object of the mental impression (saṃskāra) by virtue of being connected to its operation,
then the manifestation of a past state would certainly not occur;
for an operation cannot have one thing as its object while [the result] pertains to another.
The admission is that the action occurs elsewhere.

Therefore, because the action has a past object, the impression (saṃskāra), by virtue of its connection with that activity, has that very same [past] as its object, and not what is present before one.
Likewise, if the object of the sense faculty were only that which exists in a past state while it is active, then there would be no manifestation of an object present before one.
Therefore, since its object must be precisely that which is present before it while it is active, how can there be a single object even in terms of their respective operations?

The immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), however, although its object is odor from the perspective of its apprehension, has form as its object from the perspective of its activity;
it depends solely on the eye for its activity regarding the object of form.
For even when the eye is a cooperative cause, there is no cognition of odor arising from the cognition of odor.
Rather, it is simply the cognition of form.
This is not correct, because the distinction in activity is itself determined solely by the distinction in auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).
For it is not the case that even in the absence of auxiliary causes such as the eye, there is a restriction of the olfactory cognition's activity toward the object of color.
If that were the case, then from the cognition of odor, even with the assistance of the tongue and other [senses], there would arise only the cognition of form,
not the cognition of taste and so forth. Therefore, although for the eye alone form is the sole object of its operation, [the cognition of it does not depend on other senses].

Nevertheless, for one who maintains that the prior state acts as a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*), it is not at all contradictory that the very object present before one is the domain of the visual operation.

As for the objection—"How can the prior state, which is not in contact with the eye, be the domain of its operation?"—the remaining part of the argument raises this doubt: "But [is it not] the past...? etc.
In this context, would that state of being the object of its operation consist merely in its relation to it, or in the pervasiveness of that relation?
He refutes the first alternative with the words "What then? (tatkim iti).
He raises a second objection: "But surely this is incoherent."

For the status of being the object of the primary operation is pervaded by the status of being the object of the intermediate operation; thus, when that [status] ceases due to the past state, it also causes that [intermediate operation] to cease.

Now, if it is argued that in the case of a conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) about to be produced, the recollection of the previous state itself is the intermediate operation, and not the connection with the object.

The meaning is that, in that case, the contradiction of the definition (*lakṣaṇavirodha*) constitutes a flaw (*dūṣaṇa*). [The phrase] "let it not be so" means that it is not within the range of the senses; that is to say, it is not within the range of sensory contact (*indriyasannikarṣa*).
"And not" [is said].
This is the intention:
it is not the case that the past state is in every respect not in contact with the sense faculty.
This is because the relation of "qualification of the conjoined" (*saṃyuktaviśeṣaṇatā*) is possible;
since this too, like "inherence in the conjoined" (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), produces perceptual knowledge, it is included under the term "sense-object contact" (*sannikarṣa*).
Although, in the case of properties that are positive entities other than inherence, the relation of qualifier and qualified necessarily involves another underlying relation, [it is still included].
Nevertheless, although this is a secret— that this established rule pertains only to objects that are currently existing and thus there is no contradiction with the Sūtra—
nevertheless, even if one does not admit a connection with the past state, there is no deficiency in the definition;
for sensory contact does not extend as far as the entire range of what is to be cognized.
Such is the Sūtra.
What, then, is it? Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as a result is the cognition produced by the contact of a sense faculty with its object;
the object belonging to such a result and its corresponding domain is "directly perceived" (*pratyakṣa*).
Thus, perception is the means of valid cognition for establishing such a result.
This might be so:

with respect to a single effect, there is mutual cooperation between sensory contact and mental impression; but from what source does this very singleness of the effect arise? With this intention, the opponent raises an objection: "But [regarding] the preceding and succeeding... and so forth.
Following the maxim of the needle and the frying pan (*sūcīkaṭāhanyāya*), he explains first that which was mentioned later, beginning with "For instance" (*tathā hi*).
Although the mention of "that" (*tat*) does not pervade all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*),
it nonetheless exists in the case of the cognition of synthesis (*pratisaṃdhāna-jñāna*).
And its validity must necessarily be accepted by those who maintain the doctrine of permanence;
otherwise, everything would fall into total ruin.
Furthermore, that very point must be specifically refuted by the opponent as well.

For the intention is this: by the very refutation of that [rebirth], the rejection of conceptual construction—which, even in the absence of birth and so forth, is characterized by non-reconnection—is established without effort.
But surely, there might be a conjunction of contradictory properties even without difference; to this he says: "because it would follow that the three worlds are one," and thus:
The meaning is that there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the conventional usage of distinction (*bhedavyavahāra*) being accidental.
As for the phrase "and the difference of objects":
although the unity of the omniscient cognition remains entirely unimpaired even when it possesses different objects, [the conventional usage of distinction would still be undermined].
Nevertheless, even if the opponent were to accept that the synthesis has as its object a blue thing that is momentary and exists at multiple times, no desired conclusion would be established for him.
Nor is this undesirable for us; rather, it is simply that [oneness] does not pervade conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Therefore, does this [conceptual cognition] have as its object a superimposed unity, or does it have as its object an ultimate unity? Regarding these two, if the opponent were to accept the first, he would indeed favor our position. Consequently, oneness—which is the object of the opponent’s intention—exists by virtue of having as its object an ultimate unity qualified by various states.
And the intention is that this [objection] is refuted precisely by establishing a distinction between the objects.
To this it is replied:
although this cognition of "that" and "this" is indeed immediate even in its prior state,
for it is not the case that something becomes non-immediate merely because of the mention of the word "that."
If that were the case, it would follow that verbal, inferential, and conceptual cognitions—which lack the mental "pointing-out" (*tad-ity-ullekha*)—would also be direct perceptions (*aparokṣatva*).

Nor is it the Buddhist position that something is a direct perception simply because it has "this" (*idam*) as its object, for that would entail the fallacy of contradicting their own tenets (*apasiddhānta*).
Rather, whether the object is proximate or non-proximate, whatever cognition is produced by a sense organ independently of a logical mark (*liṅga*) and so forth [is a direct perception].
That very [cognition] arises in a direct form;
however, the distinction is that what is not born of the senses is indirect.
In that regard, whether indirect or direct, it is designated as "that" because its object is characterized by a previously experienced state.
"Because it has a proximate object, it is [cognized as] 'this'";
this is the distinction produced by the object.

Nevertheless, even in the context of a hypothetical admission (*abhyupagamavāda*), there is no contradiction; thus, one should understand that this is a "seizing of the counter-argument" (*pratibandigraha*).
If you argue that there is therefore no contradiction because the objects are different, must you not then provide a similar resolution here as well? "Indeed, it is the same here too."

So, is it now the case that the distinction between the conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and the object of conceptualization (*vikalpanīya*) is exactly the same as that between the "that-ness" (*tad-tā*) and the "this-ness" (*idantā*) substrates?
If this were so, then the Buddhists would have their hands forced; therefore, he says: "Because of the relation" (*sambandha*).
This [principle] applies to the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) in what follows as well.
The qualificand, however, is indeed one alone;
and the intention there is that its very nature is immediate perception (*aparokṣatva*).
As for the phrase "even he who": [it refers to one who holds a different view].
In this case as well, the connection with various directions and locations should be employed as a counter-argument (pratibandī).

Now, it might be argued that if the identity of an object connected to multiple times were established through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), there would follow the undesirable consequence of breaking the rule of mutual inseparability (*avinābhāva*);
furthermore, since such recognition is seen to be fallible in cases like the plantain trunk which grows back after being cut, it is simply not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).
Nor do we perceive any distinction whatsoever between the recognition of a plantain trunk and the recognition of a ruby.
But surely, even for you, who are connected to various directions and locations, unity is sometimes perceived;
how then can there be a certainty of that [unity] as well?

Or, if it is argued that the connection with various directions and locations does not cease without differentiating its own substratum, then it would result in the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).
Or it might be inconclusive;
therefore, this is not a contradictory [reason].
In that case, conjunction, the whole, and so forth, are established.
This is equally true even when there is a difference in time;
for if a connection between prior and posterior times were contradictory in the case of a real entity,
it would likewise be contradictory in the case of consciousness.
And likewise, consciousness too would not be unitary with respect to past and present objects.
And thus, because cognitions would have fixed objects, there would not even be a trace of recollection (*pratisandhāna*).
Consequently, due to the absence of a foundation, the world would arise as devoid of activity,
and the status of an omniscient being would be rendered a mere empty gesture.

If it is argued that even though [the object] has both past and present as its domain, a single cognition is not admitted to be both past and present—then what is this "presentness"? Is it existence (*sattva*), or is it a relation with another existent (*sadantara-sambandha*)? Likewise, what is "pastness"? Is it destruction (*naṣṭatva*), or is it a relation with another destroyed thing (*naṣṭāntara-sambandha*)?

In that regard, the relation between what has perished and what has not perished certainly exists both in the act of recognition and in the cognition of an omniscient being, because their objects include both the perished and the non-perished;
for if these were not their objects, neither recognition nor omniscience would be possible.
If it is argued that existence and destruction are mutually contradictory, and therefore cannot both exist in a single point of reconnection (*pratisandhāna*),
then in that case, even a ruby (*padmarāgamaṇi*) exists in its own nature from the moment of its production until the disintegration of its own parts.
There is no connection with its state of having perished;
rather, that very [object], being conjoined with something existent and with something non-existent, is as if a synthesis of both existent and non-existent objects.
Thus, there is no conjunction of contradictory properties.
Consequently, differences in magnitude and other such factors, which involve the association of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmasaṃsarga*), must be addressed.

With the intention that the same resolution applies—namely, that where these [contradictions] do not exist in the case of a ruby (*padmarāga*) or similar objects, there is simply the universal unity (*ekatva*)—he concludes by including space: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
Furthermore, the difference belonging to another related factor, time (*kāla*), does not constitute a difference—that is, a plurality (*nānātva*)—in another object, such as a ruby gem.
And as for the phrase "not by means of the sense-faculties":

if the opponent's intention is that sense-object contact is not the cause for any cognition belonging to the class of conceptual construction because of its deviation [from such cognitions], then the answer is simply an admission of that point.
For we do not assert that it is the cause of mere conceptual construction; rather, we assert it as the cause of direct perceptual cognition (*sākṣātkārivijñāna*).
And the essential point is that such cognition does not occur even without the contact of the sense faculty with its object.
This objection based on non-conceptual cognition, however, is intended to make this point easily understood.
This might be so:
for if conceptual construction were possible in both ways, then, due to the deviation of the general property, one would determine the causal relationship by taking up a specific instance.
However, it has no specific property such as direct perception and the like.

Anticipating the objection that "it [the nature of the self] is due to adventitious conditions" (*aupādhikatvāt*), he refutes it with the words: "nor is it located in conceptual construction" (*na ca vikalpagataḥ*).

It is undisputed that a property characterized as direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*) is experienced when it resides in conceptual construction; however, its being adventitious is not established by experience. Thus he says: "all... (*sarvā*)... [and so forth].
"Indeed, thus," and so forth.
Therefore, the construction is as follows: conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) whose function is perception are born from the contact of the sense-faculties with their objects;
nor is this merely a logical possibility (*aupapattika*).
The intention is that [this objection] has already been refuted prior to the discussion of its arising.
Now, if a word were to operate upon the very same object as the sense faculty,
it too would produce a conceptual cognition that is directly perceptual (*sākṣātkārī*).
The sense faculty as well functions through the operation of conceptual construction (utprekṣā),
because there is no distinction in cognition in the absence of a specific object.
Therefore, a conceptual construction that proceeds by taking sound alone as its object does not touch upon the domain of the sense faculty.

Anticipating the objection that its nature as a direct perceiver (*sākṣātkāritva*) is not intrinsic if it does not contact its object, he raises and refutes it with the words "nor [is it] by means of sound" (*na ca śabda*).
The meaning is that in one case (perception) the sense organ is the cause, while in the other (verbal cognition) it is sound and so forth, independent of that [organ].
Although this [objection] is to be disregarded as trivial, he refutes it for the benefit of the students: "nor [is it] by means of fire," etc. (*na ca vahnīti*).
The meaning is: from the cognition of fire, that is, from the cognition of heat;
there is the departure of the cold substance, or, upon its departure, the non-perception of it.
Alternatively, the absence of suffering caused by that [cold] is called the "removal of cold";
and this is accomplished through the application of a warm substance, not through the perception of it.
Otherwise, even when applying heat (svedana) to one whose humors are deranged by a *sannipāta* disorder, there would be no removal of the affliction.
The meaning is that because no hot substance is perceived,

if the Omniscient One were situated within a cave of the Snowy Mountain (Himālaya) and possessed direct perception of the submarine fire (vaḍavānala), there would be the melting of the Snowy Mountain.
He refutes the meaning of the Vārttika beginning with "yasyāpi" (even for whom... with the words "na caikena" (nor by one...).
"Upādhis" refers to existence and so forth; "being qualified by them" means the connection with those qualifiers.
This is the meaning.
The ultimate truth is that it benefits all limiting adjuncts by means of a single intrinsic nature alone.

In that case, because the benefactor possesses a single nature, there would have to be a unity of the benefits— which are the delimitations— and of the beneficiaries, which are the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), provided that they were admitted to be included within the nature of the benefit;
however, we do not maintain such a position.
You too must establish this very same point; the only difference is that you do so by way of its having an unreal object.
If this principle were applicable even to ultimate reality (paramārthasatya), what kind of fault would there be?
He says "Moreover" (*api ca*) to show that this argument of yours applies not only to conventional discourse based on conceptual construction, but even to the ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*).
The term "having atoms as its intrinsic nature" (*paramāṇu-svabhāva*) is a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound;
it should also be understood to mean "atoms are the intrinsic nature of cognition."
If [atoms] were the very nature of cognition, it would follow that cognition itself is manifold;

and thus, if each individual atom were restricted [to its own cognition], even the coarse appearance—which is indeed an error—would not occur. Furthermore, if atoms were the nature of cognition, it would follow that atoms themselves are unitary, and because they would be non-material, the same aforementioned fault would ensue. Having set aside such obvious refutations, he states another: "Of all those..."
Regarding cognition: it must also be observed that if atoms possessed the nature of a single cognition, they would not be known by a second [cognition].

Even though the Buddhist accepts a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) as the connection between cognition and the object of cognition for the sake of determining the relation between subject and object—even in the absence of identity (*tādātmya*)—nevertheless, even in the case of a causal relationship...
The objection "Who is the controller? applies equally [to all].
Therefore, he answers by means of intrinsic nature itself: "It is intrinsic nature alone."

We too maintain that the relationship between existence and non-existence, between inherence and its substratum, and between the object and the subject, is indeed mutually conferred by their very natures (*svabhāva*).

Although the relationship between substance, quality, action, genus, and their possessors is a case of the qualifier and the qualified by nature alone, nevertheless, the relationship being actually experienced cannot be disregarded in the absence of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*).

The meaning is this: just as you did not disregard the causal relationship when the relation between object and subject is based on intrinsic nature (*svabhāvika*), so too, when there is a relation distinct from that, the proof of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) remains as a subverting argument (*bādhaka*).

It is not that distinguished linguistic usage (*viśiṣṭa-vyavahāra*) does not exist at all, for it is impossible to deny its manifest presence, and because in its absence, the consequence would be the non-existence of all linguistic usage.
Therefore, this [distinction] must be established by some other means than through envy toward the method we have stated.
Regarding this, he says: "Even though they are not the object of distinct cognitions.
The word "even" (*api*) is used merely to indicate that the objection is superficial.
[Objection: Is it not the case that there is conventional usage, but it is not real? And that...
He raises the following objection: "Even if it could somehow be sustained through the medium of latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
those for whom this [object] is real must consider its sustenance through the medium of the object itself"— thus he says, "by both of these."

If this worldly transaction were indeed real, by taking as its basis the very door of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that you have described, then what fault would there be? With this intention, he says: "Let it be so for now.
Furthermore, to the question "Even so, what is the proof that this is indeed real? he says: "That being the case..."
The meaning is that, since this [cognition] arises from the contact of a sense-organ with its object, its very nature as direct perception (*sākṣātkāritva*) is itself the proof [of its validity].
The remainder [of the argument] is that one would have to postulate the mediation of non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) without any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
For if [the lack of conceptualization] did not arise by the power of its own cause, it would follow that even mental cognition (*mānasa*) would be devoid of conceptualization.
With this intention, he says: "Ah!

The opponent does not intend to maintain that the mind has all things as its objects by virtue of being necessarily connected to an operation, for even the contact between a sense organ and its object is established as having such a character when accompanied by a latent impression (*saṃskāra*).
Therefore, would it exist because it is connected to practice, or because it is the substratum for all latent impressions (*vāsanā*)?
He refutes the first [option] with the words: "If it were the former..."

The meaning is this: although our mind has all things as its object, it is not "non-universal" (asarvaviṣaya) by virtue of being bound to a specific cognition, because it is not of the nature of a non-cognition.
Nor does he say that [it is not the agent] by virtue of being the substratum for all latent impressions (*saṃskāra*); rather, he says, "because it is insentient, it is not an investigator.
This means that it is not the substratum for any of the latent impressions conducive to investigation.
And with the intention of refuting that the mind (manas) as conceived by you is the substratum of all latent impressions (vāsanās), he says: "Therefore, the Self alone [is the substratum].
The meaning is that established knowledge is the "impression of knowledge" (jñānavāsanā). The reason for this is stated: "For that [knowledge] is mental" (bauddha). Herein...
"Valid cognition" (pramāṇa) means that which is "to be cognized" (gamyate).
Therefore, it has this capacity [to function] in recollection;
the word "and" (ca) indicates a reason.

Now, if the sense organ is indeed presided over by such a consciousness, then at the very moment of the arising of indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*), it should produce conceptualization (*vikalpa*) itself, since it would already be accompanied by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). To this he says:

"That [consciousness], indeed... The construction is as follows: having first perceived [the object], and being aided by the memory produced from the awakening of latent impressions, it subsequently conceptualizes.
In that case, then, from the contact of the sense organ with its object arises indeterminate perception;
from that, the awakening of latent impressions; and from that, memory.
And since its associate (the mind) performs the conceptualization, there would be no utility whatsoever for the eye; therefore, he says: "by means of the eye."

Now, if such a causal complex, even when assembled, were not to produce a conceptual cognition in the absence of the operation of the eye, then that [operation] too would have to be postulated as a cause;
but this is not the case, and therefore he says: "This is a cow."
By this, it is shown that its positive and negative concomitances (anvaya-vyatireka) exist with respect to direct realization (sākṣātkāra).
Having this very point in mind, he states the following verse, beginning with "yathāha" (as it has been said).
That which exists together with consciousness (cetanā) is "sacetana" (possessed of consciousness).
Nevertheless, what benefit is established? To this he says: "by that.
The mention of the "relation between the signified and the signifier" (jñāpyajñāpakabhāva) is an elliptical expression;
it should be understood that the "relation between cause and effect" (kāryakāraṇabhāva) does not exist in all cases either.
In some cases, however, the word "exists" (*asti*) is not cited for substances, qualities, and actions.
When there is a recollection following from the consideration of those meanings, those two are called the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*).

The meaning is that the assistance rendered by the qualifier to the qualified consists precisely in the production of a cognition that excludes [the qualified] from what does not have that as its locus.
Although he will state in various places that an inherent relation of qualifier and qualified does not depend upon a causal interaction,
nor does this relation of benefactor and beneficiary require another causal interaction; for if it did, it would lead to an infinite regress.
Nevertheless, it should be understood that this is stated here according to the predominance of possibility.
Now, if the relationship of qualifier and qualified between these two were inherent, why would it not have been apprehended when the inherent nature was first apprehended?
And it is not the case that the inherent nature was not apprehended at that time; therefore, he says: "For the objects... (arthau hi).
Indeed, it is not the case that because tactile and other atoms do not exist by way of their own nature within the atoms of form, they consequently fail to enter the path of cognition.
If you argue that this is not so because of the absence of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*),
the point is that this [reason] is equally applicable here as well.
For this very reason, that which was argued on the assumption that a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) must pervade its entire object is also not the case; therefore, he says: "by that" (tena).
We certainly accept that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has a universal application (*kṛtsnavṛttitva*) with respect to its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).

However, with respect to the intention of natural, universal connection (*svābhāvikasamastasambandha*), it brings about the invalidity of all cognitions other than those of the Omniscient One. Having thus summarized this conclusion appropriately, he says: "But the conceptual [cognition]... The construction is: "...arising even subsequently," with the word "from the initial sensory perception" (*ālocanāt*) being understood as the ellipsis.
Therefore, everything is equal; intending to show that only the dispute regarding momentary destruction remains, he says: "Even for that which is non-sequential," and "those under dispute."
The meaning is "that which is directly realized.
By this, other [cognitions] are excluded.
The phrase "within its own domain" is for the purpose of excluding the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
By the phrase "the yellow conch," etc., the qualification "provided there is non-deviation" is added for the purpose of excluding deviation;
and an effort has been made regarding this point.

And it should not be thought that this is the [intended] commentary, because since doubt is observed to arise even without the contact of the sense-faculties with their objects, there is no possibility of this [definition] applying [to such cases] due to its not having those as its cause;
how then could there be an exclusion when [the definition] is being restated? This is the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position.

Even if not every doubt is born from the contact of the sense-faculties with their objects, nevertheless, that which possesses direct manifestation (*sākṣātkāravat*) must necessarily be produced by them.
Therefore, the meaning of the section is that exclusion (vyudāsa) is what is being enjoined.
It might be argued as follows:

the mind alone, operating externally independent of the senses, produces direct perceptions, doubts, and so forth; for its activity is observed toward objects such as jars, which serve as qualifiers for the subsequent reflective cognition (*anuvyavasāya*).

Because even when the operation of the sense organs has ceased—as in the case of a flash of lightning and the like—an ascertainment of an object that arose all at once is subsequently cognized even in darkness;
and because that subsequent cognition (anuvyavasāya) belongs to the same class as direct perception (sākṣātkārin).
Therefore, the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) does not arise again.

For, by means of the mind—which is in contact with the substantive characterized by the cognition currently being determined (anuvyavasīyamāna)—the jar or other object, which is not itself in direct contact, is determined as its delimiting factor (avacchedaka).
This is just as when the eye, being in contact with the jar, perceives it in its previously observed state.
However, a doubtful cognition does not have the perception of a future object as its domain.

Nor is it the object of the memory of either a post or a person; rather, its object is the upright entity whose specific nature as either a post or a person has not yet been determined. Furthermore, the mind is not in direct contact with that [object].

Furthermore, how could the mind produce cognition with respect to an external qualificandum when it is not in contact with it? Or, if it were to produce it, it would produce it even for the blind, the deaf, and so forth; such is the established conclusion (siddhānta).
That [occurs] previously, at the time of the arising of the resolve;
the phrase "for the sake of the perfection of reaching their own objects" is the ellipsis.
And likewise, even in the production of doubtful cognition; the phrase "as a cooperative cause" is the ellipsis.
The bystander raises an objection beginning with "by way of non-pervasiveness," and the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) offers a rebuttal;
this is done so that no further doubt may arise in the bystander's mind.
Therefore he says [the following]:
the proponent [of the prima facie view] states that there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding pleasure and so forth.

The phrase "leaving aside direct perception" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. For if those [cognitions] were of the nature of consciousness, then their being self-cognized would also be a ground for suspicion; this is the ellipsis. Now, one might object: since the Commentator says, "indeed, it exists as a sense-organ," he clearly accepts that the mind is a sense-organ. To this, he replies: "And not that... [and so forth].
The meaning is that the acceptance of the mind (*manas*) as a sense-faculty (*indriya*) in the work of Vātsyāyana contradicts the *Gautamīyasūtra*.

Even if this sūtra were not intended to be an exhaustive classification, nevertheless, if the author of the sūtras had intended the mind to be a sense-faculty, he would have defined it within the very section on the sense-faculties; therefore, he says: "And in that case... (*tatra ca*).

Since it would have been appropriate to define [the mind] as a faculty within that very same section, the fact that he treats it elsewhere indicates that some additional characteristic of its nature must be understood;
it does not mean, however, that he cannot tolerate its being a faculty.
For the author of the Vārttika will demonstrate this in the following passage, beginning with "past and future," in order to dispel any confusion.
In this case, it is the word that is faulty, not the intended meaning;
and this is merely an illustration.
The status of the eyes and other [senses] as sense organs consists in their being endowed with qualities (*saguṇa*);

however, the mind (*manas*) is not a sense organ endowed with qualities. In this regard, "being endowed with qualities" means that a sense organ functions together with a quality belonging to the same class as the specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) it perceives.

If the author of the Bhāṣya intends to mean that the mind lacks any such quality belonging to the same class as the perceived specific quality, then this too constitutes a point of difference (*vaidharmya*).
However, this cannot even be expressed by these very syllables;
yet the commentary (*bhāṣya*) becomes easy to understand through the modification of case endings.

For instance, the "possession of qualities" (*saguṇatva*) of these [senses] which have become faculties refers to the connection of the eyes and so forth with the objects of perception as their qualities.
However, for the mind, which has indeed assumed the form of a sense organ, there is neither possession of qualities nor a connection with a quality that is an object of apprehension;
therefore, here too, the same fault regarding the word applies.
But one should not think that there is the fault of falling into a precipice.
One might object: "Surely the intended [object] is established by the negation of what is unintended. To this he replies:
"Not so," [meaning] "because of the non-existence [of that].
For if the intended were obtained through the negation of everything unintended, it would result in an excessive burden of complexity (*gaurava*).
Because it is impossible to establish a negation without first presenting the specific object to be negated;
the point is that when there is a prescription of a particular case, the negation of the remainder is more concise.

Since a statement containing the word *satrā* (together) is a subject of dispute, how can there be a determination by that very [word]? To this, the author of the Bhāṣya supplies the answer: "He says...

By the term *śābda*, the Vārttikakāra intends to exclude the cognition "this is a horse" which arises from the conjunction of the sense organ and the word; thus he removes the opinion of certain [scholars] who hold otherwise, stating: "Certainly not..."

For since [the property] must reside in the qualificand when it is apprehended as a qualifier by way of being denotable (*vācyatva*), it was therefore illustrated in that very same manner even during the discussion of denotability alone.
Furthermore, because there is a deviation from the absence of the sense organ, its absence was not suspected;

for it is observed that when the nature of a horse has been apprehended, even in the absence of sensory contact with it, the cognition of denotability arises solely from instruction such as, "This lump which you see is that very horse."
Therefore, the function of the sense organ consists solely in presenting the related object.
Likewise, in subsequent cases as well, the meaning of that [word] is the specific intention of the communicator.
Although the intention of another person, or the object conditioned by it, is not within the range of the sense organs, [it is nevertheless understood].
Nevertheless, [the author] raises an objection even while conceding the point: "Now, this too...
For this matter—namely, that "this is perceptible" and "this is beyond the senses"—is to be inferred from direct perception and non-perception.
In that case, since it consists of a clear apprehension and is designated by the term "direct perception" (sākṣātkāra), it would be logical for this [cognition] to be sensory;
however, it is not so even on account of its lack of directness.
Furthermore, you yourself must consider which of these two is cognized here by the mind.

In this regard, if it is the position that [perception] is of a direct nature (*sākṣātkāritva*), then this is simply perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself; therefore, it need not be excluded [from the definition].
And if it is the position that it is not of a direct nature, then it is already ruled out by the first term [of the definition] as being "not derived from the senses" (*anaidriyaka*).
Thus, there is no room for the term "non-verbal" (*avyapadeśya*); such is the meaning of the verse.

"For what purpose, then, is the term 'indescribable' (avyavadeśya) used, and what is the meaning of this Vārttika? To this he says: "But by the term 'of the nature of determination' (vyavasāyātmaka). Although he considers the inclusion of a single term to be clear, he explains the inclusion of two terms, saying: "by the two terms."
Showing the utility of the subsequent section, he says: "Thus, in this way.
This is the definition of inference (*anumāna*).
And that [definition] becomes easy to understand through its distinction from what merely appears to be inference (*tadābhāsa*).
The meaning is that this undertaking is made by one who intends that [perception] occurs when those appearances (tadābhāsa) have been manifested.
For in the phrase "from that object" (*tato 'rthāt*), the ablative case indicates that the object is the cause with respect to the cognition.

And the particle *eva* ("only") is connected to that [cause] as follows: that cognition for which the object denoted by the designation is the cause *only*, and not even a non-cause, is perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Thus, it is indeed the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*).
Nevertheless, since the author of the *Vārttika* must also refute the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), he has shown both in his commentary.
If that [result] arises from that very [cause], [then the latter is excluded].
There is no contradiction because it is not designated as being other than the object, nor as being non-designative.
[Objection: But surely, some particular kind of inference arises from that which is non-verbal;
therefore, its exclusion has not been accomplished. To this he says: "In the phrase 'from that object,' for...
This is the definition of the genus of perception.
And since its counter-correlate is precisely the class consisting of inference and so forth, it is the exclusion of that very class which is intended.
The meaning is that he is established by this much alone.
"In whatever [locus] and of whatever kind [the object] is"—
that is, the non-connection of that designator by way of being its cause; "that is not perceived" means that designation is intended as a determination conditioned by that [cause].
Furthermore, knowledge is not defined by its agent or its instrument, but rather by its object alone; this is the meaning.
This is because the denotation does not terminate—that is, because the operation of the word does not terminate [without reaching the object].

The meaning is that the word *tat* has been conventionally established (*saṅketita*) only for a previously introduced referent, because if it were not to denote that, it would follow that it is non-expressive (*avācaka*).
And what was previously introduced is precisely the designator (*vyapadeśaka*).
The meaning is that the object itself is obtained as the qualificand because it is invariably concomitant;
since the Vārttika does not state this [explicitly], he says: "But having granted... (abhyupetya tu).
For the purpose of excluding [the possibility of] inference and so forth, there is the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*);
and that [exclusion] is established even when there is the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*). This is the meaning.

[Objection: But surely the exclusion of other causes (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) is impossible, since even non-designating factors such as the sense organs (*indriya*) are causes of that [cognition]. To this he says: "Even in the case of the exclusion of others.

For although the sense organs and so forth are non-designating, they produce cognition only through the sovereignty of the designating [mind]; thus, because they are not contradictory [to the function of designation], they are not to be excluded.

The meaning is that the gender-markers (*liṅga*) and so forth, being independent of designation and sovereignty, are contradictory to those [other factors]; therefore, they alone are the others to be excluded.
[Objection: But is not the *Vārttika* statement, "And everything [arises] from its own object," entirely inconsistent?
For memory, inference, and error do not arise from their own objects; therefore, he says: "Insofar as they are of the nature of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). [Objection:
But even erroneous cognition does not occur without a designation (*vyapadeśaka*).
Why is it not [produced] from that which is other than this? To this he says: "the one present before" (*purovartī*).

Although the phrase "even from that which is other than this" (*atasmād api*) is not explicitly heard here, the meaning is that it should be understood as not being produced even from that which serves as its designator (*vyapadeśaka*).
This has been stated as follows: "That specific form by which it is designated does not arise from that.
Therefore, the meaning is: that which arises from that very source necessarily arises from it; and that which does not arise from that source does not arise from it.

Now, one might object: "Is this not merely a verbal quibble (*vākchala*), since you have introduced the challenge that [the effect] does not arise from what is non-designatable—or rather, that it arises from what is non-designatable—by saying that it does not arise from silver that is unreal? To this, he says: "For [it does not arise] from that form which is superimposed (*āropita*). This is the meaning: The sense is as follows: [The objection is invalid because] the effect does not arise from that superimposed form. This is the point.
