For the elimination of false cognition must occur either by excluding connection with something else (anyayoga-vyavaccheda) or by excluding non-connection (ayoga-vyavaccheda).
It cannot be the first case.
For even in that case, there is the exclusion of connection with anything else;
otherwise, it would not exist if it belonged only to that which is inexpressible.
In a marketplace, independent silver might be the cause [of the cognition];
but this is not the case.
Thus it has been said: "For a false cognition does not arise from that which is superimposed, which is non-existent there [in the substrate]."
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, precisely because that which designates [an object] must be its cause.
If it is argued that silver is the designator but not the cause?
But how could silver be the designator, either independently or as the nature of the object present before one?
It cannot be the former, because grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) would then be untenable.
Furthermore, because it would follow that [the object] itself is false;
and in another cognition, that [object] becomes the designator in its capacity as the "presently existing" (purovartin) entity;
and since that "presently existing" entity is indeed the cause, this is a case of exclusion of non-connection (ayogavyavaccheda).
This has been stated: "The superimposed silver is its object by virtue of having the form of that which is being perceived.
However, this might be the intended meaning:
perception is a cognition produced from an object in whatever form that object is designated.
However, this is not the meaning of the defining terms;
nor can another person be made to understand through mere purity of intention alone, because that does not pervade recognition and self-awareness.
And this will become clear in the Jaiminīya [Mīmāṃsā] system.
This definition, even if intended with a specific underlying purpose (*ābhiprāyika*), might perhaps be possible according to our own system;
however, in your view, it is both contradictory and unestablished—this is what was stated by the author of the *Vārttika*.
He explains this very point with the words: "Even though this... and so forth.
For an object that serves as a designation is, by virtue of its presentness, the object of perception everywhere.
If that [object] were the very reason [for the inference], it would thus be past;
and in that case, when perceptibility is the probandum, non-perceptibility itself would be established—this is the meaning of the term "contradiction" (*viruddhatva*).

Alternatively, if it is the present [cognition] alone that serves as the designator, then because they would be simultaneous, the expression "from that object" (tato 'rthāt) is unestablished; thus he says: "tatsamāna... (having the same [time] as that).
As for what has been prattled by someone— that "presentness" consists merely in being illumined by an immediate cognition—
that is trivial and was therefore disregarded. For,

if all objects were of a single time simply because they are illumined by the immediate consciousness of an omniscient being, then, like the left and right horns of a cow, even the very discourse regarding the relation of cause and effect would be cut off.
And the previously mentioned objection remains exactly as it was.

By the passage beginning with "How can that which belongs to a different time be apprehended," the opponent has established in his own words that the relationship of apprehended and apprehender is in fact nothing other than the specific relationship of cause and effect, and that this occurs only between two things existing at different times.
Nor do we deny the specific nature of the causal relationship between two things existing at different times;
however, the appearance of the past as present, or its reality, has not been established by this [argument]. This is the meaning.
Surely, this has already been established by you yourself when you stated that [the object] is "capable of imparting its form to the cognition.
For by this, it is not shown that an object is designated as "grasped" by virtue of its appearing [in the cognition];
rather, it is shown to be so by virtue of its imparting a form.
However, it is the aspect (ākāra) itself that is the object of apprehension by virtue of its appearing;
and since that [aspect] exists as being identical with the nature of cognition, there is no contradiction whatsoever. Therefore, he says: "not characterized by ego" (anahaṃkāra).
[This refers to] the experience of blue and so forth as distinct from consciousness.
If it is real, there is no perception of the form residing in cognition;
if it is unreal, then perception is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). This is the meaning: this is a rope with a noose at both ends.
Moreover, let there be the cognition of the form,
or let there be the object's capacity to impart its form; nevertheless, the cognition derived from that object is direct perception (pratyakṣa).
Thus, the definition is unestablished;
for indeed, cognition is designated only of that which is appearing, and not of that which is not appearing.
And the object appears as its form, yet it is not its producer;
therefore, that which designates is not the producer, and that which produces is not the designator.
Here he raises an objection: "If not," etc.
The meaning is: it is not the case that [the object] is designated by means of its appearing form, nor is it the producer [of cognition].
Why?
Because it would follow that [the usage] is merely figurative.
To the question, "What follows if this is so?", he says: "Nor is it figurative or primary," and so forth.
For just as the word *gaṅgā* [applies] to the bank only by including the relation of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*),...
The meaning is that the word "lion" applies to the boy by including the connection with qualities perceived [in him],
whereas the perception of smoke does not apply to fire, nor does the perception of a lion apply to the boy;
for if it did, it would entail the consequence of the abolition of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This is what was stated: "because they follow different systems."
By this, the following [view] is also refuted: "The object is inferred by means of a form established through perception; thus, in effect, the object is perceived.
What is the meaning of "is inferred"?
It is said that [the object] shines forth in inference;
however, even in a dream, this is difficult to find according to the Buddhist system,
because even inference terminates in nothing other than either its own form or the unreal [object].
And how can that which is in every respect beyond the range of cognition be designated [as an object]?

Therefore, on the position of the theory of forms (ākāravāda), the external object must be abandoned; or, if that [external object] is admitted, then it is the theory of forms. With this intention, he says: "Therefore, [consciousness is] formless."
He suspects [this], for among the Buddhists there exists no such thing as a "denotable" (vācya) entity that has any real ontological status;
rather, by means of a defining statement (lakṣaṇavākya), merely conventional usage (vyavahāra) is established.
And that [definition] means being restricted to the exclusion of those [other things].

One might ask: "How could all objects be reduced to the status of perception when cognition—being free from conceptual construction—is itself being established as perception? To this he says: "For not...
[Dignāga’s definition], because it is over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*), is not a valid definition.

The established conclusion is that fame, because it is not all-pervasive, is not subsumed under either conceptual cognition or perception; furthermore, since that [perception] is demonstrated to be of the nature of perception, and because the mere mention of what is undesirable leads to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
In order to show that this is a *vārttika* intended for the purpose of establishing his own philosophical system, he raises an objection with the words "Now, if... (*nanu yadi*).
The remainder of the *vārttika* is: "endowed with a universal" (*sāmānyānvitam*), "is denoted" (*abhidhīyate*).
The meaning is "possessing the genus of humanity.

The point is that although the word "human" (manuṣya) does not denote a Brāhmaṇa by virtue of his possessing the genus of Brāhmaṇahood and so forth, it certainly does denote him by virtue of his possessing the genus of humanity.
Avoiding the charge of redundancy, he says: "Now, [the story] of Aśvakarṇa."

[Objection: But would it not be the case that even when the terms are transposed, there would still be "contact with the existent" (*satsamprayoga*), yet no specific object would exist as the referent for those respective words because they are not the subject under discussion? To this he says: "by means of cognition" (*buddhyā*).
Although, by this definition, even perceptual knowledge itself would certainly not be perceptible with respect to its own self, [the definition still applies].

Nevertheless, since the mere fact of being produced by the contact of a sense-organ with its object exists even in those cases, the opponent might perhaps say so; therefore, he says: "from inference and so forth. By this, the remaining intention of the phrase "from that object" is refuted, because it is not pervasive (avyāpaka) in the case of recognition and self-awareness. // 4 //
Now, inference based on that is of three kinds: pūrvavat, śeṣavat, and sāmānyatodṛṣṭa. (NS 1.1.5)
// Purity //
He recites the Sūtra; the words "in order to explain" are to be understood as the ellipsis.
To one who cannot tolerate even the mere introduction of the Sūtra, he says: "In this regard."
For [the phrase] "possessing a restriction" is understood to be by way of similarity;
and this is merely an illustration.
It should also be understood as being by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*).
The prescription of non-authoritativeness is indeed the negation of authoritativeness.

For, by this specific negation—namely, "perception is not a means of valid cognition"—the negation of the authority of inference is intended explicitly (*kaṇṭhataḥ*), while the prescription of the authority of perception is intended implicitly (*arthataḥ*).

And neither of these two is established without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, it was considered in the opening statement that perception alone is not capable [of establishing them] here, nor are verbal testimony or comparison.
Because there is no room for those two [arguments] in the case of one's own cognition, and even in the case of another's cognition, the locus (dharmin) is not established;
and even if it were established, there would be no certainty regarding the other person being a reliable authority (āpta).
Therefore, since it is impossible to establish or refute that which transcends the senses without accepting inference, the meaning is that inference cannot be denied.
And the phrase "the similarity with the observed is necessary" is the ellipsis.
What is intended here is merely a contradiction: how can that very [inference] be invalid by means of itself?
Therefore, this is the meaning: if inference is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), how can the establishment of affirmation and negation be achieved by it alone?
Or, if the establishment of affirmation and negation is achieved by it, [then it must be a valid means of knowledge].
How is it that this [scripture] lacks authority?

Furthermore, even the employment of words to communicate with others would be impossible without accepting inference—because it is impossible to understand the cognitions of another without that [inference].
And if there is no communication with others, [the scripture is useless].
He says "api ca" (moreover) to show that this indeed reveals the insanity of the speaker.
Since there is also a distinction [of types] in the Sūtra, he states [the following] by way of exclusion: "He states the intended meaning of the definition-sūtra.
One might object that this is over-extensive;
in this regard, it should also be understood as being under-extensive.
Therefore, there is a contradiction between the exposition and the conclusion regarding both [the first and third perceptions].
The phrase "the demonstration of the three-fold form" means that the three-fold form is to be observed.

Those who follow the literal commentary argue that since inference is established by the second perception of the mark alone, aided by the memory of pervasion (*vyāpti*), there is no need for the postulation of a third perception; [the author] refutes them with the words "not so."

This fault has been stated against one who accepts an additional awakening (udbodha) of the latent impression (saṃskāra). But as for one who thinks that there is no such thing as "awakening" other than the acquisition of auxiliary causes (sahakārin), he says in response: "of that which is in a state of perishing."
For inference does not arise from the mere recollection of pervasion, nor from the mere perception of the mark;
what then?
[Inference] arises from the perception of a mark (liṅga) qualified by pervasion (vyāpti).

Now, the mark qualified by pervasion is not the object of either [of the two means of knowledge, perception and inference] individually, nor even of both together; rather, each of the two [means of knowledge] independently [grasps] its respective part for both [together].

Moreover, even when there is knowledge of both [factors] independently, the cognition of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) does not arise. This is what was stated: "Because they are unaware of each other's affairs and because they terminate in their own respective independent objects, there is no possibility of mutual connection; this is the meaning of the impossibility of the cognition of a qualified entity."
Nor should it be argued that these two [the recollection of pervasion and the second perception of the mark] will independently bring about the inference merely by being inherent in a single self;

for does the second perception of the mark assist the recollection of pervasion simply by having the mark as its object according to the actual state of things, or by its being characterized by the form of the mark itself?
It cannot be the first case.
For it would follow that even the cognition of a distant object as being smoke would have to act as a cooperative factor for the recollection of pervasion, which arises through a different means;
however, this second [alternative] does not exist at all in the case of the second observation of the mark (*liṅga*).
This has been stated: "One should connect this by means of its function (vṛtti), not by its form (rūpa), nor merely by its inherence in both, because that would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga)."
Therefore, he states "tasmāt" (therefore) to show that one must accept a third observation of the mark (*liṅga*) which explicitly involves the mark itself;

for in this context, if those two [essential identity and causal origination] were themselves the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), or if the necessary connection had the same means of apprehension as those two, then the ascertainment of the connection would not occur upon the ascertainment of the essential nature of essential identity and causal origination.
Or rather, the conclusion regarding the necessary connection (pratibandha) rests upon those two alone; or those two themselves are the means for ascertaining the necessary connection.
In that regard, their status as a means consists either in the determination of concomitance (sahacāra), or—
Or, regarding the removal of suspicion of deviation (vyabhicāra):
whether by means of observing a limiting condition (upādhi), or by means of the suspicion of a limiting condition.
Or is it merely by investigating the deviation between two objects that have been repeatedly observed together?

In that regard, the determination of their concomitance arises dependent upon the contact of the sense organs; and even if its production is not certain, it is established in the case of fire and smoke.

Furthermore, the suspicion of deviation is dependent upon an adventitious condition (*upādhi*) capable of being perceived, and is therefore dispelled simply by the non-perception of such a perceptible condition.
However, we shall explain how even suspected adventitious conditions (*upādhi*) that are beyond the senses, when observed elsewhere through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), are excluded;

whereas a suspicion regarding an adventitious condition that has not entered the path of valid cognition undermines even the certainty of the production [of the effect] from that [cause]. How then could such [a suspicion] [be tolerated]?
Therefore, he says "it must be turned back" by stating "to this it is replied.
However, the suspicion of deviation based merely on the observation of deviation between two things that are commonly associated is equally applicable to cause and effect.

If it is argued that the suspicion is removed once the specific character of "origination from that" (tadutpatti) is established through the operation of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), [then...]

Then, for us as well, once an essential connection (svābhāvikasambandha) is established, the removal of doubt occurs precisely through the operation of a subverting proof (bādhakapramāṇa) against the contrary case; thus the resolution is the same.

The distinction, however, is that the essential connection possesses pervasion (vyāpakatva), whereas causality and the like do not possess it—this is what he states with the words "Moreover" (api ca).
This has been stated: "And it is either this one or that one.
Nor is it correct to argue that because the means are the same for both, the lack of certainty regarding one does not entail certainty regarding the other;
for even when the invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) is not certain, the relationship of cause and effect between fire and ash is nonetheless ascertained.

Even when the relationship of cause and effect is not ascertained, because the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between fire and smoke is understood, one infers fire precisely as that which has not yet passed away; thus he says, "Moreover, from the effect. He refutes the position that the necessary connection is restricted to those two alone by saying, "Moreover, from taste."
As for what Prajñākara asserted—that when there is difference, the relation of pervader and pervaded is itself the relation of cause and effect—that is more wicked than even sin.

For instance, in the absence of a restrictive factor (*niyāmaka*), the non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) between two distinct things is difficult to ascertain because it is marred by the stain of doubt; it was to remove that doubt that he introduced the relation of cause and effect.
If that [relation] is nothing other than their very nature (*rūpa*), then how can the ascertainment of non-deviation follow from the ascertainment of that [nature] alone?

Nor is this approved by Kīrti, since he has stated an alternative means for the inference of color from taste. Furthermore, if one were to set aside what is established for all the world and proceed with conventions based on definitions created by oneself, then even the phrase "when there is a difference" (bhede sati) should be abandoned.
Let it simply be that "origination from that" (tadutpatti) is the mere absence of deviation (avyabhicāra).
In this case, the definition would indeed be concise.
If it is argued that this [definition] applies to the self as well,
then let the *śiṃśapā* tree also be an effect of a tree.
If it is asked, "How can that be performed by that very same thing?"—
what is the fault?
That which is unestablished is established by means of that which is already established.
If it is argued that "the very same thing is both established and unestablished," then alas,
how can even a future thing be a cause merely by virtue of being a pervader, since it is unestablished?
And how can even a present thing be an effect merely by virtue of being a pervaded, since it is established?
In this way, even if they exist at the same time, how can they be related as cause and effect merely by virtue of being inseparable?

For in the state of non-establishment, there is no difference between the two in their lack of proving power, and in the state of establishment, there is no difference between the two in their lack of being provable.

Therefore, it is more appropriate to hold that causality is the restriction of existence at a prior time, and effectness is the restriction of subsequent existence; whereas inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is simply restriction in general.
Furthermore, would the determination of the causal relationship between taste and color be established through perception and non-perception— as in the case of fire and smoke—
or by means of the principle that "from one aggregate [of causes] another aggregate arises," as established in the proof of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*)?
The former is simply impossible in the case of two moments.
Because direct perception does not apply to those two;
since it lacks determinative power regarding them,
the [distinction] between the two continua is also difficult to comprehend.

For ordinary people do not perceive a rule of temporal priority for color as they do for fire, nor a rule of posteriority for taste as they do for smoke; moreover, the logic for establishing momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is not accessible to ordinary people. Thus, in reality, there would be no inference of color from taste for ordinary people—this is what [the author] states with the words: "And this for ordinary people..."
Furthermore, by the phrase "and moreover" (*api ca*), the view that those two [identity and causality] alone constitute the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is refuted.
He states "and moreover" (*api ca*) because identity (*tādātmya*), on the contrary, is contradictory to the relationship between the signifier and the signified (*gamyagamakabhāva*).
For it is not the case that the very same thing is both the object to be established and the means of its establishment.

The meaning is that [the subject] would be both the agent of determination by its own certainty and the determiner [of the object], because there is a mutual contradiction between the certain and the uncertain.
Let it be that the relationship of the signified and the signifier exists even in the case of non-difference; however—
Nevertheless, the inference of "treeness" from "śiṃśapā-ness" is not possible because it is undermined by the lack of occasion [for such an inference].

For there is no possibility that the universal remains uncertain while the particular is certain; having raised this objection which was defended by someone, [the author] refutes it with the words "yat tu" (as for what...).

He argues that the relationship of the signifier and the signified exists only between two distinct exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*), but because of the connection with the non-different object of determination (*adhyavaseya*), identity (*tādātmya*) is conventionally attributed even to those two.
If, on account of their connection with the same Devadatta, one were to treat even the umbrella and the earring as non-different, who could prevent it?

It is only with the intention of showing the exclusion of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the purpose (*prayojana*), as well as the contradiction with worldly convention, that he concludes with the words: "Therefore, from this... and so forth.
"This is the effect of that" and "this is the cause of that"—this is one type of relation.
Having set aside the natural relation, he states its essential nature with the words "for thus" (*tathā hi*).
The meaning is that it is natural and free from adventitious conditions (*nirupādhi*).

Although it is a rule that pervasion (vyāpti) is characterized by deviation (vyabhicāra) or non-deviation (avyabhicāra), and that these two are respectively characterized by being conditional (aupādhikatva) or unconditional (anaupādhikatva),
yet those two [conditions] cannot be without a cause, for if they were, it would follow that they would occur everywhere.
Furthermore, these two are perceived as having restricted objects;
nor are they without cause,
for if there were non-deviation even when a condition (*upādhi*) is present, and deviation even when no condition is present, it would follow that there is no fixed rule at all.
If that were the case, it would follow that there is also deviation of the nature of the effect from the nature of the cause.
Therefore, deviation necessarily exists where there is an adjunct (upādhi), and non-deviation necessarily exists where there is no adjunct.
Where there is deviation, there must necessarily be an adjunct; where there is non-deviation, there must necessarily be an absence of an adjunct.
Nevertheless, where deviation is manifest, the pursuit of a limiting condition (upādhi) is useless, because that [pursuit] is for that very purpose. But when deviation is not manifest, it is useful.
However, the search for whether there is deviation or no deviation is not required for the sake of establishing the presence or absence of a limiting condition.

Since the examination of whether a condition (*upādhi*) exists or not is fruitless once deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and so forth have been established, he states "But when... after having pointed out the deviation merely for the purpose of demonstrating mutual pervasion (*anyonya-vyāpti*). This is because [the relation] is neither intrinsic (*svābhāvika*) nor unconditional (*nirupādhika*).
Therefore, the meaning is that it is neither certain nor non-deviant.
Now, one might ask: how is the relation between smoke and so forth with fire and so forth natural? To this he says: "But the natural... [is as follows].
But surely, if deviation is not evident, the pursuit of a limiting condition (upādhi) is fruitful.
Why, then, is this not evident here? To this he says: "Because no deviation is observed in certain cases.

But surely, deviation might occur at some time or place, and yet remain unseen due to [the object's] unfitness for perception; to this he says: "Because even that which is unperceived cannot be postulated," meaning that there is an absence of any limiting condition (*upādhi*) that would serve as the medium for postulating an unperceived deviation.
Therefore, "fixed" means "invariable."

[Objection: But surely, in the absence of a limiting condition (*upādhi*), there is no room for the postulation of an unperceived deviation; yet from where does that very absence of a limiting condition arise? [The author] raises this doubt with "And not... and provides the answer with "Necessarily...".

For a limiting condition (*upādhi*) must indeed be stated as having entered the path of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Otherwise, the suspicion that some thing might be a limiting condition— though unperceived by anyone at any time or place due to its very nature— could not be dispelled even by Brahmā, despite his production of that [thing], because even an omniscient one who directly perceives objects within the scope of various means of knowledge might, by their very nature, fail to perceive some object.
And non-duality, or primordial matter and the spirit, or the lack of intrinsic nature in the world, might at some time be devoid of all means of valid cognition.
Or else, the Vedas would lack authority.
In that case, how could a monk engage even in such acts as the worship of a shrine (*caitya-vandana*)?
If it is argued that engagement occurs because of doubt regarding the purpose (*artha-saṃdeha*), [then...]
Where the demoness of doubt spreads by disregarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how could there even be any possibility of the existence of an object?
Let alone activity directed toward the next world, even activity in this world does not exist.
He says "it may be so"—namely, "at the very least."
Although it is observed that after a specific diet there frequently occurs nourishment, equilibrium of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), and so forth,
whereas death occurs only immediately following a disease or similar condition,
nevertheless, a particular kind of food might sometimes be the cause of death itself.
Otherwise, how could there be the perception of that interval at the end?
As for the fact that he did not kill [the victim] for so long, it is like fire restrained by a mantra.
Because it is obstructed by something else,
one might even suspect that the very thing acting as the obstacle is the cause of nourishment and so forth;
yet, it is actually the disease and such that are the causes of nourishment and so forth.
However, that [cause] is not perceived at the time of nourishment and so forth precisely because it is invisible.
For it might sometimes be thought that the causes of nourishment and so forth must necessarily be visible;
furthermore, just as there is a cessation of inference due to the suspicion of an unestablished condition (*upādhi*) or the suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

The meaning is that, in the same way, the cessation from consuming specific foods and so forth occurs solely through the suspicion of an unestablished harm. Therefore, like a certainty regarding an imagined object, that suspicion is also fruitless; however, like a certainty regarding what is actually known through valid cognition, even a suspicion can be useful for one's purpose. Thus he says: "Therefore..."
Thus, this is the summary:
deviation itself is the absence of a necessary connection; and the suspicion of deviation arises solely from a limiting condition (*upādhi*).
Only that which is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) may be suspected as a limiting condition (*upādhi*).
It must be determined as a limiting condition in the probans (*sādhana*) when it is present there, and as being without a limiting condition in the probandum (*sādhya*) when it is absent;
anything other than this is otherwise.
Lest it be argued that some limiting condition (*upādhi*) might exist even among those things already observed by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says: "with effort" (*prayatnena*).
This is the meaning of the effort [expended here]:
first, those [causes] perceivable by direct perception are already refuted by the non-perception of the capable (yogyānupalabdhi).
Furthermore, if even those pervasive factors observed through other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) were to function as limiting conditions (upādhi), it would follow that fire must be omnipresent.
If even non-pervasive eternal things were considered limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it would follow that fire would always persist [wherever smoke exists].
However, non-eternal things are of three kinds: those that do not deviate from either [the probandum and the reason], those that deviate from both, and [those that deviate from one or the other].
And [there are those] that do not deviate from either one.

Among these, the first and second are not *upādhis* precisely because they lack the definition of an *upādhi*. Those that do not deviate from either one are of two kinds: those that do not deviate from smoke alone, and those that do not deviate from fire alone.
In the former case, because of the very absence of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), there are no limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Even those that do not deviate from fire alone are of two kinds:
those consisting solely of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and those consisting of both forms.
The former are as before;
however, those of both forms arise from a causal complex (*sāmagrī*),
nor do the latter exist.
And that [nature] is not a limiting condition (upādhi) anywhere, because there is an essential connection (svabhāvasambandha) with it just as smoke has with fire,
and because fire itself is included within the causal complex (sāmagrī) that produces fire.

Nor is "being of a different class from the property to be proven" (sādhyadharmajātīyetaratva) an upādhi here, as it is in the case of the relationship between being produced and being non-hot— where "being of a different class from fire" serves as the upādhi—
because that [latter upādhi] is restricted solely to cases where there is sublation by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇabādha).

For this very reason, even though we do not perceive a limiting condition (*upādhi*), we delay for a moment in our inference due to being preoccupied with ascertaining the presence or absence of a contradictory means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Thus, because no limiting condition is perceived in any way, the ascertainment of its absence—just as in the case of the connection with smoke—is to be seen elsewhere as well;
and reasoning (*tarka*), being most effective at dispelling all doubts, prevails.

Objection: Is it not the case that when a thing is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is what is relied upon, but the determination of the thing does not occur solely by relying on its intrinsic nature? With this intention, he asks: "But by what [is it grasped]?
[The answer is: the non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) between fire and smoke is grasped by the very first perception.
Setting aside the view of some who hold that the subsequent [reasons] from the second onwards merely remove doubt, he elaborates upon the subject at hand with the words "When, for one...

Herein lies the ultimate truth: when a certain thing, having taken up a limiting adjunct (upādhi), becomes connected with another, it is the indicator of that other in its state devoid of adjuncts, just as fire is the indicator of smoke.
Even in a state where there is an adjunct (*upādhi*),

if the capacity belongs to the [subject] alone, then that alone is the indicator (*gamaka*), not the one qualified by the adjunct; just as, for example, when the specific transformation of the food itself is the indicator, being the son of Maitra is not.
But where the mere adjunct (upādhi) itself is deviant, there even that which possesses the adjunct is indeed an indicator;
as for example, fire possessing wet fuel [is an indicator] of smoke.
For what reason is that?
"Because that which is distinguished [from the universal] is without a limiting condition (nirupādhi)"—this refers to "repeated observation" (bhūyodarśana);
the meaning is that it is the sense organ conjoined with the mental impression (saṃskāra) produced by that [observation].
And since this very point has been clarified at the outset, there is no contradiction.

Regarding the phrase "like the reality of the distinction between jewels": just as a jewel becomes the object of various conventional designations through its respective specific qualities, [so too does the self].
And that which brings about the various distinctions in the fruits for the one who maintains [the teaching] is inferred;
those subtle particulars are inferred by investigators through repeated observations,
and it is the same here as well.
For instance, first of all, repeated observation is for the purpose of excluding the "crow-and-palmyra-fruit" logic (i.e., accidental coincidence);
thereafter, it is for the purpose of determining specific qualities such as continuous upward motion.
Therefore, for the purpose of dispelling doubts regarding limiting conditions (*upādhi*),
there is no utility in restricting the number of repetitions here,
because men possess diverse capacities due to the differences in their intellects— whether they be dull, middling, or superior.
And this being the case, the treatises on definitions (lakṣaṇa-śāstra) are not rendered useless;

for just as there is instruction for the practice of yoga culminating in the direct realization of reality characterized by specific days of the week, so too here there is a rule culminating in the cognition of an unconditional relationship.
This very same path applies even to the comprehension of the relation between cause and effect.

But it is not the case that [the cause is established] by means of fivefold perception and non-perception; for even if there is perception immediately after something that did not exist there and has not come from elsewhere, it cannot be ascertained as being produced from that alone, because it could have arisen from something else entirely, since it is possible for it to occur by mere chance, like the maxim of the crow and the palm fruit.
If, however, no deviation is observed upon further occurrence,
there would likewise be no observation of a limiting condition (upādhi);
but if both are admitted, then the relation is necessarily restricted to that [limiting condition].
It might be argued:

although there is no difference in terms of being based on repeated observation between smoke and the like, and [the property] "being the son of Maitra" and the like, from what cause does this distinction arise such that one is a prover while the other is not? To this he says: "And not...
as for what was stated here:

For just as there is no smoke when fire lacks fuel, so that specific kind of fuel related to the fire is its limiting condition (*upādhi*); likewise, if someone born of Maitra were observed to be dark-skinned despite the absence of the intended transformation of food, that [absence] would have been identified as the limiting condition.
But this is not the case;
for even if that were so, the doctrine of the limiting adjunct (upādhi) would be useless,
since Maitra’s son would be a non-cause precisely because of [the logical] deviation (vyabhicāra).
Thus, this objection raised through similarity and dissimilarity by one who has not ascertained the definition of a limiting condition (upādhi) amounts to nothing at all.
For it is not the case that there is a certain deviation from the probandum (sādhyavyabhicāra) in that which is qualified by a limiting condition (upahita).
What, indeed, is the definition of a limiting condition (upādhi)? It is being a pervader of the probandum (sādhyavyāpakatva) while not being a pervader of the probans (sādhanāvyāpakatva).

Moreover, with respect to the smoke and blackness that are intended as the probanda (*sādhya*), the two [factors]—the specific transformation of moist fuel and the specific transformation of food and drink—are equally pervasive (*vyāpaka*); and with respect to the fire and being Maitra’s son that are intended as the probans (*sādhana*), those two are equally non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*).
This, however, is the distinction:
Just as with smoke and fire, a direct absence [of the probans] is perceived even in the case of wet fuel;
however, in the case of the son of Maitra, his dark complexion is inferred from the digestion of food and drink only by means of an adventitious condition (*upādhi*).
Now, what is the adventitious condition for the reason "being composed of earth" (*pārthivatva*) with respect to the property of being scratchable by iron in the case of a diamond (*vajra*)?
[The opponent says: It is the state of having loosely joined parts.

[The proponent replies: In that case, when that [looseness] is absent, it would follow—just as in the case of iron—that even in substances like crystal, the quality of being scratchable by iron would be absent;
for indeed, there is no distinction between the two on account of the density of their parts.
It is not because of the density of its parts that crystal [is transparent], but rather precisely because its parts are loosely joined;
for it is not the case that the earth is denser than water and therefore not loosely joined in its parts.
However, this much is the distinction.
To the extent that there is a removal of softness, to that same extent is the excellence of effort on the part of the carver.
However, if softness were not a necessary factor, then even the excellence of effort applied to clay, wood, stone, and so forth would be fruitless,
since the quality of being earthen (pārthivatva) is indistinguishable across all of them.
If it is asked how this cognition occurs in the case of crystal,
it is precisely because of its being scratchable by iron;
for there is a coextensive pervasion between the property of being scratchable by iron and the property of having loose constituent parts.

Therefore, the occurrence or non-occurrence of one of these two [properties] entails the occurrence or non-occurrence of the other, but the occurrence or non-occurrence of earthiness does not entail the occurrence or non-occurrence of being scratchable by iron, because this is not observed in the case of a diamond (*vajra*).
Furthermore, because [the property] is observed in water and so forth;

as for the probans "being produced" (kṛtakatva) used to prove that fire is not hot, its "limiting condition" (upādhi) is the characteristic of being other than what belongs to that same class, and since that [condition] is restricted solely to the domain of sublation (bādha), there is no over-extension— so it has been said.
Keeping all of this in mind, he says: "beginning with these," and so forth.

Although in some cases the second perception of the mark produces a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) only while it is in a state of perishing along with the memory [of the first perception], nevertheless, where smoke that has ceased upon the cessation of the fire is reflected upon at a later time due to a desire for knowledge,
both perceptions of the mark are past; it is with this intention that he said "although," and so forth.
And by one who does not accept *parāmarśa* (the act of consideration), the fourth member of the syllogism, *apana* (the conclusion), must likewise not be accepted.

If it is argued that its utility in inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) lies in establishing the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), whereas in inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*) that [property] is already understood from the second observation of the mark (*liṅga*) alone—so what is the use of *parāmarśa*?—[we reply: No.
For it is the property of the subject (pakṣadharmatā), when conjoined with pervasion (vyāpti), that is useful for inference;
and such [conjunction] is demonstrated by the application (upanaya), but not by the second observation of the mark (liṅga).
But for that [second perception], its scope is merely the property-of-the-subject (pakṣadharmatā) devoid of an investigation into pervasion (vyāpti);
and that is not useful for inference. Therefore, the purpose of the application (upanaya) is not the object of a second observation of the mark (liṅga).

Therefore, if there is a utility for it in inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), then surely the third [member], the consideration (*parāmarśa*), must also be accepted. If it is not present there, then in inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) as well, the application (*upanaya*), which has the same purpose as the consideration of the mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*), should not be respected either.
Intending to show that these two have the same object because their objects are identical, he states their commonality of object by saying "the relation," etc.
Is it not the case that being an object consists in being connected with an operation, and being connected with an operation consists in being an object— thus resulting in mutual dependence?
Or is it that being an object consists precisely in being connected with an operation?

Nevertheless, raising the doubt as to how it is that only this [cognition] is connected with the operation [of inference], given that there is no difference in their lack of connection, he provides the following resolution: "And there is no over-extension" (*na cātiprasaṅga*).

Fire is not the object of the operation of the cognition of smoke in its own right, such that an over-extension would occur because there is no difference in their lack of connection; rather, [fire is the object] of the cognition as qualified by the object of knowledge (*jñeya-viśeṣaṇasya*).
And for that smoke which is being cognized, the restrictive relation with fire is indeed a relation of essential identity (svabhāvasambandha);
therefore, there is no over-extension—this is the meaning.
Previously, on the occasion of the question regarding the referent of the term *lakṣya*, the answer given was that it has the sense of "that by which one infers," meaning the cause (*kāraṇa*).

Now, in response to the inquiry arising from the desire to know whether inference (*anumiti*) constitutes the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in some state or not, the answer is that it is either the state (*bhāva*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
Or else, there would be tautology.

Therefore, the author of the *Ṭīkā* also, having raised the objection that [the action] lacks authority because it is a mere activity (*vyāpāra*), established its authority on the grounds that it is a cause for a different result.

Here, although the exclusion of the determination of refinement (*saṃskāra*) and [the determination of] cognition occurs under the heading of either cognition (*vijñāna*) or authority (*pramāṇa*), [the point remains as stated].
For, within the section on consciousness (*vijñāna*), the connection with the Sūtra is that inference is preceded by that [consciousness] and has experience as its cause;
however, such specificities as formative predispositions (*saṃskāra*) and ascertainment (*nirṇaya*) do not exist [as causes],
because they are not causes with respect to experience.

Even in the section on the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that same meaning [of inference] is established by implication, because of the connection with the aphorism: "Inference is the instrument of valid cognition preceded by that [perception].

Nevertheless, intending that both [definitions] will be connected to both [sections] through alternative formulations due to a difference in intended meaning, he explained it in such a way as to present each one individually, based on its primary application to each respective section.
In reality, however, the essential point is that both [terms] are connected to both [positions].

In the Vārttika, the term *vipakṣāvṛttiḥ* is established as a bahuvrīhi compound where the absence (*vyatireka*) functions as a subordinate qualifier; by extracting that absence and presenting it as the primary element through a tatpuruṣa compound, it is shown as "the absence from the dissimilar instances" (*vipakṣāvṛttir vyatirekaḥ*).

Therefore, there is no contradiction with the Vārttika regarding the co-referentiality of the reason (*hetu*). "Absence of negative concomitance" (*vyatirekābhāva*) means the absence of the determination of negative concomitance.
Here, the fact that a non-entity (*avastu*) is the object of the linguistic usage of affirmation and negation is either due to conformity with worldly practice, or—
It is like mother-of-pearl appearing as silver or a rope appearing as a snake due to conformity with the means of valid cognition;
or it is like earth or water in relation to smell,
or like primordial matter (pradhāna) or a hare’s horn, due to mere verbal assertion.
Either because of compliance with the questions of the deluded, or else, as before, out of fear of contradicting one's own words regarding another property.

Among these, the first [type of negation] is impossible with respect to a non-entity (*avastu*), because worldly engagement and withdrawal have as their object only entities; and since it enters into the second type and those following it by way of a succession, it is not refuted separately.
To refute the second [position], he states the method of conventional usage for the negation of that which is established by valid cognition: "By the two existent things," etc.

Whether non-existence has a nature distinct from those two, or whether it has a nature over and above both, in either case it is defined solely by means of the object to be negated and the locus of negation.
The meaning is: "but not by a single negated entity, nor by a single locus of negation."

Now, one might object: "Surely, that which exists will simply cease to exist due to some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*. To this he says: "other than the subject" (*pakṣād anyasya*). By this, the definition of cessation when there is no locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is refuted;
the underlying intention is that in the case of cessation, silence alone is appropriate.
"Non-occurrence itself is what is prohibited.
But one who is deluded objects: "If it does not cease.
Taking up the investigation, he answers: "Of that which..."
Indeed, it is observed that where an entity is not determined in any way whatsoever, its non-existence is determined with respect to another locus where it has been perceived elsewhere—
just as, for example, the non-existence of horns, which are seen in a cow, is determined in a hare.

But where even the non-existence of a horn cannot be ascertained, as in the case of a sky-lotus and the like, there the horn itself is what is being ascertained; thus the meaning is that this is "extraordinary" (alaukika).
Again, the deluded one raises an objection: "Then what now? etc.
He anticipates the fear of contradiction with one's own words, saying: "But if... (nanu ceti).
As it was said by Jñānaśrī:
"Regarding some phenomenon that is not an entity, is there here any conventional practice of negation or affirmation established by the mind, or not?"
If it exists somewhere, why are there not so many refutations?
If it does not exist at all, then the contradiction of one's own words is established.
Thus,
although even out of fear of contradicting one's own words it is impossible to accept an object that cannot withstand analysis in any way—
according to the maxim that "analysis is weightier than mere speech"—
Otherwise, the fact that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and words do not have real entities as their domain must be avoided [as a position] precisely because it contradicts one's own statement.

For, since the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—by virtue of its uniqueness—is incapable of being the object of linguistic convention, and since the operation of words depends upon convention, and conceptual construction has that same [conventionally constructed entity] as its sole object; [therefore, they cannot refer to the real].

In the investigation that neither of these two has a real entity as their object-domain, does there exist, with respect to any real entity, any conventional operation of negation or affirmation established by the means of valid cognition through words, or not?
If it does indeed exist, how can there not be so many refutations?
If it does not exist at all, then the contradiction of one's own words is established.
Thus, the intimidation is equal;
nevertheless, determining the reality, he refutes it with the words: "Not indeed in reality."
Now, if there is neither the negation nor the affirmation of either one, then is it the affirmation or the negation of both?
If that were so, it would result in something even more difficult to establish; therefore, he says: "Certainly not" (*no khalu*).
[Objection: But even the statement "it is not the object of any worldly transaction" (*sarvavyavahārābhājana*) could be sustained precisely by its being the object of the transaction of negation.
Otherwise, there would again be a contradiction with one's own words; therefore, he says: "or in its application.

For it is out of fear of contradicting one's own words that the acceptance of [the object] as being within the scope of the conventional usage of negation would occur, provided that by doing so, that fear were removed.
But this is not the case;
indeed, the statement that "it is both a vessel for all conventional discourse and a vessel for the discourse of its negation" is not mutually contradictory.
If it is asked, "What contradiction is there in employing the conventional designation 'unfit vessel' with the intention of referring merely to the conventional usage of prescriptions?"—alas!
Is something designated as such by virtue of being unfit for all conventional usages of prescriptions and prohibitions, or not?
In either case, there is a contradiction with one's own words.
In either case, it must be a non-entity,

because it is impossible for an entity to be devoid of all conventional usage; for if one takes the position that it is not [an entity], there is a contradiction with the very conventional usage expressed by the statement that "it is not the locus of any conventional activity of affirmation or negation."
For that which is not subject to conventional usage cannot be denied;
however, in the case where it *is* subject to conventional usage, there is a contradiction simply by examining the nature of the object itself,
for it is impossible for something to be both beyond all conventional usage and yet be conventionally used.
Moreover, if a non-entity is the object of the conventional usage of negation,
why should it not also be the object of the conventional usage of affirmation?
For the absence of a means of valid cognition is equal in both cases.

If it is argued that for the son of a barren woman, the lack of being a speaker is proven solely by his lack of consciousness and so forth, whereas there is no such proof for his being a speaker— this is not so,
because even in that case, the state of being a son is present.
For it is not the case that the son of a barren woman is not a son;
if that were so, there would be a contradiction with one's own words.
If you argue that this is merely a verbal expression and that, in ultimate reality, he is indeed a son?
Since even that which is insentient possesses such a nature, it is said that what is other than sentience is simply a different intrinsic nature called "insentient."

If it is argued that here only the mere cessation of insentience (*acaitanya*) is intended, and that this is indeed possible—[we reply: no, because even there, only the mere cessation of being a non-son (*asutatva*) is intended. Since the mere cessation of being a non-son is, by its very nature, incapable of either producing or making known [the conclusion], another capable entity must be understood; for how could there be the status of a logical reason (*hetutva*) without including such an entity?
If you say this, it is not so; for this same reasoning applies equally even to that which lacks consciousness.

Furthermore, even in the case of a form characterized by exclusion (*vyāvṛtti-rūpa*), only that which is excluded from what it is not can be the indicator, just as the nature of being a *śiṃśapā* tree [indicates a tree].

If it is argued that the son of a barren woman is excluded from things such as a pot—just as he is from "non-son"—and is also excluded from things such as Devadatta’s son, and therefore cannot be a valid logical reason (*hetu*); [we reply: no.
[Objection: But is not its insentience (*acaityanya*) also of this very same nature?
For a son of a barren woman does not differ from Devadatta and others who are sentient, nor from wood and other things which are insentient;
therefore, it is not a valid reason (*hetu*).

If it is argued that speakerhood is a property necessarily restricted to a real entity (*vastu*), and how then could it be established as a property of a non-entity (*avastu*) given the contradiction?
From what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is this contradiction established?
Is it because a non-entity, being distinct from speakerhood, is invariably perceived?
Or is it because the state of being a speaker, when devoid of a real entity (*vastu*), cannot be apprehended?
First of all, that which is not a real entity (*avastu*) cannot be the object of apprehension by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
otherwise, it would not be a non-entity.
Nor is the latter [alternative] tenable, because it is equivalent [to the first].
For even "not being a speaker" is not the object of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as something distinct from a real entity (*vastu*).
If it is argued that there is at least the mere conceptual construction (*vikalpana*) of it as distinct from that [entity]?
Even regarding the conceptualization of its association with that [negation], who could prevent it?
Is it not the case that "speaker-ness" (vaktṛtva) is the agency (kartṛtva) with respect to speaking?
How then could that pertain to a non-entity (avastu)?
If it is argued that this is because its characteristic is the absence of capacity,
then how can there also be the state of being a non-speaker (*avaktṛtva*) in that case, since its characteristic is the agency of producing speech and other things?
If it is argued that the absence of the capacity for speech is not contradictory when there is an absence of all capacities,
then from what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the son of a barren woman established as being devoid of all capacities?
If you say it is because he is a non-entity (*avastu*), [we reply:]...
"But how is even this so?
If you say it is because of the total absence of all capacity,
then this person, like an indigent debtor wandering here and there with mere words to deceive honest men, does not even see the fault of mutual dependence."
If it is argued that this is because of the absence of succession and simultaneity, we say no; for even if that absence were established, the demand for proof would still persist.

Furthermore, when "sonship" is being considered, since all properties invariably concomitant with it—such as being a speaker and so forth—would necessarily follow, what opportunity is there for establishing the absence of succession and simultaneity?
How much less, then, could there be proof of a non-entity? And how much less, then, proof for [qualities] such as not being a speaker?
Therefore, valid cognition alone is the boundary for the regulation of conventional discourse.
However, if that [definition] were exceeded, there would be no fixed rule at all; it is with this intention that the following was stated:

whether in terms of utility (*upayoga*) or in terms of being the object of the linguistic practice of negation (*niṣedha-vyavahāra*), that which is "without designation" (*nirupākhya*) is not the object of the linguistic practice of affirmation (*vidhi-vyavahāra*).
The meaning is that there is a rule stating: "Whatever is negated by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in a certain locus, something else must also be affirmed in that same locus.
In that regard, when an answer is to be given to the questioner, it is not [the case that...]
Intending to state that it is improper to speak what is contradictory or meaningless, he asks: "What then?
The reply is: "Now...
Regarding a subject for which there is no answer, whatever is made into an answer by those who lack insight—
The meaning is that this very [point] is contradictory.
Moreover, it is not only the respondent here who lacks understanding;
the questioner as well is heartless.
For, unless Devadatta and others have already been perceived, no one would ask, "Is he fair or dark? except out of sheer impudence.
In that case as well, if one person, whose very object is the uncomprehended ultimate truth, gives the answer "not white," why should another not also give the answer "white"?
And this being so, no objective conclusion whatsoever is established.

Because the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the contradiction [of its existence] are equal in both cases. This is what was meant by the phrase "for those whose speech lacks heart. Now, it is indeed logical that there is no linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding that which is not cognized; however, [the opponent might argue: "But surely, even if it is not cognized, there is no contradiction in its existence. To this we reply: No, for that would lead to the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasaṅga*) that everything would exist. For if one were to say, "Even though it is not cognized, it exists," then since the non-cognition of everything is equal, one would have to accept the existence of everything. Therefore, the statement "there is no contradiction" is merely a pretense of logic (*nyāyābhāsa*). Furthermore, if one says, "Even though it is not cognized, it exists," then since the non-cognition of everything is equal, one must accept the existence of everything. Consequently, the claim "there is no contradiction" is nothing but a semblance of reasoning. Thus, the assertion "there is no contradiction" is simply a fallacy of logic. However, [concepts] such as "the hair of a tortoise" are indeed perceived;
for these conceptual constructions do not arise without delineating some distinction of an object.
Nor is there a rule that only what is based on a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) can be the basis for conventional usage; therefore, he says: "And not absolutely... and so forth.

Although even for the Buddhist who asserts that there is an absence of linguistic convention regarding what is entirely unperceived, there is indeed a contradiction with his own words, nevertheless, this contradiction has already been largely exposed; thus, setting that aside, only the mere doubt has been addressed.
For instance, would the cognition "hare's horn" be an *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension) or an *asatkhyāti* (cognition of the non-existent)?
It cannot be the former, for that is not acceptable to you;
if it were so, there would have to be something superimposed and something that serves as the locus of superimposition.
Thus, it would follow that the locus of superimposition exists in one place, while the object to be superimposed exists elsewhere; this victory belongs to the Naiyāyikas.
Nor is the second alternative tenable, because the reason for it is untenable.
Because the sense organ functions solely through its sovereignty over its own object in the production of cognition,

and because even fallacious signs (*liṅga*) and words produce the appearance of something other than what they represent; furthermore, if these two, having set aside their own referents, were to produce the appearance of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*), it would follow that conceptual constructions such as "tortoise-hair" could arise even from the word "hare's horn."
Because there is no guiding principle.
For that [connection] must be either a convention or the inherent nature of the word;
it cannot, first of all, be the former.
Because the [objection] that it is not perceived as the object of a convention has already been refuted;
for this very reason, there is no mutual dependence regarding perception. Furthermore, if activity occurs by the power of the convention of words, there is no abandonment of one's own meaning.
Thus, since word-meanings that are actually unrelated appear as if they were related, it is simply the theory of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*) that recurs.
Furthermore, if one abandons their own specific meanings, there would again be a lack of restriction,
because meanings not conventionally established by linguistic usage would be conveyed.

However, because it is the very nature of words, if there were such a restriction, it would follow that even for one who has not mastered linguistic convention, a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of that same kind would arise just as it does for one who has.
If you argue that this is due to a specific latent impression (*vāsanā*),
then is it only the latent impression that is the cause of a cognition that represents what is non-existent, or is the latent impression itself also [non-existent]?
Not the first [alternative],
because it would entail the consequence that cognitions such as "the horn of a hare" would be eternal.

If it is argued that [the effect arises] sometimes from the awakening of a latent impression (vāsanā) and sometimes from another cause— no, for even this "awakening" is itself another auxiliary condition.
Or is it the ripening of a succession of intensities?
In the first case, since it would be nothing but latent predisposition (*vāsanā*), the proposed position is untenable.
As for the second case as well, when there is a proximity to a different object, then it is just as before.
But if [the cognition] were dependent solely upon its own continuum, there would be a contradiction with the doctrine of external objects,

because cognitions of blue and so forth would also arise solely from the maturation of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*). Furthermore, regarding the position that the predisposition itself [is the cause]:
Some other reason must also be stated; when that is examined, it does not transcend the logic previously established.
Furthermore, there is no comprehension of a relationship even for words such as "hare's horn" with respect to non-existent objects.
For this reason, since the cognitions of others are not apprehended, their objects are likewise not apprehended.
Nor is there any specific causal efficiency from which one might infer a particular object and thereby grasp a convention regarding it.
Nor can there be comprehension of that [object] from the words of the signifier alone;
for all words concerning that object would fail to convey meaning, as their referents are not yet understood and thus no convention (*samaya*) has been grasped.

Nor should it be argued that when one utters the word "rabbit's horn," some intention has occurred such that its referent is easily grasped as the denotation of this word, and thus the convention (*samaya*) is easily apprehended;
for the apprehension of a convention does not take such a form.

When it is said, "Bind the cow," for one who does not understand the word's meaning, there would be the undesirable consequence that he grasps the convention [of the word] upon the mere cognition of the speaker's intention.

Nor is it tenable to claim that its denotatum is merely an object of conceptual construction (kalpanā) devoid of any other particularity, because that would entail the absurdity that even things such as a jar, a tortoise, or hair would have that status.

Nor is it tenable that all practitioners, by virtue of their own latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), partake in the cognition of a relationship between words and non-existent objects; for, due to a lack of mutual communication, this would result in the consequence that [language] is not for the sake of others.
Indeed, it is impossible to engage another in linguistic usage without first causing them to grasp a convention established by oneself.
Nor can it be made understood without recourse to conventional usage and instruction;
nor is there, regarding the non-existent object "hare's horn," any usage among the elders such as "bind the cow," nor is there any instruction such as "this is that" or "that is this."
Nor is there an extended application of a secondary characteristic (upalakṣaṇātideśa) as in the expression "as is a cow, so is a gavaya.
Nor is there here a grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with well-known terms, as in "the bee drinks honey in the interior of a blooming lotus.
Therefore, those conceptual constructions such as a hare's horn are not of the nature of the apprehension of the non-existent (asatkhyāti).

Because there would be no cause for such a state [of being as it appears], and because it would follow that it is non-practical (asāṃvyavahārika), like an earthquake or a dream; therefore, [erroneous cognitions] consist only of misapprehension (anyathākhyāti). Thus, even on this account, a non-entity cannot be the object of the linguistic usage of negation—this is the meaning.
"Let it be so; nevertheless, this [objection] does not constitute a valid critique of our proof," he says: "and its object is imagined.
For what indeed is this so-called "exclusion" (vyatireka)?
Is it that when something is excluded from another, the former is absent there?
Or is it the nature of the absence of those two?
In that regard, first of all, the absence of succession and simultaneity in a rabbit's horn is not within the scope of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
because a rabbit's horn devoid of succession and simultaneity is not an object of valid cognition, just like a mountain ridge devoid of trees.
Nor is it established by valid cognition that the rabbit’s horn consists in the absence of succession and simultaneity;
for, like the absence of a jar, the rabbit’s horn is not apprehended by any means of valid cognition.
If it is argued that the absence of a jar is also not within the scope of valid cognition—no, [it is not so].

For that [object], even though it possesses a nature both distinct and non-distinct from its absence, is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) alone; or, if it were not so established, there would be no conventional usage regarding it either.

To begin with, a jar is established by valid cognition as having a nature consisting in the absence of its own non-existence, because it is never perceived as being of such a nature [i.e., as being its own absence].
If it is argued that by this much alone the non-existence of that [other] is also established as having the nature of the absence of the jar— no,
for the non-existence of the jar is not admitted to have the nature of the absence of that [other].
Nor would another thing be established simply because the nature of one thing has come within the scope of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
If it is argued that "the jar and its absence are of such a nature that the very determination of one constitutes the establishment of the other"— no,
for if one does not accept that the absence of a jar is as established by valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*) as the jar itself, then one is not accepting the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavāda*).

For when a thing is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it serves as the basis for the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavāda*); however, it is precisely your own war-drum of victory, proclaimed here and there, that asserts: "The determination of a thing does not occur solely through the basis of the doctrine of intrinsic nature. As it was stated in the *Vārtikālaṅkāra*:
Having established whatever one considers to be the self,
one is rendered speechless therein by the state [of reality];
thus it is said that [all is determined] by the intrinsic natures of things.
Then, he shall be entirely victorious thereafter.
In that case, is it now established by no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that the pot has the nature of being devoid of intrinsic nature (*svābhāvavirahasvabhāva*)?
From your perspective, this is indeed so;

for the pot, with whatever nature it may have, has entered the path of valid cognition. If, moreover, there were some absolute non-existence (*abhāva*) of it even in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), [then your point would hold].

From the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*), that [non-existence] as well would have the nature of being devoid of that [existence], and thus it would be established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in exactly the same way;
yet this is not accepted by you.

Therefore, since the non-existence of that [existence] is also established by valid cognition—just like the jar—the distinction (*vyatireka*) characterized by their mutual absence is proven for these two.

Or, if these two [space and time] lack the status of being valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇika*), then they do not exist in that manner either; this same logic applies even to things such as a hare's horn.
[Objection: "But surely, let it be that the fulfillment of a conceptual form alone is a constituent of inference. To this he says: "Because that is easily found everywhere," etc. This means:

[it is found] in the case of establishing "possessing fire" and so forth by means of "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and the like; in establishing "impermanence of sound" and so forth by means of "visibility" (*cākṣuṣatva*) and the like; and in establishing "permanence" and so forth by means of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and the like. [Objection:
"But surely, the subject (*pakṣa*), the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) are of two kinds, distinguished as real entities (*vastu*) and non-entities (*avastu*)."

In that regard, those [reasons] which are brought forward by conceptual construction possess, within that [conceptual domain], only conceptually constructed presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
However, the distinction is that those things brought forward by means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) are indeed established by valid cognition.

Therefore, in this case, although the exclusion of "non-fire" from a conceptual [locus]— such as the property of being an object of knowledge— is established as conceptual, nevertheless, the exclusion from a real [locus] such as a lake must be sought as something established by valid cognition.
And since that [property] is not established, how can it possess the status of a reason (*hetu*)?

Likewise, even when a word accepted as authoritative is made the subject (*pakṣa*), the existence of a reason must be stated as something itself accepted as authoritative; yet such a reason does not exist in the case of "visibility" (*cākṣuṣatva*). Therefore, how could that also be a reason?
In this way, for a property such as "being produced" which is restricted to a single real entity, a real positive concomitance (anvaya) must be asserted;
and from the real entity that is the counter-example, a real negative concomitance (vyatireka) must be asserted.
Yet, those two do not exist for it.
How then can that also be a reason? This is mere idle chatter;
for without a determining factor, the conceptualization regarding the perfection does not hasten.
However, it can be said that [the reason] lags behind with respect to the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).

And thus, even though the hair of a tortoise is devoid of fire, by the mere conceptualization that it possesses smoke, smoke would not lead to the cognition of fire because of its occurrence in the counter-example.
If it is argued: "When the actual perfection of form exists, what is the use of this conceptual defect?"
In that case, if the actual [non-accomplishment] exists, what is the use of an imagined one? The situation is the same.
If it is argued that the distinction lies in contradiction versus non-contradiction, from where does this [distinction] arise?
If it is argued that because both [the hare's horn and smoke] are a thing in one case and a non-thing in the other, [smoke] is like a non-thing elsewhere,
then is even imagined smoke a real entity such that it could have a contradiction with a tortoise-hair?

If it is argued that in some cases [the absence] is a real entity (*vastubhūta*), then the absence of smoke is also in some cases a real entity; therefore, there would be a contradiction by that very fact.
Consequently, just as an imagined failure (*vipatti*) does not constitute a fault, [so too is the case here].
Likewise, even imagined prosperity does not lead to excellence, because such prosperity is easily available everywhere; this is the meaning of the *ṭīkā*.
And this has been stated provisionally—however, in reality, that which is devoid of any defining characteristic (*nirupākhyam*) cannot be the object of any conventional usage (*vyavahāra*).

Now, if there is a contradiction with one's own words due to our own lack of skill, then what answer should be given to the questioner? Concluding this remaining point, he offers a rebuttal: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
The meaning is that where a statement is in every way contradictory, silence itself is better.
By this, the conceptual constructions regarding the causes of muteness should be understood as refuted.

One might object: "How can this [reason], being of a single form and lacking [all other] forms, be indicative? Or, if it is indeed indicative, why should another form lacking [other] forms not also be so, given that there is no difference? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And not merely this much. The meaning is that, unlike the deficiency of other forms, the deficiency of the negative concomitance (vyatireka) does not bring about a destruction of the invariable relation (avinābhāva).
If that is so, then even when a counter-example (vipakṣa) exists, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) need not be sought; to this he says: "But when a counter-example is possible...
When a counter-example exists, there is the suspicion of its [the reason's] occurrence therein;
therefore, for the purpose of excluding that, the [negative concomitance] is employed.
But when there is an absence of an adverse factor, there is no doubt at all, as was stated previously.
For a conscious person does not suspect that a dying man, who is incapable even of swallowing, will eat a *śaṣkulī* cake; this is the meaning.
Regarding the phrase "but in our own view":

even a conceptual counter-example (*vipakṣa*) cannot be asserted by an opponent in this case, because if it were asserted, it would result in its being a similar instance (*sapakṣa*); and if it were not a similar instance, it would follow that it could not be asserted at all.

Furthermore, when "being denotable" is the probandum (*sādhya*), whatever reason (*hetu*) is adduced, when asked whether it occurs in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) or does not occur, what should this master of answers say?
He has merely prattled on by himself, thinking, "Let him remain silent; there is no rival to me."

However, one who asserts "by way of pervasion" (*vyāptyā*) in order to refute the charge of partial non-establishment (*bhāgāsiddhi*)— arguing that such a thing cannot be a causeless [reason] because there would be no fault, since mere lack of interest is easily found everywhere— [is being addressed].
The suffix *matup* is prescribed in the sense of excellence (*atiśāyana*), as in the previous case;
and the intention is that this excellence is indeed pervasion (*vyāpti*).
This has been stated by the author of the *Ṭīkā*: "There is a probandum for the possession of odor, but not a pervasion."

[Objection: But surely the word *śeṣa* has no application whatsoever to that which is of the same class as the probandum (*sādhyasajātīya*). To this he says: "Because the probandum has already been utilized. He dispels the suspicion of tautology by saying: "having divided the words. It should not be thought that when explaining by means of inclusion, the term *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* is to be construed in such a manner.
That which is devoid of the aforementioned specificities is called the "general" (sāmānya) only within the counter-example (vipakṣa).
In that context, [the word] "adṛṣṭam" is used;
the suffix -tasi is applied to the locative case (saptamī).
And by the cessation of the perception of the fit [subject], the cessation of the perceptible is intended;
therefore, the meaning is that [the reason] is absent in the counter-example (vipakṣa). Thus, it is as if established.
Having accepted the fulfillment of the three characteristics, he introduces the letter *ca* (and) for the sake of the fulfillment of the two remaining characteristics: "And thus..."
Thus, when the definition "inference is the consideration of the mark preceded by that" has been explained as having the purpose of defining [inference], then,
in response to the inquiry as to what the mark is and how many kinds there are, it is explained by way of restriction as being "threefold."
