When there is a desire to know what the characteristic is, it should be understood that—through an explanation as a single syntactical unit with the phrase "as before" and so forth—the object of reflection is designated, distinguished, and characterized.
Furthermore, grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is to be understood by virtue of the intention to express non-difference between the object and the subject.
The same applies to other cases as well.
For example: the inference of worldly passion from seeing a beautiful woman intoxicated with youth;
the inference of anger from seeing an enemy;
and the inference of pleasure from the enjoyment of sense objects.
The inference of suffering from disease and the like;
the inference of cognition from the application of the unimpaired sense faculties toward their appropriate objects;
and the inference of dharma from the performance of sacrifices and other rites according to the rules by those possessed of faith.
Inwardly, there is the inference of unrighteousness (*adharma*) from the performance of prohibited acts;
the inference of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) from the cognitions of intense practice and zeal;
and the inference of the future flow of saṃsāra from false cognition.
Furthermore, one should understand that there is the inference of future ash upon perceiving a mass of grass burning externally;
likewise, the knowledge of a future river flood resulting from such rain;
and the inference of the agitation of trees and so forth by means of a swift wind perceived through another modality, and so on.
"Difficult to understand" means that its nature as a *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* [inference] has not been analyzed;
its analysis is provided by way of an example.
He says that it will be so: "And because it is not included among the examples of *śeṣavat*.

Even though it possesses the defining characteristics of *śeṣavat*, this very [type of inference] will apply to the category of *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* because of its distinctness from other examples of that [category]; therefore he says: "Nor is it merely this much.
For this term does not function in the inference of the sun's motion in the same way as words such as *aśvakarṇa*.
This is because it is used by elders elsewhere as well;
nor is this a technical rule (paribhāṣā) belonging solely to the author of the Sūtra, for it would serve no purpose.
Therefore, this is stated with the intention of merely highlighting the difference from the [previous] example;
the meaning is that such a case would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Consequently, the construction is as follows: not being satisfied with a mere presentation of an example that contradicts the commentary (*bhāṣya*) of the author of the *Bhāṣya*, he explains the term *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* and then offers an alternative example.
The phrase "while not being an object of the conditions of decay or growth" is for the sake of clarity;
for by simply considering that [the self] is perceived when facing forward and becomes an object of those same conditions when turning around, its indestructibility is already established.

For when there is the destruction of a perception, that which was perceived is not recognized; even in the case of an illusion, it is only that which was not perceived that is [mistakenly] perceived as having been perceived.

Regarding the phrase "if there is perception facing forward," which is elucidated by the *Ṭīkā*, the meaning is: "when that which was previously perceived facing forward is no longer perceived facing forward.
It should be understood that this refers to another person situated in the same location.

Otherwise, even the orb of the sun would unavoidably be perceived as facing east from the perspective of a person residing in another world; thus, the qualification [of the sun] would be unestablished.
This very point is indicated by the word "man" (nara).

The phrase "due to connection with a location facing that" is intended for the benefit of the student, in order to make known the movement of the feet—which serves to avoid fallacy—by which one faces it.
For merely walking about in whatever manner does not bring about the destruction of this cause;
and it should be understood that "when [the object] exists" means "when its state of being visible exists"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
In this context, although the pointing with a finger is irrelevant (*vyadhikaraṇa*) when proving that the directions are perceptible—
since the finger is used to designate only trees, cities, and so forth—

the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the direction with the designation by the finger does not establish that the direction has the finger as its locus, because such a relationship is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddhatvāt*).

Nevertheless, since there is a designation by means of a finger—such as "that direction in which these trees stand is the east"—even through the distinction of trees and so forth, it cannot be said that [the cognition] is directly denoted as having a different substratum; with this intention, he states the meaning of the Vārttika as being established otherwise: "by way of being established otherwise" (*anyathāsiddhatayā*).
And this is merely an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).

For there is the possibility of deviation (vyabhicāra) because the pointing with a finger— such as "this wind is blowing" upon perceiving a moving banner— applies even to the wind, which is not visible; furthermore,
by the inclusion of the word "etcetera" in the phrase "the inference of touch through color," one includes the inference of color through taste,
the inference of taste through smell, and so forth.

When there is non-perception or doubt regarding a tree, there can be no certain perception of a *śiṃśapā* (a specific type of tree); therefore, inference is rendered untenable by the lack of opportunity (*anavasara-parāhata*).

Furthermore, the inference of linguistic usage characterized by the employment of the word "tree" is not for one's own sake (*svārtha*), because it is impossible for one who does not know the convention (*samaya*).
And because it would be useless for one who already knows the convention;
furthermore, if the other person is also proficient—
that is, if they know the basis for the application of the word— [the teaching is likewise redundant].
Then he would act for himself alone;
conversely, however, one who lacks proficiency would not even perceive the state of being a *śiṃśapā*.
If [the opponent] is unlearned, [then...]
Indeed, it is impossible to engage in linguistic usage without first grasping a convention;
yet this is not the manner of grasping a convention.

For if that were the case, one would conclude that the very state of being a *śiṃśapā* (the specific property) is the ground for the application of the word "tree," based on the thought: "Because it is a *śiṃśapā*, this must be treated as a tree."

Nor is the meaning of the sentence "This is a tree because it possesses śiṃśapā-ness" [the object of the inference], for it would be redundant with respect to one who already knows that ground [for the application of the word];
and with respect to one who holds the opposite view, it would result in the fallacy of being a non-established qualifier (asiddha-viśeṣaṇa).
Because it is impossible to grasp a convention when beginning with a universal;
because a convention depends solely on human will and thus cannot be restricted by its being a property of the subject (pakṣadharmatā);
and because it is improper to begin with a positive concomitance (anvaya) for one who is unaware of the convention—for these reasons, he says: "by what is heard" (śrutena).
Thus, by this [statement], all other things that are simultaneous with the probandum are indicated as being included within the scope of inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).
The meaning is that this is another explanation according to his own view (*svamata*), not a different intended meaning (*tātparya*),
because there is a single intended meaning through the previous statement: "that which has that as its pervaded probandum" (*pūrvaṃ sādhyaṃ tadyasya vyāpya*).
With this very intention, he says: "In this case also, as far as possible.
In this interpretation, there is no distinction from the previous one regarding the lack of dependence on a reason for non-inclusion.

Whether it be an effect, a cause, or something that is neither, whatever is observed and ascertained through invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitayā*) is indeed "observed in a general way" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*); such is the application.
This is what was stated: "He declares the absence of doubt.
In that context, the phrase "preceded by that" [refers to perception] as follows:

the first intended meaning is the removal of misconceptions regarding its essential nature through the power of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which removes any suspicion of the number [of means of valid cognition] being either too few or too many.

However, since the purpose [of the statement] is to remove the doubt that the definition might be impossible by making known the restriction, there is no tautology; thus, the result of reciting what has been said and what is about to be said is as described.

Although for one who has already understood [the object], inference has no utility in terms of removing doubt or error, nor does it provide knowledge of the unknown, nevertheless, the confirmation of what has been determined—which follows from the force of the thing itself—must certainly not be disregarded regarding the object under consideration; thus, that [confirmation] is also counted among the things to be established by inference.
Therefore, in the opening statement, "the understood is to be made understood," it is precisely the understood that is the one to be made understood.
However, it should be understood that one who has not yet entered [the path] is indeed one who must be led [to it].
Furthermore, in order to avoid redundancy, he reiterates what has been said and what is about to be said: "previously [it was stated] as if already established.
One should understand that the similarity between the two actions—direct perception (*sākṣātkṛti*) and inference (*anumiti*)—pertains to their objects.
Therefore, this is the meaning:
Inference where a property that is capable of being apprehended by the means of valid cognition grasping pervasion (*vyāpti*) is inferred is *pūrvavat* inference;
whereas that in which [a property] incapable of such [apprehension] is [inferred] is *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*.
[The phrase] "by those [properties] inhering in the same substrate as smoke-ness" [is used].
The qualification "constantly" (*satātparyam*) is for this reason:
fire cannot be inferred merely by upward movement,
because that is deviant (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a cloud of dust and the like.

Since the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the reason "because of having a single substance" in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), such as color and so forth, is evident, only its absence from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) has been stated.
For [the reason] is indeed of only two kinds.
However, one should not entertain the suspicion that this is a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*) merely because positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is not explicitly stated here.
Since the fact that sound originates from something of its own kind is unestablished (*asiddha*), he proves it by stating "because it is an effect" (*kāryatvāt*).
Furthermore, its being an effect is established either through perception or by the fact that, in the absence of any cause for non-perception, it is perceived despite previously being unperceived.
The reason for the statement "because it would follow that [the object] would be perceived everywhere" is its contrapositive.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: sound is non-pervasive in its occurrence, because, while not being perceived in some places even when its substratum is reached, it is perceived in other places, just like conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

Although the status of being a quality (*guṇatva*) is established by this much alone, nevertheless, the reason provided by the author of the Bhāṣya might be disregarded; therefore, having established merely that [the opponent's reason] is non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*), he applies it to the present case—starting with "the ear" (*karṇa*).
Here too, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:
Sound reaches the region of space within the ear-cavity by the analogy of waves and ripples;
this is a negative inference (*vyatirekin*) because it is perceived despite the impossibility of any other mode [of arrival].
He analyzes this for the sake of illustration with the words "But this... and so forth.
The non-difference from existence and so forth consists in the connection with being,
impermanence,
and possession of a cause.
"Possessing both generality and particularity" means that it is never perceived by people such as ourselves through direct perception (pratyakṣa) in the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin).
For the intended meaning is the object of the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*);
it is that very [meaning] which is pervaded by the intention, without which the stated thesis would not be established.
When there is a possibility of both [alternatives], and a subverting argument (bādhaka) arises against one of them, the other becomes the object of another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
In that case, where there is an absence of a positive proof (vidhāyaka-pramāṇa), it is the occasion for the operation of the purely negative inference (kevalavyatirekin). To explain:
In the argument that "the earth and so forth have an agent because they are effects," the status of being the agent of the earth and so forth is not possible without omniscience;
for it is impossible to preside over atoms, unseen potentials (*adṛṣṭa*), and the like without knowing them, and if one were to preside over them,
omniscience would necessarily follow.

Therefore, since the intended object of the proposition cannot be established without omniscience, [the subject] is pervaded by that intention; and because it is based on intention, it falls within the scope of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). However, in the case of the argument "desire and so forth are dependent [on something else] because they are qualities," the self (*ātman*) is not pervaded by intention.
For it is not impossible for desire and the like to be dependent upon earth and so forth;
rather, this [dependence] is sublated by their being cognizable through mental perception and the like,
just as the non-stickiness of smoke is sublated by its blueness.
Therefore, since it is possible in both ways, the self is not pervaded by the intention;
and because it is not so pervaded, the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) cannot be attributed to that [self],
but rather [the inference] ceases by taking merely the connection with the desire as its basis.

Subsequently, when earth and the other [elements] have been sublated and the [existence of qualities] in anything else is unestablished, the negative (vyatirekin) inference proceeds by way of negation due to the absence of any positive means of knowledge.
Bearing this distinction in mind, it was stated: "when the status of being a quality of the eight substances has been removed by sublatives."

Now, is it not the case that whatever form is established through *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* inference cannot be proven by a purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*) inference? And as for the kind of thing that is proven by the latter, such a thing [cannot be proven by the former].
It is not established anywhere;
thus, the thesis has an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, there can be no doubt regarding such a case, because the cause for it is absent.
Because [the object] is not within the range of perception for those who hold conflicting views regarding common and uncommon properties, he says: "Even though this...
The meaning is: "in its own form," that is, in its unique, specific form.
For the relationship of qualifier and qualified among word-meanings is not obstructed by the fact that the meaning of the sentence is *apūrva* (unprecedented).
If that were the case, even the related [word-meanings] would fail to arise, and thus inference would be rendered obsolete.
Nor are the categories such as those exceeding the eight substances themselves the *apūrva*.
It should not be argued that this would result in the fallacy of an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*) for the subject (*pakṣa*),

nor that such being the case, the same consequence would apply even to things like "one who wields a bow made of a hare's horn," because in those cases too, it is easy to find something where even the mere object (*artha*) [of the term] is unestablished.
Because the boundary of the rule that [inference] must be preceded by what is observed through generalization (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) is difficult to overstep;

otherwise, how could something unestablished even in a general sense be reflected upon by relying merely on the power of words devoid of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? And how could that which is not so reflected upon enter into the practical application of valid cognition?
This has been stated as follows: "it is apprehended without remoteness.
The non-remoteness consists in the establishment of the universal through the establishment of the particular;
its absence, however, is the opposite of that.
This is the meaning.
And thus, doubt in this matter is easily understood precisely because of the disagreement between the disputants;

for, while the substratum in general is established for both parties as being desire and so forth, both have raised the two alternatives of whether [the substratum] is distinct from or not distinct from the eight substances.
Alternatively, there is the principle that a doubt arising with respect to each individual member finds its resolution in the aggregate.

For instance, the nature of being a quality (guṇatva) is observed in odor and the like, which reside in earth; it is also observed in viscidity and the like, which reside in that which is distinct from earth; and it is likewise observed in desire and the like.

In this manner, the doubt arising regarding all substances— namely, whether desire and the like are dependent upon earth or dependent upon something other than that— is restricted solely to the two alternatives of the eight substances or what is beyond them, precisely because of the perception of common characteristics; this is what was stated in the passage beginning with "and in the locus" (dharmiṇi ca), etc.

The intention [of the author] in nourishing the doubt regarding the interpretation of the *Bhāṣya* passage beginning with "simply because of the statement of division" (*vibhāgavacanāt*) is as follows:

One might object, "In the statement 'Reality consists of the existent and the non-existent' (*sadasatī tattvam*), the words 'existent' and 'non-existent' denote being and non-being (*bhāva-abhāva*). Therefore, why is this current explanation—which takes them to mean 'present' and 'not present'—adopted despite its apparent contradiction? To this, he says: "For perception indeed... (*pratyakṣaṃ hi*).
Now, one might ask: "Why should it not be exactly so? To this he says: "Even though" (*yadyapi*).
This means that there is no status as a qualifier by way of independence—that is, by way of being denoted independently.
Furthermore, [the objection] "Is there not also a logical principle (*nyāya*)? is untenable in its literal sense, because it does not connect with our position.
He states the connection by way of the intended meaning with the words "there is no doubt.
For, since reasoning (*tarka*) is insufficient for reaching certainty due to the absence of formal logic (*nyāya*), the suspicion arose that doubt would remain as it was.
Therefore, it is appropriate that the refutation of that [objection] alone constitutes the answer.
There is indeed a logical principle here, for [the reason] is that it is capable of producing certainty which opposes doubt; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

If "being a cause" (nimittatva) means "being an object" (viṣayatva), that is not seen in the example of the self (ātman). If, on the other hand, it means "being material cause" (upādānatva), that does not exist in the probandum (sādhya) due to inherence (samavāya). Therefore, he says: "Being a cause (nimittatva) means being a causal factor (kāraṇatva)."
Now, pervasiveness consists either in the possession of the dimension of supreme magnitude (*paramamahat-parimāṇa*) or in occupying the same location as all things that can be conjoined;
since neither of these two is possible in the case of inherence (*samavāya*), therefore—
He says: "When there is perception" (*satyupalabdhau*).
If one were to say merely "perceptibility" (*upalabhyatā*), it would follow that even things such as jars would possess pervasiveness.
Therefore, he said "everywhere" (*sarvatra*).
The locative case is used merely to indicate the location as a delimiting factor, as in the expression "the lion's roar in the forest.
Nevertheless, the definition remains unestablished, because the self and so forth are not perceived everywhere; therefore, it is stated: "provided that the causes for perception are present."

Nevertheless, since the object itself is also a cause of its own apprehension, wherever things—from jars down to atoms—are accompanied by their own complete causal complex for apprehension, they are indeed apprehended there; thus, there would be a deviation (vyabhicāra) from the rule by those very cases. Therefore, it is said: "in the absence of" (antare). And this should be understood with reference to other causes in the form of substances (dravya).

Otherwise, one might suspect that where jars and the like do not exist, their non-perception is due solely to the absence of something other than them— namely, the conjunction with the sense organ which is the cause of their perception— and that when such [a cause] is present, there would be perception everywhere.

Nevertheless, there is a deviation [from the rule] due to qualities such as those of atoms (paramāṇu) and so forth, which exist as long as the substance exists and whose determination is dependent upon their substratum; therefore, to exclude that, it should be understood that the condition "while being related to many" must be added.
And this was indicated by the author of the Ṭīkā through the word "sarvatra" (everywhere).
And although existence is pervasive everywhere,
nevertheless, because it is difficult to understand without a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), that very [characteristic] was stated.
He asks about the reasoning (*tarka*) which serves as the methodological procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
The meaning is that the intention is this: since an instrument cannot function by itself unless it is set into operation by an agent, it is impossible for it to possess activity on its own.

Now, one might ask: why is the consequence of having no substratum (*anādhāratva*) stated in order to introduce the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthāna*), when this consequence could not simply be independent? For it is certainly not accepted that an effect has no substratum at all; therefore, he says: "This might be so."
The remainder of the sentence is that it is subsequently conjoined with the fourth [moment].
For even though it has arisen, there is no one’s certain cognition that "this is a cloth" at the first moment of its appearance while it is still unconnected;
nevertheless, this very point is established by the force of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The meaning is that even when [the cloth] has arisen in the first moment, it is held to be non-inherent in the threads; therefore, this is not a valid answer for one who stands with legs outstretched.
Thus, he says "And inherence... to show that this was stated precisely to introduce the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Although the fact that [inherence] possesses occurrence (*vṛttimattva*) and its being a property of reaching [its locus] were already refuted by the discussion of the limiting conditions (*upādhi*), [he states this again].

Nevertheless, in order to indicate that the property of being a "possession" (prāptitva) is inconclusive, he introduces the consequence of infinite regress once again with the words "Now, if... (atheti).
For fear of infinite regress, one must necessarily admit at the end that there is some possession which itself does not possess occurrence;
and therefore, in that very same way, the state of possessing a possession is inconclusive—this is the meaning.
Now, raising the objection as to what fault there is in accepting an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), he refutes it with the words: "But this...

For, if beginninglessness is accepted, it is logical that the seed-nature existing in a seed produced by a sprout—which itself was produced by a seed occurring at a time conducive to the production of a sprout—makes known its state of being preceded by that sprout, because there exists a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in the form of an unimpaired cause.

However, regarding the state of being "first," since at the time conducive to the production of the effect the future stream does not exist, if the first [moment] were not produced, its basis—the cause—would be non-existent; and because that basis would be unestablished (*āśrayāsiddha*), all [subsequent moments] would fail to produce cognition, meaning there would be an absence of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāva*). This is the sense.
Furthermore, for one who has accepted the authority of Kaṇāda, there is a contradiction with his own treatise (*śāstra*), and so forth.

If one were to propose the thesis (*pratijñā*) that "the effect possesses a non-artificial connection," then the connection of a jar or similar object with the ground and so on would also have to be non-artificial; since that is undesirable, he qualifies the thesis by adding "with its own material cause" (*svopādānena*).
The meaning is "inhering in itself.
Furthermore, the term "effect" (*kārya*) is intended as an indicator for anything that is merely inherent (*samaveta*);
otherwise, there would be a contradiction of the reason (*hetu*), since it would occur in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) such as universals (*jāti*) and so forth.
Alternatively, the proposition remains exactly as it was heard; however,

in the phrase "because of having a substratum" (*ādhāravattvāt*), by the word "substratum" (*ādhāra*), not merely a locus (*āśraya*) is intended, but rather the kāraka known as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
The meaning is: "because it possesses the *kāraka* [category] of locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
Nor should it be argued: "If [the definition] is sufficient by the mere possession of a *kāraka*, what is the purpose of including 'locus'?
For that would lead to the undesirable consequence of [the definition] applying to destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*).
The meaning is that there is no causal relationship between two effects;
rather, they are mutually connected,
which means they exist in a relationship of the supported and the support.
The meaning is that even that [inherence] does not exist in inherence, because there is no further inherence; and even if it were present, it would not cause the effect to possess a substratum,
since the effect already possesses a substratum by virtue of its own inherence.
The meaning is that in the absence of that [simultaneous production], even inherence in a single substrate would not exist. If they were produced together, the effect would be without a support;
the word "always" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

Since there is no inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa), there can be no suspicion of a non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) either, because the latter is by nature dependent upon the former; with this intention, having set that aside, the possibility of production from a mere efficient cause (nimitta) alone was raised and refuted.
Now, one might object: "In this world, there is nothing whatsoever that exists independently apart from what is being enjoined or prohibited;
so how can there be a threefold nature of dharma? To this, he says: "And here...
The meaning is that "being enjoined" refers to what is present.
"Being negated" means "not existing.
In that context, among those things which do exist, some are dependent and possess activity; this is the meaning.
The meaning is that something independent is devoid of activity;
however, those things being negated are dependent and do not exist, precisely because they lack existence.
Thus, there are three modes: that which is enjoined as independent, that which is enjoined as dependent, and that which is prohibited as independent.
In this way, a property (*dharma*) that does not exist [in the present] is designated solely by way of being prohibited;
moreover, it is not an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
However, it has been shown that [the object] is the domain of inference; and since that is untenable, he states the meaning of the *Śaṅkā-vārttika* with the words "But surely" (*nanu*), etc.,
where "non-existent" (*asan*) is the subject (*uddeśya*).
Therefore, this is the meaning:
that which is non-existent and not present is not only the object of negative linguistic usage, but also of affirmative usage.
It is also the object of ritual injunctions and linguistic usage;
thus, it is not only the object of inference, but is also perceptible.
The meaning is that in some cases it is an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). To the question "In what way?", he says: "As follows" (*yathā*).
To the question "How is this being enjoined?", he says: "While being born" (*jāyamāna*).
To the question, "How is this an object of direct perception? he says: "With eyes wide open," and so forth.

To the question, "How is this not present [in the past]? he says: "And this is not... because it is not accepted either by way of non-existence or by way of existence; for there is a contradiction between existence and the state of being in the process of arising.
The meaning is that [it is not accepted] because non-existence is the object of an affirmation (*vidhi*).
Why is it not accepted? For there is no other mode besides existence and non-existence; therefore, he says: "But by way of being the object of a negation.
For if one accepts that [non-existence] is being produced while remaining on the side of being affirmed (*vidhīyamānatā*), there is a contradiction in either case.
But the meaning is that this is not the case even in the position where [the object] is being negated.
Therefore, when a jar is being produced, there is no operation of a positive perception, due to contradiction;
for even if a negative perception were to operate toward it, it would have only that negation as its object,
and not the jar which is the object of negation.
Therefore, the conclusion is that the distinction between objects is established; this is the essential point, having set aside the theory of the pre-existent effect (*satkāryavāda*).
As for the phrase "but others": [it refers to the following].
It is merely an excess of meaning;
it is merely an excess of words regarding the meaning.
The same applies to what follows.
Now, one might ask: "Who has said that a descriptive compound (viśeṣaṇasamāsa) occurs only when there is deviation regarding both members? To this he says: "The qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇam*).

Furthermore, one might ask: "Even so, since both the words 'earth' (*pṛthivī*) and 'substance' (*dravya*) denote both [the universal and the particular], how can there be a comprehension of a specific [meaning]? To this he says: "And not... (*na ca*).
For it is not the case that "earth-ness" is "substance-ness"; this is merely an illustration.
It should also be understood that "earth-ness is a substance" and "substance-ness is earth" do not occur either.
Nor should it be said that this same logic applies even to the word "invariable concomitance" (*nāntarīyaka*) and its meaning;
for that would lead to the consequence of lack of restriction (*aniyamaprasaṅga*).

For if there were grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the meaning of "invariable concomitance" and the word [itself], then there would likewise be coreferentiality between the state of being an object (*arthatva*) and the word "invariable concomitance."
Therefore, in order to exclude that [undesired consequence], another effort must once again be undertaken.

Therefore, even though the term *nāntarīyaka* has multiple meanings, one must admit—even against one's will—that this specific usage refers exclusively to the particular sense [of "inseparable connection"]. And thus, the previously mentioned objection remains unrefuted. Now, although the desired result is achieved by the word *asati* (when absent) when combined with the phrase whose scope is not restricted, nevertheless, the "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) reason—which never occurs in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*)—must also be excluded.

For it is not the case that merely because a reason pervades the subject (*pakṣa*) and is entirely absent from the counter-subject (*vipakṣa*), its exclusion [from the conclusion] is thereby established;
for such a reason would also be of that same nature [as a valid one].

Therefore, suspecting that one must necessarily state "its presence in what is similar to it" (*tattulye sadbhāvaḥ*), he says: "What is proposed and not refuted is indeed accepted. (*prasaktam apratiṣiddham anumatam eva*).
The meaning is that since the negation applies to what is possible, the abandonment of its opposite in the case of the material cause follows by implication;
nor is impossibility even suggested, such that it would not be negated.
If that [impossibility] were also included, its opposite would have to be excluded;
however, in the first case, since possibility is to be enjoined (*vidheya*), impossibility—which is its contrary—is not included as something to be negated (*niṣedhya*).
For when particles are connected with such variety as "conjoined" (*samuccīyamāna*) and so forth, there arises the undesirable consequence of a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).

The meaning is that, if one desires syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*), one must desire the connection with the particle (*nipāta*) precisely without variety. He clarifies this very point by raising the doubt regarding the conjunction of what is being restated (*anūdyamāna*), saying "And not... For it is that which has been stated (*udita*) which is restated (*anūdyate*).

However, neither the unoffered oblation nor that characterized by both [states] is what is meant by "offered"; rather, it is the oblation in its mere generality. And thus, under the view of it being a restatement (anuvāda), the state of being both is not intended to be significant.
But if there is an intention to express both [states], this is not a restatement (anuvāda), but rather an original assertion (vāda);
and in that case, there would be a syntactical split (vākyabheda).

Likewise, in the case of the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) as well, if the reason were stated as being qualified by the exclusion of non-connection with the probandum (*sādhyāyogavyavaccheda*),
then it would be appropriate for it to be restated in that manner;
however, this is not the case.
However, the mere cause has been indicated without distinction;
this is indeed the first introduction of the discussion regarding that specific [cause].
Thus, if "of which" (yasya) is a restatement (anuvāda),...
The qualification "only" (eva) in the sense that [the reason] must exist in the object of inference (anumeya) is not intended;
for if that were intended, a qualified statement would have to be made by this very sentence,
and subsequently, this same sentence would have to be repeated as a restatement— thus, the meaning is that there would be a split in the sentence (vākyabheda).
Thus, this is the meaning of the word "place" (sthāna), which occurs subsequent to effort.
Now, one might object: "If that which is being restated (anūdyamāna) cannot be qualified, then how is *ārti* (distress) qualified by the *havis* (oblation)? To this he says: "For here, although...
Since there is no other recourse, the qualification of *ārti* is made by means of the *havis* which has already been established [by another rule].
However, "being both" (ubhayatva) has not been previously established,
nor is it impossible to understand suffering without it; the meaning is that such is the nature of the reason, namely, the exclusion of what is to be proven.
If this is so, for what purpose is there the mention of both? To this he says: "Even though duality is perceived, it is not intended [to be expressed], as a qualifier"—this is the ellipsis.
This is the meaning of the sentence:
first of all, the sacrificial oblation must be taken up as a qualifier of "distress" (ārti);

and since that [oblation] takes many forms such as clarified butter (ājya), the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), and so forth, it also possesses the quality of being "both" (ubhayatva); thus, for the sake of generality, that too has been included.
Therefore, this is established:
[the rule applies] when "a single or multiple oblation should suffer damage," and so forth.
However, on the view that both [single and multiple] are intended to be expressed, the fault would be that the rule for expiation would not apply when only a single oblation suffers damage.
Nor should it be said, "Let it be so," for the consequence of a split in the sentence (vākyabheda) remains as it was;
nor [is it the case that the probans] exists only in the object of inference (anumeya).

It might be argued: "Let this very pair of statements—'its existence is only in that which is similar'—be the prescriber of both [the positive and negative concomitances]; what is the fault? It must be said that this would result in the failure to obtain a single object in the form of a reason (hetu) endowed with the three characteristics.

For according to the logical principle that "where there is a difference in sentences, there must necessarily be a difference in meaning," he raises an objection with the words "Now, [if it be argued]...
[The response is: even though there is a difference in subordinate sentences, the great sentence (*mahāvākya*) remains one.
The meaning of the term *śaṅkā* is the attainment of the single intended object.
Anticipating the Naiyāyika’s resolution here, the Buddhist refutes it in his own language with the words "na ca" (and not).

Even if [the term] "tattulya eva" (only similar to that) were to exclude connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), its scope would still be restricted solely to the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) only if there were a contraction regarding other objects;
and since that [contraction] occurs through syntactic unity with that very [term], there is the fault of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*).

Otherwise, since there is no distinction between the two cases regarding their equality or difference, why would there be an exclusion of connection with the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) but not an exclusion of connection with the object of inference (*anumeya*)?
If it is argued that this is because the latter has been established,
then for that very reason, it is said that due to contradiction, the coherence of a single sentence is unattainable.

Because it is only when there is a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) with that [proposition] that one can state that this [reason] has the mere counter-example (*vipakṣa*) as its object; and since that [unity] exists only when that [proposition] exists, a fault that is difficult to answer arises.
Nevertheless, even so, according to the Buddhist system, if one relies on verbal convention (*śābda-vyavahāra*), the conjunction (*samuccaya*) itself would not be established.
Intending to show that this subtle analysis has been employed in opposition [to the opponent's view], he says: "The exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*).
Although this principle is general, it has been introduced here as being restricted to a specific case for fear of digression. //5//
// Purity //
The phrase "bhāvapada" (the word for the state of being) is used because [it follows] "according to the indication and from the definition.
Between the two words "he states the definition" (*lakṣaṇam āha*), the particle *iti* is to be supplied.
Furthermore, the word *api* (also/even) in the phrase "here too" (*atrāpi*) is used because of the exhaustion of the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*).
One might object: "Let it simply be that 'the means of proof' (sādhana) is that by which something is proven;
and this meaning is possible in the case of cognition being an instrument, because it arises from a well-known similarity. To this, he says: "This very [point]..."
Similarity is not something distinct from the universal,
because if that which is non-dependent were to have another as its substratum, it would follow that it is a substance;
and even if it were not dependent on another, if it were manifested by two things that are inseparably connected (ayutasiddha), it would follow that it is inherence (samavāya).
Furthermore, manifestation residing in separate, established entities such as a cow or a gavaya is untenable;

for if it were manifested in what is separately established, it would follow that it is a non-entity (abhāva), and manifestation residing in an inseparably established whole and its parts is likewise untenable.

If [the universal] were eternal and had multiple substrata, it would follow that it is a genus (*jāti*); if it had only a single substratum, its continued existence without a substratum upon the destruction of that [substratum] would be untenable, and it would follow that there is no proof for its eternity.
For a universal is established as eternal because, even when one substratum is destroyed, it is recognized as being of that very same nature in another substratum.
But since this is not so, how is it to be known that [the universal] is eternal?

On the contrary, precisely because it has a single, non-eternal substratum, its own non-eternality is inferred; for if it were to reside eternally in a single [substratum], it would follow that it is merely a particular (viśeṣa) existing as a real entity in its own right.
Because that which exists would then incur the status of being a quality [of another],
and because there would follow the loss of the conventional usage of "similarity" regarding impermanent things;
furthermore, if the impermanent were to have multiple substrates, it would incur the status of being a substance possessing qualities.
Because if it were devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*), there would be the consequence of its being a quality itself;
because if it had a single substratum, there would be the consequence of its being an action (*karman*) as the independent cause of conjunction and disjunction;
whereas for that which is the opposite of this, there is the consequence of its being a quality (*guṇatva*).

Furthermore, there would be no conventional usage of similarity regarding qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karman*), because, lacking the status of being inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*), they cannot possess impermanent properties.

If such usage were possible through similarity with their substrata (*āśraya*), then it would be impossible for qualities and actions residing in dissimilar substrata to be subject to that conventional usage.

The meaning is that the investigation of the three causes is untenable; furthermore, the establishment of similarity (sādharmya-prasiddhi) should also be understood as occurring in the Sūtra by relying on a *karmadhāraya* compound.
The meaning is that [the means of knowledge] begins with the statement "from the word of a reliable person" and extends up to perception.

By stating that "the object to be made known [is known] by virtue of being denotable by the word *gavaya*," it is shown that the indicative sentence (*atideśavākya*) is used in conjunction with a name for which the convention has not yet been established.

Nevertheless, no justification is shown for abandoning the explanation of the word *sādhana* as an instrument (*karaṇa*-vyutpatti), since the word *prajñāpana* can likewise be derived in the sense of an instrument. Therefore...
He says: "For [the word] 'of the lump' (*piṇḍasya*).
By stating that one recognizes [an object] through a resemblance that is perceptible and is thereby made known by it, he intends that resemblance itself—when being cognized—is the cause.

And thus, because the terms "probandum" (*sādhya*) and "probans" (*sādhana*) would be in different grammatical cases (*vyadhikaraṇa*) with respect to that [resemblance], and since there is no other instrument (*karaṇa*), the terms "probandum" and "probans" would become meaningless.
If it were not an instrumental action (bhāvasādhana),
one should not say that cognition itself is the instrument,
because that which lacks an intermediate operation cannot function as an instrument.
Furthermore, because it would follow that even an incorrect cognition of similarity would be [valid],
for that too is indeed a cognition of similarity.
Nor should it be said that its cessation occurs through the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Since there is no occasion for following [another rule] once the desired result has been achieved by the very operation (*vṛtti*) of the words themselves,
that [following] also merely constitutes the operation of other words, thereby producing variety in the composition. Nevertheless,
because "cognition" (*prajñāna*) is the meaning of the word as it is commonly known, and not the act of making known (*prajñāpana*), he says "for this purpose."
The operation (*vyāpāra*) of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is its specific activity, colored by the result and occurring without mediation.

The intended meaning is that, in order to reveal that similarity (*sādṛśya*)—while being itself known—is the instrument (*karaṇa*), its operation, which is conducive to the result and whose purpose is not yet fulfilled elsewhere, has been demonstrated.
Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*):
it refers to the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*) and the literal meaning (*akṣarārtha*).
For a term that is itself being characterized cannot establish the definition, due to the faults of mutual dependence (*parasparāśrayatva*) or the impossibility of comprehension (*agati*).
Anticipating the objection that "surely the indicator [the second word] is also [necessary]," he states the intended meaning of employing the second term, beginning with "yadyapi" (even though).
[The opponent objects: "In that case, let there be only the first [word];
and this is not the Aśoka grove."
Because it is the very first [of the factors], it occurs first in the mind;
for it is not possible for it to be in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "means" (*sādhana*), which denotes the result (*phala*).
Well then, let that [word "pramiti"] also be derived as an instrument (*karaṇa*).
In this way, there would also be no need for the laborious construction of supplying the word "yataḥ" (from which).
This is indeed true;
however, the opponent removes the validity of the analogy precisely by means of the reason that it lacks a result.
Therefore, in order that this may be understood, the author indicated it by extracting and showing its result;
since this will become clear later on, the commentator has not demonstrated it here.
Anticipating the objection regarding a contradiction between the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika, he says: "by the author of the Vārttika.

It should be understood that the mention of a "third-case compound" (tṛtīyā-samāsa) is merely illustrative; the *karmadhāraya* compound, which is established by the sense of the context, has likewise not been rejected.
Because it is not contradictory;
for even in the *bahuvrīhi* compound "that which has a well-known similarity" (*prasiddha-sādharmya*), the meaning of a *karmadhāraya* is included.

Likewise, regarding the phrase "similarity with what is well-known" (*prasiddhena sādharmyam*), since a third-case *tatpuruṣa* is included there, the author says "for by the Commentator... in order to anticipate another objection concerning contradiction.
Since this meaning is not heard from the words of the commentary, he says:
"having set aside," for the purpose of explaining [the result] separately after the understanding of the convention.
He says this: "namely, the designation" (*samākhyā*).
Even so, what follows regarding the contradiction with the *Vārttika*?
To this he replies: "this very [point]" (*etadeva*).
To provide an answer to the doubt beginning with "Let this person practice," he sets forth what was stated in the Sūtra: "Because of the well-known similarity. This refers to the present context.

Regarding those who hold conflicting views concerning the result of comparison (*upamāna*), he states the resolution offered by the elder Naiyāyikas such as Jayanta and others, with some reservation: "Even though...
(*yadyapi*). The "act of naming" (*saṃjñākarma*) is the act of creating a name.
[The result] is either another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), namely verbal testimony (*śabda*), or the word-meaning (*śabdārtha*) functioning as a logical mark (*liṅga*).
In that regard, concerning the position of the indicative mark (*liṅga*):
"characterized" means made known.

The connection is as follows: the individual object (*piṇḍa*), being presented through the similarity to a cow understood from the word, can be cognized as distinguished from both homogeneous and heterogeneous classes.

In the case of the word, however, it is easy to understand that the individual object (*piṇḍa*), characterized by its similarity to a cow and apprehended from the word as qualified [by that similarity], can be understood as distinguished from both similar and dissimilar classes; for similarity, like qualities, actions, and so forth, serves to differentiate an object from those of the same and different classes.

Let it be granted for now that "the gavaya is denoted by the word 'gavaya' because it is similar to a cow. However, if one asks, "What exactly is this thing that is similar to a cow? the mind remains wavering, as it lacks the capacity to dispel such doubt. This very point has been demonstrated by the phrase beginning with "someone" (*kaścit*).
Regarding the word *tatra*:
if it is argued that, in that case, let there be a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭapratipatti*) from the sentence itself, he says "not" (*na ca*).
If it is argued that it will arise from mere perception (*pratyakṣamātra*), he says "not" (*na ca*).
By this, the combination of verbal testimony and perception is also refuted.
For would that be a combination of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or a combination of results (*phala*)?
Even regarding their status as valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), is it that there is a combination when they are both valid, or is it that validity belongs to the two combined?
It cannot be the first case.

Because if there were multiple fruits, their collective synthesis would be untenable, since that synthesis consists in their mutual predominance with respect to a single fruit. Nor is the second alternative possible.
Because speech and perception belong to different times;

for even if the word and its meaning are presented by means of memory, if the sense organ and so forth—which are connected to the body of the gavaya—do not present the similarity residing therein, the determination of the convention cannot be established.
Furthermore, if the result [of all means of knowledge] were to be subsumed under a single aggregate, then inference and verbal testimony would also result in being nothing but perception.
Is that fruit, then, entirely outside the scope of those means of valid cognition, or,
if it is included within them, what is its limit?
It is the association with the respective uncommon sense-faculties and so forth.
In that case, does the eye still have an operation at the time of the cognition of similarity and so forth when it is wide open?
No, because when that [cognition] exists, the [operation of the eye] is of no use.

"Or rather, for one who has perceived an individual *gavaya* qualified by its similarity to a cow and possesses the recollection of the sentence [heard previously], the determination of the convention (*samaya*) is possible through the power of subsequent reflection even at a later time.

This [view] attacks the position of the Elder Naiyāyikas— [introduced with] "Now, indeed..."— for previously, it was held that the sentence "as is a cow, so is this," even when accompanied by the word *gavaya* whose convention was not yet understood and which served merely for the sake of usage, was the cause for the comprehension of the relationship.
They say, however, that the counter-correlate is brought to mind either by the word itself or by an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).
But the moderns say that the presentation of the counter-correlate occurs just as before, while the determination of the convention (*samaya*) results from inference based on usage.

Thinking that the employment of a non-expressive [word] is not a constituent of a sentence, and that for one devoid of it, the result culminates in the mere indication of a related entity, they present this very usage as a proof, beginning with "For he who... By this alone,
the instability [of the opponent's position] is refuted.
If the relationship is indeed known, what is the purpose of the doubt?
Or, if it is not known, [you might argue] that it is stated thus because of the persistence of expectation; but even that is incorrect.
For a convention does not reside in specific particulars, because if that were the case, it would be impossible to grasp;
rather, having made some [general feature] its cause, it resides in the mere individuality (vyaktimātra) devoid of specific distinctions such as place and time.

If it is argued that the relation itself has not been cognized, then the cognition [of the related object] is indeed [unestablished] because the relatum has not been cognized; what, then, is this confusion of the knower?
And this is not the ultimate reality.
Because when a particular object (*piṇḍa*) qualified by similarity is introduced, the basis (*nimitta*) [of that application] is also necessarily introduced.
Otherwise, even if a particular object were introduced, if the basis were not introduced, words such as *manas* or *dharma* would not be class-words (*jātiśabda*),
or they would simply be non-denotative.
Because things of that same class are eternally beyond the reach of perception.
To this, the modern Naiyāyikas reply:
the determination of the relationship between the signified and the signifier is fivefold;
one is by direct specification (*śṛṅgagrāhikayā*), like [pointing out] Caitra and Maitra, when it is devoid of both a cause and a defining characteristic.

When there is no primary cause (nirnimitta) but an internal secondary characteristic (antarbhūtopalakṣaṇa), it is by way of etymological derivation (nirvacanikayā), as in the case of words such as "cook" (pācaka).

When there is indeed no primary cause but an external secondary characteristic (taṭasthopalakṣaṇa), it is by way of conventional designation (paribhāṣaṇikayā), as in the case of words such as "space" (ākāśa). When there is a primary cause and it is an external secondary characteristic, it is by way of such a mode [of reference], as in the case of "earth" (pṛthivī) and so forth.
Regarding the case where there is a specific cause, [the result follows] through a contraction of that cause, as in the case of heaven and so forth.

Since the first and second [alternatives] are impossible therein, and since the third mode has been set aside here because its application is already known, the fifth [alternative] takes the place of the fourth; thus he establishes the fourth, beginning with "Not, first of all... (*na tāvat*).
However, what will occur for one who is unaware of the linguistic usage of the word "gavaya" will be explained immediately thereafter;
thus it has been said.

The ultimate reality is the nature of the thing itself; therefore, the relation must be apprehended as existing only in the actual individual (piṇḍa), and not in a mere individual brought forward by the indication of similarity— this is the meaning.
Now, one might object that the cause (the basis for the cognition) has indeed been understood; to this he says: "And not...
That is to say, it is not the case that [the cow] is characterized by similarity to a cow, for "characterization" (upalakṣaṇa) means either inference or recollection.
Both [theories] are untenable when the relationship is unperceived;
the example of the staff and the man is given merely with reference to memory,
and this alone would be the extent of it.
That is to say:
either the word "gavaya" would cause one to understand the property of being a gavaya,
as in "a gavaya is like a cow."
The word-meaning may either lead to inference in the case of non-deviation, but in the case of deviation, it would merely cause recollection.
Now, one might object: similarity itself cannot be apprehended without including the distinction between the classes [of objects].
Because it consists of a multiplicity of universals— such as distinct primary substances, generalities, individuals, qualities, parts, and actions—
the words "similarity" (*sādṛśya*), "as-it-is" (*yathātathā*), and so forth, are themselves the means of conveying it.
Only the doubt regarding whether [the object] is well-known or not is left remaining.
In that regard, being an elephant and so forth is excluded by the word "cow";
however, being a buffalo and so forth is excluded because it is an inappropriate object, for otherwise, even if analogy were accepted, there would be no remedy.
Thus, the meaning of "this is similar to a cow" is: it belongs to a different genus from the cow,
yet possesses a great abundance of commonalities such as qualities and parts belonging to that [cow].
This too is not more convincing:
"the moon as in a mirror," "the face as the moon," and "the lotus as the face."

In the case of "This is a lotus because it is like a lotus," since similarity is apprehended in four ways, it is not possible to establish a restrictive rule regarding the primary or subordinate status [of the objects]; therefore, the cognition of similarity is logically established even without including that [fourfold classification] within itself.
If it is argued that "what was seen somewhere might be remembered here," let it be remembered for now that this is what is understood in this context.

But we do not say that it is understood here [in the case of the gavaya]. Therefore, let the individual object (piṇḍa) characterized by the universal "cow" be the very referent of the word "gavaya," just as the agent characterized by the act of cooking is the referent of the word "cook."
Or rather, is the similarity to a cow merely external (taṭastha),

such that the individual object (piṇḍa) as qualified by that [similarity]— like space (ākāśa)— would be its denotable meaning? Or, setting aside the qualification, is it rather the case that [the word denotes] that which possesses a specific universal (jāti-viśeṣa) qualified by the similarity to a cow, just as [the word "earth" denotes] that which possesses the earth-universal (pṛthivī-tva-jāti) qualified by odor?

The "lump" (piṇḍa) of this [object] will be described as follows: by setting aside the doubt regarding the other fixed alternatives, it is precisely a doubt resting upon three alternatives that— having been overwhelmed by the old Naiyāyikas— is called the "determination of the relation," keeping in mind the possibility of ascertainment that "one of these alternatives must necessarily be the referent of the word *gavaya*."

By this, the counter-argument regarding the mind (*manas*), mental phenomena (*dharma*), and so forth, is refuted; for even in those cases, one can infer a commonality of genus among the individual instances of the mind as they are inferred through reasoning, based on their possessing identical qualities and performing identical causal functions.
But if the universal is not apprehended, then even there the grasping of the convention is impossible;
or else, the universal is not the basis for its application.
This has been stated: "because it is not apprehended in any way whatsoever.

Even if the nature of the *gavaya* is understood, the reason—"because it is employed there [in that context]"—remains unestablished (*asiddha*) as long as the relationship between the name and the named object is not understood.

For, in the absence of another mode of application, it is impossible to understand that the usage has that [the *gavaya*] as its object without knowing the connection [between the word and its referent].
If that [relation] is already understood through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), what then remains to be established by inference?
For this very reason, even when the gavaya is perceived directly, there is no occasion for inference.
Nevertheless, once the relata are understood, the sentence itself—uttered in co-occurrence with the word "gavaya"—will bring about the cognition of the relation.
Furthermore, even for that which is not expressive, co-utterance will be functional, as in the case of the position regarding analogy (*upamāna*).
For, considering that even the sentence of transfer (*atideśavākya*) is indeed a sentence, the non-comprehension of the related term itself was established in order to refute it.
For this very reason, he says: "Or from what sentence?
For this same reason, the sentence's status as being intended to express pervasion (*vyāpti*) is also refuted, because the related term (*saṃbandhin*) is not cognized.

Nor is there an intention [of the speaker] regarding exclusion (*vyatireka*), because it is conditioned by the intention of the person establishing the convention (*saṃketayitṛ*) and because it is subject to counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*).
Although there is no deficiency in the case of analogy (upamāna) even in the absence of a reason for determination (*vinigamanā*),
since the relationship is ascertained at that time when both are denotable,
nevertheless, he analyzes the actual state of things— nevertheless.
The section beginning with "What [is the example]? and ending with "he permits that" concerns the story of the camel.
He refutes [the objection] with the words: "And the mention of 'similarity' (*sādharmya*)," etc.
Furthermore, the employment of the term as an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indicator) is for the purpose of hinting at internal subdivisions; by means of this, such is the interpretation of the Sūtra.
Comparison (*upamāna*) is the means of establishing what is to be established (*sādhya*) through similarity with something well-known (*prasiddha-sādharmya*).

That well-known property (*dharma*) is either common (*samāna*), being presented as a correlate (*pratiyogin*), or uncommon (*asamāna*). However, according to the *bahuvrīhi* interpretation, it is "of that which has a well-known property" (*prasiddha-dharman*).
The remainder is as before.

The view of the Jaran-Mīmāṃsaka, who asserts that the similarity of a cow residing in a gavaya is indeed perceptible, has been refuted. Anticipating the Śabara position, he refutes it with the words "of the cow" (gostham).
It is a common saying that [similarity] belonging to one genus resides in another genus.
Nevertheless, it has not been understood that what is delimited by a particular *gavaya* is also delimited by a particular *go*;
therefore, it will be argued that analogy (*upamāna*) applies there. To this, he says: "Therefore, just as... The intent is directed toward the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "But the application" (*prayogastu*), etc.:

here, the distinction from [other] means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) should be understood as the superimposition of the meaning of a sentence that stands in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a designation whose convention has not been established.
This is because the distinctions regarding both the object and the essential nature [of the cognition] are unestablished. //6//
// Purity //
In this regard, there are three types of misconception concerning sound: with respect to its validity, its divisions, and its definition.
Among these, the first alternative is refuted by the very fact of its contradiction with the statement itself;
for it is impossible to establish the intended meaning without accepting the authority of that [statement],
and if it were established, the authority of that [statement] would be proven precisely from that [establishment].
Distinction, however, is to be examined in the section on investigation; here it is treated only briefly.
Even the conventional usage of "distinction" arises solely from the connection with a differentiating property.
The definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is likewise [to be stated]. Therefore, that very [definition] must be analyzed.

With the intention that the introduction of the investigation (*parīkṣā*) is for the sake of those who might disagree on this point, [the author], having explained the introductory commentary (*saṅgati-bhāṣya*) as if it were already established, introduces the definition with the words "Now" (*atha*).
Regarding this, some maintain that "verbal testimony" (śabda) is the means for correctly experiencing what is beyond the senses by the power of convention;
here, moreover, the first term [of the definition] refers to inference,
while the second refers to fallacious verbal testimony.

By the third [word], determinate perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) is excluded; by the fourth, the recollection of word-meanings (*padārtha-smaraṇa*); and by the fifth, the agent and the object are excluded.

Others, however, considering that [the definition] would be over-extensive since it would apply even to motion (ceṣṭā), state that [the definition] is "while there is inherence in the nature of sound" (śabdatvasamavāye sati).
In this regard, the intention of the Prācīnas is as follows:
if activity were not a means of valid cognition,
there would be no occasion for it at all.
What is to be accomplished by the phrase "given the inherence of the nature of sound" (*śabdatva-samavāye sati*)?
If it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then since it would not be included among perception and the others, it would follow that a fifth means of valid cognition must be admitted.
Therefore, gesture (*ceṣṭā*) is actually included within verbal testimony (*śabda*) itself, because it functions through the force of convention (*samaya*).

However, the worldly linguistic usage of "word" (śabda) refers to sound alone, because that is the common practice, just as the usage of "knowledge" (jñāna) and "vision" (darśana) refers to visual cognition;
those [who hold this view] are also superficial observers.
For bodily movement is useful merely for recollecting the word that resides in one's intention, just like writing;
however, it is the word itself—ascended upon the recollection produced by the movement—that is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And because it produces a recollection of the object, its status as a means of valid cognition belongs exclusively to the word as its object.
Because the result of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*) is itself the means of valid cognition;
nor is memory its intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*).
Even if it were possible that a word, though understood, would not convey its meaning without the application of a desired [result], such a case might indeed occur.
And this is not the case.

If this is so, then the linguistic behavior of the mute and the deaf would be impossible; for such a person does not possess a recollection of the word from that gesture, since they have not grasped the convention between them.
If you say this:

For this very reason, with respect to that [person], due to the force of convention (*samaya*), there is indeed an incapacity of purposeful action (*ceṣṭā*) regarding the object, just as there is regarding the word. However, linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*)— through the apprehension of the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) of a restricted object by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)— is useful for determining the occasioning cause (*pravṛtti-nimitta*), even in the case of one who is mute, solely through the inference of intention (*abhiprāya*).
Just as in the case of an elephant or a horse, [the movement] arises from the striking of a whip or a goad;
why then, even when a convention has been established, could the movement itself not be the cause?
Because there is an absence of invariable concomitance (avinābhāva),
or even if it were to cause one to remember the meanings of the words,
it would still not be a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

For that [convention] is of two kinds, based on the distinction between the commencement of the convention: that which conforms to action (kṛtyanvayinī) and that which conforms to cognition (jñaptyanvayinī).
Among these, that which conforms to action prompts activity by causing one to remember the intention of the instigator.
But it does not establish anything as valid, like the sound of a conch shell;
therefore, it is indeed not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
However, that which follows from the cognition [of the object] regarding the factors of action (*kāraka*) has the meaning of the nominal stem (*pratipadikārtha*) as its primary referent.
In verbal actions, the meaning currently being expressed is primary;
thus, just as in the case of words such as "cow," "horse," or "man," once independent word-meanings have been recalled, there occurs a mutual syntactic connection between them.

If it is argued that—just as specific case-endings within a single word determine the recollection of specific grammatical functions (kārakas)—the restriction of the recollection of kārakas and so forth arises from specific parts of the action, or from specific contextual factors and the like, [we reply]: no, because there is an absence of specific parts of the action [that could serve as such indicators].
For we do not perceive any specific part of an action that indicates whether the cooking and so forth belongs to the past, future, or present.
Context and other such factors restrict words to specific objects,
but they do not cause them to function with respect to specific times of the agent.

If that were the case, then even in instances such as "the cow, the horse, the man, the elephant," one would have to infer the status of the object (*karmatva*) and so forth to arrive at the intended meaning.
For context and other such factors are not capable of implying specific *kārakas* and the like within a mere collection of actions.
However, there is no such rule that it must consist of a collection of words;
for if that were so, there would follow the absurdity of the uselessness of the employment of case-endings that express specific time, number, and grammatical relations (kāraka).
How, then, do specific linguistic conventions arise from that?

[They arise] from either doubt or a semblance of knowledge (*pratibhā*) when no distinction is perceived regarding an object at a distance that possesses common characteristics, as in the case of one seeking a post.
Therefore, in both cases, purposeful activity (*ceṣṭā*) is not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, for whom should the inclusion or exclusion from among the four [means of valid cognition] be considered?

This was indicated by the author of the Sūtras—who, while subsuming under tradition (*aitihya*) and the rest those whose authority is plausible, also mentioned as being included within worldly practice (*sāṃvyavahārika*) gestures, corrupt forms, scripts, sounds, and parts of words—but those of dull intellect do not grasp it; thus, [this is stated] out of compassion for them.
While explaining the definition itself, he brings forth a certain point.
It is either the knowledge of the sentence or the knowledge of its meaning.
A sentence is a collection of words possessing expectancy, semantic competency, and contiguity.
Its "knowledge" means the cognition of it; that is the sense.
As has been heard previously, [the word] is primary in what follows;
however, even there, the sentence alone is primary because it is unique, like the sense organs and so forth.
However, this principle applies to all cases when distinguishing between degrees of proximity;
for the cognition of abandonment and so forth is characterized by reflective discernment (*parāmarśa*),
whereas the other [cognition] is the result of inference.

Thus, by excluding those words that lack expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), compatibility (*yogyatā*), and proximity (*āsatti*), gestures (*iṣṭā*) and the like are also excluded; this constitutes the exclusion of heterogeneous elements (*vijātīyavyudāsa*).

Since expectancy and the other factors are mediated through their own referents (*svārtha*), it follows that the grasping of the conventional relation (*saṃgati*), the recollection of the words, the recollection of their meanings, the consideration of compatibility (*yogyatā*), and the context (*prakaraṇa*) have been mentioned.
It is with this very intention that it was stated: "But the recollection of word-meanings, etc."
Thus, by this [definition], there is the exclusion of perception and other means of knowledge belonging to the same class;
and by the inclusion of the term "reliable" (āpta), the words of those who are unreliable are refuted—thereby the attainment of the general definition [of verbal testimony].

Now, one might object: "Is this not the meaning of the word *upadeśa*? Moreover, taken literally, it suffers from the fault of being too narrow (*avyāpakatā*), as it would not include established facts (*siddhārtha*) and so forth. To this he says: "Even though... (yadyapi).
He further states: "Even though... (yadyapi ca), meaning that it does not merely fail to include established facts, but fails to include anything pertaining to what is to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
Now, since both an injunction (*vidhi*) and a command (*ājñā*) or a request (*adhyeṣaṇā*) function as motivators (*pravartaka*), what is the difference between them?

Since these two are not included under the category of "instruction" (upadeśa), their dissimilarity to "command" (vidhi) was established; then, their dissimilarity even to those two [command and entreaty] was stated by the words "for those two...
[etc.]. One might ask: "Should an effort still be made to include them within command and entreaty?
He says "no," with the words "nevertheless... [etc.].
This is the intention:
although those two could also be included by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by inserting the term "agent" (*prayoktṛ*) in the subsequent position,
nevertheless, there is no loss of purpose for us even if they are not so included.
Because this treatise begins by defining a specific type of word whose object is the means to heaven and liberation, and because the scripture proceeds under that specific jurisdiction,
the general definition was explained first in that very manner, since a specific definition cannot be introduced without a general one having been established.
And he will state:

In the context of refuting Dignāga, having set aside the word *para* (other), the understanding of the sentence-meaning as "one who possesses a purpose" alone is the result; and this is precisely the utility of employing technical (*lākṣaṇika*) terminology: that both characteristics are obtained.
Furthermore, the purpose must be understood as residing in the object, being unique, and graspable.
However, the capacity of a word to convey its own meaning is common [to both parties];
and that belongs to the other person alone.
Therefore, with respect to that, the qualification "of another" would be redundant.

Now, one might object: "If the Upaniṣads are indeed purposeful, they must certainly establish some meaning and thereby incite someone toward action, since the existence of a purpose is invariably marked by such activity. If they do not incite anyone toward action, how can they possess a purpose for others? For the absence of a purpose is marked by the lack of activity. To this, he says: "Even though... (yadyapi).
In the passage beginning with "not anywhere," the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis.
Regarding the non-authoritativeness of the Buddha, the Bull among Sages, and others: the *kāraka* (causal) reason is their being caused by illusion and delusion;
the *jñāpaka* (indicative) reason, however, is their teaching of all phenomena as momentary, selfless, and so forth, which contradicts valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Thinking that what has been heard [in the commentary] is not comprehensive, he says: "By a very firm [means of knowledge].
A very firm means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is a valid cognition (*pramā*) whose possibility of error has been entirely dispelled;
thus, it is "ascertained," meaning it has been made its object.
This is not intended with reference to the pervasion of permanence and impermanence.
But surely, even for God, authorship exists only as one who presides over the causes; and since,
through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the capacity of the locations, articulatory organs, and so forth, to produce the phonemes is understood,
His authorship of the scripture would not exist in the absence of presiding over them.
And since the occurrence of places of articulation (sthāna), effort (karaṇa), and so forth is not possible without a body—

because those [places] consist of the palate and other such parts, as well as the state of being open and so on— the author, holding this intention, raises an objection with the words "even so" (tathāpi).
The commentary answers this by saying: "Therefore, he says, 'the teacher'."
We do not deny that the body is an instrument for this Blessed One, whose presence or absence follows the specific requirements of his task—

just as dyads and so forth are required for the production of triads and so on— since the employment of such a body is also accepted for the accomplishment of effects that follow the positive and negative concomitance of the body.
However, it is not accepted as his abode, nor as the means for sustaining his agency, nor as all-pervasive, because he lacks experience (bhoga).

The explanation provided by one who intends [to argue] that agency is eternal, because the effect has an unconditional relationship with the agent, and because the body is non-deviant, is as follows: "the place and the instrument," etc.
In that case, from what means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) can such a trustworthy person (āpta) be ascertained,
given that the mental states of others are not perceptible (apratyakṣa), and since bodily and vocal activities are preceded by cognition?
