Anticipating the objection that [the Veda] might be possible otherwise, the author, while explaining the intent of the Bhāṣya with the words "for even the Mlecchas," also briefly shows the means for its ascertainment: "those who are devoid of the perception of a cause."
This is the intended meaning:
for there are two kinds of persons, namely the non-omniscient and the omniscient.

Regarding the former, once the absence of passion, hatred, and delusion is established by the very same means of valid cognition that proves his existence, his status as a non-authoritative person (*anāpta*) is refuted.

Furthermore, regarding the Teacher, his knowledge, intention, effort, the vocal organs (*sthāna*), the articulatory points (*karaṇa*), and their proficiency are indeed ascertained by mere instruction alone;
thus, there is no dispute among anyone on these points.
However, as for his knowledge, it may be either true or false.
A doubt remains as to whether the speaker's intention might be a desire to explain, or a desire to deceive;

even in that case, when one has reached a state of familiarity and there is a general certainty that "this is the meaning intended by him," there indeed arises a certainty regarding the truthfulness of that cognition.

This is just as travelers, having reached a state of familiarity with a forest, form the certainty: "This is the forest of these Mlecchas; therefore, these people here know the distinction between the right and wrong paths."
Furthermore, the desire to deceive is pervaded by the perception of a reason; that [deception] would exist only when a reason is present.
And that reason is of two kinds:
either benefit to oneself or benefit to another.
In that regard, first of all, when travelers set out on a wrong path, there is no benefit to the barbarians and others,
because [the travelers] have already been taken hold of by themselves, and because there is nothing further to be done for the mere body, or if there were, it would not be abandoned.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, for those who are not insane do not inflict harm upon one who has done them no wrong.
Nor is the mere harming of others the goal of human endeavor; if that were so, everyone would harm everyone else—thus even the desire to deceive is refuted.

However, regarding an object that has not yet reached the stage of repeated practice, the cessation of delusion and the desire to deceive occurs either through the efficacy of the initial activity or through corroboration by another means of valid cognition.

The meaning of the word "api" (even) is this: since even *mlecchas* become authoritative when they come within the scope of one's cognition, what doubt can there be regarding the ascertainment of reality by those of great intelligence and by the noble ones (*āryas*)?
By this [it is shown that] whatever is not ascertained in a certain form...
That [person] is not designated as such by that [reason], just as a street person is not [designated] as omniscient;
nor is the intended person recognized as authoritative. Thus, it has been stated that the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).
The definition of an authoritative person (*āpta*) as provided by others is not all-encompassing,
because [the qualities] as they have been heard do not exist for both Aryans and Mlecchas.
The meaning is that if one were to add further qualifications, then one would necessarily accept our own definition.
This question arises from one who is mistaken, and such error is rooted in fallacious means of valid cognition (pramāṇābhāsa).
Therefore, he says: "It exists."
Anticipating the charge of partial unestablishedness (*bhāgāsiddhatā*), he says: "In this case, as much as... Now, one might object:
"Is this not the fallacy of *prakaraṇasama* (neutralization), which consists in employing a different argument independently without refuting the opponent's argument?
Furthermore, if there is a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*), how will the perceptibility of heaven and so forth ever be established? To this, he replies: "But in that which is born of yoga..."
Because there is no effect in the absence of a cause, there is no valid cognition when the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is absent;
the external mind is dependent upon its objects as described for the eye and other senses.
Thus, since these reasons are at first sight indeed counterbalanced (satpratipakṣa), he says: "But for us, [the reason] is sound."
This is the intended meaning:
for it is observed that even when the external senses have ceased their activity, there occurs in dreams a direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of objects situated in distant places and times.
Nor should it be said that this is merely a vivid memory (*smṛti*).
For even regarding the distinction between memory and experience, the Witness need not be questioned.
What then? This matter is self-evident through the cognition "I remember this" and "I experience this.
Nor is the character of being an experience superimposed upon it, because there is no sublation.
Because there is no mention of its being a memory, and because there is the appearance of something unperceived, such as the cutting off of one's own head.
If it is argued that "this is a distortion of memory," does this mean it is a distortion regarding the object of memory?
In that case, we agree.
Alternatively, if the meaning is that this error consists in the attribution of the status of "experience" to memory itself,
then that has already been refuted.

Nor is this even possible; for an object that has become the object of a determinative cognition (*vyavasāya*) in one form cannot be subsequently determined (*anuvyavasīyate*) by another cognition as a delimiting factor (*jñānāvacchedakatayā*) in a different form.
And thus, when a memory arises such as "that jar," for one who is erring, there would occur the thought: "I am experiencing that jar."
But the form of the memory "this is not that pot" or "this is not a pot" is not [of that nature];
therefore, this must be accepted as being simply an experience.
Moreover, there is truth in some dream-experiences as well, due to their correspondence with reality; and even if that [correspondence] occurs by chance (*kākatālīya*), it is not without a cause,
for otherwise it would follow that all dream-cognitions possess such [truth].
And here, the cause is indeed *dharma* itself;
and like that born of action (*karmaja*), it is also to be understood as born of yoga (*yogaja*),
because action and the method of yoga share the same security and outcome.

Therefore, the experience of yogis is valid cognition because it is born of dharma; it is the result of perception because it is a direct, manifest cognition. However, that which arises from a cultivation (*bhāvanā*) that does not produce dharma is not valid cognition; such is the distinction.
Thus, it is well said that the reason "because of being devoid of that causal complex" is unestablished (*asiddha*).
In our case, however, the particle *ca* is used in the sense of *anvācaya* (conjunction with an additional element), meaning "and [he is] a member of the assembly" and "and [he is] many.

Even though, for us, the establishment of an intermediate omniscient being does not follow from the establishment of the supreme omniscient one, and thus there is no loss of the subject at hand; nevertheless, since there is evidence for his existence as well, he too does not deserve to be neglected.

In this context, Dignāga refuted the term "instruction" (*upadeśa*) by analyzing it according to whether it functions as a *bhāva-sādhana* (an action-noun) or a *karma-sādhana* (an object-noun); but why was the position that it functions as a *karaṇa-sādhana* (an instrument-noun)—which we ourselves accept—neglected? To this he replies:
for direct connection with the object belongs to perception alone, whereas indirect connection belongs to inference.

The meaning is that he considers the theory of the instrumental derivation (*karaṇavyutpatti*) to be impossible: for if this verbal cognition were directly connected to the object, it would follow that it is perception;
if the connection were indirect, it would result in its being inference;
and if there were no connection at all, it would simply lack validity. Thus, [the definition] is untenable.

In this context, according to the view that the suffix -tva has an abstract (bhāva) sense, the result of the word is either the ascertainment of the speaker's reliability or, by means of that, the ascertainment of the meaning of the sentence.
But one might object: for those who have been ascertained as reliable, what else remains that would constitute non-contradiction?
To the question "How is this to be ascertained?", he says: "The meaning is 'of the teachers and the seers'."
The construction of the words is as follows: "perceptuality" (*pratyakṣatva*) is the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of an object.
By this, the meaning is as follows:
authoritative instruction (*āptopadeśa*), while producing certainty regarding that very authority...

He says "this" (imam) to refute both [positions]: that verbal testimony (*śabda*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or else that, having established certainty regarding a trustworthy person (*āpta*), it produces certainty regarding the meaning of a sentence as its companion.

He raises the second position—that [compassion] is accomplished through action—by means of inference, based on [the reasons] such as being devoid of the observation of causes for the practice of compassion.
In this case as well, the result of the word is either the certainty of attaining the object indicated, or, by means of that, the certainty of the reality of the object.
Regarding these, he first demonstrates the former with the words "because" (*yasmāt*).
He shows the second [point] with the words "and thus" (*evam ca*).
It means that the object being taught has been attained, or because it has been ascertained as having been attained.
Alternatively, the construction of the sūtra is "ascertained as suchness";
he says "he refutes" because he refutes both [positions].
[Objection: But surely, the reality of an object being ascertained through the attainment of that object is ascertained precisely by means of a logical mark (*liṅga*).
So how can it be said [in the verse] "by perception" (*pratyakṣeṇa*)? To this he replies: "For by attainment... (*āptyā hi*).

He stated that the ascertainment of the reality of the object is also [effected] by perception in order to show that even when there is an ascertainment of attainment, the word has no further function.
The meaning is that it is because he is the fundamental basis.
Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that an object apprehended through verbal testimony is sometimes understood even by means of inference? To this, it was said: "mostly" (*prāyeṇa*).

Furthermore, although it would have been appropriate to raise the doubt as to whether the result—the determination of the validity of the word—is the same for both positions (the two views) which prioritize respectively the fact of being spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*) and the efficacy of its application (*pravṛtti-sāmarthya*), such a doubt was not raised;
for the determination of the object and the determination of its reality are inseparable from the determination of validity.

[The phrase] "by one who thinks that [the latter] is included within those two" means that this very [cognition] is neither accompanied by the state of being a reliable person (*āptatva*) nor accompanied by the certainty of the state of being a reliable person.
By means of attainment;
that is to say, by means of the certainty of attainment.

"Indeed, we do not perceive any distinction between what is accepted [as authoritative] and those positions that are not accepted; therefore, he says: 'This is what is meant'. [The phrase] "not caused by trustworthiness" means not caused by the certainty of trustworthiness. "Non-contradiction" means the certainty of non-contradiction.

By this sūtra, it is demonstrated by way of the meaning of scripture (*āgama-artha*) and by way of the fruit of scripture (*āgama-phala*). Nor should it be understood as the suchness of the object (*artha-tathātva*) or the ascertainment of the suchness of the object;
rather, two modes have been illustrated as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).
However, as it was explained in the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), so should it be understood here as well.
To the question, "What then is its fruit? he says: "But rather... (kiṃ tu).
The meaning is: that cognition which is made the object by this reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) characterized by such a description.

If this is so, then what is the use of ascertaining that [the scripture] was spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*)? To this he says: "And reliability" (*āptatvaṃ ca*). The meaning is: "and the fact of being spoken by a reliable person. Now, one might object: validity (*prāmāṇya*) is the non-deviation from the object.

Indeed, how could that [means of knowledge] possibly cause one to understand the object without first having made the object understood? Consequently, since the ascertainment of the object follows from its being the word of a reliable person (āpta), he says: "And not because... The word "the object of cognition" (*prameya*) implies "independently."
However, its manifestation as a delimiting factor (avacchedakatayā) is indeed admitted,
by means of the mind itself;
this refers to the jar.
Thus, this is the summary:
validity consists in being a teacher of the actual state of affairs; that very quality would not belong to a word that does not point toward its object of cognition.
Likewise, what could be ascertained by the reason of being "spoken by one who is not authoritative"?
And in that case, how could even the object manifest itself as having a delimiting function (*avacchedakatva*)?
Therefore, just as perception is produced by unimpaired sense faculties abiding in their mere state of existence, [so too must the word be understood].

Just as [a cognition] is determined to be valid by means of the absence of defects in its birth, so too is verbal testimony produced as a means of valid knowledge by a trustworthy person who exists merely by virtue of being existent;

however, it is determined to be such [i.e., valid] by a teacher whose trustworthiness has been known. Thus, like perception, its establishment regarding its own object consists in the fact that it would lead to the inference of mere cognition.
The ellipsis is "even though it is [already] understood, it is as if it were not understood."
This is the intended meaning:
there is no dispute that a determination of a specific meaning indeed arises from a sentence;
nor, however, is this [determination] inferential (laiḍgika).
Because mere speech is inconclusive, and because the quality of being spoken by a reliable person (*āptoktatva*) has already been proven unestablished; furthermore,
even if speech were taken as a logical mark (*liṅga*), there would be no probandum (*sādhya*) whatsoever.
For instance, identity with the object and reaching it are not possible;
nor is origination from the object, because even the words of authoritative persons regarding past and future objects do not originate from those objects, even indirectly.
Therefore, the meaningfulness of words consists solely in their capacity to indicate an object;
nor can that very capacity be inferred, for you do not admit its existence as something independent.
Or, if it were admitted [that the mark is known], the dispute would be resolved;
nor is it the case that the mark's very production of inferential knowledge regarding itself is what is to be inferred, because that [inferential knowledge] has another mark as its object.
Therefore, in the position where the mark is mere speech, one should cite as an example: "Whatever is speech is preceded by cognition.

For cognition arises by delineating something [as its object]; thus, by its very nature, it acquires only that which is delineated, yet even therein there is no distinction between what is real and what is unreal.
But there is no further differentiation of types;
therefore, it is well said that [the mark] should lead to the inference of mere cognition.
To the question, "What follows if this is so?", he says: "And thus" (*tathā ca*).
Even though [the nature of things] is established through both linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) and experience (*anubhava*), there would be no conformity [to that reality];
the meaning is that it would follow that the effort expended in learning [the conventions] would be futile.

[Objection: But surely the specific nature of the object will be established by the very specific nature of the cognition; to this he says: "And not... [The object] must be established by means of cognition, yet there exists no specific feature whatsoever in that [cognition], such as a form imparted by the object and so forth.

Even if it possesses a form, since that [cognition] does not arise from the object when its domain is the past, the future, and so forth, one must state that the distinction lies precisely in the object being that which is to be delineated. If that [distinction] is already included within the establishment of cognition itself, what else remains for it to be proven?
If it is not included therein, then again, the meaning is that cognition remains exactly undifferentiated.
It might be argued as follows:
let the object be established from the very beginning as the delimitor for the establishment of that cognition,
even though [your] mere statement merely alludes to a specific object.
Although this deviates from the rule that [verbal cognition] must be preceded by knowledge,

there nevertheless exists a necessary rule: whatever specific collection of words causes a particular set of word-meanings to be remembered, that [collection] is preceded by a knowledge of their mutual relation (*saṃsarga*).
If it is argued that there is thus a utility for grasping the conventional relation (*samaya*) as well—[we reply:
no, because of the deviation [of this rule] in cases such as the series of words "cow," "horse," and "man.
If it is argued that there is no deviation when [the words] are situated in the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), [we reply:]...
This relationship of qualifier and qualified does not exist by way of their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), because words are mutually independent;
nor does it exist by way of their referents (*artha*).
Because that [relation] is not apprehended;
or, if it were apprehended, what other relation among the word-meanings would there be, which is intended to be inferred as the delimiting factor of the cognition?

If it is argued that there is no deviation [from the rule] because of the qualification "provided there is expectancy and so forth," then what is this expectancy? It is certainly not non-separation (avinābhāva), whether in terms of its own nature or in terms of its meaning.
For even in its absence,
there is comprehension of the meaning of the sentence;
and even when it is present, there is no such comprehension.
If it is argued that "expectancy" (*ākāṅkṣā*) consists in the non-termination [of a sentence] until the meaning of the sentence has been communicated,

then the intended meaning of the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: "That collection of words which communicates a specific sentence-meaning must be preceded by a cognition of the connection between the meanings recalled by those words."

And so, concluding that one who desires the establishment of a specific reason (*hetu*) for the sake of establishing a specific probandum (*sādhya*) must already seek the cognition of the specific meaning of the sentence from the sentence itself even beforehand, he says: "Therefore... (*tasmāt*).

This might be so; however, if that which is unrelated were to illuminate [an object], there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). To this he says: "And not... Now, it may be argued: it is not the case that something is a signifier merely because of a connection, for that would lead to over-extension; rather, it must be an inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*). And since such a relation does not exist between a word and its object, he says: "Nor is it through non-separation..."
As for what was stated here—
that the eye also illuminates form precisely because it is an effect of form— that is incorrect.
For if it were to indicate that [object] solely because it was produced by it,
then it would indicate taste and other qualities just as it does color; or else, it would have to depend upon the cognition of its non-existence in the absence [of the object].
For this is not the power of inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) that it should cause cognition by its mere existence alone;

for if that were the case, fire would be cognized from smoke as well, even when it exists merely as a presence, just as it is from the eye. Furthermore, an object is manifested either at the same time as the cognition, or...
Or it is the immediately preceding moment;
and therefore, there is no birth from the eye itself,

but rather this acquisition of a distinct nature arises solely from its own causes— namely, that which, though non-self and not a cause, [functions as such] despite the lack of distinction in being a cause.

Or, if it is argued that even form itself, while being unknown, manifests [itself], and thus its existence is established solely by the force of observing the effect characterized by the apprehension of form— since that [apprehension] cannot be denied—
then, for whatever thing there is no connection (pratibandha) with respect to something else...

"It has no validity there, just as a donkey that is unconnected to fire [has no validity regarding it]"; thus, you yourself have made the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
What is there for us to say here?
What, then, is the basis for the conventional usage of valid cognition regarding words, which is the same basis as that for the eyes and other sense organs?
If it is asked, "What is the basis in that very case? [the answer follows].
This is great erudition that there is still doubt even regarding the established *mātṛkā*.
For everyone, even a child, says that the conventional usage of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) everywhere is based on the production of an experience of the actual object;
by that very logic, the same applies to the word as well.
The distinction between intrinsic natures is established as having arisen from their own causes,
because each respective thread of conventional designation conveys its specific meaning;
nevertheless, since linguistic convention depends upon persons, why does this person employ only those words that are conventional for worldly transaction?
If it is argued that doubt does not cease because one wonders whether he himself now establishes the convention for distinct objects— no,
for this is impossible in either case.
For if he were the communicator [of the convention], why would he utter words whose conventions have been deposited solely within the secret cave of his own heart?
For he certainly knows that these proponents are not unaware of the conventions [of language].
Now, even if he is a deceiver, what is the use of establishing another convention,
since deception is possible through well-known conventions alone?

For even where transactions are conducted by means of secret conventions, the convention need not be concealed from the person being instructed; rather, it is to be kept secret from those who are untrustworthy. Keeping this in mind, he says: "Therefore... (7).
It is not twofold, because its purpose is either seen or unseen. (1.1.8)
// Purity //
The words of the commentary are transparent, pure by nature, exceedingly weighty,
difficult to grasp, difficult to restrain, difficult to hold onto, and difficult to conceive—
like clear droplets of mercury.
Indeed, those who are under their control—verily, the entire world is under their control. //8//
The *Pramāṇanibandha* is completed.
Thus ends the section on the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
// The Chapter on the Objects of Cognition //
// Purity //

Now, one might object: "If it is indeed the object of knowledge (*prameya*) that the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) desires to understand, why was the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) mentioned first, bypassing that? To this he says: "And that... [referring to the statement *tacceti*]. Then, one might ask: "Since the means of knowledge have now been stated, let them be examined; what is the use of the definition of the object of knowledge (*prameya-lakṣaṇa*)? To this he says: "And the definition... [referring to the statement *lakṣaṇaṃ ca*].

"In that case, let only the definition of the object of knowledge (prameya) be stated; what is the use of the definitions of perception and the other means of valid cognition? To this he replies: "And not... [na ca]. Now, one might object: surely the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) should be stated first of all.
That the latter depends upon the former has already been established previously.
Now, however, there arises the inquiry as to which [topic] among the fifteen should be stated first.
Furthermore, when considering the logical connection (*saṃgati*) of what is to be stated, it follows that doubt and the other [factors] should not be mentioned at all, since they are of no utility.
From where does the rivalry regarding priority and posteriority arise? To this he says: "And because it is unexamined.
By demonstrating the utility of doubt and the other [categories] through this, their necessity for discussion has been shown.
This is due to this specific distinction within the section on the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The collective meaning is that there is an omission of the sections on doubt and so forth, and an addition of the section on the objects of cognition (prameya).
To the objection, "In that case, let the definition of the objects of cognition be commenced; what is the use of this superfluous division? he says: "Regarding that, here... (tadiha).
The state of being inseparable from the object of cognition (*prameya*) means having the object of cognition as its objective support and result.
The question posed by the author of the Bhāṣya—“What is that collection of objects?”—is twofold:
“What is its definition, and how many kinds are there?”
In this context, because a specific definition cannot be introduced without a general definition— just as in the case of "division"—
there is no answer in the second reading of the Sūtra;
however, in the first, the intention of the Bhāṣya is that it is provided by means of an etymological explanation of the word.
In this context, it has been shown by the phrase "in order to introduce the aphorism on the enumeration of divisions" that the meaning of the second question [is addressed];
whereas by the phrase "but the first [object of knowledge] remains unestablished even now as a specific object of cognition," it is shown that the question is for the sake of that [first object].
Therein, the author of the Vārttika, having taken up the general definition indicated by the word "tu" (but), states that the question pertains to the classification [of objects of knowledge].
In this regard, the author of the Vārttika, taking up the general definition indicated by the word "tu" (but), poses a question concerning its classification, stating: "And that is the particular."
"Now, if this alone is the meaning of the Sūtra, it follows that the meaning of this Sūtra is merely a classification;
and thus, the specific point intended [by the author] would not be obtained from the Sūtra.
Furthermore, such a classification of mere objects of knowledge (prameya) would be both useless and untrue. To this, he says: "Of those... (yeṣām).

The meaning of this sūtra—and by extension, the meaning of the Vārttika—is that its division [of pramāṇas] applies only to those objects of knowledge (*prameya*) specifically characterized as being relevant to the subject at hand.
By the words "of which" (*yeṣām*) and so forth, two definitions are given in their respective order; furthermore, the particle *na* is to be construed with the word *tattva*.
And the word "directly" (sākṣāt) is to be supplied [to the verse].
Liberation (apavarga) is the cessation of false knowledge,
because it is the first of those [stages].
Saṃsāra consists of attachment and aversion, because it is a part of that;
the mention of "atoms" is an illustration.
Therefore, it is bodiless and devoid of sense organs, [applying] to dyads and so forth which consist of those objects, as well as to their qualities and actions.

Now, if the resolution is that when directions and so forth are already expressed, they are [nonetheless] implied by the sense, then one must also justify what purpose there is in expressing them; therefore, he says: "It is merely a display of skill. (9)
// Purity //

But is it not the case that direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the self (*ātman*), since even our opponents accept the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) "I"?
Nor is this [construction] devoid of a real object (*avastuka*) or one whose object is doubtful (*saṃdigdhavastuka*).
Because it is not verbal and because it is not subject to refutation;
nor is it inferential,
since it arises as one's own cognition even for one who has not inferred a logical mark (*liṅga*).
Nor is this [cognition] memory, because recollection is impossible regarding that which has not been experienced.
Furthermore, it is not tenable to claim that this objectless conceptual construction is beginningless due to the power of beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
For it is equally easy to say this regarding conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) such as "blue" and so forth;
since they occur only occasionally, the postulation of a real entity (*vastu*) in those cases is identical here as well.
Furthermore, it is not tenable to claim that there is a state of reality (*vastusthiti*) because of the establishment of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) or the proof of the authority of the Sūtras.
Because even the certainty regarding the stability of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) can be subverted by taking recourse to latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
for this very reason the argument that "it proceeds from another means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇāntara*) is also refuted.
Therefore, setting aside the doctrine of latent impressions alone, some adventitious cause must also be stated.
And is that [the object] either the words "authoritative" and "unauthoritative," or the sign and its semblance, or direct perception and its semblance?
In this regard, just as the conceptualization of blue ultimately takes recourse in the last of the aforementioned modes due to the absence of the first two,
so too does the conceptualization "I am."
In this regard,
when [the conceptual cognition] arises immediately following a direct perception, it possesses a real object directly;
however, when it appears as that [perceived object], its possession of a real object is due to the root [perception] through a mediated succession.
Thus,

it is not the case that [the object] is rootless merely because external perception has ceased, for that would entail the consequence that even mental conceptualization (*buddhi-vikalpa*) is rootless.
In that case, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is the basis, and here too it is mental cognition (*mānasa*); thus, there is no difference whatsoever.
Therefore, he says "I" (*aham*) to address the question: how can the commentary be a refutation of perception with respect to the self?

Although this [notion of self] has a real object (savastuka), nevertheless, because it is grammatically co-referential with the conditions of the body, it might also be thought that its object is precisely those [conditions].

Therefore, it cannot be established as a real entity distinct from them for as long as a self separate from the body and so forth is not proven by another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); such is the meaning.
This is what was stated by the word "suddenly" (drāk).
"Like the cognition of a jar, etc. is a negative example (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*).

For just as the cognition of a jar, etc., because it is not in the same locus as the notion of the body and so forth, can immediately be established as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to an object distinct from that [body], [so too is the case here].
The meaning is that it is not so.
Now, even if it is not [established] all at once,
it will nonetheless be proven by means of the process of investigation; for instance:

Since the notion of "I" would otherwise entail over-extension by taking as its object the body, the intellect, or their collection regardless of any specific relation, it must be said that this notion of "I" refers to the body and so forth only when they are related to oneself.
In that regard, one must consider what constitutes "one's own" apart from the self.
For all entities, being non-different [from the self] is what constitutes "belonging to oneself."

And so, when that [object] is experienced by that very [subject], then because the perceiver is non-different from the object of perception, there would be the notion "I. If it is argued that for this very reason, jars and the like never have a non-different experiencer and thus never become the locus of the "I," then,
in that case, even in your own view, this cognition "I" must be merely of the nature of a superimposition upon the body and so forth.
Because the cognizer is [then] something other [than the cognition].
If it is argued that [the self] is primary in relation to the intellect (*buddhi*), we say no;

for while that [intellect] is experienced as an action, there is an experience of its agent as distinct from it, namely "I know," just as in the case of "I cut. Thus, just like the form of the object to be cognized—such as blue—the form of the cognizer is also [established] solely through this very perception. This is the Self.
If it is argued that it appears in such a way, then—
since it shares the same status as the form of the object to be cognized— the form of the cognizer is also established, which is exactly what we desire.
If it is argued that it consists merely of its own material cause, we say no.
For if that [object] were to appear, it would follow that the form of the object residing therein would also necessarily appear;
since a substratum cannot be perceived in the absence of its form.
This stream of consciousness, which is the cognizer, is indeed distinct from the stream of the active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
If it is argued that they call it the *ālayavijñāna*,
then in that case, an additional cognizer— beginningless and endless, and the substratum (*upādāna*) of the active cognitions (*pravṛttivijñāna*)— is established.
Is that [cognizer] of the nature of a continuous stream of cognition?

The consideration remains as to whether [the self] has a nature contrary to that; and since the arena for such a consideration is the refutation of momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅgabhaṅga), he says "by others" (para-).
This means [the argument] is more firmly established and focused on specific particulars.
Together with memory, there is the state of having a single object for both preceding and succeeding cognitions, which constitutes the domain of verbalizable knowledge.

Through a single subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), there may occur this synthesis— or recognition— of the prior experience, its effect (the memory), and the experience that is the effect of that memory.
Or is it the restriction to a single continuum between cause and effect and their specific qualities?
In the first case, recognition is unestablished in reality and contradicted by mere appearance.
The [reason] is not distinct [from the fallacy of] inconclusiveness (anaikāntika);
and even in the second case, contradiction (virodha) itself is established—thus it is refuted.
He says this with the words: "By this... (tadanena).

In this regard, when the opponent has put forward the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) as the basis for recognition, is it intended to raise a doubt regarding its exclusion from the heterologous class (*vipakṣa*) by way of being a limiting condition (*upādhi*),
or rather to establish the systematic arrangement of recognition within one's own system?
The underlying intention is that the very proof of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) serves as the sublation (*bādhana*) of recognition.

In this context, having taken "recognition" (*pratyabhijñāna*) to mean "reconnection" (*pratisandhāna*), and desiring to remove the defining characteristic of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), [the opponent] refutes the mutual pervasion (*vyāpti*) between causal relation and reconnection with the words "for it is not the case that... and so forth.
Again, the Buddhist [speaks].

For we do not claim that the mere relation of cause and effect is the basis for recognition; rather, it is [the relation] qualified by similarity. Thus he raises the objection with the words "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*).
This has been stated:
Regarding the phrase "among those that are homogeneous," he refutes this by means of a deviation from the negative concomitance (vyatireka-vyabhicāra), stating "that is not so.
The meaning is that even a specific causal relationship is not the determinant for recollection, because even when that [causal relationship] ceases, this [recollection] does not necessarily cease.

Nor is it tenable to claim that mere similarity alone should be the basis for that [recognition], because even that is subject to deviation when difference is perceived. Since the position of not perceiving difference must be addressed, the author sets that aside and, taking up the synthesis intended by us, raises an objection with the words "pūrvāpara... (the former and the latter).
Where there is a unification (pratisandhāna) regarding an agent, there necessarily exists a causal relationship between the cognitions being unified;
and wherever such [a causal relationship] exists, there necessarily is a unification regarding an agent— this is the meaning of "it does not deviate."
He refutes [this] with "Alas!"—
the phrase "the realization of selflessness becoming one's own nature" is intended as an indirect characterization (*upalakṣaṇa*) of omniscience.
This, then, is the meaning:
an omniscient being is, at any rate, a point of non-dispute for both parties.
Does he connect [past and future] by way of being the single agent of multiple preceding and succeeding cognitions of himself, or not?
In the first case, the oneness of the synthesizer is established precisely by that synthesis itself;
for while the diversity of cognitions and the instability of the intellect are perceived by everyone,
the momentariness of the synthesizer is not perceived even by an omniscient being.
If, however, it does not reconnect, then the reconnection in the agent is not based on the relation of cause and effect;
for it is impossible that something which does not persist even when another thing persists should be based solely upon that [other thing].
"And that very [existence]," and so forth, is said with irony.
"In vain" means that since the view of existence (sattvadṛṣṭi) cannot be denied as long as its own basis persists.
And there must necessarily be a reconnection [of consciousness] for that [intermediate state];
otherwise, how could he teach? Furthermore, a teacher must necessarily be accepted.
If it were certain that speakers regarding matters pertaining to the next world are merely deceivers, then even out of mere possibility, discerning persons would not engage [in such actions].
Therefore, in both cases, the oneness of the synthesizer is established.
Here he raises an objection: "Now, even if it does not exist... and so forth.
Consequently, there would be no relationship of cause and effect, nor would that [relationship] be its basis, because of the lack of invariable concomitance.
Nor would there be the consequence of [the cognition] being without instruction.
Because there exists a reconnection based upon that [prior state],
nor is there any room for the objection, since that [reconnection] occurs spontaneously and serves as its cause.
The meaning is that [the object] is to be apprehended by this [means]. He raises an objection with "na cet" (if not);
this [objection] is to be understood as applying only when the relation of cause and effect exists.

The meaning of the objection is this: "But instruction [occurs] precisely through the excellence of the practice of compassion brought about by the force of prior recollection; it is like the awakening of one who was asleep by the force of recollecting a contradiction. The reply is: "In activity," etc.
Furthermore, it is not tenable that there is a perception of difference among cognitions by avoiding the coloring [of the intellect] by objects, as in the case of a crystal.

Because, like a crystal, it is impossible to perceive the intellects apart from their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); for if that were the case, and the distinction between them were not grasped by the intellect alone, then one would not perceive the difference between a tree as "earthen," wood as distinct from the tree, charcoal as distinct from wood, and ashes and so forth as distinct from that.
And it is indeed perceived.
Therefore, upon the cessation of the cause, there would be no reconnection;
or, if there were such reconnection, it would imply another underlying cause—this is the meaning.
Furthermore, instruction would not be possible without the process of reconnection (pratisandhāna);
for that [instruction] has the desire to speak as its source, and that [desire to speak] has the recollection of conventional words and so forth as its source.
And that very thing is the reconnection.

[Objection: "But surely, the reconnection [of the series] will occur because of the non-apprehension of a difference in the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). To this, he says: "The storehouse...

For that stream of the storehouse-consciousness, which is the locus of the notion of "I," must it be something entirely distinct from the active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), or rather, must it consist of various occasional notions of "I" included within those [active consciousnesses]?
Not the first [alternative],
for two independent streams of consciousness are not experienced as competing with one another in a "I-first,

I-first" manner; nor, even if they existed, would there be a connection consisting of the mutual recollection of objects experienced, because they stand in a relationship of neither being the material cause (*upādāna*) nor the effect (*upādeya*) of one another.
Or, if that were the case, the same consequence would apply to Caitra, Maitra, and so forth.

Or, if both [the ālayavijñāna and the pravṛttivijñāna] were the material cause of both, then even a single entity would be supported by many; what, then, have the whole (avayavin), conjunction (saṃyoga), and so forth, done wrong?
Nor is it logical to say that the *pravṛttivijñāna*, which is appropriated by the *ālayavijñāna*, does not appropriate anything at all.
If that were the case, it would not even function as a causal condition (*nimitta*),
because being a causal condition is necessarily pervaded by being a material cause (*upādāna*).
And thus, if it were to take another cognition as its material cause, [the same problem would follow].
In that case, there would be the undesirable consequence of the commencement of an unprecedented and infinite series [of moments].
Therefore, the meaning is that the *ālayavijñāna* is neither based on experience (*ānubhavika*) nor is it based on logical necessity (*aupapattika*).
Regarding the second [alternative], he says: "I."
This is the intended meaning:
for this [error], would the non-apprehension of difference pertain to its own nature (*svarūpa*) or to its object (*viṣaya*)?
Is it by its own nature, or from the mere cognition "I was previously," or even from the active cognitions (*pravṛttivijñāna*)?
It cannot be the first [alternative].
Because the cognitions "I knew," "I know," and "I shall know" cannot be accounted for without a determination of difference based on their respective temporal states, such as pastness and so forth.

Even if the difference [between them] is somehow not apprehended, it is appropriate that there be a synthesis (*pratisandhāna*) of their objects alone, not of the active cognitions (*pravṛttivijñāna*);
and it has already been stated that there is no non-apprehension of the difference even from those [objects].
Nor [is it established] by way of its object;
for would that object be its own form, or another real entity, or something false?
Not the first, because it has already been refuted by the previous critique;
for by this [cognition], its own form is not superimposed upon itself as something distinct,
but rather its own self is shown to be its very object.
And its distinction is certain;
nor is the second [alternative] possible, because it is not accepted by [the opponent] himself.
Nor is the third [alternative] tenable,
because it has already been established that the conceptual construction "I" possesses a real objective basis (*savastukatā*);
and even if it were without a real basis (*avastukatva*), the apprehension of a distinction relevant to the present context could not possibly occur therein.
For that difference is either not apprehended despite being present,
or it is non-existent,
or it is superimposed.
Or is it that a non-existent entity has been superimposed?
It cannot be the first case, because if a false thing were to possess a difference that is not cognized as such, it would follow that it is not false.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable,
because an ultimate absence of difference must result in an ultimate identity;
nor is it the case that, from the perspective of ultimate reality, that which is falsely imagined through various conceptual constructions possesses a single nature, since it lacks any self-nature.
Or, if that were the case, what would be the utility of the non-apprehension of difference,
since the synthesis as one would occur simply because of their being one?
Nor is the third [alternative] possible.
Because it is contradicted by a logical inconsistency:
for if there were indeed a superimposition of difference upon that [object], how could it not be perceived?
Or, if that [identity] is not apprehended, how can there be the superimposition of difference?
Furthermore, when there is the superimposition of difference, there is no room for the superimposition of non-difference.
Nor is it the fourth [alternative].
Because it would entail the consequence of self-dependence and the consequence of an ultimately real distinction;
for the distinction between a jar and a cloth that is ultimately real—
If it is argued that the conceptual distinction between a rabbit’s horn and a human’s horn is not what is being grasped here, and therefore this is a "contemplation of non-difference"— we say no;
for if one fails to perceive a distinction in one object and yet superimposes non-difference upon another, it would lead to an over-extension of the principle (atiprasaṅga).

However, if there is no apprehension of the distinction between that which is described as being free from the four alternatives and that which is not, then by the superimposition of non-difference, there follows the undesirable consequence of the identity of the three worlds.

If it is argued that there is indeed a grasping of difference in that case, then it is better to maintain simply this: superimposition of non-difference occurs precisely when that difference, as it actually exists, is not grasped.
Furthermore, this [recognition] is not possible on the view that its object is unreal; therefore, it is superior to hold that the cognition of existence has only a stable entity as its domain.
The intention is that momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) will be refuted later.
Thus, this aforementioned form of recognition is pervaded by having a cause, because if it were causeless, no such regularity could be established.

And since that [succession] does not exist when there is more than one agent, it is excluded from the dissimilar class (vipakṣa) by the non-perception of the pervader (vyāpakānupalabdhi). Thus, as it turns away from the dissimilar class, it comes to rest in the state of having a single agent who possesses the causal conditions; this is the establishment of the necessary connection (pratibandha). With this intention, he concludes with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
All of this has been stated while accepting the relationship of material cause and effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*) among cognitions;
however, in reality, the dispute concerns precisely that point.

For instance, if cognitions separated by time were produced by a single agent, where would there be the relationship of material cause and effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*) among cognitions? And if that relationship exists, where would their status as having a single agent reside?
For that [relation] consists precisely in having a single material cause (*upādāna*).
Nor is the relation of material cause and effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*) merely the production of one thing from another when they belong to the same genus;
otherwise, it would follow that the cognitions of a teacher and a student would also stand in such a relation.
The claim that "it is when there is no apprehension of difference" is also not tenable;
for even between the cognitions of the disciple and the teacher, there is an apprehension of difference due to the acceptance or rejection of all their respective adjuncts (*upādhi*),
since in the present case as well, there exists an apprehension of difference characterized by adjuncts.
Because the non-apprehension of a difference in bodies is not invariably concomitant with another birth;
because it would lead to the over-extension [of the argument] to a child whose father has not been perceived;
and because it would lead to the undesirable consequence that the pot and its shards do not possess such a relationship.

Nor is it logical to maintain the rule of a single substratum (*ekādhāratāniyama*), because in the theory of momentariness (*kṣaṇikapakṣa*), there is an absence of moments that could serve as such a real substratum for the objects and their cognitions; furthermore, a merely conceptual [substratum] would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
For indeed, everyone has the conceit (*abhimāna*) regarding a jar that...
Just as fragrance is in that very place where form, taste, and touch are, so too is cognition in that very place where the body is.
By this, the non-delusory equality and the single determination regarding nature and transformation are established. Therefore...
The definition of cause and effect as consisting of the relationship between the material cause (*upādāna*) and its product (*upādeya*) is thus refuted.
Furthermore, how is it determined by you that charcoal is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the nature (*prakṛti*) of wood?
For why might it not rather be a modification of fire itself?
If it is argued that [the effect] arises from wood alone when there is contact with fire—no, for why could it not be the case that it arises from fire alone when there is contact with wood?
If it is argued that this is because of the certainty that what is earthen has only an earthen material cause—[we reply: no.
Whence is this [known]?
If it is argued that it is because such is observed in the case of homogeneous moments, then from what is that [known]?
If it is argued that this is due to the determination of a single, non-erroneous sameness— no,
for it would entail the consequence that blue atoms, when perceived as contiguous and without interval, would be mutual material causes (upādāna) of one another.
For when those [aggregates] arise, there exists for them a sense of "mine" and a conceited determination of oneness;
however, in an ultimate sense, this is not the case anywhere.
Furthermore, it is also not tenable that all the atoms of form and taste, when aggregated, serve as the material cause (*upādāna*) for everything.
Because it is not accepted by [the opponent] himself that a single [entity] has multiple occurrences,
and because there is an absence of co-location for those things that are well-known [to be distinct];
by this, the alternative reading "an illusory determination of oneness" is also refuted.
Because this is equally true for worldly people who accept it as an error,
and because for investigators it is likewise non-existent even in the case at hand;
therefore, only the mere relationship of cause and effect remains.
Nor can that [condition] be an adventitious attribute (*upādhi*), because it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, the claim that "only a certain cognition arises by the power of its own causal complex (*svakāraṇasāmagrī*) such that it examines only certain conditions belonging to a particular causal continuum,
and not others" is also not well-founded.

Otherwise, even for a disciple, there would be the undesirable consequence of the arising of a cognition that reflects upon the teacher’s mind, since they too would lack any volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāraka*) in that regard. If it is argued that this is not so because [the teacher] lacks such effort, then why is this the case, given that there is no difference in their being causes or in their being cognitions?
For the power of causes is indeed manifold. So why this excessive persistence?
If it is argued that one should postulate a cause in whatever way an effect is observed to occur?
In that case, the inquiry as to what kind of thing possesses capacity, and where, remains entirely unanswered.
If this were so, then because one could not have confidence in any indicators or producers whatsoever, the world would arise as being devoid of causal activity.
If it is argued that this is postulated because the cause of reconnection is refuted by the proof of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*)?
If it is argued that this [scripture] does not invalidate that [inference] because it is faultless,
then another fault must be stated regarding this [scripture].
If it is argued that because no distinction is perceived, let there be a state of counter-thesis (satpratipakṣatva) for both [reasons], we reply:
"Indeed, we shall remove this misfortune of yours as well; do not be in such a hurry"—this is the remainder of the concluding statement.

For if the mind of an omniscient being is cited as an example of the mind of someone like us serving as an objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), one might object that because of their dissimilarity—like a staff and a jar—it does not effect reconnection (*pratisaṃdhatte*). To this, it is said: "The mind of a yogi as well...
[This implies] that there would be reconnection even by means of the yogi's mind, because the possibility of a reversal of the reason exists;
for the opposite of the reason is also possible, such that there would be reconnection even by means of the yogi's mind. Thus, the objection is refuted.
Or is the third [case] used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārtha*)?
Here, does experience produce memory occurring at a later time, or is it the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by that [experience] which [produces it]?
Is that [self], which is beyond the senses, established by direct perception?
And even if it is beyond the senses, does it persist at that particular time, or is it a continuous stream?
Is it also unestablished by direct perception as being either the nature of a continuous stream of cognitions subsequent to that [object],
or something other than that, or a specific quality thereof?
Is this distinction merely the fact of being produced from experience, or is it a difference in the nature of the continuum of the experiencer?
Regarding these, he refutes the first [option] with the words: "For it is not that which has not arisen..."
But that which is established by direct perception is [known] from the form of the subsequent stream of cognitions;
any other [kind of self], however, is sublated by non-perception and is not admitted by them.
A distinction characterized merely by its origin in experience is no distinction at all;
for a seed does not produce a sprout only when brought into contact with soil by the hand of a laborer,
but rather even such a seed [produces a sprout] if it has not fallen into negligence.

Likewise, whether the continuum of the experience of blue and so forth is brought about by the experience of yellow and so forth, or by the experience of blue and so forth itself, there is no distinction made by its own nature (*svarūpa*).

Thus, the consequence of recollection would apply even to what has not been experienced, and not to what has been experienced; therefore, a difference in kind (*vaijātya*) must be the distinguishing factor.
Just as the *āmalakī* tree, by the application of milk, avoids acidity and, persisting while assuming sweetness, brings forth sweetness even in its fruit at a later time;
and just as the cotton seed, by the application of lac-dye, avoids whiteness and, persisting while assuming redness, brings forth redness in its flowers—
yet such a thing is not possible in the present case.

Just as crystal, though it continues to exist by discarding its coloration from objects such as a hibiscus flower and assuming whiteness instead, remains as mere crystal-nature; so too, cognition, though it continues to exist by discarding the coloring of objects and assuming mere consciousness-nature, possesses all forms in all cognitions. However, the notion that "one form is clear while others are indistinct" is merely a matter of faith in one's own philosophical system.
Since there is no fear even regarding the superimposition of contradictory properties,
even in the position that [cognition] is formless (*nirākāra*), cognition is clearly manifest with respect to whatever object is its domain;
however, that which it does not clearly manifest is not its domain.
Or, if that were the case, there would be no distinction between the object and its opposite;
therefore, the *saṃskāra* remains as something beyond the reach of the senses.
If it persists for a period of time, [then...]
"Surely that material cause (*upādāna*) must likewise be stable; for the effect (*upādeya*) does not persist even when the material cause has ceased. With this intention, he says: "arisen previously.

Anticipating the objection that "there will be a subliminal impression (*saṃskāra*) which, though continuous, is beyond the senses," he raises the doubt with the words: "again, another," and so forth.
For a separate continuum of formative forces (*saṃskāra*) is neither accepted by the opponent nor logically tenable, since the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) has already been refuted;
furthermore, if it were something additional to that, it would follow that the results such as memory would arise from that very [separate continuum] alone.

Therefore, because there would be no opportunity for the fruit within the continuum of the active process, and because it would lead to the over-extension [of the principle] that the fruit exists elsewhere than in the formation (*saṃskāra*), and because there would be no opportunity for the fruit within the continuum of the active process, and because it would lead to the over-extension that the fruit exists elsewhere than in the formation— therefore, because there would be no opportunity for the fruit within the continuum of the active process, and because it would lead to the over-extension that the fruit exists elsewhere than in the formation... [and so on].
Because it would lead to an over-extension regarding the result;
therefore, it is most logically established that where there is experience, there is a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), and where that exists, there is the result such as memory.

And thus, the proof for momentary destruction remains as an obstacle; regarding this, he says: "For it will be established," by which [he means] that whatever conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskāra*) is deposited in some continuum, [is subject to momentary destruction].
The claim that "it is capable of yielding fruit only there and not elsewhere," and so forth, is refuted;
for an additional *saṃskāra* (latent impression) lacks a proven substratum (*āśrayāsiddhi*),
and its specific definition lacks essential proof (*svarūpāsiddhi*).
And because it is contradictory to the definition of a continuous stream of subsequent effects that is undifferentiated;
furthermore, the mention of the reason "impermanence" as excluding specific [cases] is for the purpose of establishing its status as a quality (*guṇatva*).
For this very reason, there is no suspicion of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
Having established dependence through impermanence, one then establishes [its] being a quality (*guṇatva*) by means of that; however,
since that for which "being a quality" was established has already been established by the very same [reason] that established it, its [separate] establishment remains redundant.
He summarizes that [point] with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*).
Now, one might ask: if the author of the *Vārttika* has already kept its futility in mind, why then did he set forth this very reason? To this, he says:
That too was stated previously, but it was not proven;
and since what is unproven cannot be called a "proof," this results in a "withering of the embryo."
This is the meaning:
just as impermanence is inseparable from dependence on a substance, so too is quality-ness.
And just as it is with those [other] desired things,
so it is with quality-ness (*guṇatva*) as well; thus,
there is no distinction whatsoever between these two with respect to their being means of proof (*sādhana*).
What is intended [by the definition] is merely the absence of the time for inference;
that too does not exist, because even when a single reason has been established, there remains the desire to know another reason.
Furthermore, it applies even to one who does not keep impermanence in mind, provided they employ the conventional usage of "quality" (guṇatva) due to its connection with that definition.
For it is observed that desire and the like—which possess a commonality and are non-mobile by nature—are associated with other qualities.
In this regard, however, the presentation of impermanence and so forth serves as the point of contention;
such is the meaning of the particle *api*.
It establishes both dependence through impermanence and its supporting quality of being a subordinate attribute (guṇatva).
He states the utility for the subsequent section: "And this is not... and so forth.
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is "qualified by dependence on a substance.
To the question "From where is this qualification established? he says: "Even though... and so forth.
This is the intended meaning:
first, its parts that are capable of being apprehended by perception have already been refuted by means of perception and non-apprehension;
as for those [parts] beyond the senses, inference is the valid means of knowledge.
And that [reason] is of two kinds: co-extensive and non-co-extensive.
Although the negation of the probandum does not necessarily follow from the negation of the second kind, it must nonetheless follow from the negation of the first.
For instance, in some cases, the capacity of a substance to initiate [another] might be postulated on the basis of its possessing a touch that is perceived;
and when such an initiator exists, that resulting substance would be established as having parts, like air.
However, since there is no possession of a perceived touch here, the possibility of initiation does not exist.
In the absence of that [composite], there would be no possession of parts, just like space.
This is what was stated: "because there is a lack of evidence for the postulation of its parts. It is not, therefore, an atom.
The meaning is "pervasive," because the negation of a specific case has as its scope the permission of the remainder.
To the question "Why? he says: "In each of those cases."
The meaning is that it is only when this is so that the universal occurrence of desire and the rest is logically established;
he demonstrates this with the words "in some cases," etc.,
where "either one" refers to the body and so forth.

In some cases, [the attainment] begins from the production of the effect-substance by its own nature, starting from the conjunction of its causes and so forth. Now, why does it not reach each [object] simply through motion? To this he says: because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the postulation of motion.
For corporeality (*mūrti*) is indeed the means of valid cognition for the postulation of motion.
Even though it is not perceived by her, a movement is postulated in the mind and in the atoms,
yet its absence is found in the self.
For instance, desire and the like do not have the atoms as their substratum.
Because it is perceptible to us and others while being impermanent, like sound;
and for one who seeks to prove that [sound] resides in a partless substance, its residing in a substance with parts has already been refuted.

Therefore, as before, it should be understood that because it is formless (*amūrta*), motion is impossible, since form (*mūrti*) and motion possess a relationship of co-extensive pervasion (*samavyāpti*).
[Objection: But surely not even one of these is found in the Vārttika; to this he says: "This [is implied] by the inclusion of 'etcetera' (ādi).
[Objection: Even so, what is the point of this laborious construction, since it is possible to establish that these [qualities] possess the nature of *guṇa* in another way as well?

For instance, [the argument] that "desire and other qualities, being non-eternal, possess a genus perceptible by a single sense-organ, like color and so forth," and so on; therefore, he says: "by this [reasoning]," etc. (10).
Purification.
That for whose sake liberation (apavarga) is sought has already been characterized.
Now, since it is the person (puruṣa) who is most desired, it is appropriate to characterize liberation;
why, then, is there this intermediate characterization of the body and so forth? To this he says: "The self," and so on.

Because liberation (*apavarga*) is of the nature of a non-entity (*abhāva*), it is defined in dependence upon its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*); thus, it is inferior to suffering. Furthermore, because that [suffering] arises in dependence upon its causes, it is inferior to its causal factors, such as the sense organs (*indriya*) and so forth.
Since even those [sense organs] exist only by depending upon the body, they are inferior to the body. This is the summary of the logical connection (*saṃgati*).
"Directly by depending on the body" means that while the sense organs,
the mind, and a portion of the objects and so forth depend on the body through a traditional succession,
the same applies to cognition, the defects, and the portion consisting of the objects and so forth.
He states that the commentary (bhāṣya) is on this very point: "for the purpose of introducing that."

For here, in the view that movement (ceṣṭā) is not non-deviant from the body, the conjunction of the object and the sense organ is untenable, because a qualifier is meaningful only when there is the possibility of deviation.
Furthermore, in the view of their conjunction, the question "How can it be the locus of movement for one who perceives deviation? is itself untenable.
For it is only when there is a mutual deviation [of the two terms] that a conjunction (samuccaya) is possible.
Therefore, taking up the alternative (vikalpa), he introduces the commentary with the word "here" (atra).

Although "effort" (ceṣṭā) is an activity of the body, nevertheless, because that very [body] is the object to be defined, one must state merely "activity" (vyāpāra) for fear of mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya); thus he says: "effort is activity."
The word *prayuktasya* is used with a specific intention;
therefore, he explains it as "of that which has been employed, i.e., of that for which effort has been produced.
By this, the definition of *ceṣṭā* (volitional action) is established through its instrumental cause.
Voluntary action (*ceṣṭā*) is the motion of the ultimate composite [body] which has as its non-inherent cause the conjunction of the self with that which possesses effort.
By way of its result, however, it has the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful as its fruit.
Both of these aspects have been stated here according to the speaker's intention: "rather, it is a specific operation."
Therefore, in the definition by way of the effect, the example of deviation is [the case of] a wooden machine and the like;
however, in the definition by way of the cause, it is the vital air (prāṇa).
As for the mind, hands, feet, and so forth, they are excluded by the very term "ultimate composite" (antyāvayavin).
In this context, pointing out the deviation from both [premises], he says "wooden machines" and so forth.
He avoids both [objections] with the words "in another corporeal [entity].
And here, the word "corporeal" (*mūrti*) is employed with the intention of defining it according to the view of others, namely that corporeality is the dimension of a substance possessing touch.
And by that [it is meant]: "provided there is no application of another substance possessing touch";
and application (prayoga) is a quality conducive to action, and in the case of wooden machines and the like, it consists of impulsion (nodana) and so forth.
Effort, however, resides in the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Therefore, although the mind is indeed the instigator of the body, it nevertheless does not possess the quality of touch (*sparśavat*).
And although effort is also exerted there by means of the body,
nevertheless that [effort] is not other than it;
this is the result of grasping it as non-other.
Therefore, the qualification is not unestablished (*asiddha*).

And this qualification is as it is heard [in the text], in accordance with the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vārttika*. However, upon a thorough examination of the forthcoming *Vārttika*, it becomes clear that this very word *ceṣṭā* (volitional effort) functions in this way to denote a specific meaning; thus, one should not suspect that the Sūtra is deficient.
Regarding the passage beginning with "stone" (pāṣāṇa) and so forth:

it should not be argued that even such a thing possesses movement characterized by the contraction and expansion of limbs such as the eyes and belly, on the grounds that it is a living being and thus inferred to have inhalation and exhalation;
for there is an absence of space for inhalation and exhalation, and because a final composite whole (antyāvayavin) is devoid of action.
Moreover, in order to avoid the over-extension [of the definition] to a dead body, capacity alone is the refuge;
nor is it necessary to insist upon an illustrative example.

Now, even if the sense organs do not inhere in the body, they nonetheless come into contact with it; by that much alone, the meaning of "substratum" (āśraya) is established. Therefore, he reveals the intention of the author of the Vārttika with the words: "But by way of being conjoined."
Although the eye is indeed impaired when the eyeball (golaka) is struck and benefited when it is nourished,
nevertheless, because no specific distinction is made, this should be understood as referring to all the sense-faculties.
For when the eyeball alone is damaged or benefited, the skin and other faculties are neither harmed nor benefited.
Just as all [faculties] become either impaired or perfected through the injury or benefit of the body by means of old age, youth, and so forth—
this very point has been clearly demonstrated by the authors of the Bhāṣya and Vārttika through their use of the plural form "are benefited" (anugṛhyante) and "are injured" (upahanyante); therefore,
[the author] disregarded [the objection] that the faculties do not depend upon the body in its own nature.
The phrase "avoiding under-extension and over-extension" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
Now, one might object: "The fact that objects are the cause of the perception of pleasure and so forth is a nature [of those objects] conditioned by their effect;
it is not the effect itself. To this, he says: "The purpose [is stated] because activity toward them occurs on account of that [purpose]."
Therefore, this is the meaning of the definition:
that [entity] within which the self experiences objects is the body;
thus, there is no deviation [of the definition] with respect to the self. Nor...
The self is not delimited by the self itself,
nor by the mind, because the mind does not function without being delimited by the body.
Nor [is it experienced] by the sense organs, because if experience were to arise there through their limitation, it would follow that experience would also occur externally.
This very point has been clearly demonstrated previously by the author of the Bhāṣya himself when he stated, "This is the locus of its experience."
It is not elaborated here.
"Codayati" (it impels) means that having established the comprehension of the meaning, [the word] impels the comprehension of the verbal form; this is the ellipsis.

In the Vārttika, the plural form in the phrase "ceṣṭādayaḥ sāmānyaśabdāḥ" is used either because it includes other words such as "brahman" and so forth as examples, or because it intends to express the distinction in the application of the word to its various substrata; therefore, this [objection] has been set aside as being based on a weak doubt. Furthermore, the description of the logical impossibility—namely, that it is impossible to feed every single Brahmin—is merely incidental, since this point will be discussed later under the specific treatment of this position.
For this very reason, setting that aside, he explains what is relevant to the present context with the words "by means of a distinction" (*viśeṣeṇa*).
This is to be connected with the phrase "being brought near by [states such as] hunger and so forth.
Here, the meaning is: "among these two," namely, those included within the compound *prakaraṇādi* (context and so forth).
The meaning is that "impossibility of a means of valid cognition" (pramāṇāsambhava) refers to non-establishment (anupapatti) or sublation (bādha).
Even in a case where corporeality is sublated by a means of valid cognition, the state of being a locus of activity remains established.
Now, regarding the phrase "with the intention of [denying] inherence":
here, in the expression "the locus of the sense-faculties" (*indriyāśraya*), there is either a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound or a *bahuvrīhi*.
In that context, with the intention of refuting both [possibilities] through the denial of inherence, he says: "Even so... (*tathāpi*).
And this is an elliptical indication;
it should also be understood that [the same applies] to the body in relation to the sense-faculties.
For, in the first position, there would follow the undesirable consequence of corporeal entities occupying the same location.
Because a single substance does not initiate [another],
and because earth does not initiate substances such as water;
whereas in the second case, it is because heterogeneous substances do not initiate [one another].
The meaning is that the ear and the mind do not originate substances.
He specifies the particular sense organ with the words "of the nose";
this is a syntactically connected sentence.
In this regard, the following inquiry arises: is there an inherence (*samavāya*) or a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) of the nose with another part of the body?
Even regarding the first case, there are two possible alternatives.
Or, [the question may be] whether the nose is inherent in a part of the body, or whether that [part] is the nose. With reference to these two possible inquiries, he says: "Not of that," and so forth.
Because it does not inhere in the body by virtue of being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of the body's parts;
for the meaning is that a cause does not inhere in the effect of its own effect—this is the interpretation according to the *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound.
Furthermore, even according to the *bahuvrīhi* interpretation, it is because [the quality] does not inhere in the body.
The meaning is that the effect does not inhere in the cause of the cause.
As for the claim that there is inherence of the sense of smell in a part of the body, that is simply impossible;
for it is stated clearly in the *Ṭīkā* that the coexistence of two corporeal entities in a single substratum is untenable.
He adopts the position of conjunction—namely, "then it has that as its substrate.
In this context, the meaning is "conjoined.
Here too, there are two possible courses.
Whether by way of being a commencing agent (*ārambhakatva*) or by way of not being a commencing agent (*anārambhakatva*):
therein, he first refutes [the former] with the words "even so" (*tathāpi*).
For a substance that is being commenced is commenced only by its constituent parts (*avayava*) which are themselves perceptible by the senses, as is the case with a jar.
Alternatively, there is a pervasion (vyāpti) such that [an object] is perceived by supersensuous [faculties] alone, as in the case of a dyad (dvyaṇuka) and so forth,
but not by mixed [faculties];
the consequence of non-perceptibility was stated in order to refute that [pervasion].
If there were no undertaking [of action], it would be a mere substance in conjunction, like hair and so forth;
and since, in that case, the inherence of a body therein would be impossible, he disregarded this by asking, "What is the use of even such a doubt?
By this, the claim that "this [consciousness] is inherent in the body" is refuted.
