Because there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of such perception even by another person; therefore, even when whiteness is cognized, it is only with reference to the substance of the conch-shell which is its substratum. "The absence of water," and so forth.
And this is not merely a case of dissimilarity, because the supporting element necessarily exists without being separated [from the supported],
just as the earthy portion exists within gold.
In oil, milk, and ghee, water exists as a constituent;

yet in broth, water is not merely that which is conjoined with other substances, because if it were not so conjoined, the status of being broth would cease to exist. It is for this reason that it is designated by those [names].
By those qualifiers, there is the exclusion of that which is to be excluded;
and here, that [exclusion] is intended as being based on experience.
For it proceeds in this manner:
"This sandalwood is fragrant, bitter, white, and cool."
However, the word "but" (tu) is employed as a designation for the purpose of dispelling the delusion of identity, as in expressions such as "the white color of sandalwood.
Considering this to be not very profound, [the author] adopts it exactly as it was heard, and states the intended meaning: "For there exists... and so forth.
It is understood that the opponent accepts the critique of sandalwood not only by examining the nature of the reason, but also by examining the thesis itself;

for one does not prove the non-difference of form and so forth regarding something that has not even been perceived. If that were the case, the subject (*pakṣa*) would have an unestablished qualificand (*aprasiddhaviśeṣya*).

Alternatively, if existence were to be proven as independent [of other categories], the reason would be unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*); thus, he has set this aside here, intending to explain it in the third chapter. The phrase "in order to exclude a one-sided designation" is intended to indicate another formal argument (*prayoga*).
For instance: "This object of visual perception, sandalwood, is distinct from taste and the other [sensory qualities]."
Because this [consciousness] is perceived even when that [object] is not perceived;
for if something is perceived even when another thing is not perceived, it is distinct from that thing,
just as sound is distinct from form and so forth.
And so it is with this sandalwood;
therefore, it is "thus.
However, the exclusion based on the mere word is doubtful; in that case, the designation itself is the reason.
He states another argument:
because the reason of "dissimilarity" is inconclusive with respect to individuals,
and unestablished with respect to universals.

And because the distinctness from the object is what is to be proven, the intended meaning is that [the opponent] does not accept [the cognition] as being characterized by a form imparted by that [object]. The ellipsis is to be supplied thus: "the one who has this intention. And here, having made pervasion (vyāpti) primary as the reason, the reason is stated in the genitive case.
And the probandum (sādhya) ends in the fifth case [the ablative].
For example: "This mountain possesses fire; why? Because it possesses smoke."
What is the reason?
It is because [the relationship] is like that between possessing smoke and possessing fire.
However, for fear of making the text too cumbersome, he explains it according to the literal reading—as "of the cognition of a jar."
The object is the jar itself;
the cause is "jar-ness.
For it is by taking that as the cause that the cognition of "jar" occurs with respect to the jar.
The cognition of a jar, moreover, is both an experience and a recollection;
thus, this is the purification of the formal argument (*prayoga*).
The cognitions of "one" and so forth regarding jars and other objects arise dependent upon a ground for application distinct from the grounds already mentioned.
Because [the cognition] arises even in the absence of the stated cause;
just as, for instance, the cognition of "blue" arises with respect to those very objects such as jars or blue things.

In this context, if one were to state merely that it arises even in the absence of the jar, then there would be a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to the cognition of a jar arising with respect to another jar when the first jar has been discarded.
This is because even for that which has become such [i.e., a conceptualized object], there is no dependence on another cause.
However, if the argument were merely "without that cause," there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the non-conceptual cognition of a jar,
since that too does not depend on another cause even while being independent of that specific cause.
Even with the mere phrase "without that cognition," there is a deviation [from the rule] by that very same case.
Even when both the first and second words are included, there is a deviation due to the recollection, the subsequent reflective awareness (anuvyavasāya), and the error regarding that [object];
for these arise even apart from the object, the cause, and the basis of that cognition.
Nor is there a dependence on another basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*).
There is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the second and third [definitions] due to non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*);
and there is also deviation with respect to the first and third due to the cognition of another jar. Therefore, all [three] are mentioned together.
Therefore, it completes what was deficient: "even here [in the case of] 'the vessel'.
This is the distinction between the cognitions of "one" and so forth and the cognition of a jar and the like.
Thus, it is correct to say that a post is a substance.

Nor is there a confusion of genus (*jātisaṃkara*), because the genus *khadira* does not appear therein. Rather, the conventional usage [of the name] is due to the possession of its qualities, like the usage of "lion" for a young boy; and the usage of "belonging to it" is due to being composed of its parts, like curds [being said to belong to] milk.

Since a single ultimate composite, such as a serpent, does not originate [from parts], and because its constituent parts are already occupied by their own effects, it is clear that the "serpent-coil" is merely a configuration (*saṃsthāna*).
Regarding the phrase "of the statue":
because it lacks the characteristics of a body, the word "body" is not used in its primary sense there.
In this context, the term "abiding" (*saṃsthāna*) is used figuratively (*aupacārika*) because of its inclusion within that same referent, due to similarity with it;
however, in the expression "the head of Rāhu," there is merely a figurative application of the word "head" to the abiding [of the head].

In the case of the expression "the gold ring" (*suvarṇāsyāṅgurīyakam*), it is clear that the ring is merely the shape (*saṃsthāna*), because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a confusion of universals (*jāti*), given that rings made of silver and other materials are also seen.
Recalling the reasoning stated in the passage concerning "the stone statue" (*śilāputraka*), he says: "In this way... (*evam*).

If there were a distinction based on the teaching of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), then the reason would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the intellect (*buddhi*) and the body (*śarīra*) alone; therefore, he says: "not being of the same nature" (*atādātmya*). //14//
// Purity //
He introduces the *Saṅgatiprakaraṇa-vārttika* by first explaining its meaning with the words "of the self and so forth.
It has already been stated that even though the mind is a cause [of cognition], it is excluded [from being the object].

To the objection—"If these [words] were to apply to other objects as well, just like the word 'cow' according to a convention known to all people, then what contradiction would there be?"—he replies: "In that case, a convention known to all people is not capable... [of establishing such a usage].
The phrase "by way of their own denotata" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Therefore, this is the meaning:
that which is the single ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of these words when they are being used [in discourse].
"Because of its association with that [object], the intellect (buddhi) is distinguished from others"—
this is what was stated by the author of the Sūtras as "it is not something other [than the object].
By this, the aforementioned [objection] is refuted.
By those who have undertaken this convention (*samaya*), the increase must be distinguished from both similar and dissimilar classes;
and when that [increase] has been so established, the convention must be accepted by them—thus there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*).
However, if conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is what is to be proven...

Regarding the phrase "having the self as its locus" (*ātmāśrayatvam*): one might suspect that since "intellect" (*buddhi*) and "knowledge" (*jñāna*) mean the same thing, what is the purpose of uttering multiple words? Anticipating this and wishing to refute the views of others, the author says: "The Commentator himself [has stated] clearly"—that is, "because it is established by reasoning.
He explains a portion of the *Bhāṣya* with the word "synonym" (*paryāya*).
In this context, the category of "arising" (upapatti) is explained by the phrase "designation by means of synonymous terms";
the remaining portion explains the category of "capacity" (sāmarthya).
Therefore, the meaning is as follows:
The capacity of the logical justification— characterized by the designation of synonymous terms— is its implication of the negation of multiple meanings.
"Therefore" refers to this aforementioned refutation which has been indicated.
The author of the Vārttika asks about that which is to be established by reasoning: "What, then, is the reasoning here?
[The answer is: "The sense organs have non-conceptual functions;
the mind has conceptual functions."
Ahaṃkāra is the function of the conceit of entitlement;
buddhi is the function of the determination of what is to be done;
and the puruṣa is indeed devoid of function, though it is attributed with the functions of the imagined buddhi.
Therefore, this is the meaning: the *puruṣa* is neither cause nor effect;
primordial matter (*prakṛti*) is the original cause.
Intellect (*buddhi*) is the first effect; from that arises the creation beginning with the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).
The Person (*puruṣa*) is of the nature of immutable consciousness (*kūṭasthacaitanya*).
The Sāṅkhyas maintain that everything else is insentient (*acetana*).
In this system, the intellect (*buddhi*) possesses three constituent parts:
the coloring by the *puruṣa*, the coloring by the object, and the entry of activity.
For there occurs the thought, "This is to be done by me.
The coloring by the notion of "by me" is unreal, like the reflection of a face on a mirror, due to the non-apprehension of their difference.
The coloring by the object, expressed as "this," is real, like the contact with impurity on a mirror; it is a transformation through a specific channel consisting of the sense organs.
The engagement in activity also depends upon both of these;
therein, cognition (*buddhi*) is characterized by such activity,
while knowledge (*jñāna*) is characterized by the coloring (*uparāga*) by the object.

Their secret doctrine is this: the perception of that unreal superimposition upon the person—just as the face reflected in a mirror appears to possess the dirtiness inherent in the mirror—is due to its connection with that [person].
He brings this forth with the words, "It is said that the intellect... and so on;
yet that [perception] does not, first of all, belong to the intellect.
"Because of its lack of consciousness.
Even though the Sāṃkhya school accepts that it is only the unconscious [pradhāna] that undergoes delusion—as they say: "Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind"—[the author replies:]...
Thus, these [cognitions] are indeed valid knowledge, doubt, error, dream, and memory;
nevertheless, there is an objection raised on the basis of pervasion (vyāpti).
For where there is an illusion of association or an illusion of identity due to the non-apprehension of the non-association between the conscious and the unconscious,
that [illusion] belongs to the conscious being alone.
It is like the relationship between a mirror and Caitra, or between a body and its possessor;
for in those cases, there is no delusion on the part of the mirror or the body.
Furthermore, it would be the intellect (*buddhi*), while cognizing the self, that would be deluded.
Nor is it perceived by a person;
for neither of these two cases is tenable due to the very reasoning previously stated.
Furthermore, it is not logical to claim that cognition, being unmanifest either intrinsically or extrinsically, undergoes error.
For a mirror that is not even being seen does not produce a reflection merely through the presence of a friend in the case of one with cataracts.
Therefore, by way of a conclusion, he says—“Therefore, wretched”—indicating that in both ways, consciousness has become innate to the intellect. //15//
// Purity //

Since the mind has been excluded from the discussion on the sense organs (*indriya*) due to its dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), its turn comes between those two because it is to be inferred through the sequence of cognitions (*buddhi-krama*) and because it is the cause of their activity; thus he says: "The one whose turn has arrived" (*kramaprāptam*).

He explains that the *Vārttika* beginning with "Because" (*yasmāt*) is a commentary on the *Bhāṣya* which establishes the reasons stated by the author of the Sūtras and by himself, using a division of sentences; hence he says: "Not a sense organ" (*anindriya*).
Although space (*ākāśa*) is also excluded by the phrase "another cause" (*nimittāntara*) alone, [it is mentioned here for clarity].
Or rather, by the term "non-pervasive" itself [the self is excluded],

as is the case with the self and so forth by the term "cooperative cause," since it is well known that only that which is distinct from the material cause (upādāna) can be a cooperative cause (sahakārin).
Nevertheless, the distinction is established according to the speaker's intention, following the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*);
that is, either by making the sense-faculty (*indriya*) primary, or by speaking of the self as having auxiliary causes (*sahakārivāda*).
[Objection: But is not the mind (*manas*) all-pervading (*vibhu*), because it is a substance that is always devoid of contact?
Because it is a substance devoid of specific qualities;
because, while being eternal, it is a substance that does not initiate [other] substances;
because it is the substratum of the conjunction that is the inherent cause of cognition; and so forth.
How then can it be said that [the reason] is non-pervasive?
This is not so, because all of these are, at first glance, unestablished in their own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*).

For instance, when the mind is inferred as an instrument (karaṇa) because the apprehensions of pleasure and so forth are actions (kriyā), at that time its status as a substance (dravyatva) is not established,
since even that which is not a substance can function as an instrument.
Now, since these very [faculties] are perceived as direct instruments, they must be inferred by way of their being sense organs;
nevertheless, given that a limb of the body serves as their limiting adjunct (upādhi),
their functional activity is obtained only within that much.
Furthermore, if there were cessation of activity due to a defect in that [organ], it would follow [absurdly] as in the case of the ear;
therefore, the body alone must be declared to be the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
And thus, when activity is obtained through that limitation, one says, "I have a pain in my head."
There is a contradiction with the cognition that "there is pleasure in my foot" and so forth, which indicates non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛttitva*);
for pervasive effects are restricted to specific locations in accordance with their non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).

Furthermore, if one were to postulate limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) ranging from the body and its parts down to the atoms, it would result in the fault of excessive conceptual complexity (*kalpanāgaurava*).

And because a restrictive rule (niyama) would be untenable, one must postulate some other single subtle, supersensible entity as the limiting adjunct (upādhi). Even so, if its status as a sense organ were inherent, there would be no evidence for postulating anything further; thus, the means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (dharmin) would be contradicted.
Now, if that inference [of the mind] is based on its cooperation with the sense organs according to the sequence of cognitions, then the previously mentioned defect applies all the more.

However, if it is argued that even though the mind is omnipresent, its sequential activity is possible due to the power of unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), then, since the mind itself remains unproven, the reasons for its omnipresence suffer from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhi).
Now, where the unseen (adṛṣṭa) has utility through the removal of visible causes, in that case the effect is indeed produced when that [unseen] is complete;
otherwise, even from the final conjunction of threads, a cloth might sometimes not be born.
Or even if it has arisen, it might at some time be devoid of qualities;
for instance, a wheel, though impelled by a firm staff by a powerful potter, might not spin.

But where the operation of an unperceived factor occurs through the correlation with what is perceived, there the non-arising of the effect follows from its deficiency, as in the case of the motion of atoms. Therefore, in this case as well, if the mere conjunction of the object, the sense organ, and the self were the cause of cognition, then the effect would always occur whenever those [factors] exist.
For there is nothing further than this that could be brought about by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa),
nor does the arising of knowledge occur at all times;
therefore, something additional must be required.

And although that [power] pervades all the sense organs, nevertheless, because it possesses the nature of an instrument (*karaṇa*), the sequence of actions is logically consistent. However, if that [power] were not postulated, this principle would not hold.
If it is argued that there must be an internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) because the eyes and other [senses] lack the nature of being an agent and are multiple,
[we reply: even so, let there not be simultaneous cognitions.
But by what can simultaneous cognition be prevented?

If it is argued that a single cognition having multiple objects as its support (samūhālambana) indeed occurs— no, for that would lead to the undesirable consequence [of such a cognition] even in the case of objects grasped by different sense-faculties, just as it does in the case of those grasped by a single sense-faculty.
If it is argued that [the sequence] indeed occurs even in those cases, we say no;
for at the time of divided attention (*vyāsaṅga*), the sequence of the objects of dispute is inferred through the sequence of cognitions.
If it is argued that the sequence of actions during divided attention is due to a specific desire to know (*bubhutsāviśeṣa*), this is not so.
For this is not the power of the desire to know (*bubhutsā*):

that even when the causal complex for knowledge (*jñānasāmagrī*) is present, no knowledge arises regarding an object that is not intended to be known, but rather there occurs a cognition that deposits a specific latent impression (*saṃskāra*).
However, if it were the case that [the desire to know] would obstruct the causal complex itself regarding what is not intended to be known, [then its power would be established].
And thus, an eye opened for a jar would not show a cloth;

therefore, we consider it logical that even the desire to know (bubhutsā) is useful for the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions by drawing the mind away from another sense organ and directing it toward the sense organ that grasps the desired object, but not by its own inherent nature.
Therefore, it was well said: "it is non-pervasive" (*avyāpī*).

Regarding the *Vārttika*—"provided there is a difference from the activity of odor and so forth"—this, taken literally, is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because of cognitions of substances, actions, and so on; therefore, he explains it as "from the eyes and so forth.
[Objection: But in memory and the like, there are latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) and so forth.
They exist; therefore, these [cognitions] are not capable of being accounted for by the postulation of other instruments. Hence he says: "And here...
The meaning is that those produced by the sense organs are produced by instruments in the form of substances conjoined with the body.

[Objection: "But surely the mind (*manas*) is also a producer of memory and so forth precisely by virtue of being a sense-faculty (*indriya*); if it were so, there would follow the consequence that [memory] is a direct perception (*sākṣātkāritva*).

This objection is raised in the *Vārttika* beginning with "Now" (*atha*), taking up the fact that [the reason] appears to have a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇatā*). And this is the resolution offered by the "partial proponent" (*ekadeśin*).

He states clearly that the resolution—based on the actual nature of things—is that "the pervasion between two [terms] residing in different loci is impossible to grasp," by saying "it is from the Sūtra" (sautram). //16//
// Purity //
He states the reason why activity [continues] even when there is an excellence resulting from a future state, despite a deficiency of the mind: "Of the mind also... and so forth.

Since "activity" (*pravṛtti*) is not all-encompassing due to its exclusion from both conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and aggregation (*samuccaya*), this cannot be the general definition [of karma]. Furthermore, one might suspect that without it, there would be no room for a specific definition (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*). Anticipating this, he analyzes the words of the Sūtra: "Initiation" (*ārambha*) is activity.
"Initiation" is the effort (*prayatna*) that is the cause of birth and which produces a lasting specific quality (*sthirātma-viśeṣaguṇa*).
Nor is there a lack of pervasion by compassion and the rest [in that case],
because even there, an effort toward that end exists;
for if activity were merely desire, mere knowledge, or mere aversion, occurring without any effort at all, [then such a fault would arise].
