Nevertheless, since this would not include the contemplation of specific deities and so forth, he says: "And that is of two kinds.
Effort, whether for the purpose of knowing or for the purpose of making known, is in both cases a cause of knowledge;
by this, effort within the sphere of speech is also included.
The effort to do or to cause another to do [an action] is the cause of action in both cases;
by this, even the effort directed toward ignorance and so forth regarding theft, violence, and the like, is included.
He states what is established by this with the words "therein."

In that regard, the effort that produces knowledge has as its object a cause that makes [the object] known; thus, by characterizing speech as a single part of such a cause, the delusion that it is caused solely by the knowledge inherent in itself is also dispelled.
Regarding the phrase "having the body as its cause" (*kāyanimittā*): that whose cause (*nimitta*) is the body (*kāya*) by way of being its object (*viṣayatayā*) is so described.
Indeed, the effort directed toward giving, stealing, and so forth, has the body as its object.
Thus, that effort which is directed toward objects such as compassion or malice, having the mind as its cause, has the mind as its object; this is not to be doubted.
Otherwise, there would be no human activity whatsoever for which both body and mind are not the cause. //17//
Defects are characterized by their activity. //18//
// Purity //
He states the reason why, when there is an increase in rebirth (*pretyabhāva*), there is a decrease in the activity of the defects (*doṣa*): "by means of the motive" (*prayojya*).
The meaning is that they cause the person to act, making him possessed of an intensified effort.
Because of their immediate sequence, it should be understood that delusion (*moha*) also causes one to act.
"Inherence in the same object as delusion" means inherence in the same object as the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of delusion;
or [it means] with another instance of delusion.
He states this very point: "For as long as this... and so forth.
"Of that" refers to the commentary; "of its meaning" refers to the objector.

And here, although inherence (*samavāya*) is not an operation (*vyāpāra*), nevertheless, for delusion (*moha*) and the rest—which are the motivators—there exists an intermediate operation consisting in the production of passion (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*) inherent in their own substratum.

This state of being an instigator (*pravartakatva*) should be understood as the relationship between a related entity and its relation, without any great distance. Thus, delusion and attachment, or delusion and aversion, which have the fruit as their object, or delusion and attachment, or delusion and aversion, which have the means to that fruit as their object, instigate a person by generating them.

Therefore, the actual state of affairs is this: attachment, aversion, and delusion directed toward the fruit are the motivators (*pravartaka*), whereas those directed toward the means—which are inherent in the same object as that fruit—are the inducements (*pravartanā*).
Furthermore, since activity must be conducive to its effect, attachment and the others are said to be "defects" (*doṣa*) because they act as the causes of engagement (*pravṛtti-hetu*). //18//
Rebirth is re-arising after death. //19//
// Purity //

Dharma characterized by attainment, preceded by the relinquishment of everything from the body up to the defects (doṣas), is "pretyabhāva" (rebirth); therefore, its occasion follows immediately after that. Thus he says: "according to the order of enumeration."
Is it not the case that [the definition] "because of the abandonment of the previous body, etc. does not exist in the Sūtra?
Nor is mere birth "pretyabhāva" (re-existence after death), because such a designation would then follow even for a single lifetime.
Furthermore, this is not the meaning of the word *punaḥ*, because it has the sense of mere repetition;
therefore, the author of the Vārttika stated "again" (*punar*).
He explains this: "The word 'again' expresses repetition.
The meaning is that while stating the repetition, he simultaneously demonstrates—by the very necessity of the case—the relinquishment of the previous body and so forth.
Even so, what is the purpose of this indirect mode of expression (*vakrokti*)? To this he says: "And thus... (tathā ca).

This is the objection raised by the author of the Vārttika, who considers the following: "Is there not a contradiction? For in the second sūtra it was stated that the causal relationship between suffering and so forth constitutes *saṃsāra*, whereas here it is said to be 're-arising' (*punar-utpatti*); how then is there no contradiction?"
What, then, [is meant by this]?

Pretyabhāva (rebirth) is characterized by the abandonment of a previous body and so forth and the acquisition of another body and so forth, occurring when there exists a causal relationship between suffering and its causes.
Therefore, if that flow were to be interrupted in such a manner, saṃsāra—which is synonymous with pretyabhāva—would be brought to an end.

The response— "of suffering and so forth"— is intended by one who holds that there is no contradiction because that very [state] is called "saṃsāra" there due to having an identical basis for its application (*tulyapravṛttinimitta*).
This [response] is based on mere recollection.
He explains:
"This is the collection of Vārttikas.
Now, if this aforementioned rebirth is the transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) of the insentient mind, why should it be brought to an end?

Now, the author of the *Vārttika*, harboring the concern that its cessation might be impossible for the self—since even one who is liberated, through the abandonment of the body and so forth belonging to transmigratory existence, could potentially obtain another body and so forth—raises the doubt: "This very [person]... He then refutes this, harboring the intention that rebirth qualified by experience is not what constitutes *saṃsāra*: "If..."
In this regard, he clarifies the unclear term with the words "the action" (kriyām) //19//
The object produced by the activity of the defects is the fruit. //20//
// Purity //
Dispelling doubt, he establishes a connection with the words "even though" (*yadyapi*).
For it is those things known in a general way that can be known in their specific character;
therefore, there is an occasion for the specific definition of those things already characterized by their general form.
The meaning is that both forms are included because they are both useful for the cultivation of world-weariness (nirveda).
And in this sūtra, two words are redundant. Regarding that, he states their primary utility: "And here...
Although defects are also exceptionally useful for dharma and adharma—which are the effects of activity—even in terms of their own essential nature, [the two words are still redundant].
And he will say:
"For the grains of karma are shrouded by the husks of the defects," and so forth;
nevertheless, since they are the subject at hand in the Sūtra, the utility of the defects with respect to the fruit of engagement must be demonstrated.

Furthermore, there is no conventional usage of the term "fruit" (phala) for merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma). Therefore, he states their utility by way of their functional operation (vyāpāra), beginning with the words "but rather" (api tu).
He elucidates that very gateway [of operation] with the words "in the water of the defects" (doṣasalile).
Therefore, one should not fall into the error of thinking that there is a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the scriptural mention of *dharma* and *adharma*.

As for their status as intrinsic natures, the author of the Sūtras himself will state in the fourth [chapter] that the defects (*doṣas*) act as auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) toward the engagement in action.

Now, does this mean that pleasure and pain do not exist for one who is free from defects? Is it that the accumulation of previously acquired karma remains in its current state, or that it perishes without having yielded its fruit? To this he says: "And it does not exist."

We do not say that there is no enjoyment whatsoever for one who is free from faults; rather, it means that there is nothing like that which serves as a cause for cyclic existence— that is, nothing which produces further defects.
He states the purpose of the term *artha* as follows: "In the Sūtra," [verse 20].
// Purity //
The connection was stated with reference to primary suffering;
he speaks [next] with the intention of referring to it in a secondary sense: "not unspoken."

Now, if the word *lakṣaṇa* were to denote the essential nature (*svarūpa*), there would be the fault of non-pervasion regarding secondary suffering; or, if it were repeated, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Therefore, wishing to maintain the unity of the sentence, he says: "And here... (*atra ca*).
And thus there is a lack of proof; he refutes that with the words "for that very [nature]," meaning it is primary by its own essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*).
The secondary [application of the term "suffering"] is based on the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of being an object of suffering that is to be enjoined.

Nor does this entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), because the status of being its object is established by its nature as suffering, and its nature as suffering is established by its being the object of the cognition of affliction (*bādhanābuddhi*), which is well-known in the world; thus, its status as something to be abandoned (*heya*) is demonstrated.

For one who, even while knowing that the body and so forth are suffering or its cause, or that pleasure is merely attached to them, does not wish to abandon them because his mind is overwhelmed by thirst for pleasure—
toward such a person it is said: "Suffering, ending with the body and so forth, is to be abandoned," meaning that it must be relinquished,
because it is characterized by affliction (*bādhana*).
That which is not to be abandoned is not like that,
such as the true nature of the self and liberation;
[he who is] a master has conquered ignorance.

Although dispassion (*vairāgya*) is the absence of passion (*rāga*), nevertheless, because it exists in states such as deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and so forth, it is not conducive to liberation; therefore, what is intended here is absolute dispassion.
And that is established through the cessation of the capacity of the causes [of bondage].
Then that very [equanimity] was demonstrated:

even when sense objects are presented, what is this indifference? It is the intellect characterized by the exclusion of the categories of the rejectable and the acceptable, whose latent impressions of ignorance have been entirely uprooted by the powerful direct realization of reality; such is the meaning.
The meaning is that [the result] regarding the body and so forth must be understood exactly as it has been described.
Now, one who maintains that happiness is the absence of suffering does not find it undesirable that dharma has non-existence as its fruit;
nor is this an unobserved phenomenon. Therefore—
He says: "Even though...

Just as the prolongation of time for pleasure is based on scripture (*āgamika*), so too should it be understood that the excellence of its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is both based on experience (*ānubhavika*) and based on scripture (*āgamika*).
Nor should it be argued that an increase [in the result] is possible through an increase in its counter-positive, as is the case with darkness;

for if the fruit of dharma is the absence of suffering, it must be stated to be a *pradhvaṃsa* (destruction), since prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the other types of non-existence cannot be produced.
And for that [suffering], there is indeed no limitation by time;
nor is there a rule regarding the existence of a limit of the same kind, as is the case with darkness.
For there is no determining factor to suggest that suffering must necessarily occur immediately after the enjoyment of the Brahma-world.

Just as the cessation of suffering is equal when the stomach is filled by means of a special rice soup or the like, or by a lump of boiled grain (kulmāṣapiṇḍikā), so too it is with the positions of Indra and Brahmā; thus there would be no distinction whatsoever in their essential nature.

Furthermore, one who desires heaven, having performed sacrifices and the like, might at some point experience the suffering of hell due to unrighteousness (adharma) incurred from obstructed livelihood, and only thereafter experience heaven.
However, there is no fixed rule that [liberation] occurs immediately after the fall of the human body; otherwise, this would not be possible,
because dharma has the destruction of suffering as its primary fruit.

Furthermore, there can be no destruction of that which has not arisen; therefore, having practiced the Dharma, one would necessarily have to experience the sufferings of hell and so forth first, even if one were unwilling, and only thereafter would those [sufferings] cease.
Thus, the Dharma would be rendered useless; for it is better to avoid touching the mud from afar than to wash it off.
According to this principle. //21//
// Purity //

Since the objects of negation, such as the body and so forth, have been defined, the occasion for defining liberation (apavarga), which consists in their cessation, has arrived; thus he says: "In sequence," etc.
Although the mind is not born, nevertheless, because it is incapable of functioning without the support of karma, that [karma] itself is its birth; thus it was said, "all [beings] are being born.
And in this context, since the correlates—the body and so forth—are internal (ādhyātmika), their destruction as well is exclusively internal.

Liberation (mokṣa) is the absolute non-existence of suffering for that [self] distinguished [by the attainment of knowledge] subsequent to liberation while living; thus, there is no deviation [of the definition] by means of the absolute non-existence of suffering residing in space and so forth.
For transformation (pariṇāma) would consist either in the cessation of a prior substrate and the arising of another substrate, as held by the Nihilists (vaināśika); or—

Either there would be the cessation of the previous dharma and the arising of another dharma, as for the Sāṃkhyas; or else, one conceptualizes these two alternatives: "either in its entirety" or "in the former [case]. Regarding the first:
Let alone immutability; the meaning is that even transformational permanence (pariṇāminityatā) would not exist.
Regarding the phrase "in one part":
if there were an absolute non-difference between the property and the substratum, or if there were both difference and non-difference, [the following would occur].
In either case, there is no such thing as immutable permanence.
But if there were absolute difference [between Brahman and the world], how could it be said that "all this is indeed Brahman"?
The meaning is that he respected the words of the Śruti.
"Because of having parts" means because of having constituent elements;
that is to say, because of possessing the properties of arising and passing away which have become one's own nature.
"Like a jar and so forth":
the meaning is that just as jars and other such things, which are attributes of Brahman, are impermanent, so too Brahman— whose nature is non-different from them— would also be impermanent.
Nor should it be argued that Brahman must be a transforming eternal;
for the doctrine of non-absolutism (anekāntavāda) has already been refuted,
and the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryavāda) will be refuted later.
Nor should it be said that this manifold expansion of the attributes of Brahman must be absolutely distinct [from it],
because the production of the manifest from the manifest will be established through the authority of direct perception in the upcoming investigation of material causes and so forth,
and because the eternality of atoms has already been established.
But if [the object] were merely its effect, it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanāt*).
Therefore, he states "the meaning of this" (*asyārthaḥ*) because the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "eternal" (*nityam*) does not, as it stands literally, set forth the opponent's position.
"This is the meaning" (*ityarthaḥ*).

"Accepted by others" means that the self is postulated as possessing eternal happiness, setting aside other causes, because it possesses qualities of that same class which are eternal— just as, according to the Mīmāṃsā system, space is postulated as possessing eternal sound because it is the substratum for sound produced by color.
In the Satkāryavāda system, however, the self possesses eternal bliss,
because that [bliss] is being resorted to by it.
"Whatever is supported by something must be eternal like that [support],
just as threads are [supported] by a cloth"— having raised this [objection], he refutes it, saying "And here...
He introduces an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in order to strengthen the point that [the reason] is inconclusive (anaikāntikatā).

Now, one might object: since Brahman is distinct from pleasure and its perception, and since Brahman—whose nature is pure and enlightened, and whose form is neither rising nor setting—is established by itself alone, what room is there for an inquiry into the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) therein?
For all means of valid cognition have experience (*anubhava*) as their ultimate limit.
Furthermore, why consider such things as manifestation (*abhivyakti*) and so forth?
Even the consequence that there would be no distinction between the states of liberation and saṃsāra has been raised, yet it is not undesirable; therefore, he says: "This is the intended meaning.
Is the self merely the experience of sensory pleasure, or is it something distinct from that?
He refutes the first [position] with the words "pleasure" (*sukham*). Having recalled the previously stated reasoning, he states another [argument] with "for not" (*na hi*).
Now, one might object: "Are not the arising and passing away of pleasure and its perception merely apparent, and not real?"

Nor can a superimposition of contradictory attributes—which is merely imagined—be the cause of difference, for that would lead to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that even a crystal would be differentiated by the redness, blackness, and so forth produced by its proximity to lac, the *tāpiccha* flower, and the like. Anticipating this objection, the author refutes it with the words "nor indeed the self [of the substrate] alone.

The sense is that it is impossible for a crystal, while manifesting as one and the same in preceding and succeeding moments by virtue of its own nature, to have its identity excluded from blue and other colors while being superimposed as having the nature of blue and so forth.

It might be argued as follows: although self-awareness has the nature of the Self, by the power of beginningless ignorance it manifests as non-Self; and though it is unified within the Self through recognition, it manifests as if divided due to the coloring of various objects—just as the reflection of the sun in the sky, though experienced as one, appears divided in water due to the diversity of ripples. To this [it is replied]:
He says: "And this is not non-existent.
The meaning is this:
it is simply not possible for that very same person to be both deluded and non-deluded at that very same time with respect to that very same object.
Therefore, the so-called "inexplicability" (*durghaṭatva*) of ignorance is nothing but an ornament (*alaṅkāra*); this should be countered by the maxim of "stretching out the foot.
This [objection] would be based on seeking a sublation (*bādhaka*) regarding the cognition of difference;
however, we shall explain that such a sublation does not exist.
But in the case of a reflection, the error is indeed quite evident. He refutes the second [position] with the words, "And it is not adventitious.
Now, who says that consciousness is eternal in the self?
However, since the Self alone has the nature of eternal consciousness, he says: "Nor is it the Self itself.

Nor should it be argued that there is indeed a recollection in the form, "I slept happily," because then there would follow the undesirable consequence of a recollection in the form, "I sleep happily" or "I knew that [sleep]," just as there is the recollection, "I know this jar" or "I knew that [jar]."

In that case, is this [experience] "I slept happily" merely an inference of the absence of suffering, like the inference of the absence of cognition expressed as "I slept and was not aware of anything"? Or is it by what mark [is it known]? By the non-recollection of that which ought to be recollected.
What is the subject (*dharmin*)? Is it the self (*ātman*) as being presently experienced, or as being recollected, or as being recognized through re-cognition (*pratyabhijñāyamāna*)?
If it is asked: "Even so, since the state of deep sleep was not experienced, and for that very reason was not remembered, how can it be referred to by the word 'that'?"— it is not so.

Because the identity between the prior and subsequent states is recognized through the general application of the middle state as well—just as a jar perceived previously and perceived later is inferred to have been characterized by an absence of cognition during the middle state, such that one thinks "this was not known"—nothing is untenable. Let it be that the self’s cognition and pleasure are distinct from each other; nevertheless, if a cognition consisting of pleasure is not experienced within the self by another cognition, [then the objection remains].
"This is so; however, [the claim] that it does not manifest even by itself is unproven," he says, "and pleasure also.

Thus, one must accept that pleasure is eternal in the self and is manifested by a distinct cognition that is indeed different [from the self]. Regarding this, he says in the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vārtika*: "Thus, therefore.
Now, when the cognition of pleasure derived from sense objects is to be produced, why should the contact of the self and the mind be required as something distinct from pleasure?
For even in that case, if there were a dependence on the mere object, it would follow that the perception of form and so forth occurs through the mind alone;
if the rebuttal is that the external [perception] depends on the mind while the internal does not, then that same [rebuttal] applies here as well.
Therefore, he clarifies the Vārttika with the words: "in the state of saṃsāra."

He clarifies the intention residing in the heart of the opponent, the author of the *Vārttika*, who seeks to avoid the futility of the effort undertaken, in order to connect it with the *Siddhāntavārttika*: "Indeed, in your view...
For just as one who acts according to a treatise is one who ought to act, so too is he [the one who acts] capable of accomplishing the goal.
And it is not possible for that which is eternal [to be produced];
for it cannot be brought into existence because it is eternal,
nor can it be modified because it is unchanging.
Nor is there anything to be attained;
for its attainment cannot be characterized by a relationship, because it is non-transmigratory, nor can it be characterized by identity,
because that is impossible in either case— whether [the self] is already established or not yet established.
Nor is it characterized by cognition,
because that too has been discarded through the alternative of being either eternal or non-eternal;
nor is it characterized by the state of being an object.
Because there is no excess [of properties];
and because, if that were the case, since it would have already arisen, upon its destruction there would again be no connection;
for an excess over the six categories is unestablished.
If it were a positive entity (bhāvatva), it would necessarily be included within that [category];
if it were a non-entity (abhāvatva), its counter-correlate (pratiyogin) would be untenable. Nor is it something to be refined (saṃskārya).
Because it is incapable of having any excellence added to it.
Therefore, because it is impossible [to achieve], eternal happiness is not a purpose; rather,
the cessation of suffering is the purpose, because that is what is to be accomplished— such is the nature of reality.
On this point, they say: But surely even suffering, along with its causes, does not exist in an ultimate sense. Therefore, of what could there be an absence that is possible to achieve?
For activity directed toward pleasure is likewise identical to activity based on the manifestation of ignorance.

Regarding this, he says: "Dharma and adharma. Having kept this previously mentioned point in mind, he states: "They can be exhausted through experience. Not only is this view of eternal happiness useless for liberation, [but it is also untenable].
On the contrary, he says it is contradictory: "But otherwise...
Therefore, others should not grant even the slightest opportunity for this [objection], but rather should strive solely toward the cessation of ignorance, because that is possible.
The meaning is "because it is not contradictory.

Therefore, the teaching of the Supreme Lord—who speaks in a manner that is logical and faultless—cannot possibly be without purpose, nor can it have a contrary purpose; thus, he states "therefore" to show that it is only logical that the scriptural passages concerning bliss (*ānanda*) are figurative (*bhākta*).
If it is argued that eternal happiness exists,
and that even if one does not initiate or grasp anything, one will nonetheless exist by performing some action through being a causal condition (*nimitta*),
this is not so, because the meaning of the commentary has not been understood.
For the state of being a cause (*nimittatā*) is pervaded by the state of being a material cause (*upādānatā*).

Otherwise, even for things such as form (*rūpa*) that are not material causes, if one were to admit that they serve as some kind of causal sign (*pratinimitta*) for cessation, it would follow that the cessation of the entire continuum [of existence] would occur.
If you say, "Let it be so"?
Regarding this, the answer is given in the commentary:
thus, although the two who speak excessively regarding gain and loss have agreed upon the definition of liberation as intended by us, they have been refuted;
however, those such as the Sāṃkhyas have not been raised [for discussion] because they do not hold such a view.
For they indeed dispute intensely regarding these modes; and that must be investigated in each respective case. //22//
Thus concludes the section on the definition of valid cognition.
// Chapter on the Characteristics of the Limbs Preceded by Logic //
// Purity //

Since the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is dependent upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and since it is that which is most desired to be known, doubt (*saṃśaya*) and the other categories are subordinated to those two.

Furthermore, when the system of logic (*nyāya*)—along with its primary and secondary members—is to be explained, the section on doubt and the rest is elevated above other treatises because it serves as a preliminary member.
Even within that [section], the consideration of the purpose (*prayojana*) and so forth occurs only when there is doubt.
Nor is it the case that doubt arises only after one has investigated the purpose; thus, even in this sequence of definitions, the rule is that doubt comes first.
With the intention that the statement of the definition and the mention of the subject matter form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), he says "doubt" (in the commentary).
For this very reason, he explains the second reading as "in some cases."
Now, if this is the general definition of doubt,
let it be simply that "doubt is deliberation" (*vimarśaḥ saṃśayaḥ*).
If, however, these are the specific definitions?

Since there is no occasion for those [subsequent categories] until the general definition has been established, and since either the term "investigation" (vimarśa) or "doubt" (saṃśaya) would otherwise be redundant, he says: "And here...
The word *lakṣaṇa* refers to the sentence that constitutes the definition.
By the term "vimarśa" (reflective awareness), both the general definition in terms of its object and its essential nature are indicated.
Regarding these, he states the first [definition] with the words "in one [object].
As for the enumeration "reflective awareness of four contradictory objects," it is purposeless.
In the case of "Is it a post or a person?", because there is a consideration of an infinite number of substances and so forth;
and if [you argue that] it is by way of predominance, then [it would apply] only to two [possibilities].
For this negation is not the primary one.
He states the second [alternative] with "What indeed" (*kiṃsvit*);
the word *kim* introduces the inquiry.

The word *svid* indicates an alternative view (*pakṣāntara*). Thus, the meaning is: "Is this so, or rather is it thus? It should be understood as recurring (*anuvartanīya*) or being repeated (*āvartanīya*) according to the requirements of the sense.

Since the term "deliberation" (*vimarśa*) implies the intended meaning [of doubt] through its proximity to the term "doubt" (*saṃśaya*), he stated [the definition] together with that very term. He says, "here, the qualified [doubt]," indicating that there are three distinct types of doubt characterized respectively as follows: one in which both members are primarily affirmative like mutual negations (*parasparaniṣedha*);
another in which both members are primarily negative while implying each other's affirmation;
and yet another in which the affirmation and negation consist in the nature of mutual exclusion (*parasparaviraharūpa*). Thus, the "qualified" doubt is what is being defined.

"The word 'lakṣya' [means] the referent of the word 'lakṣya'. He states that "the object of definition (lakṣya) is that which pertains to the quality" by saying "here, the qualified [is the object]. [Thus,] the word 'lakṣya' [denotes] the referent of the word 'lakṣya'.
Similarity residing in qualities is indeed a specific intermediate universal (*avāntarasāmānyaviśeṣa*),
because it is on account of this that the cognition "these two have equal height and circumference" arises;
he demonstrates that very [universal] by way of its cause, namely the individual instances (*vyakti*), in the words "number, dimension," and so forth.

"Connection with the general properties of largeness and length" means connection with the mere general properties of largeness and length. Here, the author of the Vārttika—having raised an objection by stating that the mere existence of common properties (as in the phrase "from the occurrence of common properties," etc. is not a cause for doubt, and that perception is not explicitly mentioned—he explains the three-fold resolution: "Even though... and so forth.
In the first [case], the word *anupapatti* denotes existence (*sattā*) and refers to that;
however, by the phrase "perception (*upalabdhi*), however, depends on specific qualities," this is implied.
In the second [case], although this word *upapatti* has multiple meanings, it is employed here as denoting perception (*upalabdhi*).

But in the third [interpretation], it is precisely a word for existence (*sattā*) that, through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), has perception as its primary meaning. In that case, the phrase "dependent on particulars" would imply a cognition of the universal, provided that it were negating the cognition of the particular.
But this is not the case; therefore, he says "viśeṣa" (particularity).
This is due to the force of the sentence, that is, by virtue of the capacity for syntactic connection (*anvaya-yogyatā*).
Although the word "dependent on particulars" does not directly negate the perception of particulars, [it implies it].
Nevertheless, it is directed toward that [meaning] by way of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā).
And this [indication] proceeds because of an obstruction to the primary sense,
because of a connection with the intended meaning, and because of a purpose in employing a term that is not directly expressive.

Regarding that primary [position], he states the sublation: "And not... To avoid the objection concerning the purpose, he indicates its nature as a worldly definition and states the relationship by means of an example: "Just as...

For just as there is an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) between the Gaṅgā and its bank by including their conjunction, so too, by way of having a single object, there is an inseparable connection between the non-grasping [of the object] and the desire to remember, established by a fixed sequence of priority and posteriority, with doubt interposed between them.
The meaning is that such is the connection, due to a particular ease [of understanding];
its purpose can also be stated.
For it has been stated that doubt is "dependent on particulars" (*viśeṣāpekṣa*) because it requires a particular;
and thus, when it is said that it generates an inquiry regarding the particular, its result has been demonstrated.
This is what was meant by the statement: "Because it exists when there is doubt."
By this, the general definition [of perception] should also be understood as being established by way of its result.
However, regarding the second [definition], the objection is that there is a lack of evidence for a decisive criterion (*vinigamanā*).
Having raised this, he answers it with the *Vārttika*: "It might be so," and so forth.

Regarding the third point, there is the objection that there is no purpose [for defining it]; he refutes this through the *Vārttika* itself: "And this definition is not unworldly," and so forth—the implication being that it is not something for which one would have to rely on a specific purpose.
Now, one might object: "But isn't 'being produced' (*kṛtakatva*) the reason (*hetu*) for the determination [of sound as impermanent]?"
It is not [the case] that this applies to exclusion (*vyavaccheda*); therefore, he says: "but rather, of impermanence.

Now, even so, since a property that exists in what is intended and in things of its own class, while also existing in others, is denoted by the word "similar" (*samāna*), from where does the restriction [of the definition] come? To this he says: "For it is similar...
Here, the refutation remains until the introduction of the subsequent [passage].
But once that [exclusion] has been entered into, there is no further attachment [to the object].
For if a common property were the cause of exclusion, how could there be an absence of both proving and subverting means of valid cognition?
This is because the absence of those very [means] constitutes that [exclusion] itself.
If it is asked, "How then is this a cause for exclusion?
[the answer is: Nor does a term such as "perception" (upalabdhi) and so forth preclude the capacity of its opposite to either establish or subvert [an object].
One might object: "But surely there is a specific definition of that [object];

therefore, even if that [definition] were absent, there would be no room for what is to be said. To show that this argument has been stated for that very purpose, he says—while avoiding the charge of redundancy—"preceded by deliberation" (*vimarśapūrvakam*).
For previously, the merits and faults of performing and not performing [an action] were not considered; now they are being considered, and thus there is no redundancy.
For this very reason, he said earlier: "he joins."
Now he says: "it determines," as in the case of "taste in the seventh. For instance, taste as the seventh might be the object as the locus (*dharmin*) in a cognition of doubt.
Or by way of its intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*)?
Never indeed does the world doubt in this manner: "Is this the seventh taste, or a post, or a person?
or "Is it a substance (*dravya*), or a quality (*guṇa*)?"
Nor can it be doubted in this way: "Is this perceived object the seventh taste or the tenth substance?
If it is argued that there certainly does arise a doubt as to whether the seventh taste exists or not, we say no;
for there is no recollection of what has never been experienced.
And because that which is not remembered cannot be the object of doubt, [the author] says: "Not so.
For even when there is the perception of a similar object, the failure to remember occurs due to the absence of intense practice, respect, or a clear cognition.
For just as the mental impression (saṃskāra) is produced by such conditions, so too is that which is awakened by it;
thus, "two" means by way of duality.
The meaning is that the intention is to speak of the immediate [offense] (*ānantarya*) when both [factors] are combined.

By means of its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), [the author] states the unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) consisting of multiple attributes. In this regard, the author of the *Vārttika* states an objection to the primary [interpretation] under the guise of refuting the explanation of certain partial interpreters (*ekadeśin*);

therefore, he says "multiple," etc. Since the state of being produced by conjunction (*saṃyogajatva*) does not apply to all things such as substances (*dravya*), he specifies it as "in the case of an effect-substance" (*kāryadravya*), and so forth.
Thus, regarding the primary [meaning]:

As if showing that the author of the Bhāṣya has explained the Sūtra by resorting to a secondary interpretation because he perceived an obstacle, he introduces the Vārttika with the words "by the explanation of the Bhāṣyakāra.
He asks again: "If this word is technical (lākṣaṇika), what is its connection?"—the intended sense being, "who [would ask this]? as the remainder of the sentence.

Having summarized the meaning of the Vārttika as "the relationship [of *viśeṣa*] is the state of being the delimited (*avadhi*) and the delimiting (*avadhimat*)," he says, "This is what is meant," in order to show that by its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *dharma*, the word *viśeṣa* is precluded from having an abstract sense (*bhāvasādhana*). He says,
"This is what is meant," and adds "is supplied" (*adhyāhṛta*) to indicate that the word *viśeṣa* is precluded from having an abstract sense through its coreferentiality with the word *dharma*.
If this is so, then the commentary [would be] "of that which is manifold" without a basis; therefore, he says: "by means of the generality of relation.
"Another seed" means another relation.
For it was previously stated that sound, by virtue of being produced by disjunction and so forth, is distinguished from those things possessing the opposite properties within its own substratum.
The intention [of the author] is that, however, in the present case, because it is indeed a different word from its own substratum, it is not excluded;
therefore, the relationship of the "excluded" and the "excluder" constitutes another reason (bījāntara).
The meaning is that this has been explained as follows: that very property of the manifold which functions as the excluder is itself called "the manifold."

Now, if this is the case, what is the purpose of the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), since the word "manifold" (*aneka*) may simply be taken in its primary sense? For previously, it was argued that "the property of the manifold" (*anekadharma*)—if it were understood through direct inherence (*samavāya*) or other such relations—was already covered by the word "common" (*sāmānya*) itself, and thus [the term *anekadharma*] was rejected. However, as a means of exclusion (*nivartaka*), it is indeed possible for the manifold to exist; therefore, he says: "But not here."
Why? Because [the author] will demonstrate this:
if the word *aneka* (many) were merely a term denoting a relation (*saṃbandhi*), it would not be in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the word *dharma*.
And thus, since a *bahuvrīhi* compound could not be formed, the *dharmin* (the subject possessing properties) would not be obtained; such is the meaning.

Having thus concluded the Vārttika that follows the Bhāṣya and having introduced an independent Vārttika, he first explains it in accordance with the definition, beginning with the word "prakāra": "one" means belonging to a single genus; "many" means not belonging to a single genus.
The meaning is "of a different genus.

Therefore, having metaphorically attributed non-difference between the qualifier and the qualified on the grounds that both are causes for the cognition of the qualified (viśiṣṭabuddhi), the author—intending to show that this word *aneka* (many), which primarily denotes the qualified object, is here applied to the qualifying property (*dharma*)—says: "the meaning is that it is the cause of the cognitions of both difference and non-difference."
For this very reason, he will state in the conclusion: "It is manifold through metaphorical designation because it is the cause of those cognitions.
[The phrase] "than the others" means than substance, quality, and action, but not merely than words.
Because the exclusion of that [property] is of no use for doubt, he confirms this very point with the *Vārttika*, saying: "This is what [the author] says.

Although it might seem to have little purpose to state that [the uncommon property] is the cause of a single cognition when an uncommon property is intended to be expressed, [it serves a specific function].

Nevertheless, when a doubt arises from an uncommon [reason], it culminates only in the state of belonging to that class (*tajjātīyatā*), and not in the state of being that specific individual (*tadvyaktitā*); for even members of that same class are seen to possess different properties, yet they are not *that very thing*.
To indicate this, the fact that [the reason] resides in multiple individuals has been shown.
Therefore, he justifies the singular number with the word "jātyā" (by way of genus).
Now he explains in accordance with the examples, [saying] "beginning with 'existent'":
the meaning is that in this explanation, he states an appropriate example.

To clarify that the intent is to provide examples, he dispels the doubt as to why "existence" (*sat*) and so forth—which are indeed common [to both sides]—were introduced at an occasion when only uncommon [reasons] were required, by stating: "in the categories such as substantiality" (*dravyatvādikoṭi*).
"Existence" (*sat*) means possessing *sattā* (being-ness).
"Impermanent" (*anitya*) means subject to destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*).
It possesses substance by virtue of being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*);
it possesses an effect, characterized by prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*);
and it possesses a cause, both as a non-inherent cause (*nimitta*) and otherwise, as well as universals and particulars, and intermediate universals.

Regarding what we previously stated— that doubt, characterized by the predominance of both affirmation and negation of each other, is to be defined as the second characteristic— it is now demonstrated, in the context of discussing the established tenets (siddhānta), by beginning with negation and concluding with affirmation: "Is it a quality (guṇa), since it is excluded from substance (dravya) and action (karman)," and so forth.

But surely this objection is itself untenable; for there is no proof for a disjunction produced by a disjunction, since even a thousand disjunctions occupying the same location arise simultaneously. To this he says: "This is the intended meaning."

Although the Vaiśeṣikas maintain that after the disjunction of the two bamboo halves there is the destruction of their conjunction, and from that the destruction of the substance, and then— depending either on the time characterized by that destruction of the substance or on the independent part— the disjunction residing in the two halves produces a disjunction from a location such as space;
Nevertheless, because it is not the subject at hand, the sequence of the destruction of conjunction and the destruction of the substance has not been set forth.
For the action under discussion must produce two disjunctions either successively or simultaneously.
Not the first [alternative],
because it is certain that action acts without delay when beginning a separation, since it is independent; or, if there were dependence, [it would not act].
One should not effect even the first division immediately;
for when a subsequent conjunction is to be produced, there is a delay due to the dependence upon the destruction of the prior conjunction.
However, the independence [of the cause] was stated with reference to adventitious states.
Not the second [alternative], for the Vaiśeṣikas maintain that when an action produces disjunction from a location such as space, it simultaneously produces [disjunction] from another part; however,
both of these positions, taken literally, are untenable.
For when the first division is to be performed, that very time [of the original action] applies because of the independence of the rite;
but when the second is to be performed, independence exists precisely at the time immediately following the first.
Therefore, there is no lapse of time—this reasoning is also established.

The phrase beginning with "yadā" (when) refers to the state [of the atoms] while they remain within the opening buds of lotuses; therefore, he explains its meaning by stating, "for there is action in the parts.
The expression "kāryaikārya" (at the same time as the effect and the non-effect) indicates proximity.
Now, let it be granted for the time being that there is indeed no ascertainment of the aforementioned pervasion;

nevertheless, an action which initiates a disjunction that is the antithesis of a non-constituent conjunction of substances does not [also] initiate one that is the antithesis of a constituent conjunction of substances.

Or, if that were the case, since it would be possible for both types of disjunction to arise simultaneously from any action whatsoever, it would follow that whenever a part moves, all substances [in which it inheres] must perish; yet this is not so.

Therefore, once it is established that "the action which produces the opposite of a non-productive conjunction does not produce the opposite of a productive conjunction," its converse is also established. To this, he says: "But because of the difference in the nature of the action."
This is the meaning:
a distinction in the case of disjunction must necessarily be admitted, otherwise the restriction [of its occurrence] would be untenable.
In accordance with that [distinction], one must necessarily admit a distinction in action as well, whether based on its genus (*jāti*) or on its auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).
This distinction results, in one case, from being the producer of two disjunctions that are the opposites of two conjunctions— both of which are productive (*ārambhaka*)— and in the other case,
from being the producer of merely a disjunction that is the opposite of a non-productive (*anārambhaka*) conjunction.

Alternatively, it cannot be determined that [the action] in one case produces only a disjunction that is the opposite of a productive conjunction (*ārambhaka-saṃyoga*), while in another case it produces only a disjunction that is the opposite of a non-productive conjunction (*anārambhaka-saṃyoga*);
for even a disjunction that is the opposite of a non-productive conjunction—
It will do so; what contradiction is there?

Just as an action, while being a producer of a non-productive posterior conjunction, may—due to some specific distinction—also be a producer of a productive posterior conjunction, otherwise, by this very same reasoning, one would have to postulate that even in those cases, the conjunctions between cause and non-cause must be preceded by conjunctions between mere causes.
And just as there is no proof for that sequence, so it is here as well:
[the first case] is a single division residing in only two parts,
while the other [case] is a twofold division residing in two parts and also residing in both the part and the non-part.

And as for this distinction, it is better that it be so: namely, that one [disjunction] produces a disjunction which is the opposite of a non-productive conjunction, while the other produces a disjunction which is the opposite of both a productive and a non-productive conjunction.

Therefore, there is no evidence for a disjunction between cause and non-cause preceded by a disjunction between causes alone; thus, he says "therefore" to clarify that this non-acceptance has as its sole result the manifestation of this much.
However, he says "but that which... to show that a disjunction between effect and non-effect preceded by a disjunction between cause and non-cause is accepted as being based on valid proof.
In some readings, "inherence in a single object that is the effect" (*kāryaikārthasamavāya*) is given with reference to a tree;
"inherence in a single object that is both effect and cause" (*kāryakāraṇaikārthasamavāya*) is given with reference to a finger.

The word "sa" (that) refers to the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*): "produced by a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) belonging to the same class as the uncommon cause. The phrase "because it is the first sound" (*ādyaśabdatvāt*) refers to the meaning of the reason (*hetu*).

Although, in the case of sound, the uncommon cause is indeed that disjunction which has another disjunction as its expectant cause (*apekṣākāraṇa*), it would have been more appropriate to state that very thing [as the reason].

Nevertheless, the author of the Vārttika spoke thus by accepting a division produced from the division of the cause alone; he says accordingly: "Thus, in this way," and he supports even this [point] as being subject to deviation: "That too.
Even so, although the reason "because it is born of division" remains entirely faultless, [the objection persists].
For the birth of a substance or of an action is not possible from disjunction;
indeed, that [disjunction] is inherent in that which does not initiate a substance and is thus simply not a cause.
However, that [conjunction] inherent in the originating cause is indeed the destroyer [of the action] by way of destroying [the original] conjunction;
for even in the case of action, disjunction cannot be the cause of the first [action], because if that [original conjunction] were absent, the disjunction itself would be impossible.
Nor can it be the cause of the subsequent [action], since that arises only upon the cessation of the preceding action.
But when that [sound] ceases due to a subsequent conjunction, then [the substratum] also [ceases] due to disjunction; how then could the production of a subsequent action arise from disjunction?
Therefore, the fact that sound is produced by disjunction—which possesses an unambiguous pervasion—is indeed a proof for its being a quality.
Nor does the defect of being "uncommon" (asādhāraṇya) arise by taking into account its specific sub-varieties;
for if that were the case, even smoke would be non-informative.
Nevertheless, this should be understood as merely an explanation of the examples stated in the Bhāṣya.

[Objection: Is this reasoning not one that leads to a conclusion contrary to what was intended, namely, that [the universal] exists only among things of the same class? To this he says: "Even though... (yadyapi).
The meaning is that this very same reasoning as before has been stated out of respect for the author of the Bhāṣya.
By reminding us of what preceded, he introduces the Vārttika while clarifying that it represents a different approach: "Previously... (pūrvam).

For a property that is common (*samāna*) and resides in the subject (*pakṣa*) is of the same nature as the properties of both the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*);
and this negation of that nature is what is meant by "manifold" (*aneka*).
Thus, it is stated that for a property residing in the subject, there is a difference in nature from the properties of both the similar and dissimilar instances.

And that property which belongs to the subject (*pakṣaga*) and is of a different class from both the properties of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), is indeed "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*); thus, because it is inseparably connected with the thing to be expressed (*abhidheya*), it falls outside the scope of the definition (*lakṣaṇa*).
This is what was stated by the words "only by way of secondary indication" (*lakṣaṇayāiva*).

He applies the *vārttika*: "By the word *samāna*... Even though the non-common (*asamāna*) [attribute] is also presented to the mind as a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), since its status as a cause of doubt is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), that which must be stated is it; therefore, we understand from the fact that the author of the Sūtra employs multiple words that this indeed is the intended meaning.
The meaning of the construction is that [the author] has demonstrated this by means of this turn of phrase (*vacobhaṅgī*).
By this, the agreement of the author of the Sūtras with all the aforementioned modes is shown.
It should be understood that the purpose of the various types of definitions has been demonstrated by the passage beginning with "pṛcchati" (he asks).
First of all, it must be established in the second [chapter] that there is no recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) whatsoever directed toward an individual (*vyakti*), such as the letter *ga*.
Even when such recognition does exist, its object is doubted in terms of its referent: is it the individual or the universal (*jāti*)?

Even when the object is indeed an individual (vyakti), there remains the doubt as to whether it is a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) or not; with this intention, he states vaguely that it is possible even through similarity (sādṛśya).
This is itself doubtful.

Although a proponent of the view that the universal alone is the referent of a word does not accept that individual cows and so forth are "qualified" by cowness and so forth— just as one might say they are qualified by the universal—
nevertheless, through the firmness of one's own system, the opponent must also be made to accept this.

Otherwise, how could there even be the cognition of an inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) with the denotable object through the individuals? And in the absence of that, how could there even be indication (*lakṣaṇā*)?
How is it not so, and so forth?

Nor should it be argued that even if there is doubt regarding the nature of sound, there would be no fault if the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) were established by its being ascertained in the case of a jar and so forth.

For if the pervasion were ascertained through a universal induction—namely, "whatever is produced is necessarily impermanent"—then the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) would indeed produce certainty regarding sound.
It is only because of the presence of a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) that it does not establish the probandum (*sādhya*) in the case of sound.
If it is argued that [the reason] functions with respect to the intellect and so forth by way of being unimpeded—

no, for even when one refutes the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the proof of the counter-position (*pratipakṣa*), there is no contradiction in the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) as long as it remains possible.

If there were such a contradiction, the probandum would not be established even from a non-defective [reason], which would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the total destruction of all inference.
And this very point will be stated immediately hereafter.

If it is argued that, because there is an absence of universal inclusion (*sarvopasaṃhāra*) regarding the fault of over-extension (*vyāptidoṣa*), how can the probandum (*sādhya*) be established in the case of cognition and so forth by the force of that [reasoning], and that therefore the pervasion (*vyāpti*) must exclude sound whose reality is doubtful;
then, in that case, one should state: "because it is produced, while being other than sound."
And likewise, if by chance sound were in fact non-eternal, then there would be the fallacy of an ineffective qualification; thus, it is a case of "doubtful ineffective qualification.

Therefore, it was well said: "Since the state of being eternal or non-eternal is doubtful in the case of sound, the property of being produced does not necessarily follow [from it], and is thus not inherently connected with non-eternality."

The meaning is as follows: because each [reason]—whether through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—fails to lead toward either of the two alternatives (due to the variation in conditions, the gradation of intensity such as "intense" or "more intense," and the fact that each has its own counter-reason), it cannot be a cause of doubt.
Nor can it be a cause of certainty, because it lacks the essential form of having no counter-reason (*asatpratipakṣatva*).
"But when they are combined, they possess uniqueness (*asādhāraṇatva*).
The meaning is that, in that very form, they serve as the cause of doubt and not otherwise.
For nasalization (*anunāsikatva*) and the like, being particular universals (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*), when they are perceived, must necessarily reside in perceptible individuals.
Furthermore, a particular (*vyakti*) perceived by one sense organ and a universal (*jāti*) perceived by another do not both fall within the range of a single cognition.
Thus, even though the particular which serves as the substratum for universals such as nasality (*ānunāsikatva*) is itself audible, its impermanence is established for both disputants;
it remains only a matter of whether that particular has space (*ākāśa*) as its substratum, or—
Or else it has another locus; such is the disagreement.
Let this matter rest for now.

[Objection: Even so, in the view of the Naiyāyikas, properties such as nasality (*ānunāsikatva*) reside only in the substratum of sound (*śabda*); thus, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from the subject (*pakṣa*). [Reply:
No, because the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) of the reason is established by the existence of that property even in something whose nature is not the phoneme *a*.
If it is argued that this [reason] is also a subject (*pakṣa*), we say no; for when that [subject] is observed, the reason is exposed as being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) by way of contradiction,
and since it is in fact a property of sound, it suffers from the fallacy of "mis-timing" (*kālātyayāpadeśa*).

Furthermore, form and the other [sensory objects] are not the causes [of their own cognition], because they are eternal and are each apprehended by a single sense organ such as the eye, just like the universal "form-ness" (rūpatva) and so forth; this is because they share the same logical status [as the probandum].
“Because of the misconception,” and so forth.

And because this doubt, which has been defined, consists primarily of an affirmation and a negation that are mutually exclusive, the commentator himself has clearly shown the example: “The self exists” and “The self does not exist. Therefore, it was not elaborated upon by the authors of the Vārttika and the Ṭīkā.

This is merely an illustration; indeed, this alone should be taken as authoritative, because when the self has never been perceived before, it cannot be the locus of doubt for something that has not entered into memory.
Alternatively, since it is impossible to deny [the existence of sound] entirely given that it has been perceived,
this point will be elaborated upon in the third chapter and is therefore set aside here;
some maintain that sound is eternal.
"Others say no," and so forth, should be cited as examples.

"By way of difference in cause" means that it is threefold according to the distinction of its characteristics: that which is primarily affirmative, that which is primarily negative, and that which is primarily both negative and affirmative.
And it is not the case that [the person] has reached a state of non-habituation.

For if it is intended that— given the perception of one who has reached a state of non-habituation— there arises a doubt regarding truth or untruth because of the perception of the generality of "cognition" (*buddhitva*) while there is no certainty concerning the subsequent existence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), this is already covered by the very first word [of the definition].

If it is argued that what is intended here is a doubt regarding the meaning of those [two] doors, then does that doubt concern them in terms of their essential nature (*svarūpa*), in terms of place and time (*deśakāla*), or in terms of their mode (*prakāra*)?
First of all, the first alternative is inconsistent precisely because of contradiction.
For it is not possible [to think] "is this so, or is it not?

By ascertaining the absence of disturbances such as sleep, the first alternative—having that [disturbance] as its sole cause—is excluded; thus the second [alternative] is also rejected. However, if there is doubt regarding a disturbance, the doubt remains strictly internal.
Regarding the third case, however, he says: "neither a serpent nor a tree. Thus it is "inappropriate.
However, there is this distinction: in the case of "a post or a person," perception and non-perception remain unsettled precisely because they have not arisen.
In the case at hand, however, the cognition of water that has indeed arisen is not established because of the suspicion of its invalidity.
Thus, regarding the term "unfit" (ayogya):

if doubt were to arise from the non-perception of the unfit accompanied by the recollection of specific features (*viśeṣasmṛti*) without including the subject (*dharmin*), that doubt would not involve the alternative of absolute non-existence (*atyantānupalabdhi*),
because in that case there would be an absence of recollection.
Nor does it delineate the limit of perception.
For it is not the case that one can say "an atom exists" or "it does not exist," since it certainly does exist.
If you argue that it exists "here," then its existence is established only by taking a locus characterized by specific space, time, and so forth as its substratum.

And thus, being perceived, it would cause one to remember the particulars either through positive concomitance (*anvaya*), negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), or through contradiction (*vipratipatti*), but not by its own essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*); this is the meaning of "prior inclusion" (*pūrvānupraveśa*).
This has been stated: "There is no doubt without the perception of common characteristics and so forth.
When there is a distinction [in doubt] due to a difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), the threefold nature is based on the object;
however, it is indeed manifold.
The meaning is that each individual cause lacks the capacity to establish the specific determination of its object. //23//
// Purity //

It has been stated that although there is no difference in their being prior members [of the treatise], when doubt arises, one pursues the purpose (prayojana), and thus the purpose is placed after them. Furthermore, having pursued the purpose, one who wishes to investigate the reasoning (nyāya) that serves as its means follows the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta); therefore, in the enumeration, the illustrative example is placed after this [purpose].
He says "uddeśa" [etc. to show that this same connection applies here as well.

Considering that the word *artha* (object/purpose) is redundant in the definition because it contributes nothing [to its exclusion], he states the intended meaning (*tātparya*) with the words "herein" (*atre*).
Since the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*), even after restating the word *artha*, has not explained it, he says: "those together with their means" (*sasādhanau*).
[Objection: But if this is so, there is a contradiction with the subsequent commentary.

Because the word "that" (tat) in the phrase "one practices the means for the attainment and avoidance of that" refers back to the object (artha), and because the phrase "the means for the attainment and avoidance of pleasure and pain" connects with what has been previously introduced, he says: "And not...
In this regard, they supply the words "although... nevertheless" (yadyapi tathāpi) into the commentary (ṭīkā).
"Because it is observed," and so forth.
Thus, the meaning of the sentence is that precisely because it is authoritative (*prāmāṇika*), the purpose need not be stated.
[Objection: If this is the case, then the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) itself should also not be explained.
And since you have explained that very point, he says: "Nor is such a thing a means of valid cognition" (*na ca pramāṇam īdṛśam*).

The phrase "and just as" (*yathā ca*) means that for one who asserts that what is established by a means of valid cognition must not be spoken [contradictorily], there is a contradiction with his own conduct (*svacaritavirodha*).
How is this [agent] employed as a means—whether it be existent or non-existent?
If it is non-existent, is it by way of its own cognition or by another operation?
And where does it employ [the object]?
The meaning is that it must be established through investigation whether [the agent] exists in its own self or in its own instrument,
