Now, enough with this secondary characterization; let the mere statement itself be the means of proof (*sādhana*), for by that too its own object is established—that is, it is communicated. To this he says: "But if... [and so on].
For this would mean that the proof (*sādhana*) is the statement that establishes the probandum (*sādhya*);
and in that case, the thesis (*pratijñā*) itself would be the reason (*hetu*).
Alternatively, if the meaning is that the proof is the statement that establishes [the probandum] while excluding the word for the probandum itself—
To this, he says: "Now" (*atha*).
This objection was stated under the assumption that no other meaning was intended;
however, if it were formulated thus—that a statement which, by means of indicating a logical mark (*liṅga*), determines the proof of the probandum (*sādhya*)—then [the definition would be correct].
In that case, there would be an unwarranted insertion of words not heard in the original text (*aśrutādhyāhāra*).

Furthermore, it should be understood that the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)—if it were to include "by similarity with the example" and so forth—would either fail to be pervading (*avyāpti*) or would be unattainable.
Such being the case in this interpretation...

The doubt as to why the author of the commentary (*ṭīkākṛt*) himself introduces the phrase "situated precisely in the words of the aphorism" (*vacanapadamasūtrastham eva*)—namely, that there might be contradictions or over-extension—is thereby dispelled. [An opponent objects: "Even so, does this not lead to an over-extension (*prasaṅga*) regarding the application (*upanaya*)? To this he replies: "Even from the application (*upanayāt*).

For in the expression "the statement of the probandum and the probans" (*sādhyasādhanavacana*), the meaning understood is "the statement of an object qualified by the state of being a probans" (*sādhanatvaviśiṣṭārthavacana*).

Nor is there an application (upanaya); for even if it has as its object a thing that is such [as the conclusion], it does not express it as such, because it is devoid of the specific case-ending that manifests its status as a means of proof (sādhana).
For this very reason, there arises the expectation [of a reason], namely, "from what?
Thus, it does not follow from the statement "this is produced," but rather precisely from the statement "because of being produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*).

If so, what kind of thing is understood from the application (upanaya)? To this he says: "But rather... [It is] "inhering in itself," meaning devoid of properties such as being a means of proof (sādhanatva) and so forth. Why? Because the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadikārtha) is primary.
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "because it is employed with a case-ending that expresses only that much, due to its being directed toward that.
What is meant is this:
for the application (upanaya), unlike the reason (hetu), does not proceed when there is an expectancy as to "why" [it is so].
Nevertheless, once pervasion has been demonstrated by means of an example— let us grant this for the moment— even so,

when there arises the expectation as to whether or not the subject under discussion, which is the object of dispute, is qualified by that pervaded property, that very doubt is removed solely by the statement, "And this [subject] is likewise produced."
But this is not the case with the [reasoning] "because of being produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*).
Therefore, the meaning is that there is no confusion between the reason (*hetu*) and the application (*upanaya*), whether in terms of their meaning, their form, or their purpose.

Now, one might object: even if there is no such contingency when [the definition] is characterized as "speech" (vacana) with respect to either cognition or its object, nevertheless, in cases such as "the probandum and the probans" or "here, 'being produced' is the reason," there is indeed a contingency regarding speech itself;
for this too conveys an object of such a nature. To this, he says: "in a syllogistic statement" (nyāyavākya).
By this, the suitability for satisfying the expectation is shown.

Furthermore, when the question "Why? arises, neither the statement "the probandum and the probans" nor the statement "the property of being produced is the reason" is suitable for fulfilling that expectation.
Therefore, the meaning is that there is no such undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) regarding things of this kind.

Consequently, the designation of the object to be defined (*lakṣya*) as "the reason [is] by virtue of its being directed toward a specific [quality]" is not untenable; this is the remainder [of the sense].
[This refers to] "of the prescription of a qualified [entity]."
Nowhere has "similarity" (sādharmya) been prescribed as a defining characteristic of a logical reason (hetu),
such that a positive injunction (vidhi) here— qualified by its adjunct— would apply to the adjunct alone.
Nor is there here the adoption of similarity devoid of qualification, such that the injunction would have that much alone as its scope.
Furthermore, because there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) if both were intended as independent meanings,
this must therefore be a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭa-vidhi*), as there is no other recourse, just like the case of the "red turban" (*lohitoṣṇīṣa*).
Thus, the meaning is that the prohibition— which consists in the similarity of not being an example due to the absence of a non-red turban— is established by the force of the context.
He states another alternative:
the sense is that there is no fault even if the admission [of the thesis] consists merely in the cognition of a non-distinct common property (*aviśiṣṭasādharmyamātra*).

Now, if the subject at hand is established by the general rule alone, what is the purpose of mentioning the examples? And if it is not, then what is the use of the general rule? To this he says: "Because of similarity" and so forth.

Exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) will dispel over-extension (*atiprasakti*). By demonstrating its example, the definition of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is that which excludes. Exclusion is the cognition of avoidance.

For the purpose of ensuring that those [faults] which have been specifically identified are avoided within one's own discourse—by means of such methods as exclusion and so forth—even though this is already implied by the sense, it is stated explicitly;
such is the meaning of "its characteristic" (*tallakṣaṇam*).
"Not prescriptive" (*na vidhāyakam*) means that it is not in any way at all a prescriptive [statement].
The refutation of Dignāga is easy to understand.
To the question, "When the reason (*hetu*) ought to be illustrated, what is the purpose of stating the proposition (*pratijñā*)," he says: "In this context.

The sense is that once the reason has been illustrated, one must apply the definition [to it] and analyze the meaning of the reason; therefore, by way of occasion (*prasaṅga*), the meaning of the proposition is also analyzed.
Nevertheless, since destructions are manifold and there is no encompassing universal (*jāti*) or the like for them, how can pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth be established?

If it were argued that this is established merely by the non-difference of the objects to be characterized (*upalakṣya*), then the practical usage (*vyavahāra*) to be accomplished regarding Devadatta wearing earrings would also be accomplished regarding him wearing a staff; therefore, he says: "the contradictory" (*virodhī*).

For just as mere absence, by virtue of its very relation to a positive entity (*bhāva*) as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), becomes the cause of a single practical usage through a contingent universal (*aupādhika-sāmānya*), [so too is the case here].

The meaning is that, likewise, even with respect to its specific instances, there is no contradiction in their respective linguistic usages because they stand in a relationship of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) with preceding, succeeding, or other substrates.
Nor is it the case that [the action] has already attained its arising;
for in all cases, the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) as colored by the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).
And cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is the operation of the causal factors (*kāraka*). However, in the expression "the jar arises," the jar is not a causal factor because it does not yet exist.

Consequently, there must be either a metaphorical application of that [arising] to the non-factor due to its extreme proximity to the causal factors, or else a metaphorical application of the term for the effect to the causal factors themselves.
In both cases, the use of a verb occurs precisely at the time of entering into the operation [of the action], and not at the time of entering into the mere meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).
For people in the world do not say "he cooks" (*pacyate*) with reference to the mere meaning of the root when the cooking is already finished.
Why is that?
Because there is an absence of engagement with activity;
it is the same here as well. //34//
// Purity //
But surely, the absence of being a similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is not heard here in this sūtra, nor is it implied by the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*),
since its occurrence in the subject (*pakṣa*) is established through pervasion (*vyāpti*); [otherwise] one might suspect that existence in the similar instance is absolute.
But the [charge of being] "partial" (pākṣika) remains applicable.
And thus, even when a purely negative (kevalavyatirekin) reason is obtained, the "positive-negative" (anvayavyatirekin) reason is not thereby excluded.

Likewise, even in the absence of a similar instance (sapakṣa), the applicability of a reason that pervades the subject (pakṣa) while occurring in only a portion of the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) remains exactly as it was; thus he says: "nevertheless" (tathāpi).

The example "impermanent because of being corporeal" has been cited specifically to demonstrate that the restriction [of the reason] to the subject (pakṣavyāpti) maintains an indifference toward the absence of a similar instance (sapakṣa).
In reality, however, one should regard as a non-confused example: "This living body is not soulless, because it consists of flesh and so forth."

In order to exclude both of these, the word "only" (*eva*) is used with the example of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). Since the pervasion of the subject (*pakṣa-vyāpti*) has already been established by the preceding restriction, the phrase "only dissimilarity" (*vaidharmyam eva*) serves to exclude the nature of similarity (*sādharmya-rūpatā*); this would be the meaning.

[If it were so,] since the property that pervades the subject must necessarily be of the nature of dissimilarity from everything else, what possibility would there be for either of the two [similarity or dissimilarity] to occur?
Only the fault of being over-exclusive (asādhāraṇa) would follow;
and that is refuted by specifying [the reason] through an example of the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa), which demonstrates the absence of a similar instance (sapakṣa).
For if positive concomitance (anvaya) were intended only when a similar instance exists, then the statement "in the same way, due to dissimilarity" (tathā vaidharmyāt) would be entirely unnecessary.
Because the meaning is already established by the previous definition alone;
if a distinction from the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) were intended, it would be redundant.

Therefore, the term "dissimilar instance" (vipakṣa), employed as the limit for the point of difference (vaidharmya), has as its sole result the comprehension of the absence of a similar instance (sapakṣa). This is the meaning.
One might object: "Even so, in the phrase *vaidharmyāt tathā*, the meaning of the word *tathā* is [determined] by the example (*udāharaṇa*).
Since an example can also be a similar instance (*sapakṣa*), how is the specific distinction obtained? Anticipating this doubt, he explains with the words *vipakṣa*.

The sense is that it has been stated in various places that "the understanding of the specific [meaning] comes from the explanation (*vyākhyāna*); for there is no lack of definition due to doubt. This is the intended meaning.

Now, it will be stated that an object whose nature as an effect has been ascertained is to be proven by a *kevalavyatirekin* (purely negative inference), for otherwise there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*);

and in this case, effort (*prayatna*) is such [an object] in relation to breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth. If that were the probandum (*sādhya*), there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) and the impossibility of a purely negative inference (*vyatirekyasaṃbhava*), because in one's own body the concomitance (*anvaya*) with one's own position is possible through the ascertainment that breath is preceded by effort. To this he says: "by breath and so forth."

Nevertheless, since the employment of words lies within our own control, one might employ something that is non-expressive; therefore, he says: "devoid of a cause such as the vital breaths, and devoid of a cause such as desire.

The meaning is that this was stated in order to establish the presence of the reason in the other's body—which is included within the subject—and to establish the absence of the reason in the pot and so forth, which serve as counter-examples (vipakṣa) and are devoid of the property to be proven (sādhya).
[Objection: But surely, by negating the absence of an inherent cause for desire and so forth, its possession [of such a cause] would be established.

And thus, once again, there is no establishment of the self; nor is it a case of pure negative-only (kevalavyatirekī) inference, because that much is established by positive concomitance (anvaya) itself. Therefore, he says: "And that which...
For by means of positive concomitance, only its cause-in-general is established.
However, by this very [reasoning], that which is distinct from earth and the other elements is established; thus, the *vyatirekin* (negative-only inference) is not without scope.
Nor is there a failure to establish the Self (*ātman*), because it is precisely such a thing that is denoted by the word "Self"—this is the meaning.
By the passage beginning with "for one who has grasped the inseparable connection" (*gṛhītāvinābhāva*), the non-establishment of pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been demonstrated.
The establishment of the property of being a subject-attribute (pakṣadharmatā) should also be understood by this same method:

because the subject (pakṣa) is that which is qualified by the property one wishes to know, and because that which is doubted is what is to be known; furthermore, doubt arises when there is a recollection of specific [contrary] attributes.
And because that [cause] is absent in what has not been previously perceived.
For there are two ways of understanding what is distinct from the nature [of the subject]:
as an effect (*kārya*) and as possessing an effect (*kāryavat*).
Among these, the effect has been shown in the definition of inference (*anumāna*).
For example: desire and so forth reside in a substance distinct from the eight substances, because they are effects while not residing in those [eight].

Here, however, the possession of effects is shown; the meaning is that this living body is not devoid of a self, nor is it lacking a specific substance that serves as the inherent cause of desire and so forth.
"Because of possessing desire and so forth" means because of possessing effects such as desire and the like.
Explaining both of these by including them within this very [context], he first prioritizes the effect and says: "This is the meaning.
Being effects such as desire and so forth, they cause those [causes] to be known.
The remainder [of the argument] is that these too must be treated as impermanent.
To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "In the case of non-momentariness.
He refutes the objection regarding the unestablished qualification of the reason by stating: "body and sense-faculties."

The meaning is that when there is a negation based on the fact that these [properties] do not inhere in any one of the body, the senses, or the mind— because they are perceived solely by the mental [perception]—
this [reason] is a "purely negative" (kevalavyatirekin) one that is beyond reproach.

Having thus established the first [point], he establishes the second—namely, "tadasya" (that belongs to this)—while simultaneously refuting the impossibility of doubt regarding its unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) by means of the general principle (*sādhāraṇanyāya*).

This has been made clear in that very [section]. Now, one might object: even if the exclusion of any general inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of desire and so forth from jars and the like is understood, what does that have to do with the absence of a self (*nairātmya*)? To this, he says: "even by the word 'nirātmaka'..."
Having thus clarified the meaning and applied the commentary (*vārttika*), he states "this is what is meant" while making the second [point] primary.
He raises an objection with "if not," etc.

The meaning is that, just as in the inference for God (*īśvarānumāna*), the intended specific property will be established by the force of the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) alone. Now, one might ask: what has been refuted regarding the purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*) by one who establishes a specific property through a positive concomitance (*anvayin*), such that he would remain indifferent toward it even when it is possible?
Or, because it would be equally easy to state the reverse by that very same [reasoning] in the case of refutation (*khaṇḍana*), he says: "by the straight path.
For pervasion (*vyāpti*) is indeed the path to proof (*siddhi*).
He avoids the objection that "straightness" is simply its non-deviation and "crookedness" is its deviation— by stating "of the mere cause.
It has already been explained how, in this sense, the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is not applicable.
For the intended meaning is the object-domain of that [intention]; and it is pervaded by the intention,
such that the word-meaning cannot be understood without the establishment of that [intention].
Nor is it impossible to understand their inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) without perceiving something beyond the eight substances.

For there is no contradiction in asserting that earth possesses those qualities—such as desire and so forth—even when earth is the inherent cause of them, just as it is stated in the word [of the scripture] that they are preceded by an agent characterized as the employer of causes whose efficacy is observed, such as the knowledge that is the cause of dyads and the like. This is the meaning.
He raises an objection again: "By way of elimination (*pariśeṣāt*).

First, it is established that their being dependent (*āśritatva*) belongs only to the *anvayin* [type of sound]. Furthermore, the negation of their dependence on the eight substances is also established only for the *anvayin*.
The meaning is: what else remains that could be established by a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*)? The answer is: "That very same [thing].
This is the sense.
From the former [reason], its being dependent is established; from the other [reason], its not being dependent on the eight substances is established.
However, the establishment of its dependence on a substance distinct from those is not possible from even one [of these reasons].
And in the absence of that [dependence], there would be a contradiction between these two as well.
Therefore, from that meaning, the subsistence in something other than the eight [substances] is established; yet that meaning is not a positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
For there is no positive concomitance such as: "whatever subsists while not subsisting in the eight substances necessarily subsists in a substance other than those eight."
And the positive concomitant (*anvayin*) is merely a figurative expression (*vakrokti*),
being a proliferation of the purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*) due to a difference in intention.
Therefore, the actual meaning is indeed the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
Thus, it is well said that the "residual" [reason] is that which possesses negative concomitance (*vyatirekin*).
Now, he indicates the proof for establishing the qualification with the words "yadi hi" (for if).
This is an application by way of contraposition (*viparyaya*):
the body and the sense organs are not the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of desire and so forth, because they are elemental (*bhūtatva*), like a jar and similar objects.
Surely, this is appropriate where the thesis is that [the body] is supported by a substance other than the eight substances;

however, where it is stated that "this is not soulless" (*nirātmakam*), one who asserts that the very same meaning is expressed here by the word "soulless" (*nirātmaka*) has effectively accepted that the meaning of the thesis is precisely the negation of the absence of an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) such as desire and so forth.

And thus, while concluding the objection—namely, "How can the body possess a material cause for desire and so forth that is distinct from the eight substances?"—he provides the answer with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
Here too, the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is: "The living body possesses a material cause for desire and so forth that is distinct from earth and the other [elements].
The meaning of the reason (*hetu*) is: "Because it possesses effects such as desire which are inherent in it. Now, [an objection]:

Nevertheless, for a Buddhist, this remains a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because he too maintains that the material cause (*upādāna*) of desire and the other mental states is indeed something distinct from earth and the rest; therefore, [the author] says: "And not of these...
The words "given their stability" (*sthirye sati*) are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

[Objection: Even so, is the exclusion of desire and the like from insentient things such as jars caused by their exclusion from substances of that nature, or is it caused by their exclusion from the specific transformations of the elements themselves? Since the probans is thus subject to a doubtful limiting condition (upādhi), it is non-conclusive. To this, he says: "And just as...
[and] "even by way of negative concomitance."
If there is no concomitance of this [reason] with the probandum anywhere at all, then the meaning is that this is indeed contradictory (*viruddha*).
It is not intrinsic (*svābhāvika*).
The meaning is that we do not deny the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of this [reason] with the object to be attained (*upeya*), but rather its [positive concomitance] with the means (*upāya*).

Nevertheless, there is no difference between this [reason] possessing positive concomitance and the positive concomitance that constitutes the object to be attained, because it possesses positive concomitance through that very positive concomitance; therefore, he says: "By this much alone.
Now, one might object: in reality, the subject (*dharmin*) which possesses the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is itself the similar instance (*sapakṣa*).
And that [reason], being known in such a way, is designated as such by others;
consequently, even though it is accompanied by that [property], the reason is indeed one characterized by both positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatirekin*).

He raises the objection—“And not merely in the case of the subject (*pakṣa*)”—on the grounds that for those who are ignorant, it is not designated in that manner, which is a different matter altogether.

Intending to show that the logical concomitance (anvaya) of the means of legal procedure is what is being considered, and not the object of the procedure itself, he offers this rebuttal: "The object of inquiry... and so forth.
Now, if there is no exclusion of this [reason] from the similar instances (sapakṣa), how is it not "uniqueness" (asādhāraṇya)?
And if there is such exclusion, how is it not a positive concomitance (anvaya)?
Now, even if that [self] is negated, there is no positive concomitance (anvaya) based on that alone.

If this is so, then just as in the case of the similar instances (sapakṣa), even in the case of the subject (pakṣa), the existence of a self does not follow even when the self is negated; having thus refuted the opponent's objection, he reads that passage beginning with "in the body and so forth.
For it has been established by means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that only when a dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) exists is the exclusion (vyatireka) of some existing thing perceived.

And since that exclusion (vyatireka), which is established by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), is negated by a means of valid cognition only when it actually exists even in the subject (pakṣa), the establishment of a positive injunction characterized by negation is logical. However, the similar instance (sapakṣa) is not established by any means of valid cognition; therefore, in its case, neither the presence (anvaya) nor the absence (vyatireka) of that [exclusion], nor their negation, can ultimately be cognized by any means of valid cognition.
Thus, the meaning is: how could there be the application of either affirmation or negation?
If it is non-deviating from the similar class (*sapakṣa*), then the meaning is that there is no exclusion from the similar class;
[thus] it is positive (*anvayin*). If, even so, it is not positive, [then it is negative].
Rather, it is indeed a case of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

Now, if you think that even the negation of negative concomitance with respect to the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) results merely in the negation of negative concomitance itself, and thus does not result in positive concomitance (*anvaya*), then the meaning of the *Vārttika* is this: even when the absence of self (*nairātmya*) is negated in the subject (*pakṣa*), because it results in nothing more than that [negation], it does not result in the presence of a self (*sātmakatva*).

This has already been refuted, because we do not admit that absolute affirmation or negation can apply to a non-entity (*avastu*). Nevertheless, this [position] is struck down by its own internal contradiction; therefore, he says: "And this [has been stated] by us..."

The meaning is that there is no deviation even in its negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*), because as a property of negative concomitance, it is impossible for it to exist in the absence of that [subject].
Regarding the phrase "he avoids" and so forth:
just like deviation, non-deviation is also a property of that [subject]; therefore, how could that [non-deviation] exist in the absence of that [subject]? This is the meaning.

The phrase "by the absence of exclusion" means by the absence of the determination of exclusion. He explains it clearly, even though it is already evident, in order to dispel the confusion regarding the upcoming Vārttika, saying "And here...
He wards off that confusion, saying "But not..."
To the question, "But what would be the fault if the meaning of the Sūtra were only this much? he says: "If that were so.

This refers to the remainder of the refutation of other words in the Vṛtti, such as "established in the similar instance" (sapakṣe siddha) and so forth, under the heading "the definition of inference" (anumānalakṣaṇa).
The term "Sautrāntika" is used for the purpose of excluding the Vaibhāṣika view;
for in their system, it is possible for things such as space to be eternal and even non-produced.
As they say:
"Space and the two types of cessation—these three are the unconditioned.

The term "two cessations" refers to the distinction between cessation characterized by a homogeneous continuum of similar moments and cessation characterized by destruction; the technical designation for these two is "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
In this regard, Dignāga [distinguishes] between the valid reason and its fallacies by means of the statement beginning with "present in the similar class" (*sapakṣe san*).
For the purpose of illustrating that,
[the author] presents the category of the probandum (sādhya) by means of the passage beginning with "eternal" and "non-eternal."

By the words "the object of cognition" and so forth, the category of the means of proof is established; the similar instances (sapakṣa) are space, a jar, intellect, the atmosphere, the sky, and the firmament.
A flash of lightning in the sky, two jars of lightning, and likewise an atom of space.
Thus, for the class of similar instances (sapakṣa): *kumbhaḥ*, *viyat*, *taḍit*, *vyoman*, *ghaṭaḥ*, *kumbhaḥ*, *taḍit*, *ghaṭau*,
*kumbhaḥ*, *vayad*, *ghaṭaḥ*, and *buddhiḥ* are, respectively, its dissimilar instances (vipakṣa).
Having thus elaborated upon the section on opposing views,
the reason is determined by the passage beginning with "therein," and so forth.
In this regard, having abandoned conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), he sets forth only as much as is necessary to determine the reason, [introducing it with] "here" (*atre*). //35//
An example (udāharaṇa) is an instance which, through its similarity to the subject of the thesis (sādhya), possesses the property of that [subject]. //36//
// Purity //

Regarding the application [of the reason], he removes the doubt— namely, whether the sequence found in the Sūtra alone should be adopted or some other sequence— by demonstrating the purpose of the example with the words "in the case of the reason" (*hetau*).
For a reason does not remain as a valid reason, nor does it become focused on the proof of the probandum, unless it is pervaded and its pervasion is well-established.
Therefore, since it is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that one wishes to know, it is that alone which is fit to be demonstrated; this is the remainder [of the argument].
Nevertheless, one might ask: what occasion is there for the example (*udāharaṇa*)? To this he says: "And not... (*na ca*).

For it is established for all the world that one employs a means of proof (*sādhana*) whose capacity is already recognized toward the probandum (*sādhya*), rather than first employing it and subsequently seeking to ascertain its capacity; this is the summary of the connection.
Nevertheless, since there is no occasion for the specific definition (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*) without the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) and its divisions, he says: "the aphorism" (*sūtramiti*).

Now, why is the example (*udāharaṇa*), though not the primary subject, being taken up as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), and why does one who is afraid [of complexity] abandon the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) which is the primary subject?
To this he says: "The example" (*dṛṣṭānta*).
The meaning is that the mention of the "indicatory mark" (*upalakṣaṇa*) is solely for the purpose of establishing the definition of the subject at hand; thus, neither fault applies.

This means that the basis for the definition is a fixed connection, which is to say, a restrictive factor (*niyāmaka*).
Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that no conclusion to this discussion is observed?
Therefore, why is an objection raised by means of the proponent and the opponent? To this, he says: "In this [context]. Here, the word "debate" (*vāda*) is an illustration for "discussion" (*kathā*).

Now, one might ask: why should this not be the very definition of the conclusion of a debate (*kathānirṇaya*), by which both the objection and the rebuttal would also be appropriately included? To this he says: "Not at all," etc.
The meaning is that it is not so, because the doubt has already been raised.
If it is then argued that [the objection] has been answered by this refutation, he says: "But having granted...
The meaning is this:
although there are no proponent and opponent during the formal investigation (*parīkṣā*),...

Because the second [party] is engaged merely by the initiation of the questioning; because even if those two were possible, they would result only in the description of the subject matter; and because the role of the examiner belongs solely to the arbiter (*stheya*).

Nevertheless, because the four-limbed judicial proceeding (*catuṣpādavyavahāra*) is demonstrated through the distinction between the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), the rejoinder (*uttarapakṣa*), the deliberation (*pratyākalita*), and the final conclusion (*niṣkarṣa*), there is no practical difference [between the two views]; for even if there is only a single speaker, this entire complex of operations remains present during the investigation. Therefore, although the objector (*codaka*) is not skillful, his objection still has its place; thus, [the author] accepts it exactly as stated and refutes it.

Now, one might object: "How can there be a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*) in a treatise (*śāstra*) that is independent of doubt? For if that were so, it would follow that *mīmāṃsā* (critical inquiry) is purposeless. To this he says: "Not so" (*na hi*).
Indeed, it is the treatise itself that is being investigated therein;
and in that context, doubt is not prohibited.

The meaning is this: since the determination of that [object] is to be accomplished through investigation, when its determination of the subject matter must be performed by means of a treatise (*śāstra*), how could there be doubt?
For the subject matter of a treatise cannot be a locus for doubt, as it has never been perceived in any other way.

Now, one might ask: why should there not be doubt regarding the determination of the argument (*kathā*)? Otherwise, how could the author of the Commentary himself state in the fourth [chapter] that the fruit of the debate (*vāda*) is the removal of doubt? To this he replies: "only when both are certain. Although they may have been doubtful prior to the debate, at the time of its engagement, they are indeed regarded as certain due to their self-assurance (*abhimāna*).
The sense is that otherwise, the possibility of grasping a thesis (*pakṣa*) and a counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*) for those two would not exist.
Now, one might ask: "In the conclusion of the objection, the author of the *Bhāṣya*, by stating 'the determination belongs to him who remains,' indicated the instrumental case in the word *tābhyām*.

Why, then, was that [instrumental] disregarded by the author of the *Vārttika* when he stated 'from the thesis and from the counter-thesis' (*pakṣāt ca pratipakṣāt ca*), which implies an ablative? To this [we reply]:
He says: "Now then" (*nanu*).

Does it follow that, because it shares the same status of security and success as debate (*vāda*), the determination in a treatise (*śāstra*) must also proceed solely through a thesis and a counter-thesis?
Since this is not possible, he says: "But in a treatise, there is only determination."
The meaning is that there is neither deliberation nor the positions of proponent and opponent.
He states this very point with the words "But not... (na tu).
That which was mentioned will become clear in the Vārttika.
Thus he says: "in the apprehension of the object.
Now, one might object: since a debate sometimes consists of four or five stages (*kakṣā*), how can there be a restriction to three stages? To this he replies: "the first is the proof" (*sādhana*).
Even the thousand *kakṣās* (stages of debate) are included within this very [classification];
for if they were not so included, it would follow that they are something other than the subject matter at hand.
The meaning is that being excluded from the means of proof (*sādhana*), the refutation (*dūṣaṇa*), and the rebuttal thereof (*taduddhāra*) is of no utility to the present topic. //41//
Thus ends the first daily lesson in the first chapter of the *Tātparyapariśuddhi* by Udayana.
Thus ends the section on the subsequent members of the syllogism.
